name: Moshood Abiola Balogun
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 60286/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8. The applicant was represented by OA Solicitors, a firm of lawyers practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms L. Dauban of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was convicted on 21 February 2007, at the age of twenty, of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced into letting his premises be used for the preparation and sale of drugs. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, and on 18 October 2007 was notified of the Secretary of State’s intention to deport him. The applicant appealed against the decision and his appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. The Tribunal noted his previous criminal record and noted his claim to be in a relationship of some years' duration. It was not therefore accepted that he was in a serious or permanent relationship. The applicant was taken into immigration detention on 10 November 2009 and directions for his deportation to Nigeria were set on 12 November 2009 for 19 November 2009. The High Court, in refusing the application, stated that the applicant had no family life in the United Kingdom, and that the interference with his private life was proportionate. The Tribunal took into account the case of Üner v. the Netherlands [GC], no. 46410/99, ECHR 2006‑XII, in finding that, on balance, and having due regard to the public interest, the applicant’s deportation was. proportionate, and found that, despite the applicant having been in the country since a young age, it was not considered that these ties were sufficiently strong to render his deportation. The applicant notified authorities in the immigration detention centre that he had taken an overdose of paracetamol on 29 December 2009. He was assessed by the medical team and found only to have taken a few tablets. No further concerns as to his well-being appear to have been raised and the applicant was released from immigration detention on 13 January 2010. He does not claim to have made any further attempts at suicide. The Government also considered that there were sufficient mental health facilities in Nigeria, which would be available to the applicant if needed. The applicant would be escorted up until the point of arrival in Nigeria. If deemed necessary, a medical escort would be provided.

The case originated in an application (no. 60286/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Nigerian national, Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun (‘the applicant’) The applicant alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The applicant was represented by OA Solicitors, a firm of lawyers practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Ms L. Dauban of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) The applicant was convicted on 21 February 2007, at the age of twenty, of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. Indefinite leave to remain was granted to the applicant, outside the immigration rules, on 1 December 2003. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, and on 18 October 2007 was notified of the Secretary of State’s intention to deport him. The applicant appealed against the decision to deportation and his appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. It was not accepted that he had family life in the United Kingdom. Even allowing for his long stay in the UK, only four years had been with valid leave. A deportation order against the applicant was signed on 14 October 2008. The applicant made an application to have the order revoked on human rights grounds, which was rejected by the Secretary of State on 3 June 2009. An application for judicial review of this decision was refused on 30 October 2009. On 13 November 2009 the applicant sought interim measures from this Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his deportation. He was taken into immigration detention on 10 November 2009 and directions for his deportation to Nigeria were set on 12 November 2009 for 19 November 2009. The High Court, in refusing the application, stated that the applicant had no family life in the United Kingdom, and that the interference with his private life was proportionate. The applicant notified authorities in the immigration detention centre that he had taken an overdose of paracetamol on 29 December 2009. He was assessed by the medical team and found only to have taken a few tablets. No further concerns as to his well-being appear to have been raised and the applicant was released from immigration detention on 13 January 2010. He does not claim to have made any further attempts at suicide. The Government also considered that there were sufficient mental health facilities in Nigeria, which would be available to the applicant if needed. The government therefore invited the Court to lift the interim measure which had been indicated in respect of the applicant.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. On 9 March 2010 the Vice-President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The case was heard by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, Mr Justice O'Shea, and the case was adjourned until May 1, 2011. The ruling was made in favour of the applicant, Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun. The applicant lived in foster care from 2002 until he was eighteen, when he began to live alone in council accommodation. He was convicted on 21 February 2007, at the age of twenty, of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced into letting his premises be used for the preparation and sale of drugs by a group of people whom he feared because of a previous attack in 2005. On 18 October 2007 he was notified of the Secretary of State’s intention to deport him. His appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. A deportation order against the applicant was signed on 14 October 2008. The applicant made an application to have the order revoked on human rights grounds. The High Court, in refusing the application, stated that the applicant had no family life in the United Kingdom. The Tribunal took into account the case of Üner v the Netherlands [GC], no. 46410/99, ECHR 2006‑XII, in finding that, on balance, and having due regard to the public interest, the applicant’s deportation was proportionate. On 13 November 2009 the applicant sought interim measures from this Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his deportation. He was taken into immigration detention on 10 November 2009 and directions for his deportation were set on 12 November 2009 for 19 November 2009. On 18 November 2009, the Acting President of the Fourth Section decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. Rule 39 was initially applied for a period of two weeks, in order to give the Government the opportunity to comment on the applicant’s mental health history and to state whether any special measures had been put in place to alleviate the risk of suicide prior to and during his proposed removal. The Government informed the Court that they had not previously been aware of the applicant's attempted suicide, but had now considered the psychiatric report of 14 September 2009. All appropriate measures to protect the applicant from risk were already in place at the centre at which he was detained. The applicant was released from immigration detention on 13 January 2010.

name: Witold Siwiec
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28095/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he had been unable to present his civil case to the courts on an equitable basis vis-à-vis the opposite party. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made by a Polish national, Mr Witold Siwiec (‘the applicant’), on 14 May 2008. The court issued a decision dismissing the applicant’s request for the witness C.O. to be heard as a witness. The applicant appealed. He argued that the first-instance court had assessed the evidence wrongly and reached untenable conclusions. The court found no grounds on which to accept that he had suffered any damage or that the defendant had been acting unlawfully. The hearing was held on 11 June 2007 and lasted five minutes. The defendant stated only that she did not accept the applicant's claim. He was neither present nor represented. The case was dismissed on 25 June 2007, after the applicant failed to submit copies of his request to the court. The Lublin Regional Court refused to grant legal aid to the applicant. The court was of the view that the fact that his claim had been dismissed was not tantamount to a finding that the applicant was unable to argue his case. The applicant appealed against this decision in so far as it related to the refusal of legal aid. On 6 February 2008 the Lublin Court of Appeal granted the applicant legal aid for the purposes of preparing a cassation appeal. The Lublin Bar Association assigned M. K. to the case on 11 February 2008. By a written legal opinion dated 25 February 2008, the lawyer informed the applicant that he was refusing to prepare an appeal in the case. The court ruled that there were no legal grounds for an appeal. The appeal was served on the applicant shortly afterwards. The judge ruled that the appeal could not be launched as it was not in the public interest. The case was dismissed and the appeal was dismissed on a technicality. name: Frédéric Foucher
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 25 January 1996 and by the French Government on 6 February 1996. It originated in an application (no. 22209/93) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a French national, Mr Frédéric Foucher, on 16 April 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The case was heard in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 25 November 1996. The applicant and his father were charged with using insulting and threatening words and behaviour towards public-service employees in 1991. They were both summoned to appear before the Argentan Police Court under the direct committal procedure. The Court heard addresses by Mr Békés, Mr Masure, Mr Dobelle, Mr Fèvre and Mr Marchi-Uhel. The hearing was adjourned until a later date, which was set by the President on the Commission's request. The case was decided by a jury of five, with the decision of the Court of Appeal the last to be heard. The applicant decided to conduct his own case and his mother went to the police court registry on 25 July 1991 to consult the case file and procure copies of the documents it contained. In a note that same day the Argentan public prosecutor stated that copies could not be issued to individuals except through a lawyer or an insurance company. The defendants should have been allowed access to their case file in order to prepare their defence, says the judge. The court set aside the proceedings against the applicant and his father on the ground that the rights of the defence had been infringed. It declared inadmissible applications by the National Field Sports Board and the two game wardens to join the proceedings as civil parties. Gérard Foucher did not appear at the hearing in the Caen Court of Appeal on 16 March 1992. His mother went to the registry to obtain information on how to gain access to the case file, but met with the registrar’s refusal. Relying on the official report drawn up on 13 February 1991 by the two game wardens and on the statements made by another hunter, the Court of appeal fined the applicant and his father FRF 3,000 each for insulting each other. In a judgment of 16 March. 1992, given after proceedings that were adversarial in the case of the applicant’S father. and deemed to have been adversarial for the applicant, the. Court of. Appeal reversed the judgment of 2 October 1991 and refused the application for the proceedings to be set aside for. having violated the rights of the defence. On 15 March 1993 the Court of Cassation (Criminal Division) dismissed the applicant’s appeal on the following ground: “In holding that the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms did not require that the case file be made available to the defendant himself, and that he had been informed, by means of the summons in due form served on him, of the charges against him and the relevant legal provisions, the court of Appeal did not breach the provisions of that Convention’”. The applicant had lodged an appeal on points of law against the judgment of 16 March 1992. In his grounds of appeal he cited Article 6 of the Convention (art. 6)

name: Jerzy Bobrowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Jerzy Bobrowski. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the court’s unreasoned decisions to refuse to grant him legal aid in connection with the preparation of an appeal against a first-instance judgment infringed his right to a fair hearing. On 10 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant requested that a legal‑aid lawyer be assigned to the case for the purpose of preparing an appeal to the Supreme Court. The Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the request on 20 March 2000. The applicant appealed. On 26 May 2000 the Wroclaw Court of appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal, prepared and lodged by a lawyer, holding that no appeal was available in law against the contested decision. On 28 June 2000 the court granted the applicant partial exemption from court fees. On 1 September 2000 the applicant requested the court to assign a legal-aid lawyer to thecase, referring again to his very difficult financial situation. On 19 September 2000, the applicant appealed against it. The applicant appealed against a decision dismissing his compensation claim against a trustee in bankruptcy of “Westa’s” Insurance Company. The Wrocław Court of Appeal rejected his appeal, holding that no appeal was available against the contested decision. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court refused to entertain that appeal on 22 November 2001. name: Gösta Håkansson
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Immediately prior to its opening, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence and on 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application from a similar applicant (Rule 40 para. 1). The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. The applicants maintained that a representative of the County Administrative Board had stated, at the public viewing of the property on 27 November 1979, that, in this case, the requisite permit would certainly be granted speedily. In support of these allegations, the applicants submitted three affidavits, each of which was signed in 1989 by a person who had been present either at the auction or at a public viewing. The applications for a permit to retain the estate Risböke 1:3 were granted on 5 February 1980. The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture (lantbruksstyrelsen), which rejected the appeal on 5 September 1980. A new request, dated 4 January 1982, for a permit to retain Risböke 1:3 was rejected by the County Agricultural Board on 25 January 1982. The Board stated that the estate was considered to be a unit suitable for rationalisation purposes, which ought to be used to consolidate properties within the area that were capable of further development. It added that, as neighbours were interested in acquiring the property, the request might be refused under section 4 para. 1, sub-section 3, of the 1979 Act. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court (fastighetsdomstolen) of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. In a judgment of 11 December 1981 the court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. The applicants appealed to the Göta Court of Appeal (Göta hovrätt), which on 1 July 1982 confirmed the judgment. On 14 July 1983 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. In April 1984 the Senior Land Surveyor of the County of Kronoberg made a new valuation of the property, resulting in an estimated market value of 125,000 SEK. On 10 November 1983, the County Administrative Board ordered the compulsory resale by auction. In 1984 the Enforcement Office determined that the estate had a value of 125,000 SEK. The applicants challenged this before the Göta Court of Appeal but the court dismissed the action on 4 June 1984. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers. In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000SEK. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (‘the 1985 auction’) at the auction. At the auction, there was, in fact, only one bid. The Court of Appeal refused to grant the request for a new appeal. The appeal was made under the terms of an earlier ruling. The case was dismissed on August 27, 1987. The new appeal was denied on August 30, 1987 and the appeal was not heard again until August 31, 1987, when the new decision was made to grant it. The decision made by the Court was made on the basis of the fact that the case was brought by an individual, rather than by the court. The application was denied due to a lack of evidence that the application was made in good faith. The court's decision was later overturned on appeal and the case is now being heard again.

The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14. The case was heard at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1989. The hearing took place in public in the human rights building. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence. On 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application from a similar applicant (Rule 40 para. 1). Risböke 1:3 was bought for 240,000 Swedish crowns (SEK) at a compulsory sale by auction (exekutiv auktion) in 1979. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. According to a valuation made public before the auction, the market value (saluvärde) of the property was estimated at 140,000 SEK. The applicants maintained that a representative of the County Administrative Board had stated, at the public viewing, that, in this case, the requisite permit would certainly be granted speedily. The County Agricultural Board rejected the applicants’ request on the ground that the estate was a “rationalisation unit’ (rationaliseringsfastighet) which ought to be used for the purpose of consolidating other properties in the area that were capable of further development. The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture (lantbruksstyrelsen), which rejected the appeal on 5 September 1980. A new request, dated 4 January 1982, for a permit to retain Risböke 1:3 was rejected by the County Agricultural board on 25 January 1982. The Board concluded that the real estate at issue lacks the prerequisites for remaining as a separate cultivation unit. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court (fastighetsdomstolen) of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture. The Government, recalling that the case had been finally settled by them on the latter date, decided on 14 March 1985 not to take any further action in respect of the request. At the request of the County Agricultural Board, the County Administrative Board ordered the compulsory resale by auction on 10 November 1983. The Enforcement Office (kronofogdemyndigheten) in VäXjö was responsible for arranging the auction. In April 1984 the Enforcement Office determined that the estate had a value of 125,000 SEK. The applicants challenged this before the Göta Court of Appeal but the court dismissed the action. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers (see paragraph 37 below) In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000SEK. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (“the 1985 auction”) The Enforcement Office decided that the lowest bid which could be accepted would be 172, 000 SEK and it was accepted by the County Agricultural Board. The decision by the Court of Appeal was made on 3 July 1985. On 17 January 1986, the decision was approved by the Supreme Court. The decision was later overturned by the European Court of Human Rights. The Supreme Court ordered the decision to be appealed. The case is still pending in the European Courts of Justice. The final decision is expected in October 2015. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. The applicants had intended to build up units which would create opportunities for employment and, in the long run, become financially sound properties to be exploited by their children. In the opinion of the County Agricultural Board, there was only room for one active farmer in the region. Finally, Mr Michael Borg, who leased two neighbouring properties, one of which was owned by his father, had shown a great interest in acquiring the applicants’ property. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court (fastighetsdomstolen) of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. In a judgment of 11 December 1981 the court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. In April 1984 the Senior Land Surveyor (överlantmätaren) of the County of Kronoberg made a new valuation of the property, resulting in an estimated market value of 125,000 SEK. On 10 November 1983 the County Administrative Board ordered the compulsory resale by auction. The Risböke 1:3 estate was sold at auction on 18 June 1985. At the auction, there was, in fact, only one bid. It was an offer of 172,000 SEK made by the County Agricultural Board and it was accepted by the Enforcement Office. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK. The applicants appealed to the Göta Court of Appeal requesting that the compulsory sale be annulled. They argued that the property had not been sold at the market price, as required by law, since the valuation had been based only on an assessment of the yield from the property. In 1985 the Swedish government accepted a request from a private company to buy a large piece of land in the south of the country. The company was not required to make the purchase. The decision was made on the basis that the land had already been purchased by the company. In 1986, the company applied to the Supreme Court for a permit to buy the land, which was granted. In 1987, the government accepted the request and the company bought the land for $1.5 million. The purchase was approved by the Court of Appeal in April 1986. The land was sold to a private firm and the sale was finalized in March 1987.
eval_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence and on 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application. The hearing was adjourned until the next day at 10am on 27 September 1989. The verdict was handed down at 10:30am on 28 September. Risböke 1:3 was bought for 240,000 Swedish crowns (SEK) at a compulsory sale by auction in 1979. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. The applicants submitted three affidavits in 1989 by a person who had been present either at the auction or at the public viewing. The applications for a permit to retain the estate were denied on the grounds of its size, situation and nature. The sale contract was drawn up on 7 January 1980 with the County Agricultural Board drawing up a sale contract in which the applicants were reminded of the wording of section 16 para 1 of the 1979 Act. Risböke 1:3 had an area of 41 hectares of which 18 hectares were forest and 8 hectares pasture. Mr Sturesson’s estate, which comprised 63 hectares of forest and 10 of pasture, was 25 kilometres away. The applicants had intended to build up units which would create opportunities for employment and, in the long run, become financially sound properties to be exploited by their children. In the opinion of the County Agricultural Board, there was only room for one active farmer in the region. Finally, Mr Michael Borg, who leased two neighbouring properties, one of which was owned by his father, had shown a great interest in acquiring the applicants’ property. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court (fastighetsdomstolen) of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. In a judgment of 11 December 1981 the court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. In April 1984 the Senior Land Surveyor (överlantmätaren) of the County of Kronoberg made a new valuation of the property, resulting in an estimated market value of 125,000 SEK. On 10 November 1983 the County Administrative Board ordered the compulsory resale by auction. Auction of Risböke 1:3 took place on 18 June 1985. The Enforcement Office determined that the estate had a value of 125,000 SEK. The applicants challenged this before the Göta Court of Appeal but the court dismissed the action on 4 June 1984. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers (see paragraph 37 below) In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000SEK. At the auction, there was, in fact, only one bid, made by the County Agricultural Board and it was accepted by the Enforcement Office. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (“the 1985 auction’) Court of Appeal refused to grant permission for the merger. The decision was made on 17 January 1986. The merger was finally approved on 12 July 1986. It was the first time the Court of Appeal had been asked to approve the deal. The deal was struck with the owners of the land, the Stromberg family, who owned the land. The agreement was signed on 18 January 1986, and the sale was approved on 16 March 1986, with no delay. The sale was completed on 12 October 1986, following an appeal by the owners. The acquisition was made possible by the acquisition of a number of farms, including the Duchy of Stromburg, which had been given permission to sell the land for the intended sale.

name: İhsan Güler
train_texts: The case was brought by two Turkish nationals, Mr İhsan Güler and Mr Sinan Uğur. The applicants were active members and regional leaders of the Party for a Democratic Society (Demokratik Toplum Partisi (DTP) They took part in a religious ceremony (mevlût)0 on the premises of the DTP in Altındağ (Ankara) in which they paid tribute to three members of the PKK who had been killed by the security forces. The participants read out passages from the Koran and said prayers, and showed a film about the lives of the deceased. In their defence they stated that they had taken part in the ceremony for the observance of their religious duties. In its judgment, the Assize Court observed, firstly, that the persons in whose memory the ceremony had been held were members of a terrorist organisation. It also took the view that the choice of venue for the ceremony – the premises of a political party –, and the fact that the PKK flag had been spread over the tables contributed to raising serious doubts as to the actual reasons for the gathering that had been given by the applicants in their defence. The applicants were imprisoned for the duration of their sentence. Their conviction was upheld by a final judgment of the Court of Cassation on 8 March 2010.

Two Turkish nationals took part in a religious ceremony (mevlût)0 on the premises of the DTP in Altındağ (Ankara) in which they paid tribute to three members of the PKK who had been killed by the security forces. The applicants alleged that their conviction for propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation, which had been based, in their view, on their participation in a commemorative religious ceremony, had entailed a violation of Article 9 of the Convention. The case originated in two applications (nos. 31706/10 and 33088/10) lodged with the Court. The two men were convicted of taking part in a ceremony in memory of the 'martyrs of the PKK' The court ruled that the people in whose memory the ceremony was held were members of a terrorist organisation. The court also took the view that the choice of venue for the ceremony – the premises of a political party –, and the fact that the PKK flag had been spread over the tables and photos of members of the organisation had been displayed, contributed to raising serious doubts as to the actual reasons for the gathering. The applicants were imprisoned for the duration of their sentence. Their conviction was upheld by a final judgment of the Court of Cassation in March 2010.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their conviction for propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation had been based, in their view, on their participation in a commemorative religious ceremony, had entailed a violation of Article 9. The application was brought by two Turkish nationals, Mr İhsan Güler and Mr Sinan Uğur, on 5 May 2010 and 13 May 2010 respectively. They were active members and regional leaders of the Party for a Democratic Society (Demokratik Toplum Partisi (DTP) The ceremony was held in memory of ‘martyrs of the PKK’. The Ankara Assize Court sentenced the two applicants to ten months’ imprisonment. In their defence they stated that they had taken part in the ceremony for the observance of their religious duties. The applicants were imprisoned for the duration of their sentence. Their conviction was upheld by a final judgment of the Court of Cassation on 8 March 2010. The applicant Mr Güler was arrested and taken into police custody on 28 December 2006. He was released the next day. The court observed that the persons in whose memory the ceremony had been held were members of a terrorist organisation and had been killed by the security forces during an operation against that organisation.

name: Gürcan Keman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68446/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Gürcan Keman. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Manisa, Turkey. In 1991 the applicant sat a competition for admission to the civil service. Following his success in the competition, the General Directorate of Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution conducted a pre-employment background investigation. It found that the applicant had not mentioned his criminal record in his application form. In 1980 the applicant was convicted of issuing threats against one of his teachers. The applicant claimed he had suffered pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage as a result of the decision dated 14 January 1992. The General Directorate appealed the decision, arguing that the applicant had not suffered any damage and that therefore the legal costs should be borne by him. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the Ankara Administrative Court's ruling was in conformity with law and procedure. The court further decided that legal Costs should be shared by the parties, given that it partially acceded to the applicant's claims for compensation. The application was dismissed on October 31, 2001. The appeal was dismissed again on May 30, 2002.

The case originated in an application (no. 68446/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr S. Özay, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 26 April 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theapplication at the same time. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant had fulfilled all the requirements of the vacant post in question as prescribed under Law no. 657. The applicant brought a new action in the Ankara Administrative Court against the General Directorate requesting compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage which he allegedly had suffered as a result of the decision dated 14 January 1992. The court awarded the applicant a certain amount of compensation. The General Directorate appealed the decision, arguing that the applicant had not suffered any damage and that therefore the legal costs should be borne by him. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 30 May 2002, holding that the court's ruling was in conformity with law and procedure.

name: Hıdır Adıyaman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31880/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The judge elected in respect of Turkey withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was convicted in 1989 and sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment. The case was referred to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence under Articles 146 and 146-1 of the Criminal Code of Turkey.

name: Waldemar Krasuski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61444/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a “reasonable time’, as required under Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The applicant was represented by Mr L. Cyrson, a lawyer practising in Poznań, Poland. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant and his wife concluded a contract with E.W. and W.W., the owners of a company W. ona Góra, Poland, to carry out building work on the applicant’s house. On 24 November 1994 the applicant, considering that the company was in breach of the contract, withdrew from it. The plaintiffs sued the defendants in the Zielona Gorra Regional Court seeking compensation for the serious damage to the house allegedly caused by the defendants. On 19 November 1998 the court gave judgment and dismissed the claim, but the plaintiffs appealed. In the meantime, the applicant had made two unsuccessful applications for his claim to be secured. In 2000 the judge decided to obtain a fresh expert report. The applicant applied to the court. for an exemption from payment of the court fee for the increased claim. On 12 October 2000 the court refused their application. That decision was later upheld by the Poznań Court of Appeal. The Government maintained that at the hearing held on 8 May 2001 the plaintiffs had increased their claim and had stated that they would not seek an exemption. The applicant denied that they had altered their claim. A hearing scheduled for 12 July 2001 was adjourned at the plaintiffs’ request. A subsequent hearing was held on 6 September 2001. On 11 October 2001 the court heard evidence from the parties and closed the trial. On 30 November 2001 the applicant appealed against the judgment.

The case originated in an application against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a ‘reasonable time’ He also alleged a breach of Article 13 of the. Convention in that he has no effective domestic remedy in respect of the excessive length. of the proceedings. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant’s wife, Mrs Józefa Krasuska, informed the Court’S Registry that the applicant had died on 30 December 2004. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late husband's stead. The case was brought by a Polish man and his wife in Zielona Góra, Poland. They sued E.W. and W.W., the owners of a company that was to carry out building work on the applicant’s house. The court ordered the experts to revise their report. The plaintiffs appealed the first-instance judgment. On 20 February 2000 the expert report was submitted to the court. The Government submitted that on 16 May 2000 the plaintiffs had altered the amount of the damages they had sought. Subsequently, they applied for an exemption from the court fee due due to their claim. The judge dismissed the claim and remitted the case. The Government maintained that at the hearing held on 8 May 2001 the plaintiffs had increased their claim and had stated that they would not seek an exemption from the court fee. The applicant stated that this was not true. He maintained that, in a pleading of 11 May 2001, after the experts had again revised their valuation of the damage sustained, he had indeed extended the amount of the damages sought to 300,000 Polish zlotys (PLN), mostly because he had been forced to do so by the court. On 4 October 2001 the court heard evidence from the parties and closed the trial. On 11 October 2001 it gave judgment, awarding the applicant PLN 50,000 plus statutory interest. Since the applicant refrained from lodging a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court, the judgment became final on that day.

name: Sofiika Vasileva
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52792/99) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 9.30 p.m. on 11 August until 11 a.m on 12 August 1995. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant was charged with refusing to reveal her identity in August 1995. She was released at 11.00 a.m. and hospitalised for three days with high blood pressure. The Chief Constable of Århus ruled against her claim for compensation on 18 July 1996. The outcome of the applicant's dispute with the bus company is unknown. The case can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice by the applicant. The application was dismissed by the Chief Constable on 14 June 1996, but the case is still pending in the Court of Appeal. The applicant claimed compensation for having been detained. The appeal is expected to be heard in May or June 1996. The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision. She complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg, who refused to grant her compensation on 6 February 1997. The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. A court session was held on 26 June 1998, in which the applicant, represented by counsel, explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station. The applicant did not disclose her name and address to the two [named] police officers. The City Court decided that she infringed section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act, which authorises the imposition of a fine. The applicant is entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice. The application was settled out of court in 1998. The court ruled that the application should be dismissed and that the police officers had not been justified in not being able to identify the applicant before she was placed in the detention cell. The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 9.30 p.m. on 11 August 1995. The applicant invokes Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. On 4 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was lodged by a Polish national, Mr Paweł Kurczewski (‘the applicant’), on 7 May 2004. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the co-accused to trial from prison. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years' imprisonment in July 2004. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. All the appeals and applications for release lodged by the applicant were to no avail. The case is now being investigated by the Polish National Court for the Judiciary and the National Court of Criminal Procedure for the Prosecutor's Office. Appeal hearings cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. Gdańsk Regional Court quashed the applicant's detention order on 3 February 2006. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld by the Gda’s Regional Court on 11 July 2007. The application was dismissed and the applicant was released from prison on 4 September 2007. For more information on the case, visit the website of the Polish Court of Appeal, which is open to all citizens of Poland, Poland, and all EU member states, or visit: www.thecourt of appeal.org.

name: Lynette Copland
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62617/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the monitoring of her telephone calls, e-mail correspondence and Internet usage. According to the Government, this monitoring took place in order to ascertain whether the applicant was making excessive use of College facilities for personal purposes. By a decision of 7 March 2006, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Government stated that the monitoring consisted of analysis of the College telephone bills showing telephone numbers called, the dates and times of the calls, and their length and cost. The Government submitted that the monitoring of telephone usage took place for a few months up to about 22 November 1999. The applicant contended that her telephone usage was monitored over a period of about eighteen months until November1999. The Government accepted that this monitoring took the form of analysing the websites visited, the times and dates of the visits to the websites and their duration. She provided documentary evidence. in the form. of printouts detailing her e‑mail usage from 14 May to 22. November 1999 which set out the date and time of e‑mails sent from her. e-mail account together with the recipients’ e-mails addresses. There was no policy in force at the College at the material time regarding the monitoring of telephone, e-mail or Internet usage by employees. The applicant was informed by other members of staff that between 1996 and late 1999 several of her activities had been monitored by the DP or those acting on his behalf. She further believed that the DP became aware of a legally privileged fax that was sent by herself to her solicitors and that her personal movements, both at work and when on annual or sick leave, were the subject of surveillance. The Court heard that the applicant, who is still employed by the College, understands that theDP has been suspended.

name: Sven Olof Göthlin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Swedish national, Mr Sven Olof Göthlin (“the applicant”), on 9 November 2010. The applicant complained, in particular, about the proportionality of the detention order under Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government of Sweden on 12 September 2012. The writ of execution was subsequently lifted and the applicant’s detention order was also lifted. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Sweden (Högsta domstolen) on 2 February 2013. The Enforcement Authority contacted the applicant in order to plan the sale of the attached sawmill. In his reply a few days later, the applicant stated that he had removed the sawmill from his property and hidden it. The Authority also handed the applicant a summons for questioning on its premises, as well as an injunction in which he was ordered to provide the Authority with the necessary information. On the same day, the District Court assigned a public defender for the applicant. On 27 May 2010, after having held an oral hearing, the D.C. District Court ordered the Authority to detain the applicant because he had refused to cooperate and give the required information. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of Appeal, maintaining its claims. The applicant opposed the appeal, maintaining his claims and adding that, if he were detained, it would amount to imprisonment to obtain a confession. In reaching its decision, the court found that the measure did not breach the Convention. It stated that a debtor had to give necessary information about his assets and failure to do so could result in the debtor being detained, if there were extraordinary reasons for detention. The court concluded that currently there did not exist such extraordinary reasons to detain the applicant. The Appeal Court said that it should be informed of any further developments in the case. The applicant was detained the following day. On 30 June 2010, the Court of Appeal held an oral hearing and decided to maintain its earlier decision. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the applicant should be kept in detention since he still had not given any information about the location of the sawmill. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court which, on 6 July 2010, refused leave to appeal. On 13 July 2010 the District Court reviewed the applicant’s detention and held a new hearing in the case as required by Chapter 2, section 16, of the Enforcement Code. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal since a new decision had already been taken. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal which, on 2 August 2010, rejected the appeal. On 9 August 2010 the District Court once again reviewed the detention and held a hearing in the case. The parties maintained their earlier standpoints. The District Court found that continued detention of the applicant would be disproportionate to the measures he had taken. On 26 April 2012 the applicant submitted a claim for damages to the Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern), pursuant to the Act on Compensation for Deprivation of Liberty and Other Coercive Measures (Lagen om ersättning vid frihetsberövande och andra tvångsåtgärder, 1998:714), in the amount of SE. He demanded to be reimbursed SEK 2,940 for costs which had been deducted from his pension during his time in detention. On 15 October 2012 the Chancellor of Justice rejected the claim. The Chancellor noted that the decision to detain the applicant had been taken by a court of law, in accordance with relevant legal provisions. Moreover, the examination of the case showed no basis for finding the decision had been made on erroneous grounds and therefore was incorrect, he said. He said there was no basis to find that the case had been found to have been decided on an erroneous basis and therefore the ruling was incorrect. He added that the judge's decision was correct and that the applicant's claims had been rejected.

The applicants objected that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the confiscation proceedings on the grounds that more than six months had elapsed since their convictions. It was agreed by the parties that the proceedings should be adjourned to await the outcome of a similar case which was due to be heard by the Court of Appeal, R v Steele and Shevki. The confiscation hearings were adjourned until 5 February 2001. On 8 March 2001, the judge held the court retained a common law power to adjourn beyond the statutory time-limit in compelling circumstances such as where the judge was unavailable. On 26 and 27 March 2001 the Court of Appeal heard and dismissed Mr E.’s appeal against conviction. The substantive hearing of the confiscation hearing was again adjourned. On 7 February 2002 the Crown Court imposed a confiscation order on the first applicant in the sum of GBP 375,000, to be paid within 18 months of the resolution of any appeal. The second applicant lodged an application for leave to appeal on the same grounds as the second applicant (see paragraph 20 above) The proceedings were adjourned to 28 January 2002 with a time estimate of three weeks. The first applicant appealed the order and was found guilty of fraud and fined GBP 75,350. He was sentenced to 21 months’ imprisonment in default. The Court of Appeal quashed the confiscation orders and default sentences of imprisonment. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4451/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 4 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. Hakkı Kaya was abducted in Diyarbakır, Turkey, in November 1996. Three men dressed in civilian clothes and carrying walkie-talkies forced him into a car. He was taken to a police station to make a statement, but never arrived. His brother petitioned the Public Prosecutor’s office to investigate his disappearance. On 17 March 1997 the Prosecutor declared a lack of jurisdiction and transferred the case to the Chief Public Prosecutor's office. The Security Directorate has been sending regular reports to the Prosecutor and checking the customs’ records to see whether Hakkim Kaya has left the country. Hakkı Kaya was missing since November 1996. The car with the registration number 06 EKN 22 was a Fiat Şahin, and not a white Toros estate car as alleged, and it belonged to a certain Y.C., who resided in Ankara. The applicants submitted a copy of a newspaper article to the Public Prosecutor for further investigation. Abdülkadir Aygan, a former member of the PKK and allegedly a member of JITEM (the Gendarme Intelligence Service), claimed to have killed Mr Kaya. The Public Prosecutor continued searching for Mr Aygan but was not able to locate him. The parties submitted various documents with a view to substantiating their claims. These documents, in so far as they are relevant, may be listed as follows. The petition of Efendi Kaya to the Diyarbakır State Security Court Public Prosecutor, dated 28 November 1996, requested the authorities to carry out an investigation into his father’s disappearance. name: Jan Górkiewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41663/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Polish nationals, Mr Jan Górkiewicz (‘the first applicant’) and Mrs Bogdana Gókiewicz, made the application on 9 July 2004. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of foreign Affairs. The applicants were born in 1948 and 1955 respectively and live in Glinica. They claimed compensation for the unlawful annulment of a contract by a contractor. The applicants sought just satisfaction in the amount of 20,000 Polish zlotys (PLN), that is, PLN 10,000 each. Both parties lodged appeals against the first-instance judgment. It appears that both parties lodged cassation appeals and the case is pending before the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) The applicants appealed under section 5 of the 2004 Act. The first hearing in the case was held on 26 January 2005. The applicants also lodged a complaint against the Gliwice and Katowice Regional Courts for their inactivity between the date the claim had been filed and the date of the first hearing had been scheduled.

The applicant was born in 1950 and was detained in the Hilvan prison, in Şanlıurfa, at the time of the case. The case concerned the prosecution of organised drug trafficking. The application was dismissed on 25 October 2005 and the case was dismissed again on 27 October 2005. The applicant and his co-accused were sentenced to six years and three months' imprisonment. The Diyarbakır State Security Court quashed the first-instance court's judgment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment on 20 April 2000. It ordered their release from detention having regard to the time that they had spent in prison. The application was later dismissed by a court of appeal. The applicant was acquitted by the Court of Appeal on 28 October 2013. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court of Justice on 3 January 2014. The case was adjourned until 16 May 2015, when the applicant was sentenced to five years in prison and two years and four months' probation.

The appeal was eventually dismissed on 28 July 2004 by the appellate court. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of France and the appeal judge has yet to make his decision.

name: Gerard Keegan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28867/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their home had been unjustifiably broken into and searched by police officers. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 11 October 2005, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled in the Court of International Human Rights (ICHR) in 2007. Police were tasked with investigating, and arresting, any further members of the gang and recovering the money from the robberies. The information which came into their possession indicated that Dean De La Cruz had often given 19 New Henderson Street as his address. A search warrant was issued permitting a search of the premises for the cash. The applicants brought proceedings against the Chief Constable of Merseyside Police for the tort of maliciously procuring a search warrant, unlawful entry and false imprisonment. They alleged that they had been caused terror, distress and psychiatric harm. Medical reports indicated that the applicants were suffering from varying degrees of post traumatic stress disorder. On 31 October 2002 the County Court Judge rejected the applicants’ claims. The judge found on the facts that the police, who were investigating serious and violent offences, had not acted with reckless indifference to the lawfulness of their acts. name: Danuta Gryziecka
train_texts: Two Polish nationals, Danuta Gryziecka and Henryk Gryziecki, made the application. The applicants alleged that their right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 10 January 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s” “Chamber”) in the Court of Justice of the European Union (‘the Court’). The case relates to 728,000 old Polish zlotys. the plaintiff’s claim in respect of the land on which the hen house had been constructed. The plaintiff's wife and daughter joined the proceedings as his legal successors. The court decided to obtain evidence from a bank and obtained three expert reports, held one view of the site and heard some witnesses. It also obtained fresh expert evidence in order to determine the value of certain construction works made by the second applicant. The case had been assigned to a new judge when it was decided to hold a hearing in 1996. The judge ruled that the case should be decided by a jury. The applicants requested that the court index the repayment of their bank loan and the payment made to the original plaintiff in 1984. The court fixed a one-month time-limit for the parties to produce the evidence. The applicants also requested to obtain documentary evidence from the land register. On 26 March 1998 the court gave judgment and partly granted the claim of the original. plaintiff’s daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claim. of the first applicant. The case had been assigned to a new judge. None of the parties submitted a notice of appeal. No one has appealed the decision, which was made in March 1998.

Subsequently, his wife and daughter joined the proceedings as his legal successors. In the meantime the plaintiff had modified his claim. The court decided to obtain evidence from a bank. It obtained three expert reports, held one view of the site and heard some witnesses. The plaintiffs again modified their claim. On 12 November 1996 the expert report was submitted to the court. On 11 December 1996 it was approved. The case had been assigned to a new judge and the case was now being heard by a different judge. The judge will decide on the future of the case at a hearing in May or June 2012. The applicants requested that the court index the repayment of their bank loan and the payment made to the original plaintiff in 1984. The applicants also requested to obtain documentary evidence from the land register. The court fixed a one-month time-limit for the parties to produce the evidence. On 16 September 1997 the plaintiffs again modified their claim. The plaintiffs withdrew their claims against the first applicant. On 26 March 1998 the court gave judgment. It partly granted the claim of the original plaintiffs’ daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claims of the first plaintiff’s wife. None of the parties submitted a notice of appeal. The case had been assigned to a new judge.

name: Abdurrahman Şiray
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29724/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who is of Kurdish origin, was arrested in Mardin and taken into police custody with three other individuals on suspicion of acting as a courier for an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK/KADEK. In his statement, given in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied any affiliation with the illegal organisation and contested F.A.’s allegations. He also explained that he had been carrying a false identity card as he was an army deserter. The applicant was charged with aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK and F.A. of membership of that organisation. He denied all charges against him, as well as retracting the statements he had made before the police, the public prosecutor and the magistrates’ court. At the sixth hearing, held on 1 April 2004, the applicant’s lawyer requested the applicant's release, claiming that the only piece of evidence found against him was F.a.’S statements made during the preliminary investigation stage. He further argued that he had. made his statements in Kurdish and had no way of knowing whether they had been translated into Turkish accurately. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court. The applicant was found guilty and convicted under Article 169 of the former Criminal Code and Section 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act for aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK. He was sentenced to four years and six months' imprisonment. On 22 December 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The case was re-examined in view of the recent legislative changes in Turkey. The new Criminal Code which had entered into force on 1 June 2005 (Law no. 5237) had provisions which would be more favourable for the applicant.

name: Yaşar Kanbur
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28291/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He was then taken to Ankara for questioning in relation to his activities in the organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The case is still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The criminal proceedings are still pending. The applicant appealed against his conviction. He was permanently debarred from employment in the civil service and placed under judicial guardianship.

name: Grattan Bond
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63479/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the United Kingdom authorities’ refusal to grant him widows’ social security and tax benefits or equivalent constituted discrimination on grounds of sex. The Court decided to communicate the complaint in connection with his claim for widows' benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his ‘second’ claim. It declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it subsequently decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law. the Inland Revenue informed him that he was ineligible for WBA as he was not a woman. The applicant decided not to appeal further since he considered that he would not be granted WBA under UK law. The application was denied and the applicant was not allowed to claim WBA for the remainder of his life. He was awarded WBA on February 25, 2011, and was awarded a pension of £1,000 a year. The amount was paid in full to the widower and his wife at the same time.

Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) and Mr Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 March 1993. Mrs Klaas was arrested and charged with obstructing a public officer in the execution of his duties. She was driven to the hospital for a blood test, which showed the level of alcohol in her blood to be 0.82 per ml (milligrammes per millilitre) The precise course of the events is disputed by the applicants (see paragraph 7 below) and the police officers. The first applicant underwent two medical examinations. Dr Schwering noticed bruises which were about 10cm long on her right arm, considerable problems in moving her left shoulder, and bruises on that shoulder. Dr Krauspe, the chief surgeon at the local hospital, examined the first applicant on 30 January 1986 and had reached an almost identical diagnosis. Police Constable Bolte had followed the applicants to the back door of the house. Mrs Klaas struggled, struck out and tried to free herself from the police officer’s grip. With great difficulty the officers managed to control the applicant, who was putting up a fight. They handcuffed her in order to avoid further criminal offences being committed, in particular injury to the person. In November 1986 the competent administrative authority imposed an administrative fine of DM 500 for having committed the “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) of driving with a blood. while under the influence of alcohol contrary to Article 316 of the said code. Mrs Klaas claimed that the police officers had used a disproportionate amount of force, causing injuries to her head, left shoulder and upper right arm. She maintained that the blood test showed the level of alcohol to be 0.80 per ml. On 18 September 1986, the Head of the Detmold District Administration, acting as the Police Department authority (Kreispolizeibehörde), dismissed her complaint. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), were dismissed. The first applicant instituted civil proceedings in April 1987 against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia and the police officers concerned. Her request to take her daughter to a neighbour’s first was granted. When the first applicant opened the door and tried to enter with her daughter, one of the police. officers held her right arm fast, whereupon she started to kick and to hit out with her left hand. She had to be handcuffed. It was not accepted that her head. knocked against the window-ledge at any moment in the course of the arrest. The Detmold Regional Court, in a partial judgment, dismissed her complaint against the officers on the ground that an official acting in the exercise of his duties does not incur personal liability. Police Constable Wildschut confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte. He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. She had resisted arrest and had been lashing out when he had twisted her arm behind her back, but he assumed she had not intended to assault either him or his colleague. Monika said she had seen through the glass door panel that one of the police officers had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. Monika did not recognise the officers involved she thought that the dark-haired police officer had a beard. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. The Chamber is admittedly convinced that the plaintiff incurred the injuries complained of when she was arrested by the two police officers. It does not follow, however, that the defendant Land is liable in damages. The plaintiff was under suspicion of having committed a criminal offence. Arrest was not disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring that the further investigations could be carried out. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff’s daughter, conflicts. The Chamber is not convinced that the officers caused the plaintiff's injuries by exceeding what was necessary when arresting her. Mrs Klaas claims to have seen one of the police officers repeatedly knocking the plaintiff’s head against the wall by the door, the two police officers deny this. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the. wall; the shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled while being restrained by the police and. when the handcuffs were being put on her. She said that she had managed to see through the plain glass door panel that the officer had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. These injuries were probably sustained by the plaintiff in the context of her arrest. The plaintiff was under suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol in road traffic contrary to Article 316 of the Criminal Code. The arrest itself was not unlawful. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff’s daughter, conflicts. Mrs Hildegard Klaas, the first applicant, submitted that, in the presence of her daughter, Monika, she had been subjected in the course of her arrest to inhuman and degrading treatment by the police. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against conviction but also certified it as a conviction. The House of Lords held that there was no right to privacy in English law. Evidence obtained improperly or even unlawfully remained admissible. The use at a criminal trial of material obtained in breach of Article 8 of the Convention did not mean that the trial would be unfair. The sole cause of this case coming to the House is the lack of a statutory system regulating the use of surveillance devices by the police. The absence of such a system seems astonishing, more so in view of the statutory framework which has governed the. use of such devices since 1989, and the interception of communications by the. police as well as by other agencies since 1985. The applicant was discharged from prison on 11 August 1994. His release was on licence until 12 May 1995. because counsel for the respondent was able to inform us, on instructions, that the government proposes to introduce legislation covering the matter in the next session of Parliament. The applicant was allowed to leave prison on licence. He was released on licence on May 12, 1995, after serving four years of a five-year prison sentence. The respondent was sentenced to three years in prison, suspended for one year, and fined £1,000. The judge ordered the respondent to serve his sentence on licence, until May 15, 1995.
