train_texts: The Adolf case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Republic of Austria. The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on 7 June 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an Austrian citizen, Mr. Gustav Adolf. The Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality and Mr G. Wiarda, the President of the Court. On 31 January 1981 in the presence of the Registrar, the. President drew by lot the names of the five other members. The applicant, an Austrian citizen born in 1918, lives in Innsbruck where he practises as a lawyer. The Government produced a document to the Court on 9 October, the Government's memorial was received on 14 April. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Herndl, Mr. Linke and Mr. Okresek for the Government and by. Melchior and Hoffmann for the Commission, as well as. their replies to questions put by the Court. Those appearing before the Court filed several documents during the hearings. The applicant's lawyer before the Commission was assisting the Delegate (Rule 29 par. 1, second sentence, of the Rules of Court). 85-year-old woman, Irmgard Proxauf, wrote to the Innsbruck public prosecutor's office. She claimed Mr. Adolf had thrown at another person, Mrs. Anneliese Schuh, a bunch of keys which had then struck her, causing her injury. Adolf denied the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. Court registered the case on 4 October 1977; under the heading “punishable act’ it specified “section 83 of the Penal Code’, which is a provision, amongst others, dealing with the infliction of bodily harm. The District Court assessed the costs of the case. Dr. Gustav Adolf was accused of injuring Mrs. Proxauf by throwing a bunch of keys. Adolf denied that he had injured her and contested the doctor's findings. He called on the District Court either to acquit him after trial or to terminate the proceedings pursuant to section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 21 below). He requested that fresh medical evidence be taken forthwith. The District Court of Innsbruck terminated the proceedings on an unspecified date in pursuance of section 451 par. 2 of the Penal Code. Mr. Adolf was served with a decision dated 10 January 1978 on his request. Irma Proxauf alleged that the accused had caused her an injury, namely a bruise on her left arm and another below her left breast, with a bunch of keys. The key first struck the back of the right hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant (geringfügig) as it does not exceed the three-day limit. The fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant. Therefore the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met. In both cases, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence (Beweisverfahren), something which should in principle precede any finding of guilt (Schulderkenntnis) The Generalprokurator said section 42 of the Penal Code was not appropriate where, on the basis of the complaint or the preliminary enquiries, no offence could be established on the facts or existed in law. A court decision terminating proceedings in accordance with section 42 could therefore only be grounded on a “suspected state of affairs’ (Verdachtslage) as disclosed by the case-file. The Generalprokurator moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated 10 January 1978 was contrary to the law. Mr. Adolf criticised the District Court for having failed to take into consideration evidence in his favour, for having declined to hear witnesses requested by him and for not having given him the opportunity to challenge the expert medical opinion. He relied on section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which places the judge under a duty to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met. The judge must have regard to all the evidence adduced and not simply to the evidence supporting the suspicion. Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on 28 February 1980. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law, says the judge. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified, he writes. The decision contains a negative ruling on the merits of the case and does not amount to a declaration, equivalent to a finding of guilt. The judgment of the Supreme Court was reproduced in an Austrian legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. The professional association to which Mr. Adolf belongs has not instituted any disciplinary proceedings against him in respect of the facts underlying Mrs. Proxauf's complaint. The file on his case, including the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated 10 January 1978, has been produced in evidence in a civil action in the matter of an easement (Dienstbarkeit) The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor is required by law to inquire into the correctness of any report (Anzeige) of an offence. The German law on criminal prosecutions means there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. The judge must then terminate the preliminary enquiries (section 447 par. 1). This provision applies, mutatis mutandis, to district court proceedings. Under the terms of section 90 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the public prosecutor may alternatively ask the investigating judge to hold that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met. If the court decides in the affirmative, it shall bring the proceedings to a close. Section 42 of the Austrian Penal Code is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings. Two circulars were issued on 15 January 1979 and 24 March 1980 by the relevant Austrian authorities drawing the attention of the courts to the problems raised by the application of this section. The Commission accepted the application on 6 July 1979. In its report of 8 October 1980 (Article 31 of the Convention) (art. 31), the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 of Article 6. The report contains three dissenting opinions. name: Abed Hussain
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 8 December 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 21928/93) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 31 March 1993 by a Pakistani national. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Singh v the UK should be heard by the same Chamber. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal. Mr Abed Hussain was born in 1962 and is currently detained in Lindholme prison. He was convicted at Leeds Crown Court of the murder of his younger brother, aged 2. The applicant had inflicted severe injuries on the infant while looking after him. He received a mandatory sentence of detention “during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) (see paragraph 23 below). Its effect was to render the applicant “liable to be detained in such a place and under such conditions as the Secretary of State [for the Home Department] may direct’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Fitzgerald and Mr Pannick.

name: Gunnar Beck
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26390/95) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that certain criminal proceedings against him in relation to fraud charges had exceeded a reasonable time, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 16 November 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required, decided the case on the basis of the case-file as it stood. Geneve and Cosmesin were accused of defrauding thousands of people. No goods containing the cultivated substances were ever marketed or produced. The companies went into bankruptcy in February 1987. One of the two leading figures in the criminal activity concerned, Mr D.R., disappeared. In November 1987 a search for him with an arrest warrant was made via Interpol. On 7 November 1990 he was arrested by the Spanish police. The Norwegian authorities requested his extradition on 23 November 1990. In October 1991 and April 1992 the police interviewed 12 cultivators. In April 1989 the police held meetings with Swedish and English police authorities. On 29 February 1988 the Probate Court (skifteretten) received the final report from the administrators of the estates ofCosmesin and Geneve. The case was submitted to the Oslo City Court on 4 September 1991. On 8 July 1991 he was released from custody in Spain, subject to a duty to report to the police. In early February 1992 he was extradited to Norway. After holding a hearing over 20 days in October and November 1992, the City Court convicted the applicant of all but the VAT charges, and sentenced him to 2 years’ imprisonment. The City Court noted from the outset that the offences for which the applicant was convicted were punishable by up to 9 years' imprisonment. It further stated that general considerations of crime prevention suggested that economic offences of the kind at issue warranted a severe penalty. The prosecution transmitted the case to the Oslo City Court in December 1991. Final investigations concerning one aspect of the case as important as the value of the cultivators and their possible use went on as late as the first semester of 1992. Two other co-defendants, including Mr D.R., who were considered to have played a more prominent role in the proscribed activity, were sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. The applicant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, alleging a procedural error in the first instance proceedings and requesting a new trial. After taking evidence on 14 December 1993 and holding a hearing on 6 September 1994, the Supreme court rejected the appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5298/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Turkish nationals, Mr Rıdvan Saruhan and Mr Abdulvahit Çelik (‘the applicants’), made the application on 2 February 2006. In 1974, a third person named B.A. inherited a plot of land from her mother, a Syrian national, but she did not have the land registered in her name at the time. On 9 July 1996 B. a’s representative signed an agreement with the applicants before a notary public, promising to sell the land to them. The applicants made a plea of unconstitutionality against the decree of 1966. On 7 July 2005 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicants’ request for rectification. This decision was not served on the applicants and they learned about the outcome of the proceedings by tracking their application through the court’s web site. The decision was made by a three-judge panel and the decision was upheld by the first instance court. The case is still pending at the Supreme Court of Justice of Belgium. The appeal was dismissed on 28 February 2005 and the appeal was upheld on 28 July 2005. The application was denied on 7 July 2006 and it was dismissed again on 7 September 2006.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals. In 1974, a third person inherited a plot of land from her mother, a Syrian national. However, she did not have the land registered in her name at the time. The applicants claimed that she had failed to transfer the ownership of the land to them, although they had paid the purchase price. The court held that on 1 October 1966 the Cabinet of Ministers had issued a decree seizing the property of Syrian nationals. As the land had been owned by the State since 1966, the court concluded that the sale agreement of 9 July 1996 signed by B.A. was void. The Court of Cassation dismissed the plea of unconstitutionality against the decree of 1966. The decision was not served on the applicants and they learned about the outcome of the proceedings by tracking their application through the Court's web site. On 7 July 2005 the Court ofCassation rejected the applicants’ request for rectification. The case is still pending at the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Luxembourg. For more information, go to: http://www.cassation.gov.uk/. For more details on the case, visit: www.casseration.org.uk. for more information about the case.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19657/12) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged a violation of their right to freedom of expression as guaranteed by Article 10. The application was communicated to the Government on 26 June 2014. The case was brought by two Danish nationals, Ms Mette Frisk (the first applicant), and Mr Steen Jensen, (the second applicant) on 27 March 2012. It concerned the treatment of pleural mesothelioma cancer, notably at Copenhagen University Hospital (Rigshospitalet) European Union approved marketing of Alimta in combination with Cisplatin for treatment of patients with inoperable pleural mesothelioma cancer in 2004. Denmark's Minister for Internal Affairs and Health replied to various questions posed by Members of Parliament in 2007. He said there was no proof that an AlimTA-based treatment was more efficient than other chemotherapy-based treatments, including that offered in Denmark. Copenhagen University Hospital produced a memorandum about pleuralmesothelIoma cancer and its treatment in June 2008. It stressed that international studies had not shown that any two-combination regime was superior to other two‑combination regimes. The memorandum also referred to a fund aimed at developing research on pleural MesoCancer in the amount of 90,000 Danish kroner. 12,000 Euros (EUR) received by S from company F, which produces Vinorelbine. The money had been used to pay nurses and students and for data collection. It emerged that there had been no financial profit for the doctors involved. The proceedings before the courts began on 27 October 2008. Copenhagen University Hospital and S instituted defamation proceedings against the Director of DR and the two applicants. The first applicant stated, inter alia: “... that she had not criticised Copenhagen University hospital for improper treatment causing death. Her message was only to point out that the substance of Alimta had been better documented” Alimta has been used for second-line therapy in Denmark since 2004, and since 2007 as first-line. therapy. Today, Alimta is used in combination with Carboplatin as the standard therapy for inoperable patients. After the programme had been broadcast ... patients started mistrusting the Vinorelbine therapy. It was not possible to perform the trial [phase II] on this drug. Nor would it be possible to obtain funding for the trial. Therefore no trial had been performed of Vinorelbsine. The approval of Alimna by the Danish Medicines Agency for the treatment of mesothelioma only means that a marketing authorisation has been granted for the drug. Copenhagen City Court found against the applicants (and the Director of DR) and sentenced them each to 10 day-fines of 1,000 Danish Kroner (DKK) The allegations were declared null and void. The court said the shift to Alimta as the standard therapy at Copenhagen University Hospital did not reflect that AlimTA was medically better than Vinorelbine. The programme had created distrust towards both Copenhagen University hospital and S. and had created uncertainty in both patients and relatives. He had received 50 to 100 ‘hate mails’ himself ...” By a judgment of 9 April 2010, the Copenhagen City Court Found against the Applicants and the Director. means that advertisement of the product is permitted. Court accepts as a fact that Vinorelbine is a drug dating back more than 20 years whose effect had been documented by clinical experience and approved by the Danish Medicines Agency for a wide range of oncological therapies. Court finds that it would seem to a non-professional viewer that Alimta was the only effective drug for mesothelioma, particularly because the programme linked the treatment of two patients with Vinorelbsine to their death. Court also finds that a drug administered to patients in a trial is referred to as an experimental drug, no matter whether the same drug is the standard therapy offered outside the trial setting. On appeal, on 10 June 2011 the judgment was upheld by the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) with the following reasoning: ‘In the introduction to the programme ‘When the doctor knows best’ a narrator states, among other things, that a Danish doctor has treated dying patients with chemotherapy that is not approved’ ‘S can freely choose the medication that he thinks is best. There is only one treatment which, in comparative studies, has proved to have an effect on pleural mesothelioma cancer. Accordingly, that is the only medication which is approved as treatment. That medication is called Alimta’ According to the calculations made by DR, close to 300 patients in Denmark have been given test medication. In the worst scenario, that may result in patients dying earlier than if they had been given the approved medication. The programme ends by informing us, among other things, that two of the patients who were interviewed have passed away. The narrator says, inter alia: ‘TJ, who was part of S’s tests with Vinorelbine, died on 4 January 2008’ With these statements, [the applicants] not only passed on assertions by patients, relatives and experts, but also took a stand, so that the programme undisputedly gave the viewers the impression that malpractice has occurred. Copenhagen University Hospital and S were accused of malpractice in a TV programme. The programme claimed the choice of medication [Vinorelbine] was chosen for S’s professional prestige and personal finances. The application was made under Article 267 of the Penal Code. The court ruled that the application must be understood in the light of Article 10 of the Convention on the protection of freedom of expression. A very considerable public interest is related to journalistic discussion about risk to life and health, or suspicion thereof, as regards public hospital treatment. The press must be permitted, as the public control- and information organ, a certain amount of exaggeration and provocation in connection with their discussion. Vinorelbine in combination with Cisplatin or Carboplatin was standard treatment at Copenhagen University Hospital. European Union on 20 September 2004 approved the marketing of Alimta for treatment of inoperable patients with pleural mesothelioma cancer. The applicants made allegations which were based on an incorrect factual basis, of which they must have been aware via the research material. It is an aggravating factor that the wrongful accusations were disseminated on national television during primetime and on DR’s homepage, by means of which the accusations had a significant spread. The allegations are not unpunishable under Article 269 (1) nor is there any basis for remitting the punishment under Article269 (2) Copenhagen High Court dismisses the appeal and upholds the judgment of the Copenhagen City Court. The applicants shall be jointly and severally liable for paying legal costs of the High Court appeal to Copenhagen University Hospital and S, in the amount of DKK 90,000. Two of the cases have been appealed against to the National Agency for Patients’ Rights and Complaints (Patientskadeankenævnet) All four complaints have been refused, one of the reasons being that the independent medical oncologists who assessed the cases found that it was in compliance with optimum medical standards to treat patients with the selected combination therapy.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant obtained a copy of his brother’s death certificate and a medical report which recorded that his brother died on 20 January 1995, after being brought to hospital from prison with a history of severe chest pain and general body weakness associated with a fever. He also obtained the summons from the Pemba police headquarters to his parents dated 25 November 1995. He made representations to the Secretary of State dated 30 January 1997, requesting that his letter be considered as a fresh asylum application. By letter dated 5 February 1997 he decided not to refer the material in question to the special adjudicator under section 21 of the Immigration Act 1971. He refused on that basis to reverse his decision. The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s refusal to refer the new material to the special adjudicator. The application for leave was rejected by the High Court. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal. In its judgment it noted that the hospital records showed that his brother had died of fever and did not support the applicant's evidence that he had been tortured. The appeal was dismissed on 1 December 1998 and the applicant was allowed to return to his home country. The judge said that he could safely return to the mainland if he went to his native Tanzania. He refused to make a reference under section 21. to reverse his decision to refuse asylum. The applicant's wife arrived in the United Kingdom and claimed asylum shortly afterwards. There was no evidence to suggest that the conclusion reached by the Secretary of State that the applicant could live without harassment on the mainland was wrong. It was recorded that she stated in her interview that the police had harassed her due to her husband’s involvement with the CUF. She had been detained for one day in April 1995 and questioned about her husband's whereabouts. The police came to her house on 12 February 1999, wanting to know if her husband was back in Zanzibar. They were angry because he had claimed asylum and tarnished the name of the President. They threatened to arrest her instead.

name: Mark Anthony Grieves
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 57067/00) lodged on 26 April 2000 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he did not receive a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law in violation of Article 6. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section. On 6 May 2003 a Chamber of that Section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, neither of the parties having objected to such relinquishment. The Grand Chamber notified the parties that it might decide to examine the merits of the complaint before it at the same time as its admissibility. The Government. and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits together with separate. submissions on the applicable domestic law and practice. The Grand Chamber subsequently decided to examine the merits of the complaint before it at the same time as its admissiblity. The applicant chose to be represented by a naval barrister. He was sentenced to, inter alia, three years' imprisonment and to be dismissed from the service and reduced in rank. The Court heard addresses by Mr Havers and by Mr Blades. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 1 October 2003 (Rule 59 § 3 of the Rules of Court). The Navy Board decided not to vary the court-martial's verdict and sentence. name: Georgiev Cvetan Rangelov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5123/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him had violated Articles 5 § 1 and 14. He had been refused important measures putting him in a position to prove that he was no longer dangerous to the public. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was convicted of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary. He was sentenced to eight years and six months’ imprisonment. He served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he has been remanded in preventive detention. The court ruled that the applicant had a propensity to commit offences by which serious economic damage was caused and was therefore dangerous to the public. The applicant is currently being held in a preventive detention facility in Regensburg, Germany. He is being held under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 40-41 below) The applicant’s transfer to a social therapeutic institution, relaxations in the conditions of his detention and preparations for his release were not envisaged as the city of Munich had issued a deportation order. The applicant’s counsel was subsequently granted access to the applicant's personal files at Straubing Prison. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. On 26 February 2004 the Regensburg Regional Court, having heard the applicant on 15 January 2004 and the applicant and the two experts W. and T. on 19 February 2004, again decided that the execution of the applicant”s preventive detention was necessary in view of its objective (Article 67c § 1 of the Criminal Code). It therefore refused to suspend the execution and to grant probation. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The Public Prosecutor’s Office would have to consider this issue when deciding on a fresh motion lodged by the applicant to suspend his preventive detention pursuant to Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint and to grant him legal aid (no. 2 BvR 1079/04). It found that his complaint had no prospects of success. There was nothing to indicate that the criminal courts had failed duly to consider human dignity and the right to freedom as guaranteed by the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that there were no suitable measures to prepare the applicant adequately for his release. The applications to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal were to no avail. The application to the Regensburg Regional Court to suspend the execution of the applicant's preventive detention order on probation was not successful. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. It conceded that it was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. The applicant could not expect any relaxations in the conditions of his detention. In practice, the latter were a precondition for coming to an assessment that a detainee was no longer dangerous to the public. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations. In these circumstances, a therapeutic treatment was without prospects of success. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria and sentenced to life imprisonment. The judgment was upheld on appeal. The applicant was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria in order to serve his sentence. He was expelled to Bulgaria on 13 December 2007 in accordance with the deportation order issued by the city of Munich on 16 April 1997. He has been living in Bulgaria since then. The application for his release was rejected on 13 November 2013. The appeal was denied again on 17 January 2014. The case was dismissed again on 16 May 2006. The Munich Court of Appeal ruled that the prosecution authorities could only exercise their discretion in a lawful manner by granting his request under the said provision.

The case originated in an application (no. 5123/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him had violated Articles 5 § 1 and 14. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant entered Germany in 1979 and has been convicted some fifteen times since 1980, notably of theft and burglary. The applicant was convicted of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary. He was sentenced to eight years and six months’ imprisonment in 1996. The city of Munich ordered the applicant’s expulsion to Bulgaria and prohibited him to re-enter Germany for an indefinite duration in view of his criminal convictions. The applicant served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he was remanded in preventive detention. The decision of the Regional Court decided that the execution of the applicant's preventive detention was still necessary. The proceedings at issue are referred to in paragraphs 40-41 of this article. The case was decided by the Munich I Regional Court in 1996 and the case was heard by the Regensburg Regional Court on 21 August 2003. The appeal was dismissed on 25 November 1997. Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The refusal of the Straubing Prison authorities to allow the applicant’s defence counsel to inspect his personal files had violated the right to a fair trial. The applicant had not been admitted to a social therapy in Erlangen Prison he had applied for in 2002. The conditions of his detention had also not been relaxed (Vollzugslockerungen) The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 26 February 2004. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time. The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. He notably argued that his right to freedom as guaranteed by Article 2 § 2 of the Basic Law was violated because his preventive detention was disproportionate. He claimed that the refusal to admit him to a social therapy due to his imminent expulsion discriminated him because of his Bulgarian nationality. On 28 September 2004 the Federal. Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’S constitutional complaint and to grant him legal aid. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that there were no suitable measures to prepare the applicant adequately for his release due to his persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences. The decision of the Nuremberg-Fürth Regional Court dismissed as inadmissible the applicant's request to declare that refusal unlawful. The Regensburg Regional Court refused to suspend the execution of the applicant’S preventive detention order on probation. The applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. there was still a risk that the applicant would commit further serious offences against the property of others (but no violent offences) if released. It was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. owing to, in particular, his foreign nationality, the applicant could not expect any relaxations in the conditions of his detention. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations. In these circumstances, a therapeutic treatment was without prospects of success. Munich Court of Appeal ruled that the prosecution's balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty was not unconstitutional. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria and sentenced to life imprisonment. The judgment was upheld on appeal and the applicant was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria in order to serve his sentence. On 13 December 2007 the applicant. was expelled to Bulgaria. in accordance with the deportation order issued by the city of Munich. on 16 April 1997. The application was dismissed on 7 November 2005 and again on 7 September 2007.

In these circumstances, a therapeutic treatment was without prospects of success. On 19 June 2007 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint. It noted, in particular, that expert A. had considered that there was no starting point for beginning with measures preparing the applicant his conditional release. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria and sentenced to life imprisonment. The judgment was upheld on appeal. The applicant was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria in order to serve his sentence. The Munich Court of Appeal noted, in particular, that it might appear contradictory to the applicant that measures aiming at his reintegration into society, such as a social therapy, were refused to him because of the deportation order against him. However, the refusal of the said measures alone did not mean that the prosecution authorities could only exercise their discretion in a lawful manner by granting his request.

name: David Hood
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government”) on 14 August 1998. It originated in an application (no. 27267/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights by a British national, Mr David Hood, on 18 April 1995. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (former Rule 30). The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the UK. David Hood is a British national born in 1970. At the relevant time, he was a soldier with the regular forces of the British army. The applicant went absent without leave from his unit in Germany three times. Prior to his third absence, he had been remanded for trial by court martial on an assault charge (later abandoned) He remained absent for almost two and a half years and he gave himself up to the civilian police in December 1993. The relevant detention took place in Germany. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 9 December 1998. The Court heard addresses by Mr Mackenzie and Mr Havers. The applicant did not return after two weeks’ leave (his fourth absence without leave) on 11 May 1994. On 27 November 1994 he was arrested at his home by the civilian police and he was taken by army escort to Brompton Barracks. On 4 January 1995 the applicant appeared before the unit adjutant and was given the abstract of evidence. The charge sheet, dated 25 January 1995 and signed by his commanding officer and on behalf of the convening officer, recorded two charges of absence contrary to the Army Act 1955 and two of desertion. The applicant, who was legally represented, pleaded not guilty and was remanded for trial by court martial. The applicant was convicted on the two charges of absence without leave and on one of the charges of desertion. He was sentenced to be imprisoned for eight months and to be dismissed from the service. The judge advocate found that Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure (Army) 1972 had been followed. After confirmation and promulgation of the conviction and sentence, the applicant petitioned the Army. By letter dated 13 July 1995 the applicant was informed that his petition to the Army Board had been rejected. His leave application to the single judge of the Courts-Martial Appeal Court was rejected on 13 September 1995 and his further appeal to the full courts was also refused. High Court rejected the application. The court found, inter alia, that the delay report had been properly completed in a timely fashion. It noted that the expressed reason for the applicant’s continued detention was to prevent his absconding and found that ‘perfectly understandable’ given the charges against him. The application was rejected by the Court of Appeal on Tuesday. The appeal was adjourned until October 31, 2014. The case was heard by a three-judge panel at the High Court in Dublin. name: Grzegorz Zabłocki
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 10104/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the lustration proceedings in his case had been unfair, in violation of Article 6 of the Court's Convention. On 24 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicants case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) from 26 February 2008 to 13 December 2008. In 2002 the applicant became a member of the board of directors of the same radio (Zarząd) In 2005 the Commissioner of the Public Interest informed the applicant that he had doubts as to the truthfulness of his lustration declaration. On 20 September 2006 the Warsaw Court of Appeal, acting as the first‑instance lustration court, found that the applicant had been an intentional and secret collaborator with the State’s secret services. The court based its findings on the statements made by Mr A.W., an officer of the Security Service (Służba Bezpieczeństwa, ‘the SB’) Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal as being manifestly ill‑founded. Appeal, acting as the second‑instance lustration court, upheld the impugned judgment. The court established that the evidence in the case had not been extensive but had obviously pointed to the fact that the applicant had been an intentional and secret collaborator with the SB. The applicant was barred from holding public office for a period of ten years in application of the 1997 Lustration Act. The Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) dismissed the applicants appeal. The appeal was dismissed as being manifestsly ill-founded.

All the documents collected in the case were classified as confidential and could be consulted by the applicant in the secret registry of the lustration court. Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal as being manifestly ill‑founded. Appeal, acting as the second‑instance lustration court, upheld the impugned judgment. The applicant was barred from holding public office for a period of ten years in application of the 1997 Lustration Act. The appeal was dismissed on 28 August 2007, and the application was dismissed in court on 30 August 2007. The application was rejected by the Supreme Court.

name: Gordon Foxley
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33274/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the decision of the authorities of the respondent State to open, read and copy to file his correspondence was an unjustified interference with his right guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The court found that the applicant had benefited from the commission of the offences in the amount of GBP 2,092,569.20. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment under section 1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1906 on each of the twelve counts, to be served concurrently. In default of payment the applicant was to be imprisoned for a further (consecutive) term of three years. On 2 September 1996, following an application on behalf of the Ministry of Defence in separate civil proceedings, the applicant were declared bankrupt. Ms S.D. was appointed as the applicant’s Trustee in Bankruptcy. This appointment was independent of her appointment as Receiver. The Order was made under section 371 of the Insolvency Act 1986 in favour of Ms S.D. in her capacity as the applicant’s Trustee in Bankruptcy. The application was based on the grounds that the Trustee was of the opinion that communications concerning remittances and useful information in respect of the applicant's assets and liabilities might be forwarded. The grounds invoked were supported by an affidavit sworn on 27 September 1996, which affirmed that it was necessary for postal packets to be intercepted immediately and without notice to the applicant. Between 27 September and 10 January 1997, a total of 71 letters addressed to the application were re-directed to the Receiver and Trustee. Although the re-direction Order expired on 27 December 1996 it was only as from 18 January 1997 that the applicant began to receive his mail directly again. During that period there were two mail deliveries to the Trustee in Bankruptcy. One delivery was received on 30 December 1996, the other on 10 January 1997. The deliveries contained ten items of mail, none of which fell within the categories described above (see paragraph 19). A number of the items were however copied to file before being forwarded to the applicant. On 25 February 1997 the applicant issued a summons for a stay of the receivership proceedings pending the determination of his application to the Commission. The hearing was listed for 16 June 1997 but was adjourned to 19 February 1998.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50034/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings in which she claimed discrimination at work took an unreasonable length of time. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. By a decision of 15 November 2001, the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant complained of a failure to transfer her to another post and the failure to assign her to a higher grade by giving due recognition to her professional qualifications. In her application, she relied on events going back to the commencement of her employment in 1989. The Employment Tribunal ruled that under section 68(1) of the Race Relations Act 1976, the applicant could not rely upon events taking place before September 1990. An offer of transfer was made to the applicant on 8 February 1994. The case lasted longer than anticipated by the parties and it was adjourned and re-listed. On 20 December 1994, the Tribunal issued its decision. The Tribunal made the applicant an award of 24,952.51 pounds sterling (GBP), which decision issued on 9 October 1995. The Council appealed to the Employment Appeal Tribunal (“EAT’) The EAT delivered judgment on 28 October 1996. It quashed the findings of discrimination. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9244/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in connection with the incidents in the Ümraniye Prison. He was accused of homicide, of starting a riot in the prison and of damage to public property. Since the applicant was a minor when the crimes in question had been committed, the case should be examined by the Istanbul Juvenile Court. The applicant was released from prison on 7 July 2001 at around 8.30 p.m.

The applicants' neighbours were granted a permission to construct a shop on the ground floor of their house. They appealed but the decision was upheld on 19 July 1993. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8456/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the International Convention. He was charged with establishing and leading an organised criminal group engaged in money laundering, illegal trading in liquid fuel and the falsification of tax documents. In his appeals, he argued that the charges against him were based on unreliable and fabricated evidence. He also relied on his personal circumstances, in particular the need to ensure that his wife, who suffered from psychiatric problems, was cared for. The authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. The courts stressed, on several occasions, the applicant's role in the organised criminal group, holding that there was a risk that if released, he would induce witnesses to give false testimony, or otherwise obstruct the proper conduct of the investigation. In one of the decisions dismissing an appeal by the applicant against a decision prolonging his detention, the Court of Appeal noted that “certain witnesses in principle admitted that they had been instructed [about what to say] in their testimony” It did not, however, specify who had exerted pressure on the witnesses or how they had done so.

name: Wacław Płoski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8 of the Convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merit of the case. The applicant applied for leave to attend the funeral of his mother. The judge rejected the application on the grounds that he was a habitual offender whose return to prison could not be guaranteed. On 6 August 1994 the applicant made an application to attend his father’s funeral. The application was in the following terms: “I kindly ask you to grant me a compassionate leave because my father Wacław Płoski has died. The funeral will take place on 8.08.1994 and I would like to attend it and to pay last respects to him.” The judge ruled that there were no grounds for granting the applicant compassionate leave. Wacław Płoski applied for leave to attend the funeral of his father in August 1994. Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused permission to grant the applicant leave. The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society.” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. He was released from prison on 27 February 1996. On 31 January 1995 the Legal Secretary advised the applicant that his requests for leave had been rejected because he had been a recidivist posing a risk of absconding.

name: Wolfgang Ohneberg
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10781/08) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was a civil servant at the Bregenz Tax Authority. He was removed from his post as head of the tax assessment division by a decision of the Bremen Tax Authority of 29 March 2005. Upon the applicant’s appeal the Appeals Commission at the Federal Chancellery (Berufungskommission beim Bundeskanzleramt - “the Appeals Commission”) set aside those two decisions on 28 July 2005. The applicant was transferred to the post of specialist without any team-leading responsibilities. The job profile did not state that any employees or civil servants were to be under his direct supervision. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Appeals Commission on 18 May 2006. He argued, inter alia, that his actual work had not changed sufficiently to justify the lower grade. The Appeals Commission replied on 30 October 2006 and stated, referring to the Constitutional Court’s case-law, that the rights and obligations. arising from employment in public service did not amount to civil rights and. obligations. The application was dismissed on 21 July 2006. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in July 2007 that the ruling was valid. The European Court found that Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights applied to the case. The court said that the decision was not in breach of Article 6 because it was based on a non-existent legal provision. The decision led to the European Court's decision not to hold a hearing on the case in the first place. The case was re-opened in October 2007 and a decision was made to hold the hearing in the second week of October. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Europe on June 23, 2008. The Supreme Court ruled that the original decision was valid because it had been made by a court of law, not by a commission.

The MNC has asked the MNC to make clear that it is not responsible for the disappearance of Mustafa Saidgı. Mustafa Sayğı was unlawfully detained by the military in the temporary military base near Yoğurtçu village. The prosecutor did not attach any weight to the denials of the military personnel. The applicant lodged an objection against the prosecutor’s decision with the Siverek Assize Court and submitted that nothing had been heard from her husband after his unlawful detention. She argued that similar unlawful detentions had peaked in that area in 1994 and that the relatives of those who had disappeared had been too frightened to complain to the authorities. The objection lodged by the applicant was rejected by the SIVErek Assized Court on 29 November 2006. The remains of a red motorbike and 30 bones were found during the digging. Forensic experts were not able to identify the type or make of the motorbike due to corrosion. The chassis numbers and letters of theMotorbike – in Russian – are reproduced in the report of the experts. The bones were examined at the Forensic Medicine Institute. It was established that the bones were animal bones. According to a report drawn up on 1 February 2010 by the forensic laboratory of the police, the soil on the motor bike parts matched the soil samples taken from the place. However, the dirt on the bones did not match the soil sample taken from that place. No prior applications had been made to the police about the disappearance. On 7 April 2010 Suruç prosecutor M.A. decided to close his investigation on the basis that the bones were not human bones. The applicant lodged an objection with the Siverek Assize Court against the prosecutor’s decision and argued that the investigation had been incomplete. She argued that carrying out an effective investigation was necessary in order to avoid ‘the State being put on trial before the European Court of Human Rights for its failure to protect the right to life of her husband’ The objection was rejected by the Sivesize Assize court on 7 June 2010. No mention was made in the decision about the points raised by the applicant in her objection.

name: Vernon John Davies
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42007/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of his right under Article 6 of the Convention to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly inadmissible on 26 September 2000. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the application was allocated to a newly composed Fourth Section. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case went to the Court of Appeal, where it was quashed. The case was adjourned until the end of 1994, when it was re-opened. The prosecution again applied for an extension of the trial, which was denied. The appeal was dismissed, and the case was returned to the court of appeal. The trial was reopened and the prosecution tried to obtain the case back to the High Court. The High Court rejected this request and the appeal was thrown out. The matter was referred to the Supreme Court, which made the decision to dismiss the case. The decision was overturned on appeal, but not before the prosecution had the opportunity to present its case again. Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached between the applicant and the Secretary of State in other proceedings under the CDDA. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the secretary of state's costs of GBP 94,000. The Blackspur case was settled with the applicant agreeing to pay GBP 90,000 of the secretary's costs as part of a settlement. The case was adjourned until after the conclusion of the criminal trial in February 1998. The judge ruled that the case should proceed since it was in the public interest to determine the “particularly serious” allegations of false accounting and trading while insolvent made against the defendants.

The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of his right under Article 6 § 1 to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly inadmissible on 26 September 2000. The Third Section declared the application admissible insofar as the applicant complained about the length of the ‘Blackspur’ proceedings. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was brought against the UK Government. The trial was to begin on 1 July 1992. It was adjourned until 29 July 1993. The case was finally dismissed on 2 May 1995. The UK government has appealed the decision. The appeal has been rejected. The judge said the case should be dismissed because it was not resolved before the start of the trial. The British government had appealed against the decision to dismiss the case. The jury was unable to reach a verdict. The decision was quashed by the Court of Appeal, and the case was dismissed. The sentence was reduced to a fine of £5,000. The defendant was allowed to return to the UK to appeal the conviction. The Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached between the applicant and the Secretary of State in other proceedings under the CDDA. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the Secretary. of State's costs of GBP 94,000. The applicant also agreed to give up his right to a hearing in the case against him. The case was adjourned until after the conclusion of the criminal trial, not to hurry them on”. The court observed that the delay had not affected the timing of the hearing or prejudiced the applicant, and that, once the proceedings had commenced, “the respondents' main concern was to delay the proceedings’.

The case was heard by the Fourth Section, which was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. The case was adjourned until November 1995. Two of the four defendants were found not guilty by reason of miscarriage of justice. The other two defendants were acquitted of all charges against them. The case was settled by a jury, who found the defendants not guilty of any crime. The judge ruled that the case was dismissed on a technicality, and that the judge should not have been allowed to consider the case. The appeal was dismissed in November 1995, and the case against the two defendants was dismissed as well. The conviction of the defendants was overturned on appeal in May 1998. The trial of the other three defendants was eventually settled in June 1998, with the judge leaving the case to the prosecution. On 1 July 1996 the Registrar directed that the defendants should serve their evidence in response to that of the Secretary of State by 29 November 1996. That order was not complied with, and on 9 December 1996 the Registry ordered that if the defendants had not served their evidence by 17 January 1997, they would be debarred from adducing any evidence. On 20 January 1997 the Registrar ordered that the Secretary. of State should serve his evidence in reply by 17 March 1997. The applicant failed to comply with this order and on 8 December 1997 he was granted an extension of time until 9 February 1998. In the event, however, the Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the Secretary's costs of GBP 94,000.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38663/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 of the convention in proceedings concerning the enforcement of their claims for maintenance against their father. The application was dismissed by the debtor and the Government applied to postpone enforcement until a decision on his action had been reached. On 23 October 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. In support of his application to postpone enforcement regarding the sale of movable property, the debtor claimed he would risk losing his property rights over the objects seized for enforcement. The applicants were not notified of the appeal. The Steyr Regional Court quashed the decision, ordering both kinds of enforcement to be postponed until the decision on the action under Section 35 of the Enforcement Act was rendered and re-setting the deposit at EUR 1,000. It held that an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was not admissible and the applicants were obliged to reimburse legal costs amounting to EUR 305.40 to the debtor.

name: Turhan Yalçın Bürkev
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Turhan Yalçın Bürkev complained about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case. The Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application admissible. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi), and the case file was transmitted to the Court of Cassation (yargıtay) in 1994. The applicant’s conviction was quashed in 1995 on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence under Articles 146 and 168.

name: Eie Enhorn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court ruled that the application was admissible on 10 December 2002. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. The county medical officer petitioned the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) for a court order that the applicant be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The court's record of the applicant's statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons. also tell his dentist [about it].” It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant’s medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1987 Act. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. While being isolated the applicant had the opportunity to go outdoors every day together with members of the hospital staff, but not on his own. Also, he was able to accompany staff members on different activities outside the hospital grounds. The applicant's compulsory confinement was repeatedly prolonged by periods of six months at a time. The boy, who was 15 years old when they met, took the initiative both emotionally and sexually. Today [the applicant] realises that he infected the boy, which he finds very regrettable. While on the run from 26 February 1997 until 26 February 1999, he had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the. applicant returned to Stockholm and began to live at his farm hostel under a pseudonym. The applicant had taken precautions against spreading the disease and, having had to visit physicians twice during his period at large, had informed them about his HIV infection. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicants had made a lunge at him. In his opinion, the applicant suffers from a paranoid personality disorder and from alcohol abuse. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. On 23 April 1999 the County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During [the applicant's] contact with the doctors in question, they did not discuss the risk of spreading the disease at all. A treatment plan was not formally signed [by the applicant]. In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease” In 1999 the applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, the following: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol.” The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [ the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued. This entails a risk of the infection spreading. The applicant showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. With regard to sexual relations, he preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. He had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. The Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger) The application was turned down by the County Administrative Court on 12 December 2001. It referred to the fact that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the applicant’s whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the further involuntary placement in isolation. On 5 October 1999 the County Medical Officer submitted an application for an extension of the compulsory isolation of the applicant. The application was granted on 12 October 1999 and the applicant was placed in isolation until the end of the year.

The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section. The Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The court's record of the applicant’s statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships.” The applicant had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. The applicant's lack of social contact and his feeling of being an outsider, in combination with possible alcohol abuse, could increase the risk of destructive sexual relations. He has had periods of extensive [alcohol] abuse as a consequence of learning that he was infected with HIV but also when he lost his job. He realises that he infected the boy, which he finds very regrettable. A relative of the applicant is now being treated at a hospital in Hamburg. He is being held in compulsory isolation and is not allowed to leave the hospital grounds. He was detained in his room from 26 February until 2 March 1999. The court ordered that he be confined for up to three months. While he was on the run, the applicant had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant has a healthy liver.”. It was noted that subsequent to his return the. applicant returned to Sweden under a pseudonym and went back to his farm hostel in Norrköping. The owner of the farm. hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The record of his statement reads, inter alia, as follows. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. The statement of the county medical officer, who gave evidence before the court, is recorded, inter alia, as follows: “During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus’. He has agreed to sign a treatment agreement.” The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection. During the time preceding his compulsory isolation, [the applicant] was not able to follow the practical instructions issued. Subsequently, he has consistently declined the help offered by the consulting physician and the psychiatrist and has instead responded with aversion and mistrust – and by escaping” The applicant had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, that he was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol. The Court has not been convinced that [the applicant] is not misusing alcohol and finds that he is likely to be unable to control his sexual behaviour. It appears from the evidence that [ the applicant] still shows aversion to the treatment offered and is considered likely to abscond.” On 12 June 1999 the applicant again abscondered, leaving his whereabouts unknown. HIV-infected man was found to have a paranoid personality disorder. Court of Appeal found against the applicant in 1999. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger), and he was found not to be mentally ill. He preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17, was celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. He was fully aware that he was carrying the HIV virus and was careful to stress he was not afraid to die. He showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned, and was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. An application was turned down by the County Administrative Court in December 2001. It appears that since 2002 the appealer's whereabouts have been known, but that there are no grounds for the applicant’s further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was made on 5 October 1999 and was rejected on 12 December 2001, with the reason given as that there was no information about the applicant. It was the first time the application had been rejected by a court in Sweden. The case was heard at the Swedish Court of Appeal (S.A. ingsrätten) on 11 October 1999.
