He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. While on the run from 26 February 1997 until 26 February 1999, he had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. He used to go shopping once a day, usually for beer, and [the witness] would estimate that he had drunk between four and six cans of beer every day. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant’s liver appeared to be healthy. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. In P. N.'s view, the applications had not made any positive progress since 10 October 1996. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease. The applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol.” The Court has not been convinced that [ the applicant] is not misusing alcohol and finds that, especially in connection with alcohol consumption, [the applicants] is likely to be unable to control his sexual behaviour. It is not correct to talk in terms of lack of awareness of a disease, since it is not considered that a disease is involved. The applicant had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. He showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. He felt that he had been subjected to persecution between 1994 and 1995. This could possibly be interpreted as a symptom of delusion. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. He preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill.” In conclusion, the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the applicant.'s further involuntary placement in isolation. On 5 October 1999. the applicant was placed in a psychiatric ward at the hospital in Bremen.

In October 1990 a. large explosion occurred at a British Army/Royal Ulster Constabulary checkpoint in. County Derry. Five British soldiers and one civilian were killed and a. number of other British army personnel were seriously injured. An hour and a half later, Irish police officers on surveillance duty noted a light in a. house approximately four miles from the scene of the explosion. The seven men in the house, including the owner and the applicants, were arrested and detained by the police under. section 30 of the Offences against the State Act 1939 (“the 1939 Act”) As later noted by the High Court (see paragraph 15 below), it was suspected that the bombing had been carried out by the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) The applicants' trial in the Special Criminal Court took place on 19 April 1991. name: Yeşim Taciroğlu
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25324/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The court relied on “the serious nature of the offences with which the applicant had been charged, the state of evidence, the content of the case file, and the duration of the detention” when further detaining the applicant. The applicant was convicted of the offence as charged and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 1 April 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction, and remitted the case back to the Istanbul State Security Court. The case is still pending. May 2000, the court also noted that the case was due to be decided soon. The court stated that the applicant's conviction was likely to be quashed soon. In November 2003 the court noted that it was expected to be heard soon. On 17 December 2003, the applicant was found guilty of the charges against him. In August 2003, he was sentenced to a life sentence in prison.

name: Ayhan Çakmak
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants complained about the length of compensation proceedings. The applicants were represented by Mr O.K. Cengiz, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court against the Ege University Medical Department (hereinafter “the defendant”) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice. The court found that there was no indication of any negligence on the part of the Medical Department in the treatment given to C.Ç. The applicants appealed against the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision of the Supreme Administrative Court was served on the applicants on 3 February 1999. The case file was sent to the Court of Appeal on 5 September 1997. The appeal was dismissed on 14 October 1998. The application was dismissed again on 28 October 1998, without holding a hearing. The Appeal Court ruled that the Administrative Court. was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants in the exercise of their duties.

The applicants were represented by Mr O.K. Cengiz, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court declared the application admissible on 23 September 2003. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court against the Ege University Medical Department (hereinafter ‘the defendant’) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice. The court dismissed the applicants' claim for compensation because the court was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties. The applicants appealed against the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision of the Supreme Administrative Court was served on the applicants on 3 February 1999. The case originated in an application (no. 53672/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' daughter, C.Ç., was severely injured in an accident in 1987. Her hair was burned and part of her scalp was damaged. She underwent surgery to repair the damage to her scalp in 1992. Following the operation, the applicants's daughter caught an infection. The Court found in favour of the applicants and ruled that they should be compensated for the loss they suffered as a result of medical malpractice. The decision was later overturned on appeal. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court against the Ege University Medical Department (hereinafter ‘the defendant’) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice. The court found that there was no indication of any negligence on the part of the Medical Department in the treatment given to C.Ç. The applicants appealed against the judgment of the first-instance court. On 3 February 1999 the decision of the Supreme Administrative Court was served on the applicants. The decision was that the Administrative Court. was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties. The application was dismissed.

It originated in an application (no. 16969/90) against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 May 1990 by an Irish citizen, Mr Joseph Keegan. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 8 and/or 14. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 November 1993. The Registrar consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the procedure (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). The Court heard addresses by Sir Basil Hall, Ms Browne and Mr Gleeson as well as replies to questions put by several of its members. The proceedings before the Circuit Court were adjourned until at least January 6, 1994. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the adoption proceedings were thrown out. The application was brought by the Government on behalf of the Applicant. The applicant applied to be appointed guardian under section 6A, sub-section 1, of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964. Pursuant to the Adoption Act 1952, an adoption order cannot be made, inter alia, without the consent of the child’s mother and the child's guardian. While a married man is a guardian of his children, an unmarried man is not unless so appointed by the court (see paragraphs 25 and 26 below). On 29 May 1989 the Circuit Court appointed the applicant guardian and awarded him custody. The High Court found in July 1989 that the applicant was a fit person to beappointed guardian and that there were no circumstances involving the child which required that the father's rights be denied. Chief Justice Finlay ruled that the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act. He considered that the Act only gave the natural father a right to apply to be guardian. It did not equate his position with that of a married father. He concluded that: “... regard should not be had to the objective of satisfying the wishes and desires of the father to be involved in the guardianship of a child’’ The extent and character of the rights which accrue arising from the relationship of a father to a child to whose mother he is not married must vary very greatly indeed, depending on the circumstances. High Court heard that the child would suffer short-term trauma if moved to the applicant’s custody. Matter was then referred back to the High Court for the case to be decided in light of this interpretation. In his judgment of 9 February 1990 Mr Justice Barron recalled that the applicant wished bona fide to have custody of his daughter and that he felt the existence of an emotional bond. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living and would be likely to remain at school longer. However, he considered that differences springing solely from socio-economic causes should not be taken into account where one of the claimants is a natural parent. An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child. In these circumstances, the welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. Accordingly the application for relief must be refused.“The father's wish and desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account.” The judge said he could not hold that the quality of welfare likely to be achieved with the prospective adopters would not be to an important extent better than that likely tobe achieved by custody with the father. The case was returned to the High Court for reconsideration.

The applicants alleged in particular that they had been subjected to torture during their detention in police custody and that ensuing criminal proceedings against the police officers involved had been ineffective. On 22 May and 24 June 2009 respectively the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the cases at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was brought before the Istanbul Public Prosecutor on 6 March 1997. She denied all accusations against her and mentioned the ill-treatment she had been subjected to. An investigation concerning eight police officers on duty at the time was initiated. On an unspecified date the applicant intervened in the criminal proceedings as a civil party. On 2 December 2002 the Istanbul Assize Court acquitted five of the police officers for lack of evidence. The remaining four officers were sentenced to eleven months and twenty days' imprisonment and disbarred from public service. The applicant appealed. On 1 April 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld the acquittal decision regarding the police officer who had been identified by the applicant during the proceedings. The applicants were born in 1965 and 1974 respectively and live in Istanbul. The applicants were taken into police custody at the Istanbul Security Headquarters on 25 November 1997. They were held until 2 December 1997 and questioned regarding their alleged involvement in a terrorist organisation. Both applicants, who were interviewed by the Fatih Public Prosecutor on 10 March 1998, mainly said that they had been blindfolded and beaten, that their testicles had been squeezed. On 29 November 2006 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. Police officers claimed that the applicants had shown resistance at the time of their arrest which explained the marks found on their body. The applicants requested that the Forensic Medicine Institute be consulted in order to determine the exact cause of the marks on their bodies. On 20 June 2003, on the basis of the evidence in the case file, the Istanbul Assize Court held that all three complainants had been subjected to ill‑treatment which fell under Article 243 of the Criminal Code. The court found M.C. and S.A. guilty as charged and sentenced them to one year's imprisonment, further prohibiting them from holding public office for a year. The case was remitted to the Istanbul Assize Court, which, on 24 June 2005, decided to discontinue the proceedings in respect of M.C. and S.A. because the prosecution had ultimately become time-barred. The second applicant appealed. On 18 April 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the Istanbulassize Court's judgment with simple reference to the hearings, evidence, the trial court's discretion and the case file in general. The case was adjourned for a. period of three months. In July 2005 the second applicant. appealed against the acquittal. The court took into account the fact that the. second applicant could not identify the perpetrators. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the investigation was insufficient.

name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1638/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the residence prohibition against him violated his right to respect for his private and family life. By a decision of 2 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between June 1999 and January 2000. He was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment, 13 of which were suspended on probation. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten years’ residence prohibition on the applicant. The applicant, assisted by counsel, appealed. He submitted that the residence prohibition violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention as he was a minor who had come to Austria at the age of six, his entire family lived in Austria and he had no relatives in Bulgaria. By decision of 19 July 2000, the applicant served his prison term until 24 May 2002. The applicant was deported to Bulgaria in 2003. He had no relatives and other social contacts in Bulgaria and was still a minor. The residence prohibition did not constitute a disproportionate interference with the applicant’s rights under Article 8, despite his lengthy residence and family ties in Austria. He was arrested on 27 November 2003 and deported on 22 December 2003. The application was dismissed in 2001 by both the Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court. The appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Public Security Authority in 2002. The applicant was ordered to leave Austria on 18 August 2003 and was later arrested and deported to Sofia, Bulgaria. The case was decided by the Austrian Federal Police Authority and the Appeals Court.

name: Allan Jacobsson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. It originated in an application (no. 10842/84) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Commission sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13, 17 and 18. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The Government’s memorial and the applicant’S memorial were received by the registry on 2 and 9 May 1988, respectively. On 6 March 1989 the Secretary to the Commission notified the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. The President directed on 21 February 1989 that the oral proceedings should commence on 24 May 1989 (Rule 38) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government and Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and Mr Tullberg, Mr Petrén and Mr Magnusson for the applicant as well as their replies to its questions. The first building prohibition under section 35 of the 1947 Act covering the applicant’s property was issued by the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen, “the Board’) of the Stockholm County on 21 September 1965. This prohibition has subsequently been prolonged by the Board for one or two years each time, leaving the property unaffected for only a few brief intermediate periods. The last decision was taken on 11 July 1985 and was valid until 11 July 1987. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one (see paragraphs 44-45 below). The application was for a one-family house and a garage on a property in Botkyrka. The applicant appealed to the Board claiming that the building prohibition was not valid. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. In April 1983 the Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. The board rejected the request on 23 March 1984, stating inter alia as follows: “The long duration of the [building] prohibition depends to a large extent on changes in the objectives of the planning procedure which have occurred twice during the time of prohibition” The applicant’s property is situated in an area to be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. On 13 February 1984 the Municipal Council (kommunstyrelsen) adopted an area programme according to which the planning procedure should be given priority. On 11 July 1984 the Board decided to issue a further building prohibition for the area in question. In the decision it was noted that the Municipality planned to carry out certain work during 1984 for the purposes of establishing the necessary plans. The applicant appealed to the Government, which rejected the appeal on 8 November 1984, referring to the on-going planning work. On 20 March 1986 the Municipal Assembly adopted a new area plan covering inter alia the applicant's property. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. The applicant again filed a request for a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision for a period of two years (see paragraphs 45 and 46 below). The application was denied on 10 July 1987. The application for the application to be granted was rejected by the Building Committee on 13 July 1987, and the application was rejected for the second time. The decision was made by the Committee to defer the decision on the application for two years. The building committee then decided to grant the applicant the request for the building permit.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. The applicant bought a property of 2,644 m², Salem 23:1, in the centre of Rönninge in the municipality of Salem, a suburb about 20 kilometres south west of Stockholm. In 1974 the applicant bought the property it was covered by a subdivision plan (avstyckningsplan - see paragraph 31 below) adopted in 1938. The property in Rönninge, Stockholm, was covered by an area plan (områdesplan - see paragraph 26 below), adopted in 1972. It was also covered by a building prohibition pursuant to section 35 of the 1947 Building Act (byggnadslagen, “the 1947 Act“) issued on 26 August 1974 and lasting until 1 September 1976. The Government also claimed that the regulations for non-planned areas (utomplansbestämmelser) applied but the applicant contested this (see paragraph 33 below). On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one. The building prohibition relates to part of the municipality of Botkyrka. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. The Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. On 6 June 1983 the Board decided to prolong the building prohibition for the area in question. In 1984 the Board rejected a request to revoke the right of the newly created municipality of Rönninge to build a house according to a subdivision plan from 1938. The long duration of the [building] prohibition depends to a large extent on changes in the objectives of the planning procedure as a result of the changes of municipal organisation. The applicant's property is situated in an area to be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. On 24 April 1986 the Government quashed the Board’s decision, holding that the Committee's opinion was not a binding decision and that, accordingly, it could not as such be subject to an appeal. On 16 March 1987 the Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, referring to the government's decision. The request to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal was rejected on 1 November 1988. On 10 July 1987 the applicant again filed a request for a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision for a period of two years. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. This plan mentioned the possibility of using the area for single or multi-family house development. According to the Government, this is the last step of the preparatory work in the making of a town plan. The application was rejected on 14 July 1987, and the building permit application was dismissed on 17 July 1987.

The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in İzmir. In 1998 the applicant and his wife bought a flat. In 1999 the applicant’s wife initiated divorce proceedings against the applicant. It was concluded that, given his financial situation, the applicant could not have contributed enough to the purchase of the flat in question to be entitled to claim a share in it. The court further noted that, at the time of purchase, the legal matrimonial regime was the system of separation of property. On 29 December 2005 and 14 April 2006 respectively, the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal and rectification requests. the flat was registered in the wife's name. The appeal was rejected on 29 December 2006 and 14 January 2007 respectively. The applicant appealed again on 29 April 2006 but was unsuccessful. The application was dismissed on 29 March 2007. The couple have since remarried and have a daughter and son-in-law. The family has three children and a step-son. The wife had no memory of the original application. The case was settled out of court and the family appealed again. The Appeal Court rejected the appeal in 2007.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9907/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to give notice to the Government of the complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the convention. In accordance with Article 29 § 3, the Court decided to examine the admissibility and merits of the cases at the same time. The application was brought by Ms Emine Araç (“the applicant”), a Turkish national, on 22 October 2001. Following an appeal by the applicant on points of law, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of 23 September 1999, finding it to have been in accordance with the law and the procedural rules. In view of the juridical and legal arguments on which the first-instance judgment was based, these grounds cannot be said to require the quashing of the impugned judgment, the court found. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the grounds of appeal did not correspond to those enumerated in Article 49 of the Code of Administrative Procedure. The case was decided on an appeal brought by the head of the Turkish Academy of Sciences.

name: Velimir Janosevic
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 September 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Thörnhammar and Ms Kalmerborn. The Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 30 September 2000, and the decision was made by the ECJ on 30 October 2000. It was decided that the application was admissible and the case was dismissed. The applicant challenged the report and requested that further investigative measures be carried out. The additional taxes levied on the applicant, including interest and surcharges, totalled SEK 1,020,300, of which SEK 161,261 were surcharges. The amounts relating to value-added tax and employer's contributions were payable on 5 January 1996 and those relating to income tax on 10 April 1996. The Tax Authority considered that the prerequisites laid down in section 49, subsection 1(2) or (3), of the Tax Collection Act [Uppbördslagen, 1953:272] for granting a stay of execution have been fulfilled. The applicant was registered as being in arrears with value-added tax and employer's contributions and the corresponding tax surcharges and interest imposed as a result of the Tax Authority's decisions. The amounts relating to income tax did not become payable until 10 April 1996. The Tax Authority rejected the applicant's request for a stay of execution, as no security had been furnished. The applicant appealed against those decisions to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm, claiming that he should be exempted from the obligation to provide security. On 21 May 1997 the Administrative Court of Appeal in Stockholm refused him leave to appeal against the County administrative court's judgments. His request for leave to appealed against the appellate court's decisions was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court in 1998. The applicant's tax liability as of 22 March 1996 amounted to SEK 653,144. The only property owned by the applicant was some vehicles, but of insufficient value to cover the debt. The applicant appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) on 18 June 1996. Leave to appeal against the appellate court's decision was refused by the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) on18 September 1996. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of appeal on 18 August 1996. By a decision of 10 June 1996, after rejecting the applicant's request for a further adjournment, the District Court declared the applicant bankrupt. In so doing it had regard to the fact that, under section 103 of the Tax Collection Act, the applicant had been found to be insolvent. The whole debt became statute-barred on 31 December 2001, at the end of the fifth year following the day it became due. On 30 October 1997 the applicant was sentenced by the District Court to ten months' imprisonment for tax fraud (skattebedrägeri) and a bookkeeping offence (bokföringsbrott) The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 16 November 1998. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 4 March 1999. Further proceedings concerning the taxes and tax surcharges concerning the applicant were referred to the County Administrative Court for determination in September 2001. Tax Authority had good reason to make discretionary tax assessments based on the information obtained during the audit. Administrative Court informed the applicant that it did not find a hearing necessary and ordered him to make his final observations in the case in writing. It considered that there had been sufficient reasons to impose the surcharges in question and that no legal basis for remitting them had been shown. In that connection, it dismissed the applicant's argument that the allegedly excessive length of the proceedings constituted by itself a reason to remit the tax surcharges. The applicant has appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, where the dispute is at present pending. The case is being heard in Stockholm.

train_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 (“the 2000 Act”) on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the cases (Rule 59 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The first applicant gave evidence on oath in the course of the hearing. Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. Each of the applicants was interviewed on twelve occasions in the following five days. Judge Philpott noted that the relevant forensic evidence was central to the investigation and that the investigation was being carried out diligently and expeditiously. The second applicant was arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Masserene Barracks, Antrim, on 7 March 2009. He was detained at Antrim Police Station on the same day. The third applicant’s continued detention until 5.52 a.m. on 28 March 2009, was granted by the Court of Appeal. The second applicant was interviewed on twelve occasions in the following five days. Neither the interviews nor the results of the forensic tests provided any evidence linking the second applicant to the murders of the two soldiers. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of Judge Philpott’s decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. The High Court of Northern Ireland heard the applications on 25 March 2009. The review of the lawfulness of the detention had to embrace an examination of the basis of the arrest, otherwise a person could be detained under the 2000 Act for up to twenty-eight days without there having been any judicial review. The High Court of Northern Ireland found no basis for the submission that Schedule 8 was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. The court accepted, however, that a review of the lawfulness of the arrest need not involve a detailed analysis of the decision to arrest and should reflect the constraints that necessarily apply in many arrests for terrorist offences. ott had been wrong to disavow any review of the lawfulness of the applicants’ arrest and, as a consequence, her decision to grant extensions had to be quashed. The High Court found that, although the judge had not focused directly on whether the applicants had toBe detained rather than released pending the outcome of the remaining forensic examinations, she had not failed to have regard to the need for detention. The High Court of Northern Ireland ruled that Article 5 required that a detained person be charged well before the expiry of the twenty‑eight day period contemplated in the 2000 Act. The court ruled that there were a range of tools available to the court to preserve to the necessary extent an adversarial procedure and equality of arms. The High Court also found that there was no authority which supported the applicants’ contention that Article 3 required that the detainee be charged before the end of the period contemplated by the Terrorism Act 2000 (‘the Act’) The court decided that the detention of a suspect without charge for more than four days was not compatible with the Applicant’s rights under Article 5(1)(c), 5(2) and 5(3) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009. The first and third applicants were not subsequently charged with any offence related to the murder of the police officer. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury. On 20 January 2012 he was acquitted on all counts of the indictment. The High Court refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The applications did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The applicants’ release from detention was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 14 November 2011.

The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 (“the 2000 Act”) on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the cases (Rule 59 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The first applicant gave evidence on oath in the course of the hearing. Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. The second applicant was arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Masserene Barracks, Antrim, on 7 March 2009. On 15 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court for a warrant extending the second applicant’s detention as the results of a number of forensic tests were pending. On 22 March 2009 a police superintendent gave evidence on oath as to the necessity of the extensions. Her Honour Judge Philpott QC delivered a written judgment in respect of the first applicant and an ex tempore decision inrespect of the third applicant. On 21 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court under paragraph 36 of Schedule 8 to the 2000 Act for a seven-day extension to the period specified in the warrant for further detention. The extension was sought as the results of further forensic tests which had been sent for analysis to a laboratory in Great Britain were expected to become available within the following seven days. Judge Philpott granted the application, authorising the second applicant’s continued detention until 7.20 on 28 March 2009. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of the decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. They submitted that Judge Phil pott had been wrong to conclude that a court was precluded from investigating the lawfulness of the arrest. The High Court of Northern Ireland found no basis for the submission that Schedule 8 was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. The court held that, although there was no doubt that the “competent legal authority” referred to in Article 5 § 1 (c) was the magistrate in the United Kingdom, the Court had made it clear that the function of “a judge or other officer” for the purposes of Article 5 could be carried out by an officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The Court also ruled that, as paragraph 32 of Schedule 8 to the 2000 Act provided that there must be reasonable grounds for believing that the further detention of a person was necessary, it therefore contained a requirement of proportionality. The High Court of Northern Ireland ruled that the provisions of the Terrorism Act 2000 were compatible with the applicant’s rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. The court also ruled that there was no authority which supported the applicants’ contention that Article 5 required that a detained person be charged well before the expiry of the twenty‑eight day period contemplated in the 2000 Act. The High Court concluded that it was satisfied that the decision given on 24 February 2011 involved the following points of law of general public importance: Whether the absence of a power to allow for conditional release on bail rendered the scheme for extending detention set out in the Act invalid. If Articles 5(1)(c) and 5(3) of the Convention cannot be interpreted in such a way as to permit the detention of a suspect without charge for any period specified by Parliament, subject only to the requirement of periodic judicial approval. The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009. The first and third applicants were not subsequently charged with any offence related to the murder of the police officer. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. The High Court refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury. On 20 January 2012 he was acquitted on all counts of the indictment. The applicants’ release from detention was confirmed on 26 March 2009 and they were released from detention without charge. The application for bail was refused by the High Court on the ground that there was a real risk of reoffending on account of suspected involvement with a dissident republican organisation.

name: Michael Becker
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Europe, Integration and Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 28 September 2009. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 22 April 2008 and ruled in favour of the applicant on 28 November 2008. The decision was published in full on 24 December 2008. The applicant appealed and argued that the DAA should have obtained the report of a technical expert on the functioning of the breathlyser. The Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The applicant was ordered to follow driver improvement training before his driving licence would be returned. The Regional Governor concluded that refusing to undergo a breathalyser test was as serious as driving under the influence of alcohol because it prevented the authorities from verifying whether a person was actually drunk. The additional measure imposed on the applicant was therefore justified in order to improve his attitude to road traffic. The DAA ordered that an appeal had no suspensive effect because it was necessary to avoid the risk that a person lacking trustworthiness for road traffic might drive. On 20 April 2001 the DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) and imposed a fine for refusal to take the breathalyser test. The applicant appealed. On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Since no decision had been taken within the prescribed time limit of 15 months after the lodging of the appeal, the fine imposed by the D AA had expired ipso iure. The Administrative Court found that an oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. It found that on the basis of the evidence before them the authorities had arrived at the conclusion that the applicant had refused to undergo the breathalyzer test.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He was sentenced to a total of fifteen years' imprisonment. A confiscation order was imposed on him on 24 September 1998 in the sum of 50,169.18 pounds sterling (GBP) The applicant's renewed application to appeal against conviction was refused by the Court of Appeal on 17 October 2000. He appealed against his conviction in November 1999, but was unsuccessful. The appeal was refused in October 2000, and he was not allowed to appeal again until December 2000. The applicant appealed against the conviction in October 1998, but the appeal was rejected in November 2000.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3042/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Nihat Konak (‘the applicant’) was taken into police custody on suspicion of being a member of the TKP/ML-TIKKO (Communist Party of Turkey//Marxist‑Leninist Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army), an illegal organisation. During the questioning, he was not provided with a lawyer. The applicant, who was born in 1964, is currently serving his prison sentence in the Tekirdağ Prison. The applicant was charged with being a leader of an armed organisation. He was released pending trial. On 26 October 2001 the first-instance court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to eighteen years and nine months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the conviction for lack of reasoning on 14 February 2002. The court concluded that the applicant had acted as district leader of the organisation in Istanbul. It further found it established that he had taken part in a number of organisation’s activities such as hanging illegal banners, throwing Molotov cocktails and participating in illegal demonstrations. It noted that, according to the confrontation and identification records, certain of his co-accused, namely M.Ş., L.L. and T.Ö, had identified him as the district leader.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 27 November 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained on 18 March 1991. On 3 June 1991 he was brought before the Strasbourg Criminal Court. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. He later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out of the Court of Cassation's list on 3 February 1992. On 4 September 1994 the applicant completed his prison sentence. However, he remained in custody pursuant to the order requiring him to serve two years’ imprisonment in default of payment of the customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. In a judgment of 28 November 1994 the Colmar Court of Court of Appeal upheld the Criminal Court's judgment in its entirety. The Court of Appeal upheld the Criminal Court's order for imprisonment in default on the ground of anticipatory default. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. The applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. He alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which sets out the non bis in idem rule, and of Article 6 of the Convention. He relied in particular on the Court's judgment in Jamil v France (judgment of 8 June 1995, Series A no. 317-B), in which imprisonment indefault was found to constitute a “penalty” for the purposes of the European Convention. Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. After being ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In a judgment of 16 September 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons. Code, which required sentences to run concurrently, had not been infringed by the trial court and could not enable a prison sentence and term of imprisonment in Default to be served concurrently. The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey.

name: Tibet Menteş
train_texts: The case was brought by a group of men who live in the town of Mersin in Turkey. The group alleges that they were denied the right to work overtime. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the men. The court's decision was made under Article 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which prohibits the use of public money for private gain. The judge ruled that the men were entitled to work over the weekend in order to make up for the unpaid time they had spent waiting for the case to be heard. The decision was appealed to the European Union's Court of Justice, which decided the case could not proceed. Workers at the company in question had worked overtime of 139.5 hours in months which had thirty-one calendar days and 135 hours in the remaining months. In the four months of the summer period they worked continuously for twenty-four hours and rested the next twenty-24 hours. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-three hours a day, seven days a week. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were not subject to wage deductions. The court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims. The court rejected claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused annual leave. The employer had been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. On the basis of his examination of the company’s timekeeping records, the expert calculated the number of hours worked as overtime in respect of each applicant, deducting three hours of rest per each day worked. The applicants raised a number of objections to the expert report. They stated that the timekeeping. records used for the calculation did not reflect the actual hours worked. In that regard, the applicants submitted that they had worked for more hours than established by the expert. The applicants were awarded overtime pay in part by the İzmir Labour Court in 2005. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds. It found that the Labour Court had not taken into account any time that could have been used for rest periods and that therefore the calculation of overtime could not be deemed accurate. It also stated that the overtime calculation should be based on weekly working hours rather than the monthly working time used in the expert report. The applicant's employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law that a person could not work more than fourteen hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift should be applied to facts of the dispute. The Court of Cassation’s Civil Division, in workplaces where there are 24-hour shifts, says a person can only work for 14 hours a day. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours per day was physically impossible. As a result of that interpretation, some of the applicants’ claims were dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report.

The case was brought by five members of a trade union. They claimed they were denied the right to work overtime. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. A decision was made in favor of the claim, but the issue is still pending. The decision will be heard again on November 5, 2015, and the case will be re-examined by the ECHR if necessary. The application was made under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits employers from refusing to pay overtime wages to employees. The ECHR says that this rule applies to employees of all trade unions, not just those that have a contract with the union. Workers claimed compensation for overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were to be paid at one and a half times the regular hourly rate. The applicants claimed for overtime pay, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave that they had not taken. The İzmir Labour Court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report. Employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. Employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. Expert also noted that the applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. The applicants raised no objections to the expert’s conclusion on the dismissal of their claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused annually leave. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: “It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24. hours; and in the winter months they worked for24 hours and then rested for 48 hours”. The employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law that a person could not work more than fourteen hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift should be applied to the facts of the dispute. However, as determined by the well-established case- law of the Grand Chamber of Grand Chamber, the case was quashed on the grounds that the applicants had had a minimum of three hours for rest. The applicants had worked continuously for twenty-four hours. The judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible. The applicants appealed against the decision. On 18 March 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision. Some of the applicants’ claims were dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. The decision was made without responding to the applicants' objections. The application was dismissed on 28 December 2009. The case was heard by the Turkish Court of Labour and the case was adjourned until 9 February 2010.

The case was brought by a group of people who claim they were wrongly denied a right to work overtime. The case was decided by the European Court of Human Rights. The European Court ruled that the workers' claims had been denied. The decision was made under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) which prohibits employers from refusing to pay overtime. This applies to the cases brought against the members of the EUHRC. The court also ruled that there had been a breach of Article 4 of the ECHR, which forbids employers from denying workers overtime pay. The ECHR ruled that this was a violation of the ECHR's right to pay workers overtime, and that they should be compensated for their time. Workers at the company in question had worked overtime of 139.5 hours in months which had thirty-one calendar days and 135 hours in the remaining months. They claimed compensation for the overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The Turkish Labour Court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave. The applicant's employer had previously been cautioned by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. The expert determined that the employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The applicants raised no objections to the expert’s conclusion on the dismissal of their claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused annual leave. The applicant said the deduction of three hours of rest per day was not based on fact but was an assumption by the expert. The employer argued that the timekeeping documents used for the calculation did not reflect the actual hours worked as they were unofficial copies kept by the employer. The applicants worked 24 hours in a 24-hour shift. They were awarded overtime. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: “It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24. hours; and in the winter months they worked for 25 hours and then rested for 48 hours.” The case was settled in favour of the applicants in part. The employer appealed and the case was again heard by the İzmir Labour Court. The applicants were awarded compensation for overtime. The applicants had worked continuously for twenty-four hours. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked for 24 hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. The Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. The application was dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. The case is still pending.
eval_texts: The case was brought by a group of five people who claimed they had been denied the right to work overtime. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled that the claim had been made in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights. The ECHR ruled in favour of the group's claim that they had not been properly compensated for the time they had spent on the case. The ECHR also decided that the case did not meet the legal requirements for a claim to be heard in court under Article 1 of the EU Human Rights Act of 1998. The decision by the ECHR was appealed and the case was returned to the ECHR. Workers claimed compensation for overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. Section 22 of the collective labour agreement provided that such periods would be counted as working time and that they could not be subject to wage deductions. The court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave. It ruled that the claims were valid. The applicants’ employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. On the basis of his examination of the company’s timekeeping records, the expert calculated the number of hours worked as overtime in respect of each applicant, deducting three hours of rest per each day worked. The employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The expert also noted that the applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company. Both parties appealed to the Court of Cassation. The Court found that the Labour Court had not taken into account any time that could have been used for rest periods. It also stated that the overtime calculation should be based on weekly working hours rather than the monthly working time used in the expert report. On 26 May 2008 the İzmir Labour Court awarded the applicants compensation for overtime as determined in the revised expert report, but the judgment was quashed on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case. The case was settled out of court in a settlement between the employer and the applicants, and the employer was compensated for unpaid overtime. An expert report calculated the applicants’ daily working time as fourteen hours. The calculation in the new report led to no overtime being found for the weeks in which the applicants had worked three days as the working time was less than the legal limit of forty-five hours. On 28 December 2009 the İzmir Labour Court rendered a final judgment in the applicants' case, based on the expert report of 21 July 2009. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. On 18 March 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the  decision.

name: Guy Laumont
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained, in particular, that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. He had been kept in custody even though the order extending his detention had expired. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 31 August 2000. On 27 October 2000 the Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled in favour of the Government. A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. The judge issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. The applicant was held for four months, twice extended for a further four months. On 30 September 1996 the investigating judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit) and made a partial discharge order. In accordance with Article 181 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, he ordered that the file be transferred to the public prosecutor's office at the Versailles Court of Appeal. The applicant was detained under the transfer order of 30 September 1996 and the Versailles Court of Appeal’s judgment of 27 November 1996. On 9 April 1997 the applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily. In a judgment of 19 August 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of [the applicant], who was under investigation for offences including armed robbery. On expiry of its validity a year later the investigating judge extended the detention three times for four months, the final extension taking effect on 19 September 1996. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. He was tried at the Versailles Assize Court, which sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. In a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims the applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken.

On 2 July 1977, within the prescribed period of ten days from service of the judgment, the applicant filed a memorial containing a “final“ statement (section189 para. 3 of the 1889 Act) of his grounds of appeal. The Chief Military Prosecutor (auditeur en chef) appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. He claimed that the Divisional Court had erred in not declining jurisdiction to hear the case on the merits. He also argued that the refusal to order a supplementary enquiry had prejudiced the defence on decisive points. The Court dismissed the appeal on 21 October 1977, but could have quashed it if the sole ground for the quashing had been misapplication of the law. The President requested a judge whom he had designated from amongst his colleagues to draft a report containing a reasoned proposal. This document was circulated, together with the papers in the case, amongst the other members. The 1889 Act was repealed by the Federal Military Criminal Procedure Act of 23 March 1979 (“the 1979 Act’) The existing system was maintained for proceedings before the Divisional Courts, and was extended to the Courts of Appeal which were set up by the same statute. As regards the Military Court of Cassation, the 1979 Act provides that “There shall be no oral hearings“ (section 189 para. 1). The Act did, however, make two innovations: in future, the Court was to deliver judgment in open court and could in no circumstances itself rule on the merits of the case. The operative provisions of the judgment were immediately served on Mr. Sutter in writing. The Sutter judgment of 21 October 1977 appeared in 1983 in volume 9 (covering the years 1973 to 1979) of the judgments of the Military Court of Cassation, under the number 136. Anyone who can establish an interest may consult or obtain a copy of the full text on application to the Chief Military Prosecutor or the military court registries. If judgments contain features that are novel or of importance for the interpretation of the law, they are subsequently published in printed form. The report contains two separate opinions, one being dissenting. In its report of 10 October 1981, the Commission expressed the opinion by ten votes to eight that there had been no violation of Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. Switzerland's government invited the Court “to hold that Switzerland has not violated Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention’. On 21 March 1983, the hearings on 21 March heard that Switzerland had violated the Convention. The U.S. government asked the Court to rule that the Swiss government had not violated the treaty. The court found in Switzerland's favour in March 1983. The Swiss government has asked the court to rule in its favour again in December 2014. The decision is expected to be announced in February 2015. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43425/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52: 1 of the Rules of Court) "Any little cretin, whether he wears a gown or not, should vent his need to intimidate others by making allusions to legal responsibility [for their acts] on his mistress, if he has one, or on his dog, but not on me," he writes. "I am not going to be afraid of any such clown who wants to intimidate me, but the truth is that my request of 18 August 1994 was addressed to the court, not to some fool," he adds. The court found that on 15 November 1994 the applicant had sent a letter to the President of the Regional Court in which he referred to all judges of the Penitentiary Division as ‘irresponsible clowns’ The court further observed that the applicant, as a citizen, had a constitutional right to criticise the State authorities. However, the impugned letter had largely exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism and was directly aimed at lowering the court in the public. It had to be understood that the. applicant had insulted the court as the State authority, and the unidentified judge could be regarded as a symbol. of that court. The court referred to the grounds of appeal in which it had been argued that the conviction had been in flagrant breach of Article 237 of the Criminal Code in that the applicant's acts, in the light of his submissions as to his motives, did not amount to a punishable criminal offence. The applicant had a long criminal record, even though he had been assessed positively by the penitentiary services. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal as unfounded. No new arguments had been submitted to the Supreme Court to show that there had been any procedural shortcomings in the proceedings. The Supreme Court went on to state that the applicant's abusive letter, referred to and quoted by the Regional Court, had clearly exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism. The appeal was dismissed as not being in compliance with the requirements laid down by the applicable procedural provisions. But the court emphasised, it was worth noting that the. Regional Court in its judgment had examined all complaints submitted in the appeal against the first-instance. judgment, including those concerning the assessment of evidence and the factual findings of the first.instance court.

name: Atalay Dede
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32981/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the proceedings against them. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59) The Court declared the application admissible on 17 October 2000 and the case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The case was settled on 1 November 2001 and the application was dismissed on 1 December 2001. The decision of the European Court of Human rights was upheld. The Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) was accused of being an illegal organisation. The applicants were all released pending trial by the Ankara Martial Law Court. They were convicted in 1989 and sentenced to terms of imprisonment. The cases were appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) It quashed the convictions of Mr Dede and Mr Dirik and referred the cases to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. The applications have been dismissed by the Supreme Court of Justice (Aksaray)

name: Ahmet Öngün
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15737/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Izmir. He was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of involvement in various acts of arson with a view to protesting against the arrest of Abdullah Öcalan, the former leader of the PKK. Two men were accused of setting fire to a car on 19 February 1999 and two buildings on 13 and 14 March 1999. The applicant retracted his earlier submissions, claiming that he had made them under duress. He further contested the verbatim records of the reconstruction of events and other evidence which incriminated him. On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges sitting on the bench of the State Security Courts were replaced by civilian judges. The first-instance court held its first hearing, in the presence of the applicant and his lawyer, on 11 May 1999. It heard evidence from the accused and three complainants, Mr A.Ş., Mr I.Ö and Mr H.K. The applicant was convicted of arson and sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison. The Court of Cassation quashed the conviction on the grounds that he should have been tried under Article 168 of the Criminal Code. In his petition, he submitted that, apart from evidence obtained under duress at the pre-trial stage, there was no evidence to demonstrate that he had taken part in these acts. He further complained that there was nothing to indicate that he was part of an illegal organisation and that therefore Article 168 should not have been applied to him. By letter dated 16 June 2008 the applicant’s representative informed the Court that the applicant was no longer in jail.

name: Philippe Bidart
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant is the former head of the Basque separatist organisation Iparretarrak. After his detention in 1988, he was convicted several times. In 2007 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 14 February 2007 to 14 February 2014, ordering to follow a seven-year programme of assistance and supervision. The Government pointed out that the applicant was the first person sentenced to life imprisonment for offences linked to terrorism ever to have been released on licence. The case has been adjourned until 15 February 2015. The applicant took part in a peaceful demonstration outside Agen Prison in support of Basque detainees being held there. The media reported on that demonstration. The Paris Sentence Enforcement Court delivered a judgment on 14 May 2008 imposing additional special obligations on the applicant. The latter judgment was quashed by judgment of the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation on 10 June 2009. On 18 February 2010 the Public Prosecutor’s Office requested that the sentence enforcement judge of the Regional Court of Paris add both the aforementioned obligations. The judge added the following special obligations: exercising an occupation or following vocational education or training; residing in Béziers; continuing, in accordance with his means, to pay into the Guarantee Fund for the compensation of victims of terrorism. Philippe Bidart was jailed in 2007 for promoting Basque separatism and supporting detainees convicted of or charged with terrorist acts. In 2010 he was told he could not discuss his convictions in public. He appealed and the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant. The Court of Appeal ruled that the obligation in question “merely prohibited commenting on or condoning the offences committed” and “that the obligation was not a disproportionate measure in the light of the need to protect public order, nor does it prevent Philippe Bidart from expressing his political convictions’. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the judgment was properly applied.

The applicant is the former head of the Basque separatist organisation Iparretarrak. After his detention in 1988, he was convicted several times: on 4 March 1991 he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment for criminal association with a view to preparing a terrorist offence. In February 2007 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 14 February 2007 to 14 February 2014. The Government pointed out that the applicant was the first person sentenced to life imprisonment for offences linked to terrorism ever to have been released on licence. On 24 December 2007 the applicant took part in a peaceful demonstration outside Agen Prison in support of Basque detainees being held there. The media reported on that demonstration. The Paris Sentence Enforcement Court delivered a judgment on 14 May 2008 imposing additional special obligations on the applicant. That judgment was upheld by judgment of the Paris Court of Appeal on 2 October 2008. However, the latter judgment was quashed on 10 June 2009, on the grounds that the sentence enforcement court did not have jurisdiction to modify the obligations for release on licence. On 18 February 2010 the Public Prosecutor’s Office requested that the. sentence enforcement judge of the Regional Court of Paris add both the aforementioned obligations. Philippe Bidart was convicted of murder and sexual assault in 2007. He was told he could not discuss his conviction in public or promote Basque separatism. His appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the obligation was not a disproportionate measure in the light of the need to protect public order. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant. The application was heard at the Paris Court of Appeal in August 2010. The applicant's appeal was heard again at the Court of Appeals in March 2011. The appeal was rejected on the basis that the judge had not properly applied Article 132-45 (16) of the Penal Code, as well as other points.
