train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41355/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. name: January Jagiełło
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8934/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was lodged by a Polish national, Mr January Jagiełło (‘the applicant’), on 2 February 2005. The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in Warszawa. He is a taxi driver by profession. On 4 February 1974 he had a car accident in Bulgaria. On 28 November 1995 he was involved in another car crash in Warsaw. The applicant filed a complaint with the Warsaw Regional Court under the 2004 Act alleging that the proceedings concerning the 1974 accident had been unreasonably lengthy. The applicant was granted PLN 4,000 [EUR 1,200] in compensation. On 5 September 2007, having examined the applicant’s complaint on the merits, the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint. The proceedings in respect of the 1995 accident are still pending. On 19 June 2008 the Warsaw court of Appeal refused to entertain the applicant's complaint lodged on 6 May 2008 on the ground that the statutory period of twelve months had not lapsed since the date of the previous complaint.

name: Linda Grant
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60 as was the case for other women. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. By a decision of 19 May 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant applied for a State pension at the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Adjudication Officer issued on 31 October 1997. He stated that she had applied “too early’, and was only entitled to a pension from 65. At this time she claimed that she was no longer able to work due to a spinal collapse fracture of osteoporotic origin. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Birmingham Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 12 March 1998, which dismissed it on the basis of established case-law. Her case was adjourned to await the House of Lords judgment in Bellinger v. Bellinger. In that case the claimant sought a declaration of validity in respect of a marriage contracted following gender reassignment surgery. Government refused to make any ex gratia payment of a sum representing her lost State pension. House of Lords disapproved of attempts to seek recognition even in the clearest cases. Parliament ([2003] WLR 1174). Further, the applicant was advised by her legal representative that the prospects of persuading the Court of Appeal to depart from the Bellinger judgment were nil. If proceedings were continued, she would further risk punitive costs orders. The applicant consented to a court order dismissing her appeal with no order as to costs. She was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate following her application under the Genderrecognition Act 2004.

The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60 as was the case for other women. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant applied for a State pension at the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Adjudication Officer issued on 31 October 1997. He stated that she had applied ‘too early’ and was only entitled to a pension from 65. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Birmingham Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 12 March 1998. At this time she claimed that she was no longer able to work due to a spinal collapse fracture of osteoporotic origin. Her case was adjourned to await the House of Lords judgment in Bellinger v Bellinger. In that case the claimant, a transsexual, sought a declaration of validity in respect of a marriage contracted following gender reassignment surgery. By a decision of 10 April 2003, their Lordships found the Government’s continuing failure to legislate to be a breach of Articles 8 and 12. The applicant was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate following her application under the Gender Recognitions Act 2004. The applicant was advised by her legal representative that the prospects of persuading the Court of Appeal to depart from the Bellinger judgment were nil. If proceedings were continued, she would further risk punitive costs orders. Accordingly, the applicant consented to a court order dismissing her appeal with no order as to costs. The Government further refused to make any ex gratia payment of a sum representing her lost State pension. On 26 April 2005 the applicant was given a Genderrecognition Certificate. The application had been made under theGender Recognition Act 2004 which had come into force on 1 July 2004.

name: Adele Ursula Price
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33394/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 September 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The applicant claims she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She also alleges that the emergency buttons and light switches were out of her reach, and that she was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. The applicant complained of feeling cold, headache and queasy (no food since admission – offered but refused) The doctor's note of his examination of the applicant at 12.35 a.m. states: “Patient complained of Feeling cold, Headache and Queasy” The applicant's. case had been heard during the afternoon of 20 January 1995, it was not possible to take her to prison until the next day. The applicant slept until 7 a.m., when she was moved to another cell and offered food and drink, which she refused. She was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. The applicant was examined by Dr Kidd, whose notes stated: “New reception. Thalidomide victim with numerous deformities including absent arms upper/lower with dislocating L shoulder and no use in R upper limb. Both lower limbs are absent with small feet.” A “continuous medical record” on the applicant was kept during her detention. The first entry, dated 21 January 1995, stated: “I asked duty Governor, Mr Ellis, to give permission for a battery charger for Adele's wheelchair to be brought in if we could arrange it. He agreed to this and whilst here we pointed out the numerous problems staff may encounter with this inmate i.e. (1) Needs lifting in and out of bed and she says this is usually done by one person standing behind her with arms around her midriff then lifting her either onto the bed or onto her wheelchair. Because of recurrent urinary infections she should take two litres of fluid daily but usually has juice and doesn't like water, therefore will probably reduce her fluid intake. The applicant claimed that a female nurse who was assisting her onto the toilet removed her bedclothes in the presence of two male prison nursing officers, thereby exposing her, naked from the chest down, to the male officers. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. Prior to her release, on 23 January 1995, the applicant was examined by Dr Kidd who found she needed catheterising due to urine retention. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve half the sentence imposed, namely, three and a half days. There is a need for us to separate Adele's little whims from her genuine problems. The applicant claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged. Counsel advised that, in the light of this case-law and the difficulties of proof which she faced, the applicant had a limited prospect of success in her claim and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling.

She slept until 7 a.m., when she was moved to another cell and offered food and drink, which she refused. On arrival at the prison the applicant completed a medical questionnaire. She stated that she had health worries but that they were ‘under control – takes it as it comes’ A ‘continuous medical record’ on the applicant was kept during her detention. They pointed out that prior to her release the applicant made a complaint to the prison governor concerning the lack of adequate facilities. It is unclear from the Government's submissions whether Senior Officer Tingle and Officer Bowman were nursing staff or whether they were prison officers without nursing qualifications. The applicant further claimed that later that evening, a female nurse who was assisting her onto the toilet removed her bedclothes in the presence of two male prison nursing officers, thereby exposing her, naked from the chest down, to the male officers. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve half the sentence imposed, namely, three and a half days. She claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. Said that Gv. Ellis had said that she could sleep on a chair and have her cell door open all night. When asked if she had any specific medical complaints – she only asked for a bath and to be catheterised. via catheter before leaving. Given that she is due for release today she said her Governor's application was immaterial. ...” The applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May 1996. In the light of this case-law and the difficulties of proof which she faced, the applicant had a limited prospect of success in her claim.

train_texts: The case of Luedicke, Belkacem and Koç was referred to the Court by the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany and the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was lodged on 1 October 1977, the request on 10 October. Their purpose is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 3 (e) and 14 (art. 6-3-e, art. 14) of the Convention. The President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. On 21 November, Mr. Balladore Pallieri, acting in pursuance of Rule 24 para. 4, granted himself exemption from sitting on the case. The Government filed their memorial on 30 January 1978. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on 17 April that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply. On 8 May, he communicated to the Registrar a note containing ‘the applicants’ observations on the question of the application of Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention’ and Mr. Koç’s observations on his case. In accordance with Rule 21 paras. 3 (b) and 5, Mr Wiarda, the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber and assumed the office of President. Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The Court rules in favour of the applicants and the Commission. The application has now been thrown out of the European Court of Human Rights. Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings, according to Article 464 (a) para. 1, first sentence, of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with the foreign language (section 185 para. 2 of the Constitution of the Courts Act). Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence in 1972. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He appealed against the decision, saying it was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. The case was referred to the Bielefeld Regional Court, which upheld the original decision. Mr. Luingicke is a citizen of the United Kingdom and was, at the time of his application to the Commission, a member of the British Forces stationed in the Federal Republic of Germany. Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany where he followed various occupations. In December 1973, he was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. He was found guilty and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. On 4 May 1973, the applicant paid the Costs of the Proceedings, including The Interpretation Costs of Mr. Mohammed Belkaciem v. feld District Court which dismissed the appeal on 31 August 1972. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted him of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and to a fine of DM 500. Mr. Belkacem filed an “immediate appeal’ against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. He submitted that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. On 13 June 1974, the Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal. The Regional Court reasoned that, since no assessment of costs had yet been made, there had been no decision capable of being challenged on appeal. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. On 6 December 1973, the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court (Schwurgericht beim Landgericht at Aachen) convicted Mr. Koç of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commuted. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), in a fully reasoned decision delivered on 5 June 1975, set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. The intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. A fair trial is guaranteed in this respect insofar as the accused must be assisted by the interpreter he needs. But it certainly does not mean that even a convicted person may not have the costs of interpretation awarded against him. According to the payment vouchers (Kassenanweisungen), the fees paid to the interpreter amounted to DM 311.50 for the hearing on 4 December 1973. The applicant was not served with a notice to pay the costs for which he was liable, including the interpretation costs, since it was noted that he had a wife and four children to support, that his income was modest and that there was thus no prospect of recovering the costs. It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. Nor does the consideration that a foreigner should not receive worse treatment in the matter of costs than a national, dictate the conclusion that permanent exemption from costs is necessarily implied. The Commission declared Mr. Luedicke’s application admissible on 11 March 1976 and the applications of Mr. Belkacem and Mr. Koç on 4 October following. In its report of 18 May 1977, the Commission expressed the opinion that the decisions concerning the interpreter's costs in the applicants’ cases were in breach of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The Commission declared by twelve votes to one, that it was not necessary to pursue its examination of the case under Article 14. The report contains one separate opinion. The Government requested that the Court strike the case out of its list insofar as the applicant Koç was concerned.

name: Christina Riepl
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37040/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Austrian nationals, Franz and Christina Riepl (‘the applicants’), applied for a building permit for an adjoining building with a garage on their property. The applicants were represented by Mr H. Blum, a lawyer practising in Linz. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Departement at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was for a double garage with a parking area. The Municipal Council quashed the building permit of 16 August 1994 and remitted the case back to the Mayor of Freistadt. In 2002 the Mayor granted a building permit for the double garage. The application was settled by paying the fees incurred by the applicants’ representation in the proceedings so far, on the condition that the applicants amended their request for aBuilding permit in accordance with the newly established building scheme (Bebauungsplan) The applicants submitted the requested plans, which, however, turned out to be incomplete. On 15 January 2002 they submitted the corrected plans and the permit was granted.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 9 July 1997. It originated in an application (no. 22954/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The application was made by Mr Mobin Ahmed, Mr Dennis Perrin, Mr Ray Bentley and Mr David John Brough. Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London, was granted leave to submit written comments on the case in September 1997. The Government’s responses to the applicants’ claims were filed with the registry on 21 April and 18 May 1998. The applicants filed observations in reply on 29 May 1998 and the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998. MacLeod, Legal Secretariat to the Law Officers. The history of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in Sections C and D below. Section C: The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990. Section D: The legal effect of the Regulations on a range of different types of applicants.Section B: The political background to the adoption. of the regulations, including their effect on the powers of local government officers. Section B: Their impact on the political activities of certain categories of officials. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials: the most senior post-holders in the local authority, senior councillors and senior members of the local council. The regulations also apply to those who hold office in a political party. They include: standing for, and holding, public elected office; (ii) holding office in the party; (iii) speaking or writing in public in a way that might be regarded as engaging in party political debate; and (iv) canvassing at elections. Local government officials in the first, second and third categories were deemed to be subject to the regulations. A local government officer could apply to an independent adjudicator to have his or her post removed from the list of posts to which the Regulations applied (section 3) The first applicant, Mr Ahmed, was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. The Council confirmed that Mr Ahmed had not attended committees during the previous twelve months, but stated that he would be involved in giving advice to committees in future. Mr Perrin was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council (a category three officer). He was responsible for leading, leading, the Housing Benefits Review Board and the Environmental Sub-Committee. Mr Perrin's post required him to give regular advice to the Council’s committees, including strategy advice on key estate management issues, and to speak to the media. His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. Mr Perrin had to give up his position as Vice-Chair and Property Officer of the Exeter Constituency Labour Party. He also had to refrain from supporting and assisting Labour candidates in Exeter City Council elections, including his wife, who was a candidate in May 1990 and May 1991. Mr Bentley's post was classified as politically sensitive (a category one post) and appropriately subject to political restrictions under section 2(3) of the Act. Mr Brough can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East. He is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. Mr Bentley's post also fell within section 2(7)(a) and (b) of the Act, and was therefore politically restricted in any event. Mr Brough did not apply for exemption from the scope of the Regulations. The application was dismissed on 20 December 1991. The applicants and NALGO (the predecessor of UNISON, the trade union of which the applicants are members and which represents public-sector workers) applied for and were granted leave to apply for judicial review of the regulations. The judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. The affidavit explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures with particular reference to the respective roles of elected members and officers. The judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees’” The judge went on to say that the regulations’ definition of ‘politically restricted posts’ was ‘unduly wide’ The Regulations go too far in prohibiting conduct undertaken with apparent intention, etc., or likely to create the impression of support, etc. They should, at most, have proscribed actual political activities. The restrictions may have an adverse effect on recruitment and lead to resignations by skilled staff. The Regulations are uncertain and incapable of consistent and fair application. The Government’s Command Paper in July 1988 spelt out the essential aim that the post-holder should be seen to be politically impartial but that otherwise, local government employees should not be subject to restrictions on their political activity. The arguments summarised in (a) to (h) above are, it seems to me, essentially arguments against the whole concept of restricting such activities, and in the circumstances cannot found an attack on Wednesbury grounds. train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 22261/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In 2000 the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources expropriated two plots of land belonging to the applicant in Erenköy village, Nizip, for the construction of the Birecik dam. On 14 September 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgments of the first‑instance court on 9 July 2001. The Government informed the Court that they had not yet made any further payments to the applicant to discharge their outstanding debt. The Court accepted the calculations made by the administration for the discharge of its outstanding debt, and the debt was discharged. The case was settled out of court in July 2008, with the Government paying back the money owed to the applicants. The debt was finally discharged in July 2009, when the Government made a payment of £1.4 million to the applicant to pay off the debt. It was the first time the debt had been discharged in over a decade. The appeal was rejected by the court, and it was decided that the debt could not be discharged until the Government had made further payments.

The case originated in an application (no. 22261/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources expropriated two plots of land belonging to the applicant (plot no. 247 in block no. 103 and plot no. 14 in blockNo. 130) in Erenköy village, Nizip, for the construction of the Birecik dam. The applicant was represented by Mr M. Birlik, a lawyer practising in Şanlıurfa. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 8 July 2008 the Government informed the Court that they had not yet made any further payments to the applicant to discharge their outstanding debt. accept the calculations made by the administration for the discharge of its outstanding debt, and order the Government to pay the debt back. The Government did not pay back the debt and the case was returned to the Court of Appeal on 9 July 2008. The appeal was dismissed on 11 July 2008 by the Supreme Court of England and Wales, and the debt was discharged on 14 July 2008, but the outstanding debt was not paid back by the Government. The case was decided in favor of the applicant by the High Court on 21 July 2008 and the decision was quashed.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court under Article 6 of the convention. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of. Human Rights (Interights) and Justice (“the third-party interveners”) were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. Three men claim they were tortured in Saudi Arabia. They claim to have been beaten, starved and subjected to sleep deprivation. They are seeking compensation from Saudi Arabia for their injuries. The case has been heard in the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The judge ruled in favour of the men's claims and ordered the case to go to the High Court of Justice in London, where it was heard for a year. The appeal was thrown out of court on appeal and the case is now back before the Court of Appeal for a new hearing, which could take place as soon as this year, if the appeal is successful. The High Court heard the case in March 2013, but the appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the case had already been dismissed. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal with the leave of the Master. The Court of Appeals published its judgment on 28 October 2004. It unanimously dismissed Mr Jones’s appeal from the decision to refuse permission to serve Saudi Arabia outside the jurisdiction. However, it allowed the appeals in respect of the refusal of permission in each case to serve the individual defendants. Lord Justice Mance, with whom Lord Phillips and Lord Justice Neuberger agreed, refused to depart from this Court's ruling in Al‑Adsani v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 35763/97, ECHR 2001‑XI. He further found that Article 14 § 1 of the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment could not be interpreted as imposing an obligation on a State to provide redress for acts of torture. Torture was to be regarded as outside the scope of any proper exercise of sovereign authority or with international crime, let alone with systematic torture. LJ did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the “servant or agent” of Saudi Arabia. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. He did not accept that general differences between criminal and civil law justified a distinction in the application of immunity in the two contexts. Mance LJ considered that whether any claim in the English courts against individuals could proceed was better determined not by reference to immunity. He was of the view that the legislation and case-law of the United States of America (see paragraphs 112-25 below) militated strongly against any such settled principle. He considered the dicta in the separate opinion of Judges Higgins, Kooijmans and Buergenthal to the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the ‘Arrest Warrant’ case to provide further confirmation that there was no settled international practice in this area. He acknowledged that the courts of one State were. pursue any civil claim. Mance LJ concluded that giving blanket effect to a foreign State’s claim to State immunity ratione materiae in respect of a State official alleged to have committed acts of systematic torture could deprive the right of access to a court under Article 6 of real meaning. He therefore allowed the applicants’ appeals in. respect of the individual defendants and remitted them for further argument, concluding: “96. ... [I]t seems to me that any absolute view of immunity. must at the very least yield in the face of assertions of systematic. torture to a more nuanced or proportionate approach.” Lord Phillips agreed with the conclusions of Mance. LJ as regards both the claim against Saudi Arabia and the claims against. individual officials. Saudi Arabia appealed to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in respect of the individual defendants. Mr Jones appealed against the. the decision in favour of his claim against Saudi Arabia itself. On 14 June 2006, the House. of Lords unanimously allowed Saudi Arabia’s appeal and dismissed the. appeal by Mr Jones. Lord Bingham considered that there was a ‘wealth of authority’ in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to show that a State was entitled to claim immunity for. its servants or agents. The fact that conduct was unlawful or objectionable was not, of itself, a ground for refusing immunity. The four defendants in the second case were public officials and the alleged conduct took place in public premises. Lord Bingham disagreed with the applicants’ submission that torture could not be a governmental or official act. Under Article 1 of the Convention against Torture, torture had to be inflicted by or with the connivance of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The applicants referred to a substantial body of authority showing that the courts of the United States would not recognise acts performed by individual officials as being carried out for the purposes of immunity. Lord Bingham considered the first to be of slight legal authority, the second to be an obiter dictum and the third not to be a accurate statement of international law. Lord Bingham found that the Court of Appeal had incorrectly departed from the position in its previous ruling in Propend. He said that the prohibition of torture did not automatically override all other rules of international law. Article 14 of the Convention against Torture did not provide for universal civil jurisdiction. The 2004 United Nations Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property (see paragraphs 75-80 below) did not provided any exception from immunity for civil claims based on acts of torture. No evidence that States had recognised or given effect to any international-law obligation to exercise universal jurisdiction over claims arising from alleged breaches of peremptory norms. The prosecution of a servant or agent for an act of torture within article 1 of the Torture Convention is founded on an express exception from the general rule of immunity. It is, however, clear that a civil action against individual torturers based on acts of official torture does indirectly implead the state since their acts are attributable to it. Were these claims against the individual defendants to proceed and be upheld, the interests of the Kingdom would be obviously affected, even though it is not a named party. The distinction between criminal proceedings (which were the subject of universal jurisdiction) and civil proceedings ( which were not) was, he said, “fundamental” and one that could not be “wished away” Lord Hoffmann found Lord Justice Mance’s conclusion that the Convention against Torture did not lend acts of torture any official character to be unsatisfactory. He also considered inappropriate the Court of Appeal's proposed approach to the exercise of jurisdiction, on the ground that State immunity was not a self-imposed restriction but was “imposed by international law without any discrimination between one State and another” He concluded that it would be “invidious in the extreme for the judicial branch of government to decide that it will allow the investigation of allegations of torture against the officials of one foreign state but not against those of another’

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court under Article 6. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of human Rights (Interights) and JUSTICE (“the third-party interveners”) were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. On 29 November 2011 the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the Case. Mr Jones alleges he was beaten with a cane on his palms, feet, arms and legs. He was also suspended by his arms; shackled at his ankles; and given mind-altering drugs. Mr Jones claims he was tortured by Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz. The case was brought in the High Court of England and Wales. The High Court ruled that Saudi Arabia was entitled to immunity under the State Immunity Act of 1978, and that Mr Jones' case should be dismissed. The appeal was denied and Mr Jones returned to Saudi Arabia. He claims he has been treated for post-traumatic stress disorder. He has also suffered from depression and anxiety due to his ordeal. Mr Jones and Mr Phillips applied for permission to serve their claim on four individuals out of the jurisdiction. The Master who heard Mr Jones’s claim refused on the basis of his previous ruling in respect of Mr Jones. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal with the leave of the Master. The two cases were joined and on 28 October 2004 the Court. of Appeal published its judgment. It unanimously dismissed Mr Jones's appeal from the decision of the. the Master to refuse permission to service Saudi Arabia outside the. jurisdiction. However, it allowed the appeals in respect. of the refusal of permission in each case to serve the individual defendants. Mance LJ did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the “servant or agent” of Saudi Arabia. Nor did he accept that general differences between criminal and civil law justified a distinction in the application of immunity in the two contexts. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. It was also incongruous that if an alleged torturer was within the jurisdiction of the forum State, he would be prosecuted pursuant to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention against Torture. Mance LJ considered that whether any claim in the English courts against individuals could proceed was better determined not by reference to immunity. He considered it impossible to identify any settled international principle affording the State the right to claim immunity in respect of claims directed against an official, rather than against the State, its Head of State or diplomats. He was of the view that the legislation and case-law of the United States of America (see paragraphs 112-25 below) militated strongly against any such settled principle and supported a contrary view. In so far as counsel for the Government purported to refer to evidence of settled practice, he noted that the case- law to which he had referred related either to the immunity of the State itself or to immunity of individual officials for alleged misconduct. Mance LJ concluded that giving blanket effect to a foreign State’s claim to State immunity ratione materiae in respect of a State official alleged to have committed acts of systematic torture could deprive the right of access to a court under Article 6 of real meaning. Lord Phillips agreed with the conclusions of Mance L J as regards both the claim against Saudi Arabia and the claims against the individual officials. In particular, he considered that the judgment in Pinochet (No. 3) (see paragraphs 44-56 below) had shown that torture could no longer fall within the scope of the official duties of a state official. It therefore followed that if civil proceedings were brought against individuals for acts of torture in circumstances where the State was immune from suit, there could be no suggestion the State would be vicariously liable. Saudi Arabia appealed to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in respect of the individual defendants and Mr Jones. On 14 June 2006, the House. of Lords unanimously allowed Saudi Arabia’s appeal and dismissed the appeal by Mr. Jones. Lord Bingham considered that there was a “wealth of authority” in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to show that a State was entitled to claim immunity for its servants or agents and that the right to immunity could not be circumvented by suing them instead. The fact that conduct was unlawful or objectionable was not, of itself, a ground for refusing immunity. The four defendants in the second case were public officials and the alleged conduct took place in public premises. Under Article 1 of the Convention against Torture, torture had to be inflicted by or with the connivance of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The applicants referred to a substantial body of authority showing that the courts of the United States would not recognise acts performed by individual officials as being carried out for the purposes of immunity. Lord Bingham found it unnecessary to examine those authorities since they were only important to the extent that they expressed principles widely shared and observed among other nations. Saudi Arabia identified four arguments advanced by Saudi Arabia which he said were “cumulatively irresistible” It claimed that State immunity ratione personae could be claimed for a serving foreign minister accused of crimes against humanity. It also claimed that torture could not be a governmental or official act. Lord Bingham found that the prohibition of torture did not automatically override all other rules of international law. Article 14 of the Convention against Torture did not provide for universal civil jurisdiction. There was no evidence that States had recognised or given effect to any international-law obligation to exercise universal jurisdiction over claims arising from alleged breaches of peremptory norms. For these reasons, Lord Bingham agreed with the Court of Appeal that the claim brought by Mr Jones against Saudi Arabia was to be dismissed. He also said that the court had incorrectly departed from the position in its previous ruling in Propend that the acts of State officials were to be considered the act of the State itself. The prosecution of a servant or agent for an act of torture within article 1 of the Torture Convention is founded on an express exception from the general rule of immunity. It is, however, clear that a civil action against individual torturers based on acts of official torture does indirectly implead the state since their acts are attributable to it. Were these claims against the individual defendants to proceed and be upheld, the interests of the Kingdom would be obviously affected, even though it is not a named party. The distinction between criminal proceedings and civil proceedings was, he said, “fundamental” and one that could not be “wished away”. Lord Hoffmann found Lord Justice Mance’s conclusion that the Convention against Torture’'s definition of torture did not lend acts of torture any official character to be unsatisfactory. He said it would be ‘invidious in the extreme for the judicial branch of government to have the power to decide that it will allow the investigation of allegations of torture against the officials of one foreign state but not against those of another’ He also considered inappropriate the Court of Appeal's proposed approach to the exercise of jurisdiction, on the ground that State immunity was not a self-imposed restriction but was “imposed by international law without any discrimination between one State and another”

However, where there was no adequate remedy in the State where the systematic torture occurred, it might be regarded as disproportionate to maintain a blanket refusal of recourse. Saudi Arabia, in claiming immunity, was not justifying torture but merely objecting to the jurisdiction of the English courts in deciding whether it had used torture or not. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones and to the individual defendants in both cases amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of human Rights (Interights) and JUSTICE were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. On 29 November 2011 the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the Case. The case was brought by two men who say they were tortured in Saudi Arabia. They claim they were beaten with a cane and given mind-altering drugs. The case was heard in the High Court in London, but the case was thrown out of court. The judge ruled that the Saudi government was entitled to immunity under the State Immunity Act 1978. The men appealed the decision and the case has now been heard by the Court of Appeal in London. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the claim was not supported by the evidence. The plaintiffs are seeking compensation for their injuries and for the cost of their legal fees. They are also seeking an apology from the government for their treatment. Policemen wanted to serve their claim on four individuals out of the jurisdiction. Master refused to do so on the basis of previous ruling in respect of Mr Jones. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal with the leave of the Master. The two cases were joined and on 28 October 2004 the court of Appeal published its judgment. It unanimously dismissed Mr Jones’s appeal from the decision to refuse permission to serve Saudi Arabia outside the jurisdiction, but allowed the appeals inrespect of the refusal of permission in each case to serve the individual defendants. Lord Justice Mance, with whom Lord Phillips and Lord Justice Neuberger agreed, refused to depart from this Court's ruling in Al‑Adsani v the United Kingdom. Mance LJ did not accept that the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture was fatal to the applicants’ claims. He did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the ‘servant or agent’ of Saudi Arabia. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. It was not easy to see why civil proceedings against an alleged torturer could be said to involve a greater interference in the internal affairs of a foreign State. Mance LJ said there was no basis for assuming that, in civil proceedings, a State could be made liable to indemnify or otherwise support one of its officials proved to have committed systematic torture. He considered the dicta in the separate opinion of Judges Higgins, Kooijmans and Buergenthal to the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the ‘Arrest Warrant’ case. He was of the view that the legislation and case-law of the United States of America (see paragraphs 112-25 below) militated strongly against any such settled principle. He acknowledged that the courts of one State were not expected to pursue any civil claim. But he said it was disproportionate to maintain a blanket refusal of recourse to the civil courts of another jurisdiction. Mance LJ concluded that. giving blanket effect to a foreign State’s claim to. State immunity ratione materiae in respect of a State official alleged to have committed acts of. systematic torture could deprive the right of access to a court under. Article 6 of real meaning. He therefore allowed the applicants’ appeals in. respect of the individual defendants and remitted them for further argument, concluding: “96. ... [I]t seems to me that any absolute view of immunity must at the very least yield in. the face of assertions of systematic torture to a more nuanced or proportionate approach.” Saudi Arabia appealed to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in respect of the individual defendants and Mr Jones appealed against the. decision. On 14 June 2006, the House. of Lords unanimously allowed Saudi Arabia’s appeal and dismissed the appeal by. Mr Jones. Lord Bingham considered that there was a ‘wealth of authority’ in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to show that a State was entitled to claim immunity for its servants or agents. He said there was no recognised rule of public international law that conferred such immunity. The fact that conduct was unlawful or objectionable was not, of itself, a ground for refusing immunity. Lord Bingham disagreed with the applicants’ submission that torture could not be a governmental or official act. Under Article 1 of the Convention against Torture, torture had to be inflicted by or with the connivance of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The applicants referred to a substantial body of authority showing that the courts of the United States would not recognise acts performed by individual officials as being carried out for the purposes of immunity. Lord Bingham found it unnecessary to examine those authorities since they were only important to the extent that they expressed principles widely shared and observed among other nations. He considered the first to be of slight legal authority and the second to be an obiter dictum. Lord Bingham said that the prohibition of torture did not automatically override all other rules of international law. He said that Article 14 of the Convention against Torture did not provide for universal civil jurisdiction. The 2004 United Nations Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property (see paragraphs 75-80 below) did not provided any exception from immunity for civil claims based on acts of torture. There was no evidence that States had recognised or given effect to any international-law obligation to exercise universal jurisdiction over claims arising from alleged breaches of peremptory norms. The prosecution of a servant or agent for an act of torture within article 1 of the Torture Convention is founded on an express exception from the general rule of immunity. name: Kemal Evcimen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21865/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged unfairness of the proceedings against the applicant. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the DHKP-C (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party- Front) The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the Court. The case-file was sent to the Erzurum State Security Court in 1997. In 1998 the court convicted the applicant under Article 168 of the Criminal Code of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the DHKP-C. The court sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. On 29 May 2004 the applicant was conditionally released from prison. On 18 November 1999 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 27 November 1998 in respect of the applicant. The cases against the applicant and his co-accused were subsequently joined before the Errzincan State Security court. The applicant was convicted of disseminating separatist propaganda and incitement to hatred and hostility.

Germany were eligible for benefits.’

name: Wim Capeau
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42914/98) against the Kingdom of Belgium lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained of a violation of Articles 5, 6 and 14 of the Convention. By a decision of 6 April 2004, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59:1). The applicant did not submit any observations within the time allowed. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52:1 of the Rules of Court) The Court ruled that the application was not admissible because it was not part of the normal course of proceedings. The Minister of Justice refused the applicant's claim on the ground that he had not “established his innocence by adducing factual evidence” The Appeals Board upheld the refusal of his claim by a decision taken on the same day and served on the applicant on 29 March 1998. It noted that the grounds for presuming the guilt of the applicant, who had always denied committing the offence, had been held to be insufficient to justify committing him for trial. It observed that, although the applicant had announced his intention of submitting a pleading setting out the evidence in the file which “amply” proved his innocence, he did not do so and had not replied to the Government's submissions.

On 12 March and 13 June 2012 the Government and the applicant submitted their observations respectively. On 16 July 2015 the Government replied to the submissions of the applicant. In 1999 the applicant fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan because of pressure from the police, who suspected him of anti-constitutional activities. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he decided to flee from Iran following deportation threats. On 18 November 2007 the applicant entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. The Van office issued him with an asylum seeker certificate. Subsequently, he registered with the Van police headquarters and started the domestic temporary asylum procedure. name: Paul Howard Ginnifer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65507/01) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Yeovil. His wife died on 17 December 1996, leaving one child born in 1991. On 20 June 2000 the applicant applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. On 3 July 2000 the Benefits Agency refused his claim for WMA. The appeal was then sent to the Social Security Appeals Service. However, such appeal was bound to fail given that no social security benefits were payable to widowers under the domestic law. The applicant receives child benefit in the sum of GBP 70.20 per week.

name: Fazia Ali
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Fazia Ali was born in 1980 and lives in Birmingham. She is represented before the Court by Mr M. McIlvaney of the Community Law Partnership. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Ms R. Tomlinson of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation within the meaning of Part VII of the Housing Act 1996. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. The Council notified the applicant that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. By letter dated 29 March 2007 the applicant notified the Council that she had not received an offer in writing and requested that the Council review its decision. While the applicant’s case was pending before the review panel, a further offer of accommodation was made to her pursuant to a different scheme, namely the scheme for the provision of housing accommodation. She did not accept this offer. The appeal was heard on 29 August 2007, on which date the judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. The applicant submitted that the County Court should hear evidence on the matter so that it could determine it for itself. Although the judge accepted that the Homelessness Review Officer was not an independent or impartial tribunal, he found that the decision whether or not the letter had been received was properly and fairly to be made by her. Although it was not specifically stated in the correspondence between the Council and the applicant, the judge appeared to consider whether or Not the Council had discharged its duty under section 193(7) (see paragraph 25 below) House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Thomas LJ stated that: “It is far from easy to draw the distinction advanced in practice. A finding of suitability is itself a finding based on conclusions of primary fact’. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. In doing so, it proceeded on the assumption that the case involved the determination of the applicant's civil rights for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The full right of appeal sought from a review officer on fact might have to be significantly different from an appeal from a court. Thomas LJ said the decision of the House of Lords in Runa Begum applied to all County Court appeals under section 204 of the 1996 Act. He further held that the decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not affect appeals brought in homelessness cases. “I consider that it does whether the decision turns on a simple issue of primary fact or a conclusion of fact based on primary facts (such as a conclusion on suitability),” he said. � “The present scope of the appeal provides a real measure of protection for homeless appellants. Lord Hope of Craighead said that cases where the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder, do not engage article 6(1). In my opinion they do not give rise to ‘civil rights’ within the autonomous meaning that is given to that expression for the purposes of that article’. The judgment of the Supreme Court held that the HBRB was not independent of the parties; it could have awarded the applicant 43. % of the benefit if it made an award in her favour. The court went on to observe that the fact that a County Court did not have a full fact-finding jurisdiction when hearing an appeal under section 204 of the 1996 Act did not mean that the applicant was deprived of what was required to satisfy the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation. She is represented before the Court by Mr M. McIlvaney of the Community Law Partnership, a solicitor practising in Birmingham. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms R. Tomlinson of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On 7 November 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was made by a British national, Ms Fazia Ali, on 15 July 2010. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. The Council notified the applicant that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. By letter dated 29 March 2007 the applicant notified the Council that she had not received an offer in writing and requested that the Council review its decision. The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court under section 204 of the1996 Act, which allowed for an appeal on a point of law only. In her grounds of appeal the applicant claimed that the applicant’s refusal of the offer of accommodation had discharged the Council's main housing duty. The appeal was heard on 29 August 2007, on which date the judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. The applicant submitted that the County Court should hear evidence on the matter so that it could determine it for itself. Although the judge accepted that the Homelessness Review Officer was not an independent or impartial tribunal, he found that the decision whether or not the letter had been received was properly and fairly to be made by her. Although it was not specifically stated in the correspondence between the Council and the applicant, the judge appeared to consider whether the Council had discharged its duty under section 193(7) (see paragraph 25 below) House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Thomas LJ stated that: “It is far from easy to draw the distinction advanced in practice. A finding of suitability is itself a finding based on conclusions of primary fact ... ii) There would be considerable complexity in administering a scheme with these distinctions. A scheme which enabled certain factual issues to be subject to a full right of appeal and others which would not be so subject would be too uncertain and too complex" Thomas LJ held that the decision of the House of Lords in Runa Begum applied to all County Court appeals under section 204 of the 1996 Act. He also held that. the decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not. affect appeals brought in homelessness cases. “I consider that it does whether the decision turns on a simple issue of primary fact or a conclusion of fact based on primary facts (such as a conclusion on suitability),” he said. The decision in the case of prospective benefit, central government reimbursed the local authority 95% of what it was required to pay, it only reimbursed 50% of backdated awards. This fact had been heavily relied upon in argument. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding that the determination by the Council, that its duty to secure accommodation for the applicant had ceased, was not a determination of her civil rights within the meaning of Article 6.1 of the Housing Act. Lord Hope of Craighead stated that the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder. He continued: “... There are a number of straws in the wind since Runa Begum that suggest that a distinction can indeed be made between the class of social security and welfare benefits that are of the kind exemplified by Salesi v Italy.” Lord Hope said separating simple, formal questions of “gateway” facts, such as the letter issue, from the expert assessment of suitability would needlessly complicate a scheme designed to be simple to administer. The court went on to observe that the fact that a County Court did not have a full fact-finding jurisdiction when hearing an appeal under section 204 of the 1996 Act did not mean that the applicant was deprived of what was required to satisfy the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. Unlike the County Court, the Supreme Court appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty to the applicant under section 193(5); however, it appeared to accept that a formal letter of offer was required by that subsection.

The application was communicated to the Government on 7 November 2012. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Ms R. Tomlinson of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 11 December 2012. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. The Council notified the applicant that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. By letter dated 29 March 2007 the applicant notified the Council that she had not received an offer in writing and requested that the Council review its decision. The Homelessness Review Officer upheld the decision that the applicant’s refusal of the offer of accommodation had discharged the Council's main housing duty. The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court. The appeal was heard on 29 August 2007, on which date the judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. The applicant subsequently appealed to the Court of Appeal and then to the Supreme Court. At each level, the grounds of appeal were that the decision taken by the Council’s Homelessness Review Officer had constituted a determination of the applicant's civil rights for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The House of Lords in Runa Begum v. London Borough of Tower Hamlets [2003] UKHL 5 found that judicial review provided ‘sufficiency of review’ House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Although the Officer could not be regarded as independent, since she was employed by the Council which had made the offer of accommodation which the claimant had rejected, statutory regulations provided substantial safeguards to ensure that the review would be independently and fairly conducted, free from improper external influences. He further held that the decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not affect appeals brought in homelessness cases. The present scope of the appeal provides a real measure of protection for homeless appellants, he said. He concluded that the Strasbourg Court relied on the decision. in reaching its conclusion and said nothing that cast doubt on the correctness of the. decision. He said there is no reason to attempt to find that the review by the County Court in cases of this kind was sufficient. I would be prepared now to hold that cases where the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder, do not engage article 6(1). name: Hasan Yavuz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39863/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the independence and impartiality of the Diyarbakır State Security Court and the length of the proceedings to the respondent Government. The applicants were taken into custody by policemen from the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the Batman Security Directorate on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation, namely the Workers' Party of Kurdistan (“the PKK”) On 13 April 1993 the applicants were brought before the public prosecutor and subsequently the investigating judge, who ordered their detention on remand. The Diyarbakır State Security Court acquitted the first applicant of the charges against him. The court further found the second applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to the death penalty under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. On 1 October 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the DiYarbakir State Security court. hearings. The first applicant was sentenced to death in March 2002. The second applicant was found guilty in October 2002 and sentenced to life in prison in March 2003. The third applicant was acquitted in April 2003 and the fourth applicant was convicted in October 2003.

name: Marek Jończyk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75870/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in Łask-Kolumna, Poland. He was granted a special disability pension from the State Insurance Company (Powszechny Zakład Ubezpieczeniowy - “PZU”). He was not satisfied with the amount of the pension and on 31 March 1992 he lodged a claim for a reassessment of the amount. The first hearing was held on 21 April 1993. The trial court held hearings on 17 May and 28 October 1993. The case began on 9 December 1994 in the Sieradz Regional Court. On 9 June 1995 the applicant requested that an expert opinion be obtained. The trial court held four further hearings between 8 April 1998 and 8 February 1999. On 12 February 1999 the District Court gave judgment. Both parties appealed. The proceedings were terminated by the judgment of the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) of 21 January 2000. The case was heard by a jury of three men and two women. The jury found the applicant not guilty of the charges. The verdict was quashed and the case was adjourned until later in the year.

He was subsequently granted a special disability pension from the State Insurance Company (Powszechny Zakład Ubezpieczeniowy - “PZU”). The applicant was not satisfied with the amount of the pension and on 31 March 1992 he lodged a claim for a reassessment of the amount with the Łask District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). The proceedings were terminated by the judgment of the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) of 21 January 2000. Both parties appealed the decision of the Sieradz Regional Court to dismiss the applicant’s claim. The application was dismissed on 30 June 1999 and the appeal was rejected on 12 February 1999. The trial court held four further hearings between 8 April 1998 and 8 February 1999 and gave judgment on 12 Feb 1999. For more details about the case, see the case file on the case page: www.sieradzy.cz/sieradsz/pensioners/Pensioner/Case-Case-Appeal-Case.html.
