name: Mehmet Göç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36590/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. On 9 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs) in compensation. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 6 April 2000 the application was declared partly admissible. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. The case was brought by a former clerk in the 2nd Court of Taxation in the city of İzmir. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant, and the Government paid back the legal aid. The judgement was published on 17 November 2002. The amount of legal aid received was converted into Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement, less FRF 4,100 (four thousand one hundred French francs) The judge also ruled that all costs and expenses, together with any value-added tax that might be chargeable, were to be converted into lira. The applicant was taken into police custody and detained at the İzmir Security Directorate on 25 July 1995. Two other suspects were also detained and statements were taken from them. The applicant later claimed that he was not permitted to contact his family or consult a lawyer. On 31 July 1995 the office of the public prosecutor of Karşıyaka decided not to bring charges against the applicant (takipsizlik kararı) for lack of evidence. The decision was served on the applicant on 19 August 1995. In the petition, the applicant's lawyer stated, inter alia, that the applicant, while in detention, had been tortured and ill-treated by being beaten and insulted for two hours. The applicant was detained for two days from 25 July to 27 July 1995. Upon his release, he obtained a medical report which indicated that he had been assaulted. The judge noted that the applicant had been given four days' sick leave by his employer. He concluded: “The complainant requested that he be granted the sum of TRL 200,000,000 in compensation” On 7 December 1995 the public prosecutor, as required by Law no. 466, submitted his opinion to the Karşıyaka Assize Court. The public prosecutor recommended the applicant be granted compensation for non-pecuniary damage in an amount to be assessed by the court. The applicant had been working in the İzmir Tax Court, had been paying TRL 3,000,000 in rent, and was divorced with two children. The complainant requested that the court award him TRL 200,00,000 for the non-pecuniary damage suffered. The applicant's lawyer contended on appeal that the amount of compensation was insufficient reparation for his wrongful arrest and detention. The Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his opinion on the merits of both parties' appeals. He advised that both appeals be rejected and that the first-instance judgment be approved, being in compliance with procedural rules and law. This opinion was not submitted to the applicant. The case file was referred to the competent division of the Court of Cassation through the intermediary of the public prosecutor. According to information submitted by the Government, the applicant never applied to obtain the compensation awarded to him by the Karşıyaka Assize Court. Having regard, inter alia, to the opinion of the Principal Public Prosecutor, upheld the judgment of 7 December 1995. According to the information submitted to the Government by the Attorney General, the applicants never applied for the compensation. The applicant was awarded the compensation for the loss of his property. The case was heard in the High Court of Justice in Istanbul. The judge ruled in favor of the applicant, and the case was dismissed. The Government has appealed the decision and appealed to the Supreme Court of Appeal.

The case originated in an application (no. 36590/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. On 9 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs) in damages. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg in 2002. The Court heard addresses by the Government, the applicant and the lawyer for the Government. The Grand Chamber decided to refer the case to the Court on 5 September 2001. A separate opinion of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen was annexed to the judgment on 9 November 2000. The judgment ordered the amount received by way of legal aid to be converted into Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement, less FRF 4,100 (four thousand one hundred French francs) The judgment also ordered any costs and expenses, together with any value-added tax that might be chargeable, to be Conversion to Turkish Liras. The applicant was taken into police custody and detained at the İzmir Security Directorate. The applicant later claimed that he was not permitted to contact his family or consult a lawyer. The medical report prepared at the hospital referred to the fact that the applicant was suffering from a common skin disease caused by the inflammation of the roots of his facial hair. On 31 July 1995 the office of the public prosecutor of Karşıyaka decided not to bring charges against the applicant (takipsizlik kararı) for lack of evidence. The decision was served on the applicant on 19 August 1995. On 5 September 1995 the applicant filed a complaint. under Law no. 466 with the Karş Turkey Assize Court (Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi) against the Treasury requesting 200,000,000 Turkish liras. by way of compensation for his detention. The Karşıyaka Assize Court appointed one of its members (naip hakim) to investigate the case and draft a report. The judge verified, inter alia, that the office of the public prosecutor of İzmir had dropped the charges against the applicant. He also obtained information about the applicant's personal, financial and social status. He found that the evidence obtained was sufficient to enable him to draft his report and decided in the exercise of his discretion under section 3 of Law no. 466 that it was unnecessary to hear the applicants. The public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be granted compensation for non-pecuniary damage in an amount to be assessed. Karşıyaka Assize Court found that the applicant had been detained for two days and qualified for compensation. The complainant requested that the court award him TRL 200,000,000 for the non-pecuniary damage suffered. The applicant's lawyer contended on appeal that the amount of compensation was insufficient reparation for his wrongful arrest and detention. The Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his opinion (tebliğname) to the Sixth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) on 17 October 1996. He advised that both appeals be rejected and that the first-instance judgment be approved, being in compliance with procedural rules and law. This opinion was not submitted to the applicant. The applicant never applied to obtain the compensation awarded to him by the Karşıyaka Assize Court. The Government said that the applicant did not apply for compensation. The judge upheld the judgment of 7 December 1995. The applicant was awarded a fine of 1.5 million Turkish lira (about £1.6 million or $2.7 million) by the court. He was also awarded the right to a £500,000 fine (around £400,000 or $700,000) and a £200,000 compensation payment. The court ruled that the compensation paid to the applicant was fair and just. The decision was unanimous.

Case originated in an application (no. 36590/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Chamber which initially examined the case. It also held, unanimously, that it was not necessary to examine separately the applicant's complaint concerning the absence of an oral hearing in the domestic proceedings. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs) The case was referred to the Grand Chamber on 5 September 2001. A hearing before the Grand chamber took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Dinç, Mr Özmen and Mrs Bulutlar Ulusoy, and also their replies to questions from its individual members. The case was settled at the rate applicable at the date of settlement, less FRF 4,100 (four thousand one hundred French francs) received by way of legal aid to be converted into Turkish liras on 9 November 2000. The separate opinion of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen was annexed to the judgment. The applicant was taken into police custody and detained at the İzmir Security Directorate. He gave a statement in which he denied that he had been involved in the incident relating to the court's case file. Two other suspects were also detained and statements were taken from them. The public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be granted compensation for non-pecuniary damage in an amount to be assessed by the court. The complainant requested that he be granted the sum of TRL 200,000,000 in compensation. In determining the amount of compensation the court should consider both the complainant's economic and social position as well as the intensity of his emotional suffering. The applicant was detained for two days and qualified for compensation. The complainant requested that the court award him TRL 200,000,000 for the non-pecuniary damage suffered. name: Hermann Walter Mork
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the execution of his preventive detention violated his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The application was adjourned until the judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above) has become final. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the applications at issue be resumed and granted priority to the applications (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). The applicant was born in 1955 and is currently detained in Aachen Prison. He was convicted of numerous counts of joint burglary committed in companies and shops. In December 1996 the applicant was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of drug trafficking. He has remained in prison since then. In a judgment dated 9 February 1998 the Aachen Regional Court convicted the applicant of unauthorised importing of drugs. (hashish and cocaine) and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The applicant claimed that he had struck a deal with the Regional Court on the latter’s proposal that the court would impose a sentence of less than ten years. The Government submitted that there was no indication in the case-file that such an agreement had been made. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed as ill-founded an appeal by the applicant on points of law. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the two judgments of the Regional Court and the judgment and decision of the Federal Court of Justice. He complained that preventive detention was incompatible with his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, which did not cover such a preventive measure. It further violated the prohibition of retrospective punishment under the Basic Law and Article 7 of the convention because his preventive detention had been ordered without a maximum duration of ten years, which had been the maximum penalty at the time he committed his offences. The court found that the applicant had failed to submit his statement of the grounds of his appeal on points of law nor had he claimed that he had complained about the unconstitutionality of the amended provisions on preventive detention. The applicant had to serve his full prison sentence as of 25 July 2007 (Article 67c § 1 of the Criminal Code) The court fully agreed with the findings of a psychiatric and psychotherapeutic expert it had consulted on the applicant’s dangerousness. In his report dated 7 May 2007 the expert considered that, if released, the applicant was very likely to commit further serious offences similar to those he had previously committed. Even assuming that the security measures taken against him by the prison authorities had not been justified, this did not alter the fact that there had. not been a consistent treatment limiting the risk that he would reoffend after his release. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 2356/07) The applicant had been sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment and another of eight years and six months. The Constitutional Court noted that the courts had not based their decision to order preventive detention globally on the fact that the applicant had failed to prove that he was no longer dangerous in the course of such relaxations. If the prison authorities refused to grant the applicant relaxations in the conditions of his detention in the future, the applicant would have to raise this issue with the competent lower courts first. The finding that the interest in public safety prevailed over the applicant’s right to liberty had been proportionate, the Court said. The court said that the decision in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) was not arbitrary. Under Article 67d of the Criminal Code, in its version in force prior to 31 January 1998, the first placement in preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. Termination shall automatically entail supervision of the conduct of the offender. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the execution of the preventive detention order. If there is no danger that the detainee will, owing to his criminal tendencies, commit serious offences resulting in considerable psychological or physical harm to the victims, the measure is terminated. Recent case-law on preventive detention has been a source of controversy in Germany. The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period in May 2011. The court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. The provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot). These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. All provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. The courts dealing with the execution of sentences had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences and if, additionally, they suffered from a mental disorder. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes.

The case originated in two applications (nos. 31047/04 and 43386/08) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot), the Court ruled. The Court also concluded that Article 66 did not comply with the constitutional protection of legitimate expectations guaranteed in a State governed by the rule of law. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. Two men were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the activities of the above-mentioned organisation. They were remanded in custody on 24 February 1994. At a hearing held on 5 August 1998, the applicants requested to be released for the first time. On 4 November 2002 the applicants, at their request, were released pending trial. name: James Roberts Hewitson
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the installation and use by the police of a covert listening device at his place of work. By a decision of 22 October 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The case as declared admissible raises complaints under Article 8 ofthe Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) An indictment was signed charging the applicant with conspiracy to import controlled drugs and conspiracy to supply controlled drugs, namely cannabis. The prosecution evidence against the applicant relied on tape recordings made from the listening device which had been installed by the police at the applicant’s garage premises. The applicant objected to the admission of the tape recordings as evidence in his trial. The judge concluded that the tapes were admissible as evidence and should not be excluded under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (“PACE”) On 5 September 1997 he was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. On 24 September 1997, the Court of Appeal held that the convictions could not be regarded as ‘unsafe’ and rejected his appeal.

name: Mürvet Fidan
train_texts: Five Turkish nationals brought an application against the Republic of Turkey under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their plots of land were illegally seized by the administration for a dam construction without any payment. The court ordered the administration to pay the applicants an amount of increased compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, starting from 1986 when the land was submerged in the waters of the dam. On 6 October 1994 the Court of Cassation quashed these judgments, holding that the authorities had paid the resulting amounts to the owners registered in the local land registry. In 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the following complaints to the respondent Government. The Baskil Civil Court ordered the administration to pay the applicants a certain amount of compensation, plus interest running from 1986. The Court of Cassation reversed its decision and held, on 10 March 1995, that the cases could in fact be characterised as compensation claims arising from expropriation. The administration paid TRL 934,027,000 to Ms Mürvet Fidan, 884,579,000 TRL to Mr Murat Fidan and TRL 2,041,230,000  to Ms Elif Özbilge. On 2 April 1998 the Court ofCassation's rulings were served on the applicants.

name: Abdülmenaf Osman
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he was not tried before an independent and impartial tribunal and that the length of the proceedings exceeded the reasonable time. On 6 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the independence and impartiality of the Diyarbakır State Security Court to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case against the applicant was dismissed on 6 October 2006. The Diyarbakır State Security Court held 51 hearings. The applicant did not attend many of these hearings in protest against the State Security Courts. On 12 March 2002 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to the death penalty under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. On 1 October 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The court held 18 more hearings. On 18 June 1999 the constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench was replaced by a civilian judge. The judges dealt with solely procedural matters. They considered the measures that should be taken to secure the presence of the accused persons.

Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal. The applicant lodged his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The court held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. The CCA also considered that the events at Corke Abbey and an association with those events, the vehicles and the contents of the vehicles, the materials found during searches as well as the meetings between both accused at the time when the applicant’s house was being searched, were all matters which came within the ambit of the phrase ‘movements, actions, activities, or associations on the part of an accused person’ The court noted that there had been no serious challenge to the prosecution evidence of the facts, connections and associations so found. The trial court was entitled to look at the established facts, when taken in conjunction with the inferences which it had properly drawn to see whether these supported or corroborated the belief evidence. The right to silence did not apply in this case. The case was referred to the Supreme Court for reconsideration. The Supreme Court ruled that the case was of "exceptional public importance" in that it had been decided that the evidence was not relevant to the case at hand. The matter was referred back to the High Court for further consideration. The trial court ruled that it was in the public interest for the case to be re-examined in light of this decision. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court. In weighing up the value of that belief evidence, the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence. The applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the trial Judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents or the documents. If the SCC had found documents of assistance to the applicant, its answer would have been different. Moreover, the undisclosed documents were demonstrably not determinative as the applicant had suggested. The author is not responsible for any of the. material contained therein. The case originated in an application (no. 19165/08) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by an Irish national, Mr Kenneth Donohoe (“the applicant’), on 8 April 2008. On 4 January 2012 the application was communicated to the Government by the Irish Human Rights Commission. The applicant was represented by Ms C. Almond, a lawyer practising in Dublin. The Irish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr P. White, of the Department of Foreign Affairs. An off-duty Garda (police) detective attached to the Special Detective Unit noticed suspicious activity and contacted a local Garda station. Five of the eight men involved were arrested and charged with being members of an illegal organisation. They were found with a lump/sledge hammer; two pickaxe handles; a torch; eight plastic bags of cable ties; black balaclavas with single or double openings; woollen gloves; rolls of masking tape; a sky blue shirt marked ‘security’; a yellow fluorescent jacket with the word “GARDA” labelled on it. The Nissan Almera contained false registration plates which corresponded to its tax and insurance discs, these, in fact, being those of an identical car that had previously been stolen. Papers found at the applicant's home contained the phone number of the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) and the man in the driver’s seat of the Transit van (PB) The trial court later found that, at the very least, the applicant was acquainted with one of the men arrested on 10 October 2002. The applicant and NB were tried before the Special Criminal Court (SCC) in October 2004. The trial lasted 8 days. 54 prosecution witnesses were heard. The accused did not give any evidence at trial nor was any other evidence tendered on his behalf. On 18 November 2004 the SCC delivered its judgment convicting the applicant and his co-accused. Chief Superintendent testified that he believed the applicant was a member of the IRA. When asked to identify his sources, he claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK’s sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him (Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000-II). The prosecution, which had no access to the confidential source material, opposed the applicant's request on the basis of the principle of informer privilege. The SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK's evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial in favour of the prosecution. Chief Superintendent PK produced files which, he asserted, informed him that the accused were members of the IRA. The SCC found that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. Later, in weighing PK’s evidence, the SCC confirmed that it had excluded any information to which it had become privy during its review of the files he had produced to the court. The court also noted that the demeanour of PK was such that the court was persuaded that he was an “honest and reliable witness’. He had 25 years’ service as a police officer most of which was devoted to combating subversion. Packaging from a Rayovac torch and a receipt dated 10 October 2002 were later found in the Nissan Micra when it was searched. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The court accepted a piece of paper containing the drawing of a key and a telephone number which the court accepted was that of MB, the owner of the Nissan Almera with the false number plates. During an earlier search of the co-accused’s home, police had found documents which contained notes of the actions and movements of a number of elected politicians from different political parties. The trial court accepted that the documentation established that the applicant was, at the very least, acquainted with the driver of the Transit van (PB) and the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) Each man failed to answer a variety of questions which, the court maintained, were very material to the investigation of the offences with which each was charged. It was accepted by the defence that each accused was afforded all the rights and privileges to which they were legally entitled during their detention. The trial court had no doubt as to the materiality of a vast number of the questions put to each accused and it was clear that each had made no effort whatsoever to answer them. For example, each accused was asked to affirm or deny that he was a member of the IRA. Each was asked whether he knew the men arrested at Corke Abbey on the night of 10 October 2002. The court was satisfied that their silence amounted to corroboration of the belief evidence given by Chief Superintendent PK. It was persuaded beyond all reasonable doubt that each of the accused was guilty of charged. The trial court added, that it was not convinced that, standing alone, either the activities at Corkes Abbey or the documentation found upon a search of their homes necessarily indicated activities or membership of an unlawful organisation.  applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (‘CCA’) was refused. applicant sought leave to appeal against his conviction to the CCA claiming that the trial court had erred in law. He objected to any review by the trial judges, as adjudicators of guilt or innocence, of material underlying the belief of Chief Superintendent PK on the grounds that to do so was unlawful and contrary to the case-law of this Court. The CCA found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the believe of the Chief Superintendent. The CCA held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. A statement to the contrary was explicitly made in the judgment itself. The trial court had noted that there had been no serious challenge to the prosecution evidence of the facts, connections and associations so found. The CCA also considered that the events at Corke Abbey and an association with those events, the vehicles and the contents of the vehicles, the materials found during searches as well as the meetings between both accused at the time when the applicant’s house was being searched, were all matters within the ambit of the phrase ‘movements, actions, activities, or associations on the part of an accused person’ The court agreed that the evidence of the two men was sufficient to prove that they were members of the IRA. The case was referred to the Supreme Court, who ruled that the right to silence was not an absolute right. The court found that the public interest outweighed the public's right to know about the alleged involvement of the men in the bombing of the Iraqi Embassy in Baghdad. The judge's decision was made on the basis that the facts of the case were in line with the public’s interest in knowing about the bombing. The Court of Appeal ruled that this was the case and that the case should be referred back to the CCA for further proceedings. The decision was upheld. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court. The CCA rejected the submission that the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence. The applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the trial Judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents or the documents. It was clear that there were no such documents: if the SCC had found documents of assistance to the applicant, its answer would have been different. The undisclosed documents were demonstrably not determinative as the applicant had suggested. The material in this article does not represent all of the. material contained therein. The SCC was persuaded beyond any doubt by the belief evidence of PK that the accused were members of the IRA as charged. It was also satisfied, having heard abundant evidence which included sightings of the applicant and his co-accused together in the middle of the night when the applicant's home was being searched, that they were ‘well known’ to each other. The court noted that each availed of the opportunity to consult a solicitor before and in the course of several police interviews. The video-recordings of the interviews were shown to the trial court. It was clear to the court that each was deliberately and offensively ignoring all that was being asked of them. The court was satisfied that not only were the relevant statutory provisions invoked and adequately explained to each accused but each was given an opportunity to protest in the event that he had not understood that explanation, an opportunity which was ignored. The defence accepted that each accused was afforded all the rights and privileges to which they were legally entitled during their detention and, in particular, that each of them had full access to legal advice. The trial court had no doubt as to the materiality of a vast number of the questions put to each accused and it was clear that each had made no effort whatsoever to answer them. The CCA found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the belief. of the Chief Superintendent. It was satisfied that a restriction on the ability to cross-examine the Chief. Superintendent, arising from his claim of privilege, did not ipso facto constitute a breach of Article 38 of the Constitution. The court held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. A statement to the contrary was explicitly made in the judgment itself, the court said. The court was fully entitled to have found that the applicant was associated with the events at Corke Abbey and its conclusion, in the circumstances, was a safe and valid one. The evidence established a complete and utter failure to answer any question at all and the court made a finding on that failure. The trial court’s entitlement to draw inferences arose, precisely, from that failure, and the inferences were correctly and validly drawn. The trial court’s finding that the foregoing facts and inferences, when taken together with the belief evidence, established beyond reasonable doubt that the IRA were involved, was upheld. name: Marcin Bereza
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was brought by a Polish national, Mr Marcin Bereza (‘the applicant’), on 18 September 2006. He was arrested on suspicion of murder, extortion, robbery and drug trafficking committed while acting as part of an organised criminal group. On 17 October 2005 a bill of indictment was lodged with the Warsaw Regional Court. There were 57 defendants in the case, all charged with numerous counts of attempted murder, extortion, robbery, drug trafficking, theft, illegal possession of firearms, battery and forgery committed in an organised criminal group. The prosecutor requested the court to hear evidence from 435 witnesses, including 5 key witnesses, and to take another 627 pieces of evidence listed therein. The courts repeated the grounds previously given for the applicant’s continued detention. They relied especially on the complexity of the case and the large number of co-accused. On 4 March 2008 the applicant was released from Detention Centre.

On 7 February 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard by the Court's Fourth Section. The Warsaw Regional Court lodged a bill of indictment against the applicant on 17 October 2005. 57 defendants in the case were charged with numerous counts of attempted murder, extortion, robbery, drug trafficking, theft, illegal possession of firearms, battery and forgery committed in an organised criminal group. In September 2006 the applicant asked for the appointment of a new lawyer on the ground that he did not ‘trust’ G.R, his court-appointed defence counsel. On 4 March 2008 the applicant was released from Detention Centre.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits and admissibility. The application was declared partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s detention in police custody for ten days without being brought before a judge to the Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant was born in 1964 and is currently detained in Midyat prison. name: Hasan Demirkaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31721/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into police custody in İzmir on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (Kurdistan Workers' Party) In his police statement, N.S. stated that he was a member of the PKK and that the applicant had acted as a PKK courier and helped him in certain illegal activities. On 18 January 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Izmir State Security Court charged the applicant and fifteen others with aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The charges were brought under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713 (the anti-terrorist law). During the trial, the applicant denied any connection with the PKK. On 20 June 2002 the Izmir State security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months' imprisonment. On 10 October 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal. It concluded that the applicant’s police statement, in which he had admitted to his involvement in the PKK, had been confirmed by other evidence in the case file.

On 16 March 2010 the applicant’s complaint concerning the right to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of detention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

name: Yaşar Kanbur
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The Court awarded the applicant 100,000 French francs (approximately 15,000 euros) in compensation. The applicant was sentenced to death, and then commuted his sentence to life imprisonment. The judgment was subject to appeal and the case is still pending. On 28 May 2004 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the death penalty had been abolished during the course of the proceedings. On 23 December 2004 the Ankara Assize Court resumed the trial. On 3 October 2006, at its fourteenth hearing, the Ankaraassize Court delivered its judgment and sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment pursuant to Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The case is apparently still pending before the Court  of Cassation. It is alleged that the applicant was the first person in Turkey to be convicted of murder in peacetime. He was also the first to be sentenced to death by hanging.

The case originated in an application (no. 9984/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 14 February 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was awarded the applicant 100,000 French francs (approximately 15,000 euros) in compensation. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Yaşar Kanbur (“the applicant”), on 4 February 2003. The first-instance court quashed the judgment on the ground that the death penalty had been abolished during the course of the proceedings. On 23 December 2004 the Ankara Assize Court resumed the trial. On 3 October 2006, at its fourteenth hearing, the court sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment pursuant to Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The case is apparently still pending before the Court of Cassation. The applicant was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 15 years and a maximum of 30 years. The sentence was imposed on the basis of Article 146, which allows courts to abolish the death sentence in peacetime. The death penalty was abolished in Turkey on 28 May 2004.

name: Ziemowit Hermanowicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44581/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Krupski Młyn. He was charged with several offences of fraud. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the convention. The court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application. The case was brought under the 2004 Act, which entered into force on 17 September 2004. The applicant filed a complaint about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time in respect of the criminal proceedings instituted against him. The Gliwice Regional Court dismissed his complaint on 12 March 2008. The proceedings are still pending before the Tarnowskie Góry District Court. The application was dismissed because the applicant failed to prove that he had suffered any damage or incurred any pecuniary losses on account of the length of the proceedings. The case was adjourned on 9 March 2007 because the defendant's co-accused's counsel had not been properly summoned.

name: Antun Petrovic
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 5 December 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20458/92) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Antun Petrovic, on 3 August 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31) Antun Petrovic claimed a parental leave allowance (Karenzurlaubsgeld) in 1989. His claim was turned down by the local employment office on the ground that only mothers could claim such an allowance. He appealed against that decision to the Vienna Regional Employment Office (Landesarbeitsamt) On 18 August 1989 he lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 October 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Marxer, Mr Laimer and Mr Okresek. Constitutional Court declined to accept the complaint for adjudication. It added that the legislature had a certain amount of time in which to adapt new rules to changes in society. Section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below. The court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. However, it added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments, the applicant's complaint was unfounded. It said that the legislation had been given enough time to adapt to the new rules.

The case was heard in private on 12 December 1991.

name: Mehmet Reşit Arslan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31320/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Ms S. Gürcan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the alleged ill‑treatment of the applicant to the Government. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Mehmet Reşit Arslan (“the applicant”), on 21 August 2001. The applicant was convicted of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The first-instance court held forty-six hearings between 12 July 1993 and 6 March 2000. In his petition, he maintained that the judgment of the first- instance court was based on his police statements which had been taken under torture. On 21 March 2001 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The applicant was sentenced to death in 2000. He died in 2008 at the age of 67. He was buried in Istanbul's Ataturk International Airport, with a guard of honour.

The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the alleged ill‑treatment of the applicant and the length of the proceedings to the Government. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the Proceedings before the Court. The applicant was convicted of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The applicant maintained that his statements had been taken under torture while in police custody. The first-instance court did not list the applicant's statements taken by the police as evidence, having regard to the doctors' reports. It nevertheless convicted the applicant holding that other evidence corroborated his statements to the police. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 6 March 2000. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The case is still pending in the High Court of Justice of Turkey, which has the power to impose the death penalty.

name: Ruslan Kurkaev
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10424/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been detained for a period of ninety-one days in an overcrowded room at the Foreigners' Department of the Istanbul Security Headquarters. On 29 September 2009 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The Russian Government did not exercise their right to intervene in the case. The Turkish Government was represented by their Agent. The applicant had been held in the men's section of the Foreigners' Department of the Istanbul Security Headquarters, which measured 220 square metres. There were three toilets, two showers, twenty bunk beds, a television, two telephones, two air conditioners and a cafeteria. According to the Government all the rooms were sufficiently lit and ventilated. Breakfast, lunch and dinner were served every day. Asylum seekers could be visited by their relatives in the visitors' room. Those who needed medical help were taken to the local State hospital and their medical expenses were born by the State. In support of his complaints the applicant presented drawings of the facility and referred to reports of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a gynaecologist, was arrested and taken into police custody at his medical practice on 19 October 1999. He alleges that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. In particular, he complains of having received electric shocks, of having been suffocated, and of being beaten and threatened. He also alleges that during the first three days of his detention, he had been deprived of food and medication and prevented from sleeping. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. The application was rejected by the Istanbul Court of Appeal and the Turkish Supreme Court of Human Rights. The case was dismissed by the Turkish High Court of Justice and the Court of Appeals on 24 May 2000. The judge ruled that the applicant had not been deprived of his constitutional rights. He was sentenced to two years in prison, but was released on 26 November 1999.

The case originated in an application (no. 11564/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a gynaecologist, was born in 1956 and lives in İzmir. He was arrested and taken into police custody at his medical practice on 19 October 1999. In the course of an investigation into the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), an illegal armed organisation, the applicant’s name was mentioned by a few detainees suspected of membership of that organisation and a convicted confessor (itirafcı)0 as having provided assistance to that organisation. He alleges that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. In its decision the prosecution noted that none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events. None of the medical reports, dated 19 October 1999, 23 October 1999 and 25 October 1999 save for one dated 11 November 1999, i.e. fifteen days after the events, noted any physical findings of ill-treatment.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors had led to their father’s death. In each case they alternatively invoked a breach of Articles 8, 13 and 14. The application was declared partly inadmissible on 18 December 2012 as being manifestly ill-founded as regards the complaints against the United Kingdom and the complaints under Article 14 of the Convention. The Government of the UK, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36, did not make use of this right. The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U. from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany where he arrived the following day. The applicant apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment. He explained that when treating the deceased he had committed a grave mistake with fatal outcome that resulted from the confusion between the drugs pethidine and diamorphine. The applicant was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. The criminal proceedings were instituted against U. in the United Kingdom and Germany. U. was found to have satisfied the requirements generally expected from locum doctors working for the TCN and had completed the compulsory induction process all clinicians had to undergo before they could be assigned to clinical shifts. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the UK established as the cause of Mr Gray’S death diammorphine poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication. Cambridgeshire Constabulary made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) on 5 March 2008. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany. The Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray pursuant to Article 152 § 2 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure in conjunction with Articles 222 and 7 § 2 no. 1 of theGerman Criminal Code. In July 2008 German and British police officers visited U. at his surgery in Witten, Germany, and informed him that criminal investigations were pending against him. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. The originals of the protocols of the witness hearings conducted as well as the material obtained in the course of the investigations were handed over to Cambridgeshire police. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. Cambridgeshire Constabulary requested the German public prosecution authorities to assure that no criminal proceedings would be instituted against U. in Germany prior to finalisation of the investigations in the United Kingdom. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U’’'s treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. The German prosecution authorities had informed Cambridgeshy Constabulary in reply to a similar request made over the phone that day that they had been obliged by operation of law to institute preliminary criminal proceedings against U in Germany and that they were also obliged under German criminal procedure to grant counsel for the accused. U. was arrested for allegedly having caused the death of Mr Gray with an overdose of morphine. On 12 March 2009 the Colchester Magistrates’ Court issued a European Arrest Warrant (‘EAW’) against U. U. did not have a criminal record, had made a full confession and had apologised to the victim’s relatives. Despite the fact that an ampoule with a fatal dose of morphine had been included in the care box, U. had declared that he would accept the envisaged sentence of 9 months in prison. Following previous discussions with the public prosecution authorities, U., represented by counsel, had expressed his intention to accept the sentence. A draft of the penal order was attached to the application. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation on 13 March 2009. The CPS asked the Ministry of Justice of the Land of North Rhine-Westphalia for information why the EAW had not yet been executed. U. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment and had thus violated basic principles of the medical profession, according to the court's decision. The court ruled that the probation period for U. was two years starting from the date the penal order became final. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued a penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters (2002/584/JI) Hamm Higher Regional Court declared U’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. No appeal having been lodged by U., the penal order of 20 March 2009 became final in accordance with Article 410 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure (see Relevant domestic and international law and practice below) Criminal investigations in the United Kingdom were discontinued. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. U. was reprimanded for having disregarded the standards of the medical profession. There was no need to suspend or revoke U.’s licence to practice medicine in Germany and. discontinued the proceedings regarding U.'s fitness to practice. The case was referred to the German authorities for further investigation in the wake of Mr Gray's death. The German authorities decided not to extradite U. as a consequence of the decision. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. U.D. in particular for having committed a grave error in the treatment of Mr Gray, and fined him 7,000 EUR. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants by consent orders of December 2009, January and August 2010. The GMC Fitness to Practice Panel considered that U. had breached several of the basic principles of good medical practice and decided to formally strike U.’s name from the medical register.

An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. The latter returned the verdict that the deceased had been unlawfully killed as a consequence of the inadequate treatment administered by U.D. Subsequent investigations and proceedings were instituted in the United Kingdom following Mr. Gray’s death. In 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cambridge PCT. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants by consent orders of December 2009, January and August 2010.

name: Richard Anderson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19859/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Glasgow. He is an advocate by profession. He owned a flat in a tenement building in Edinburgh. In 1988, a fire occurred in the building which damaged part of the applicant’s flat. The applicant refused to pay the council for his share of the repair costs. The council brought proceedings in the Sheriff Court (the civil court of general jurisdiction). The applicant brought proceedings against commercial property company and the city council. He alleged that the statutory notices were invalid on grounds of fraud and illegal conspiracy. By judgments of 17 February 1999, the Sheriff Court rejected the applicant’s claims. The case was heard in the Outer House of the Court of Session. The Lord Ordinary granted the first defenders leave to reclaim (appeal) to the Inner House against the interlocutor of 22 September 1998 in so far as it related to the disclosure of documents. This was done when the first Defenders failed to appear in court. The applicant was then informed by the court that he was required to intimate a copy of the closed record to the relevant sheriff clerk. On 26 February 1998, the court gave him leave to do so. The first defenders failed to apply for a hearing. Inner House directed the parties to lodge their grounds of appeal within 28 days. The appeal was heard on 21 June 2002. On 4 November 2003, the Inner House refused the applicant’s motion for leave to amend his appeal. However, it allowed him to abandon his appeal against the second defenders and proceed only against the first defenders. The application was dismissed on 4 September 2002 by the Outer House. In a written judgment, the Lord Ordinary found the applicant's claims to be unfounded and unspecified. The case was listed for 18 and 19 November 2003. It was heard by the Inner Court and the Outer Court. The applicant was found liable for the first defenders’ costs on 18 December 2003. The appeal was unanimously dismissed on 11 December 2003, the court finding that the applicant’s pleadings lacked specification. The applicant also sought to bring proceedings in the Court of Session against the solicitors acting for the council in the Sheriff Court proceedings. on 18 and 19 November 2003. Complaints made in relation to solicitors and advocates representing the council were dismissed by their respective professional bodies and then by the Scottish Legal Services Ombudsman on 13 November 2001 and 4 July 2003, respectively. The application was dismissed on 2 November 2003 and the appeal was dismissed two weeks later.

name: Zekeriya Karaman
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that references to his participation in a criminal offence in a judgment rendered against separately prosecuted co-suspects violated his right to be presumed innocent. The Turkish Government, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36 of the convention, did not make use of this right. The application was communicated to the Government on 18 October 2012 and the Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Court has ruled in favour of the applicant in this case. In 1999 a similar association was founded in Germany under the name of Deniz Feneri Dernegi e.V. (hereinafter ‘Deniz Fengi’) by G., one of the other shareholders and managing directors of Euro 7 Fernseh- und Marketing GmbH. During that programme, broadcast in Turkey and in Germany, the association reported on charitable aid projects being run by it and appealed for monetary donations. In 2006 the Frankfurt am Main prosecution authorities (Staatsanwaltschaft) launched investigations against the applicant and several co-suspects, including G., on suspicion of fraudulently using the majority of funds donated to the associations. The court’s findings were primarily based on confessions made by T., E. and G. following a plea bargain reached between the court, the prosecution authorities and the defence. T. had contributed to the fraudulent misrepresentation by, inter alia, fabricating minutes of virtual association meetings of Deniz Feneri in order to conceal the unauthorised use of donated funds from the tax authorities. E., for his part, also acting upon instructions from G., had omitted to record the actual use of the donations in the association's official accounts and had documented them in separate unofficial accounts (Nebenbuchhaltung) The court was therefore satisifed that G. had not been at the top of the criminal organisation’d hierarchy but had received orders from its leaders. The most relevant passages of the judgment in parts II to V of its reasoning read as follows: “It was neither the association’s chairman nor the registered members of the association [Deniz Feneri] who decided on the use of funds” The accused G. and the persons in charge of Kanal 7 in Turkey were aware that donations collected would only partly be used for charitable purposes or social projects. Since the year 2002 it had been the intention of G. to also use a large part of the collected funds for economic activities, in particular for the start-up financing of entrepreneurial projects of private-law companies in which G. or the separately prosecuted Zekeriya Karaman, ..., ... and ... became shareholders. The circumstances of the case have been established (Sachverhalt) on the basis of the confessions made by the accused and further evidence obtained in the course of the trial as set out in the record of the hearing. ... The Chamber did not follow G.’s submissions that he alone had decided on the unauthorised use of donated funds without consulting the persons behind the scenes in Turkey. The accused T. is guilty of fraud committed in his capacity as successive joint offender (in sukzessiver Mittäterschaft) pursuant to Articles 263 and 25 § 2 of the German Criminal Code. (p. 25) T.’s confession was not limited to his own participation in the commission of the offence. He also revealed his knowledge regarding the background and in particular concerning the persons behind the scenes. In the hierarchy he was placed far below G. and the responsible persons in Turkey. By keeping unofficial accounts [E.] made a significant contribution to the functioning of the overall system. (p. 30) T. and T. acted in accordance with instructions they had received from Kanal 7, in particular from Zek. G. had previously attempted to prevent [E]. from testifying before the investigative authorities by establishing contact with his first counsel and members of his family. The applicant argued that the references in the reasoning of the Regional Court’s judgment of 17 September 2008 to his role in the fraudulent use of the donated funds had violated the principle of the presumption of innocence. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as inadmissible (file no. 2 BvR 2540/08) by a decision of 3 September 2009. The Constitutional Court reiterated its established case-law according to which no measures effectively amounting to a penalty could be taken against an accused without his guilt having been established beforehand in the course of a fair trial. The finding of guilt had to become final before it could be held against the person concerned. However, in the context of criminal proceedings the presumption. of innocence did not prevent the law-enforcement authorities from making an assessment. as to whether and to what degree a person could be suspected of having committed a criminal offence. A request for legal assistance was sent to the Turkish authorities on 20 January 2009 with a view to obtaining the applicant’s examination in Turkey. No information was submitted to the Court as regards compliance with that request. The Frankfurt am Main Regional Court, by an order dated 19 August 2013, opened the main hearing in the proceedings against the applicant. These are apparently still pending. The applicant could not be regarded as guilty on the basis of that judgment and was still protected by the principle of the presumption of innocence. The fact that the establishment of the facts by the Regional Court not only concerned the accused, who were convicted at the end of the proceedings, but also the applicant was an inevitable consequence of the fact that in complex criminal proceedings it was hardly ever possible to conduct and terminate the proceedings.

The case originated in an application (no. 17103/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Zekeriya Karaman alleged that references to his participation in a criminal offence in a judgment rendered against separately prosecuted co-suspects violated his right to be presumed innocent. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Turkish Government, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36, did not make use of this right. In 1999 a similar association was founded in Germany under the name of Deniz Feneri Dernegi e.V. In 2006 the Frankfurt am Main prosecution authorities (Staatsanwaltschaft) launched investigations against the applicant and several co-suspects. Two of the applicant’s co-accused were convicted of aggravated fraud. G. and T. were sentenced to prison sentences of five years and ten months and two years and nine months respectively, while E. was given a suspended prison sentence of one year and 10 months. The full judgment, with the complete reasoning, was subsequently delivered in writing between 17 September and the beginning of November 2008. G. and the applicant, among others, became shareholders in Deniz Feneri. At G.’s request, T. had contributed to the fraudulent misrepresentation by fabricating minutes of virtual association meetings. E. also acting upon instructions from G., had omitted to record the actual use of the donations in official accounts. The court was therefore satisifed that G. had not been at the top of the criminal organisation's hierarchy but had received orders from its leaders residing in Turkey. The judgment refers on several occasions to the role that the heads of a criminal organisation in Turkey played in connection with the use of donated funds for non-charitable purposes. Deniz Feneri's. names are mentioned numerous times in the judgment running to some thirty‑two pages. The most relevant passages of the judgment in parts II to V of its reasoning read as follows: “II. ... The accused G. and the persons in charge of Kanal 7 in Turkey were ... aware that donations collected in the German association’s. name would only partly be used for charitable purposes or social projects.’ “III. ... According to the entries in the unofficial accounts a total amount of 4,504,000 euros was handed over to the separately prosecuted Zekeriya Karaman. (p. 15) The circumstances of the case (Sachverhalt) have been established (steht fest) on the basis of the confessions made by the accused and further evidence obtained in the course of the trial as set out in the record of the hearing. The Chamber did not follow G.’s submissions that he alone had decided on the unauthorised use of donated funds without consulting the persons behind the scenes in Turkey. The accused T. is guilty of fraud committed in his capacity as successive joint offender (in sukzessiver Mittäterschaft) pursuant to Articles 263 and 25 § 2 of the German Criminal Code. T. was an executing organ rather than a decision maker (mehr ausführendes als bestimmendes Organ) ... By keeping unofficial accounts [E.] made a significant contribution to the functioning of the overall system. [T.’s] confession was not limited to his own participation in the commission of the offence. He also revealed his knowledge regarding the background and in particular concerning the persons behind the scenes. His knowledge was limited since G. and the people behind him deliberately granted him only a restricted insight. In the hierarchy he was placed far below G and the responsible persons in Turkey. (p. 29) The applicant lodged a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. He argued that the references in the reasoning of the Regional Court’s judgment of 17 September 2008 to his role in the fraudulent use of the donated funds had violated the principle of the presumption of innocence. In a decision of 3 September 2009, served on the applicant on 25 September 2009,. the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as inadmissible (file no. 2 BvR 2540/08). The Constitutional Court found that while defendants were not categorically prevented from challenging a judgment delivered in proceedings conducted against third persons, an applicant did have to be able to claim that his or her legitimate interests were directly affected by the impugned decision. The application was brought by the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court in 2009. The applicant could not be regarded as guilty on the basis of that judgment and was still protected by the principle of the presumption of innocence. A request for legal assistance was sent to the Turkish authorities on 20 January 2009 with a view to obtaining the applicant’s examination in Turkey. No information was submitted to the Court as regards compliance with that request. The main hearing in the proceedings against the applicant is apparently still pending. The application has been dismissed by the German Court of Appeal. The appeal against the decision to dismiss the appeal was rejected by the High Court of Justice on 9 August 2013.

name: Nicholas Wells
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63477/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in Cambridgeshire. His wife died on 6 May 1997 leaving four children, the last born in 1987. He applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. The applicant received child benefit in the sum of GBP 150.20 per month. He was told that he had no right of appeal since his claim had not been considered by a decision maker. The Chamber to which the case had been allocated, decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

Mr Nicholas Wells (‘the applicant’) was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. By a partial decision of 10 September 2002, the Court decided to adjourn the applicant's complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. He received child benefit in the sum of GBP 150.20 per month. The applicant was told that he had no right of appeal since his claim had not been considered by a decision maker.
