train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39482/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. On 22 March 1989 at Norwich Crown Court the applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 14 May 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). Nugent and Gray were charged with conspiracy to commit murder. The pair were accused of conspiring to pay off a man who had broken his leg. The two men pleaded guilty to lesser charges and were released. The case was later thrown out of court by the Court of Appeal. The judge ruled that the pair were not guilty of any crime, but they had provided evidence of a conspiracy to break a man’s leg to cover up a crime. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty, but allowed the pair to go free on a suspended sentence. The trial was adjourned until a later date, but the verdict was not overturned. The Government says the evidence which was not disclosed at first instance, but which was disclosed prior to the applicant’s appeal, fell into two categories. The first type of evidence derived from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry to store and cross-reference all the information obtained in the course of the inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. In respect of some of the items in this article, the Government submitted that, following the applicant's conviction, and in the light of developments in the common-law duty of disclosure (see below), the prosecution decided that the data stored on the computer system did amount to disclosable material. Document no. 580 subsequently came into the applicant’s possession. It is a letter, dated 12 April 1988, from a firm of solicitors acting for Gray addressed to Detective Chief Inspector Baldry of the Suffolk Constabulary. “... Further to our several discussions concerning Mr Gray, you will of course be aware that I did visit him in Leicester Prison on 26 March. He has requested a transfer either to Brixton Prison or Wormwood Scrubs if this is at all possible.” ‘I should be grateful if you would let me know whether there is any possibility of Mr Gray receiving a transfer.’ The Court of Appeal dismissed Gray's appeal on 29 March 1994. Although the summing-up should have included a ‘Lucas’ direction, no miscarriage of justice had occurred. Nugent’s dishonesty was made perfectly plain to the jury. The money actually paid was in our view out of proportion to a plot simply to ‘duff up’ the victim. The applicant believed that an inducement was promised to Gray by the prosecuting authorities in exchange for his testifying against him. In addition to the above letter, which the applicant claimed supported his hypothesis, he referred to the fact that his tariff of imprisonment under the life sentence had been set at twenty-five years, but was subsequently reduced. Stephen Gray shot and killed Mr Nugent and had his tariff set at eleven years. Runham, who had provided the murder weapon and drove the get-away car, received a tariff of sixteen years. In April 1999 the Home Office wrote to Runham refusing to reduce his tariff. The Government denied that any inducement was offered to Gray. Under cover of a letter dated 27 June 2001, they sent to the Court undated statements from three senior officers in the Suffolk Constabulary who had been involved in the murder investigation. The court will hear the case from September 10 to 14, 2013. The trial is due to last four days. Detective Chief Inspector Abrahams, also now retired, said in his statement: “I did not personally offer Gray any inducement or arrangement relating to his sentence. Nor did I have any discussions with his legal representative with regard to his prison sentence” Gray was arrested at Mildenhall Police Station on 23 January 1988 after which the murder management team was joined by Mr Christopher Yule of the Crown Prosecution Service, Ipswich, who advised on all legal aspects of the case. Mr Yule was later joined by David Penry-Davey QC and Mr David Lamming of Counsel. I am not aware that any representations were made to the trial judge concerning any reduction in Gray’s tariff. If this had been the case then the application would have had to be made through prosecuting counsel. Gary Runham did the groundwork in planning Nugent’s murder and propositioned Gray at a later stage to do the actual killing. The jury unanimously found Dowsett guilty of murder and he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Gray appeared as a prosecution witness but Runham didn’t. The matter was investigated by an outside Police Force and was found by the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions] and the PCA to be totally unsubstantiated. The above is to the best of my recollection. I do not know what tariffs were set by the Judge in his sentencing of all three defendants but I assume credit was given for Gray and Runham’S guilty pleas.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 66484/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that in proceedings in which a court had imposed a penalty of solitary confinement on him he had not received a hearing by an impartial tribunal. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 10 January 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant lodged an appeal against the decision of 24 June 2009 to reject his appeal. He submitted that he had been penalised for exercising his right to freedom of expression. On 22 July 2009 the Gdańsk Court of Appeal quashed the decision. It observed that section 49 of the Courts Act conferred on a judge the power to immediately apply measures necessary to ensure the peaceful conduct of a hearing in a courtroom. But the case-law of the Supreme Court had made it clear that these powers could not be used in situations where insults or disparaging statements about a judge or a court had been made in writing, in a context different from that of maintaining order in the courtroom. Judge E.O. felt offended by the allegations made in the applicant’s letter. He was envisaging bringing criminal proceedings against the applicant for defamation punishable under Article 212 of the Criminal Code. In its reply dated 29 September 2009, the Gdansk Court of Appeal stated that it had not found any grounds to discipline the judge. It was true that the judge had mistakenly referred to the applicant's non‑existent ‘wife’ in one paragraph of his initial decision instead of his mother, on whose situation the applicant had relied in his application. But that did not suffice to pursue disciplinary proceedings against him, the court said.

train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were detained in Elazığ Prison in Turkey. On 14 March 1999 the police raided a flat which was used as a cell by Hezbollah in Mardin. The police officers seized, among other things, three computer hard disks during the operation. The Applicants' names were recorded on these hard disks as members of Hezbollah. On 13 January 2005 the Court joined the applications. It decided to declare the applications partly inadmissible and to communicate the complaints concerning the lack of prompt and detailed information on the nature and cause of the accusations. The applicants were accused of being members of Hezbollah. They were convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months in prison. The applicants appealed the decision, but it was upheld by the Court of Cassation on 27 May 2002. The court noted that the applicants' police statements were supported by information gathered from the archive of the organisation and further evidence. They denied the content of their police statements alleging that they were taken under duress. They had no idea as to how their names had appeared on the computer hard disks that were seized during the raid in Mardin. The application was rejected by the High Court of Justice on 1 July 2006.

name: Umar Karatepe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29766/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the treatment to which they had been subjected by police offices during their arrest had amounted to a breach of Article 3 of the convention. On 8 December 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of. the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by two Turkish nationals, Mr Umar Karatepe and Ms Sevil Ulaş, on 22 August 2003. The applicants were taken to the Bakırköy State Hospital for a medical examination. The doctor noted that the first applicant had two scratches on his right elbow and a bruise on his back. The second applicant had the presence of a bruises on her left elbow. The applicants refused to sign this report. The report further concluded that both applicants were unfit to work for three days. Following this medical examination, the applicants were released and filed a criminal complaint with the Bak Turkish police. On 3 September 2001 the Bak Turkey Forensic Institute delivered its final report in respect of the applicants. It was stated that the applicants had several bruises and scratches on their body. An Istanbul woman claimed she was beaten up by police officers during her arrest. The Istanbul Regional Administrative Court set aside a decision not to prosecute the officers. The court said the investigation into the applicants’ allegations was inadequate and ordered a new investigation. The investigator concluded that the medical reports merely indicated the presence of scratches on the arms and hands of the complainants and that there was no indication of physical violence. He therefore concluded that no permission should be given for prosecution of the accused police officers. A new investigation was carried out by the District Governor’s office. The new investigator found that the allegations were not corroborated by evidence and therefore no permission was given for the prosecution. On 15 July 2002 the Bahçelievler District Governor refused authorisation for the prosecution of the accused police officers. The applicants appealed against this decision. On 17 December 2002 the Eyüp Assize Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal. This decision was notified to the applicants on 26 February 2003. The accused officers were not charged with any offence. The case was settled out of court and the accused were released on bail. The trial was adjourned until February 2004. The verdict was handed down by a jury on 26 October 2004. name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. On 16 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention). The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Saint-Didier-au-Mont-d’Or. The applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court. They were charged with having deceived the social security scheme and the relevant health insurance offices through fraudulent practices. In a judgment of 30 March 2001 the Lyon Criminal Court held that the prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty. The applicant was accordingly acquitted. The Principal Public Prosecutor lodged an appeal against the judgment on 20 April 2001, availing himself of the two-month time-limit granted to him for that purpose by Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the time- limit reserved for him was incompatible with the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the time available to the Principal Public Prosecutor for lodging an appeal was incompatible with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In a judgment of 13 March 2002 the Lyons Court of Appeal dismissed that argument. The applicant was sentenced to a suspended term of two years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay a fine of 120,000 euros (EUR) and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. He was also ordered, jointly and severally with his brother, to pay the sum of EUR 442,573.13 in compensation for all the damage found to have been sustained by the civil parties.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49490/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant appealed and the case was dismissed in December 2008. The application was dismissed under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right of a trial. The case is still pending in the Court of Appeals of the Republic of Poland.

name: Bünyamin İnan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39428/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The case was brought by police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The judge ruled in favour of the applicant company and the Austrian Government. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy. Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon. She was kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son, abducted by the authorities. Her case was so well documented that Austria, in the form of the normally very strict Federal Refugee Office, granted her asylum quickly and without red tape. But then this country revealed its other side. The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Traiskirchen centre. One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. ‘Please help us!’ pleaded the women. Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’ Elaine B. from Cameroon demanded an interview with the head of the Traiskirchen [branch of the] Gendarmerie. She placed a pair of torn red underpants on the interview room table and described ‘through her tears’ how a drunken security officer had pursued her for days. Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. The man who claimed he had sex with the woman is interviewed as the presumed perpetrator. He claims it was entirely consensual. However, he doesn’t recognise Elaine in a photograph. He had offered to buy the woman a drink in the bakery. According to him, she followed him out of her own accord, undressed in front of him, took hold of his penis, inserted it and then got dressed again. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. Saleswoman R.Z.: ‘She gave him a kiss. She was fairly young, I’d say between 20 and 25. The two of them were talking quietly. I couldn’t describe the woman’ No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. And what of the only piece of physical evidence, the torn red underpants? ‘These have no evidentiary value’ according to Judge K. Why not? Because the accused said that the underpants had been ‘beige’ Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She should study this case. She has the right to give instructions. She bears the political responsibility if this woman, in addition to everything else, faces charges.” Judge I.K. alleges in the judgment – without giving any reasons – that the asylum seeker was driven by the basest motives. “The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment” Vienna Regional Court found against the applicant company. The court held that the impugned statements had constituted defamation under the freedom of speech law. It considered that by publishing the impUGned. statements it had merely expressed criticism, protected by the freedom. of speech. The hearing was adjourned in order to hear three witnesses proposed by the applicant. company. But on 12 December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation. proceedings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed. The third witness proposed did not appear. The Regional Court refused to hear other witnesses proposed as it considered that those persons could not make any statements relevant to the proceedings. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. According to the article, the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced, whereas the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. K.’s assertion that she had been the victim of an assault had not been excluded but because it contradicted the statements of witnesses it had been considered to be partially implausible. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. There was hardly a more severe accusation which could be levied against a judge. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. The judgment had clearly indicated the court’s reluctance to accept the version of events given by K. also. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant's company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. It was necessary to protect public confidence in the judiciary against destructive attacks that were essentially unfounded. Taking these principles into account, the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The judge should have taken into account the broad public attention the article had received and the consequences it had had for the claimant.

The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. An error in the translation of that statement could not be excluded, but that did not allow the conclusion that there had been no basis in the file for the above finding of Judge I.K. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant's company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The judge ruled that the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The court also ruled that it was necessary to protect public confidence in the judiciary against destructive attacks that were essentially unfounded. The appeal was dismissed and the judgment was upheld on June 19, 2006.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40518/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged under Article 5 of the Convention that he was not brought promptly before a judge. He further alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Diyarbakır State Security Court which tried and convicted him. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) By a decision of 10 April 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The applicant was arrested in September 1997 in Istanbul. He was handed over to the Siirt Police, in whose jurisdiction he had allegedly committed offences. He reiterated the confessions he had made in his statement at the Istanbul Police Headquarters. The applicant gave a detailed account of his involvement within the PKK and of the activities he had carried out on behalf of that organisation. He maintained that his police statements were correct and that he had nothing to add to them. The public prosecutor filed an indictment with the Diyarbakır State Security Court against the applicant and requested the court to sentence him pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The prosecutor accused the applicant of carrying out activities aimed at breaking up the unity of the State. He requested the court to sentence the applicant in accordance with Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The applicant’s appeal against the judgment was rejected by the Court of Cassation on 22 May 2001. The application was dropped by the Supreme Court of Justice on 2 May 2001 after the applicant was found not guilty of the charges against him. The appeal was dropped after the judge found the applicant not guilty by reason of his good conduct during the trial and commuted the sentence to life in prison.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39163/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that her detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) and to examine it simultaneously with the case of Łoś v Poland. The applicant was charged with fraud and forgery of documents, committed in an organised criminal group. The court found that the strong suspicion against her of having committed the serious offences and the severity of the anticipated sentence justified holding her in custody. Until 21 December 2006, the date on which the applicant was released, the Warszawa District Court held 44 hearings in the case. The judge found the request for prolongation of the applicant’s pre-trial detention justified; however, it prolonged it only by three months and not by six months. It added that it was possible for the trial court to examine all the evidence within the three‑month time-limit and that maximum efforts should be made to expedite the examination. On 21 December 2006 the applicant was released from the prison. The court pointed out that the three-month time-limit was sufficient for examining the evidence. The trial court was instructed to take all necessary measures in order to expedite the proceedings. The proceedings are still pending. The application for bail has been denied and the application has been adjourned until the end of the year. The appeal is expected to be heard by the Polish Supreme Court in December 2006. The case is currently being heard at the Court of Appeal in the town of Warszawa, Poland. The applicant has been granted bail and the case is pending at the Supreme Court of Poland.

name: Anna Young
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 60682/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant suffered from cerebral palsy, a disorder of the central nervous system which can inhibit voluntary muscle control. She used a wheelchair and could only walk a few steps with assistance. She did not have voluntary control of her bladder meaning that on occasion she either could not urinate for several hours or she urinated uncontrollably. She was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and was accorded an unconditional release date of 23 January 2000. The prison psychotherapist’s report of 31 January 2000 noted that the applicant had been referred in December 1999 given her distress and difficulties in coping with her imprisonment. It noted as follows: “Largely confined to a wheelchair, [the applicant] manifests obvious physical symptoms of cerebral palsy as well as somewhat less obvious mental ones. [The applicant] possesses an excellent vocabulary and a reasonably well-developed capacity to think logically that places her well in the highest range of mental functioning for those who have the condition from which she suffers” The report concluded: ‘The stay in [prison] appears to have been a sobering experience for her. It seems rather graphically to have brought home to her the consequences of some of her own actions’  applicant was detained in the medical wing of the prison since the normal prison cells were not wheelchair accessible. She claimed that she began to explain why she could not provide a sample but that her explanation was brushed aside. She was offered a cup of water, which she declined. She maintained that this was because she knew that the water would not assist because the problem was not whether her bladder was full or not but whether she had the motor control to provide a specimen on demand. She admitted, however, that she did not explain to them that she couldn't urinate as a result of her disability. She alleged that she was menstruating (the Government disputed this) but, in any event, she accepted that she didn't use her menstruation as an excuse. The applicant claims she was not asked about her disability or whether she had problems urinating. The matter was adjourned to the following week, to allow the relevant prison officer to attend to give evidence. In the meantime, the applicant was seen by a medical officer who certified her as fit to take part in the hearing. She did not inform the medical officer either that her disability had prevented her from providing a urine sample. The Government disputed the applicant’s account of this meeting. The applicant claimed that her request for legal representation was refused. The Governor did not ask her if there were any medical reasons why she should be assisted. The Governor found the charge of disobeying a lawful order to have been proven and sentenced the applicant to 14 additional days’ detention. She accepted that she did not inform the Governor during the adjudication hearing that her disability had prevented her from providing a urine sample. She expressed extreme distress at having to discuss her bodily functions and requested that the 14 more days be withdrawn. Her legal representatives could not contact her by telephone and were offered a visit after her initial release date. In default of which proceedings under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 would be pursued. The applicant was released on 26 January 2000. In his letter of 27 January 2000 to the applicant’s representatives (confirming a telephone conversation of 20 January 2000) The area manager was satisfied that the adjudication was conducted in a fair and proper manner. He noted that the applicant had not explained her difficulties to officers involved in the test process, nor availed herself of the opportunity subsequently to talk through the issues with the Governor. The applicant’s representatives complained to the Home Secretary about the prison adjudication matter. They received an acknowledgement dated 8 August 2000. That letter indicated that a medical officer had informed the Governor that she had been fit to appear and had made no comment to the governor that she was unable to comply with an order to provide a sample. The application was eventually thrown out in 2000.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant had taken care of her grandmother, who had fallen seriously ill, until some of the grandmother’s children had arrived from Somalia to take over the care of their mother. On 9 August 2005, three months before the applicant turned eighteen years old, she contacted the Danish Embassy in Nairobi with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in Denmark. The Immigration Service found that the applicant's residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii) According to the applicant, in June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. On 1 October 2007 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. It stated among other things: “There is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed” Immigration Service brought the case concerning section 17 and section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted. name: Ingo Hentschel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers who, owing to an inadequate investigation, had been neither identified nor punished. They complained under Article 13 that they had had no judicial remedy at their disposal to challenge the discontinuation and the ineffectiveness of the investigation. On 26 February 2016 the application was communicated to the Government by the applicants. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights in Berlin on 18 March 2016. After the match had ended the police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants. Some of these officers started hitting the spectators with their truncheons without any prior warning as soon as they reached them. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. The Government’s version of the subsequent events was that the blockade was lifted due to the aggressive behaviour of some of the spectators. The supporters’ conduct resulted in the arrest of one supporter and two police officers sustained minor injuries. The Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the. investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police. officers. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. On 14 October 2008 the public prosecutor reopened the investigation and ordered further enquiries. Subsequently, a further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. On 19 September 2011 the Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 19, 4 and 103 of the German Basic Law (Gylageerzwingungsverfahren) The applicants complained that the investigation had not been effective. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. They also filed criminal complaints in respect of assistance given in an official capacity in avoiding prosecution or punishment.

The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. A total of 227 police officers were deployed, including two squads – comprising eight to ten police officers each – of the Munich riot control unit (Unterstützungskommando). Police cordoned off the stands of supporters of one of the teams to prevent them from leaving the stadium and encountering supporters of the other team. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. On the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. After a few minutes the police pacified the situation and got the exiting spectators out. Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the. investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police. officers. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. The investigation was reopened in October 2008. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including 14 platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. They also filed criminal complaints in respect of assistance given in an official capacity in avoiding prosecution or punishment.

The applicant, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar (“the applicant”), was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. In 1998, after having heard witness statements and evaluated all relevant evidence, the Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the. Convention concerning the independence and impartiality of the İzmir State Security Court and the applicant’s. inability to examine or have examined witnesses were communicated to the Government. The applicant was accused of trafficking illegal drugs in Turkey. In 1997 the Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand in absentia. The applicant denied his involvement in the trafficking of illegal drugs. He requested to have certain witnesses, including his counsel in the United Kingdom, heard. The court rejected that request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the UK. In 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. He was acquitted by the court on 21 March 2003. The applicant was found guilty of smuggling illegal drugs in March 2003 and sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine. On 31 March 2003 the applicant appealed against that judgment. He argued that he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the İzmir State Security Court on 4 March 2004. The higher court indicated that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom. On 3 July 2008 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years and ten months of imprisonment.

name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. Uli Lutz, on 14 June 1982. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government’s memorial was lodged with the registry on 13 November 1986. The applicant informed the Registrar on the same day that he would not be filing a memorial. The Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr. P.-G. Pötz and Mr. V. Hohbach, Rechtsanwalt, Counsel. The President also granted the members of the Government's delegation leave to speak in German. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. On 9 December 1980, on the basis of the police. report, the Heil bronn Police Authority (Amt für öffentliche Ordnung) imposed on Mr. Lutz a fine (Geldbusse) of DM 125. The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz) and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49. On 24 August 1981, the District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they were time-barred. Its decision read as follows: “In the ‘regulatory offences’ matter (B) the court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings and order costs against the Treasury (Staatskasse)“ The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) Uli Lutz appealed against a fine for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. name: Helmut Malek
train_texts: The case stems from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was taken over by another Investigating Commissioner in August 1995. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the excessive length of the applicant’s detention and the length of criminal proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The application was lodged by a Polish national, Mr Sławomir Wierzba (“the applicant”), on 17 May 2004. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard in the Gdańsk District Court. The bill of indictment concerned five defendants and, in all, twelve charges were brought against them. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the applicant to trial from prison. The applicant was convicted in July 2004 and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. He has appealed, unsuccessfully, against refusals to release him and against decisions extending his detention. In all the decisions the courts stated that the grounds originally given for the applicant’s detention were still valid. The applicant lodged a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. He sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Gdańsk District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) The first-instance judgment in the case had been given before the 2004 Act came into force. The Gda’s Regional Court examined only the conduct of the appellate proceedings and found no delays for which the relevant court could be held responsible. The case was dismissed on 11 February 2005.

name: Kerem Durmaz
train_texts: The case originated in four applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. The applicants were accused of being members of an illegal armed organisation, namely the TIKP (the Revolutionary Communists’ Union of Turkey) They were also accused of taking part in demonstrations on 1 May and 8 March (Women’s Day) during which they had chanted slogans and distributed TIKB leaflets. The Court decided to join the applications, declared them partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicants’ right to a fair hearing to the Government. The applicants were found guilty under Article 169 of the Criminal Code for aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The first, second and third applicants were sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment, while the second applicant was sentenced to three years and nine months. The applicants appealed. The chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his opinion on the merits of the appeal on 24 December 1997. This opinion was not served on the applicants, but read out during the hearing which took place on 18 March 1998. On 20 May 1998 the court dismissed the applicants’ request for appeal. The decision was pronounced on 10 June 1998.

name: Thomas Wolfmeyer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5263/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) An Austrian national, Mr Thomas Wolfmeyer (‘the applicant’), was convicted under Article 209 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to six months' imprisonment suspended on probation. The applicant was represented by Mr H. Graupner, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The Austrian Government (’the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Innsbruck Court of Appeal partly granted the applicant's appeal, awarding him reimbursement of a total amount of 1,839.38 euros (EUR) for costs and expenses. It found that the Regional Court had wrongly applied Article 393a (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant's case had been the case in point before the Constitutional Court leading to the repeal of Article 209 of the Criminal Code. His case had to be treated as if Article 209 had never existed. Consequently, it could not be said that he was acquitted on grounds which occurred after the indictment. In addition EUR 748,38 were awarded for cash expenses.

name: Jan Nowiński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25924/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right of access to a court had been violated as a result of the court's refusal to accept his statement of claim. On 17 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Mr A. Bodnar from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. The applicant told the court that following his divorce he had had to move out from the apartment he had previously occupied at Gajowa Street in Wrocław. On 16 May 2005 the District Court ordered that the statement of claim be returned to the applicant. The court held that the applicant had failed to indicate his place of residence. It noted that a post-office box or a work address could not be considered as a place of residences within the meaning of Article 126 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The applicant paid the required court fee for lodging his interlocutory appeal. On 14 April 2006 the Wroc Polish Regional Court upheld that decision.

name: Raphael Rowe
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 12 March 1999. It originated in an application (no. 28901/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under former Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the President of the Court, Mrs E. Palm, Vice-President and Mr J.‑P. Costa and Mr M. Fischbach. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: Mr M. Eaton, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Deputy Legal Adviser, Agent, Mr R. Cranston, Solicitor-General, Mr J. Eadie, Barrister-at-Law, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Mr Cranston and also their replies to questions put by several of its members. The offences occurred during the night of 15 to 16 December 1988, a series of offences occurred in Surrey, England. The first, which may have occurred sometime after 1.30 a.m., involved an attack on two men in a parked car in a field in Fickleshall. Three masked robbers arrived at the Napier household in Oxted. Two of them went into Timothy Napier's room; one had a knife, the other a gun. Richard Napier (the father) was awakened by the third robber armed with a revolver. Both were told they would be shot if they did not cooperate. They attacked the robbers and forced them downstairs. In the struggle, TimothyNapier's arm was cut and an artery was severed. The other two robbers ransacked the room before all three fled taking Timothy's Toyota car. Hurburgh's car was found abandoned nearby. There was considerable interest in the above events, including publication in the national media of a reward of GBP 25,000 for information leading to the conviction of the offenders. Raphael Rowe, Michael Davis, Mark Jobbins, Norman Duncan and Shane Griffin lived at No. 25. Randolph Johnson visited the house from time to time, most recently to help repair the wiring and various electrical appliances, and he was said to have been there on the night of 15 December 1988. Rowe, Davis and Johnson were black. Duncan and Griffin sniffed glue on a regular basis. Duncan was arrested on 21 December. Kate Williamson, a 16-year-old school student and girlfriend of Rowe, produced to the police a number of items from the Spicer/Almond robbery, including two eternity rings, a yellow metal watch strap and a lady's watch. Johnson was arrested on 6 January 1989 after an extensive car chase by several police officers. He denied involvement in the offences and said in police interviews that he might have spent the night with a girlfriend. The prosecution relied substantially upon the evidence of the Jobbins Group. The latter admitted having jointly stolen the Spitfire which had been found abandoned near the scene of the first robbery and murder, and had driven the Renault and Cavalier stolen at the last robbery to a field in Sidcup where they had set fire to them. The trial of the two applicants and Johnson took place at the Central Criminal Court in February 1990. Johnson was acquitted of all charges against him. All three of the accused denied any involvement in the offences. The defence submitted that many of the witnesses for the prosecution were unreliable. It was argued that if anyone from No. 25 had been responsible for the crimes, it was the Jobbins Group, and that they had given a deliberately false account to the police in order to implicate the accused and thus exonerate themselves. The jury deliberated for just over two hours. The verdict was returned at 1.30pm on 31 December 2012. The trial was expected to last for up to three weeks. The sentence is expected to be pronounced at 2.45pm on 2 January 2013.  Rowe and Johnson were convicted of murder, assault occasioning grievous bodily harm, and three counts of robbery. They were each sentenced to concurrent terms of life, fifteen years' and twelve years' imprisonment. The applicants and Johnson appealed on the grounds, inter alia, that their convictions were unsafe and unsatisfactory because of weaknesses and inconsistencies in the evidence against them. The disclosure procedure to be followed when the prosecution was in possession of material which it believed should not be disclosed to the defence had been changed by the judgment in R.D. against the prosecution. The issue of disclosure was re-canvassed before a differently constituted Court of Appeal (although the Lord Chief Justice, Lord Taylor, participated) In 1994 the applicants applied to the Home Office for a review of the safety of their convictions. In April 1997 the Criminal Cases Review was published. This resulted in an ex parte application which was heard in camera. This application was upheld and referred to by Watkins LJ in his final judgment in these terms: 'We upheld the claim and refused to order disclosure of any kind for reasons we gave on 22nd June and which are recorded.’ The appeal was eventually dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 29 July 1993. The substantive appeal was heard on 30 September 1993 and the appeal was dismissed on 29 October 1993. In 1994 the first applicant's solicitor asked the Crown Prosecution Service for disclosure of. any reward claims made prior to the trial by any witness. Criminal Appeal. Commission (“the CCRC”) was set up under the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 and the applicants' case was transferred to it. In August 1997 the CCRC appointed an officer from Greater Manchester Police to investigate the events surrounding the prosecution of the applicants and Johnson. The investigating officer's report was submitted in January 1999. The CCRC concluded that, in the light of this new evidence, there was a real possibility that Johnson was not involved in the offences of 15 to 16 December 1988. While there was evidence linking the two applicants to the robberies, if the prosecution case against one of the three, Johnson, might no longer be sustainable, the Court of Appeal ought at the same time to consider whether the case could still be sustained against Rowe and Davis.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 12 March 1999. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the UK. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 1999. The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Mr Cranston and also their replies to questions put by several of its members. The offences occurred during the night of 15 to 16 December 1988, a series of offences occurred in Surrey, England. The first, which may have occurred sometime after 1.30 a.m., involved an attack on two men in a parked car in a field near a public house in Fickleshall. Just after the conclusion of sexual activities between the two men (Mr Ely and Mr Hurburgh), two masked men appeared. Three masked robbers arrived at the Napier household in Oxted. They entered by a back window. Two of them went into Timothy Napier's room; one had a knife, the other a gun. Meanwhile, Richard Napier was awakened by the third robber armed with a revolver. Both were told they would be shot if they did not cooperate. They attacked the robbers and forced them downstairs. In the struggle, TimothyNapier's arm was cut and an artery was severed. The other two robbers ransacked the room before all three fled taking Timothy's Toyota car. Hurburgh's car was found abandoned nearby. Raphael Rowe, Michael Davis and Randolph Johnson lived at No. 25. Mark Jobbins, Norman Duncan and Shane Griffin also lived there. They were then aged 29, 21 and 19 years respectively. Duncan and Griffin sniffed glue on a regular basis. All three had criminal records. Rowe, Davis and Johnson were black. Duncan was white and Griffin was black. Blood stains on a jacket found in Rowe's bedroom were analysed and found to be of a blood group shared by 8% of the population, including the murder victim, Hurburgh. Police found a brooch from the Spicer/Almond robbery in Rowe’s wastepaper basket. Other items were found in a storeroom. The trial of the two applicants and Johnson took place at the Central Criminal Court in February 1990. The prosecution case was that the three men had been involved in each incident. It was argued that there was evidence to link the offences: the Austin Princess stolen from Hurburgh was found at the scene of the Napier robbery; the Toyota stolen from the Napiers was found abandoned close to the Spicer/Almond household; and the vehicles stolen from latter couple were connected to the occupants of No. 25. Johnson was arrested on 6 January 1989 after an extensive car chase by several police officers. He denied involvement in the offences and said in police interviews that he might have spent the night with a girlfriend. The defence argued that many of the witnesses for the prosecution were unreliable. It was argued that if anyone from No. 25 had been responsible for the crimes, it was the Jobbins Group. The defence referred to the substantial reward which had been offered as a factor which may have motivated prosecution witnesses to give evidence. Joanne Cassar may have been an accomplice because she knew Duncan and Griffin. Kate Williamson's evidence was motivated by jealousy of Rowe's relationship with another girlfriend and was in any event inconsistent with a letter which she had sent to Rowe whilst he was in prison. All three of the accused denied any involvement in the offences. The applicants and Johnson appealed on the grounds, inter alia, that their convictions were unsafe and unsatisfactory because of weaknesses and inconsistencies in the evidence against them. The disclosure procedure to be followed when the prosecution was in possession of material which it believed should not be disclosed to the defence had been changed by the judgment in R.H. Vickers v. Johnson. The applicants were convicted of murder, assault occasioning grievous bodily harm, and three counts of robbery. They were each sentenced to concurrent terms of life, fifteen years' and twelve years' imprisonment. The appeal was heard by the Court of Appeal in 1992 and 1993. The issue of disclosure was re-canvassed before a differently constituted Court of appeal in 1993. The Court of Appeal upheld the applicants' convictions and that of Johnson, concluding that there was no basis to say there was even a lurking doubt about their safety. In 1994 the applicants applied to the Home Office for a review of the safety of their convictions. In April 1997 the Criminal Cases Review was published. The first applicant's solicitor asked the Crown Prosecution Service for disclosure of any reward claim made prior to the trial by any witness and, in particular, by one of the Jobbins Group, Williamson or Cassar. This application was upheld and referred to by Watkins LJ in his final judgment in these terms: 'We upheld the claim and refused to order disclosure.’ The Criminal Appeal. Commission (“the CCRC”) was set up under the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 and the applicants' case was transferred to it. In August 1997 the CCRC appointed an officer from Greater Manchester Police to investigate the events surrounding the prosecution of the applicants and Johnson. The investigating officer's report was submitted in January 1999. The CCRC found, inter alia, that Duncan was a long-standing police informant, who, on 18 December 1988 had approached a Sussex police officer and told him that the applicants were responsible for the crimes of 15 to 16 December 1988. Duncan had received a reward of GBP 10,300, in addition to police protection between 18 and 22 December 1988 and immunity from prosecution in relation to his admitted participation as an accessory to the offences.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6544/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Günther Paul Litwin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29090/06) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been denied access to the appeal courts, contrary to Article 6 of the convention. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised to grant him the right to appeal. The Government, however, did not take part in the agreement reached between the applicant and the public prosecutor. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Human rights. The applicant had been convicted of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery. He was sentenced to nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The court considered the fact that the applicant had eventually waived his right to the confiscated assets and had thus delivered a major proportion of his criminal profits as a mitigating factor. The applicant subsequently appointed new counsel. On 12 April 2001 the applicant’s new counsel applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the waiver of the right to appeal had been invalid because it had not complied with the requirements of the Federal Court of Justice's case-law. The applicant argued that the actual waiver of the right to appeal had been declared before delivery of the judgment. not been recorded in the court transcript, as required by the case-law of the Fourth Chamber of the Federal Court of Justice (see paragraph 19 below). In his view, this constituted a breach of the principle of a public hearing. The court observed that a waiver could not be revoked, rescinded or withdrawn. It did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement, as this fact did not call into question the validity of the waiver as such. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 5 July 2001. The applicant had claimed he had been unduly influenced when waiving his right to appeal in exchange for a maximum penalty of nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The Federal Court of Justice had failed to consider the fact that his wife, who had not been involved in the trial, had also been asked to waive any rights she had to the confiscated assets. This procedural method had been arbitrary, not in accordance with the statutory provisions governing the confiscation of assets in criminal proceedings and had also constituted a violation of the right to an effective remedy. The court refused to admit the constitutional complaint for examination without giving further reasons.

train_texts: An Iranian national, Davood Amrollahi (“the applicant’s” case, was granted legal aid by the Danish Government. He complained that he would be separated from his wife and children, who cannot be expected to follow him to Iran. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties not to expel the applicant pending the Court's decision. By a decision of 28 June 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. After consulting the parties, the Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2, in fine) The man was granted a residence and work permit in Denmark in 1990. He was sentenced to three years' imprisonment in 1998 for drug trafficking. The man has three children with a woman he met in Denmark. The family has broken off all relations with the man since his arrest in 1998. The applicant was allowed to return to Denmark after serving his sentence. He has now been released from prison on bail. He is now living in Denmark with his wife and two children, aged 8 and 11. On 17 December 1998 the applicant had served two-thirds of his sentence and was due to be released on parole. Since he did not consent to the deportation and refused to leave the country voluntarily, he was detained as from that date in accordance with the Aliens Act with a view to being repatriated. The applicant availed himself of the possibility, prior to the enforcement of a deportation, to bring before the immigration authorities the question whether he could be returned to Iran. The immigration authorities found, on 13 January 1999, that the applicant would not risk persecution in Iran of a kind which could constitute a basis for his remaining in Denmark. The applicant was released from his detention on 11 May 2000. On 7 September 2000 the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision of 3 March 2000 as it agreed that a request for a review of an expulsion order pursuant to section 50 of the Aliens Act could only be examined once by the courts. The application was denied on the grounds that it was not the right of the court to review it as it had not been heard in full. The appeal was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 3 April 2000 and the appeal was dismissed on 4 April 2000. The case was heard again on 7 March 2000.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 32602/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the assessor who had remanded him in custody had lacked independence. On 30 November 2010 the Court (Fourth Section) decided to strike out the application of its list of cases in so far as it related to the complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the convention. It also decided to adjourn the examination of the applicant’s complaint under Article5 § 3 of thevention. The application was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application. The applicant was remanded in custody until 19 March 2008. Two of the applicant’s counsel (Mr J. Majewski and Mr M. Boruc) lodged appeals against the detention order. On 12 February 2008 the Warsaw-Praga Regional Court, sitting as a bench of three professional judges, dismissed the appeals. It held that the assessor could not be considered as “a non-authorised person to give a decision” within the meaning of Article 439 § 1 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”) The Constitutional Court had struck down the provisions allowing the Minister of Justice to delegate judicial powers to assessors; however the relevant decisions given by assessors had not been automatically negated.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13258/09) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Norwegian nationals, Mr Lars Lillo-Stenberg and Mrs Andrine Sæther (‘the applicants’), alleged that their right under Article 8 of the convention to respect for private life had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. The applicants were represented by Mr Harald Stabell, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government’s Office (Civil Affairs) was represented by their Agent, Mrs Fanny Platou Amble. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine before Oslo District Court. The magazine appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett), which by judgment of 2 September 2008 found against the applicants, by three votes to two. Mr Justice U.S. gave the following reasons, which in the main were endorsed by the two other members of the majority: “I have concluded that the appeal should be allowed.” (34) The provision in section 3-6 refers, at any rate primarily, to violation of section 390 of the Penal Code. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [the applicants], there is a need to redress for violation of privacy under section 390. There is no reason for me to evaluate individual elements on the basis of whether or not they impinge on the concept of privacy. Nor will I examine whether this is a discussion of terminology or of facts. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships between the family and their friends are clearly of a personal nature. The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. It has been clearly established that the article was published without the couple’s consent. The question under consideration is whether a violation of privacy took place, cf. section 390 of the Penal Code. The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. The principles that must be weighed in this case are similar to those that must. be weighed under section 3-6, first paragraph, of the Damages Act and section 390. of the Penal Code. The issue is whether the published article contributes to a debate of public interest. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 of the Human rights Convention is the most relevant principle to be weighed. The Court of Human Rights in the case of von Hannover and the subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court in the Big Brother case have premises that seem to go far in support of protection against the use of pictures and texts concerning an individual’s private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together, and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Thus information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source. The Court reiterates the fundamental importance of protecting private life from the point of view of the development of every human being's personality. The right to protection of privacy is no weaker for well-known cultural personalities than it is for others. Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. The situation was similar to some extent in the Big Brother case. were published and the constant photographing ‒ often by photographers who followed her around ‒ constituted harassment of the aggrieved party and also an invasion. of privacy. (44) A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families. The wedding was organised in a very unusual way, and took place in an area that is accessible to the public under the Outdoor Recreation Act. The photos were taken from a headland about 200-250 metres from the islet where the ceremony was being held. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. Nor was the photographing in the nature of a breach of confidence, as it would have been if for example any of the participants had published personal photos taken during or in connection with the wedding. Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge’s general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article in Se og Hør can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. However, when weighing the right to privacy against the principle of freedom of expression in this specific case, I have arrived at a different conclusion.” Weddings have always been a subject of general interest. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them. The couple are entitled to protect themselves from publicity in such cases. This includes withholding permission for the press to publish the event. In my view the desire to hold a private wedding should be respected in the sense that the wedding ceremony should be regarded as a personal matter within the meaning of section 390. the arrangements in connection with the wedding Ceremony. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. It follows from the von Hannover judgment that protection of privacy also applies to places to which the public has access. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. The names of guests with children were also given, and pictures were shown of the children and their parents. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding and that in my view underlines the private nature of the wedding. (66) Like the first-voting judge, I consider that it has been clearly demonstrated that the opposite parties’ consent had not been obtained. (67) The next question is whether the publication is legal and justified despite the fact that the subject of the article is a personal matter. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I am of the opinion that the article in Se og Hør cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality, and that the opposite parties are entitled to redress for pain and suffering from the appellants. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion.” (70) It seems likely that the reason for using this technique was that the journalist and photographer were aware that the bridal couple would have reacted to their presence on the islet and this might have resulted in the marriage ceremony being moved inside the hotel.

The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The relationship between the family and their friends are clearly of a personal nature. There is no reason for me to evaluate individual elements on the basis of whether or not they impinge on the concept of privacy. It has been clearly established that the article was published without the couple’s consent. I would add that I see nothing in the article indicating that the couple had given the magazine permission to report on the wedding in return for payment. On the contrary, the article stated at the end that the two celebrities did not wish to comment. The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case.
