The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. The right to protection of privacy is no weaker for well-known cultural personalities than it is for others, despite the fact that their photos are published in magazines and newspapers and on the internet in connection with their professional lives. A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families, friends and other persons close to them. The wedding ceremony and celebrations are clearly part of private and family life and thus in principle should be protected. The photos were taken from a headland about 200-250 metres from the islet where the ceremony was being held. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. In spite of the fact that all individuals, including celebrities, are entitled to protection against being photographed even in public places, I consider that this must be taken into account in the assessment of legality. (52) The article contained a photo of [the second applicant] The photos do not show the most personal part of the wedding, the actual marriage ceremony. The case raises difficult and uncertain legal questions, clarification of which is in the public interest. The Court therefore allows the appeal. The article in Se og Hør also describes in words and pictures details of the marriage. together with the couple’s under-age child. Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge's general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. No award of costs should therefore be made.” Weddings have always been a subject of general interest. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them. The couple are entitled to protect themselves from publicity in such cases as well, and this includes withholding permission for the press to publish the event. In my view all the relevant circumstances indicate that in the present case the wedding was a private event. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. It follows from the von Hannover judgment that protection of privacy also applies to places to which the public has access. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding and that in my view underlines the private nature of the wedding. In the present case the publication was a celebrity article written for the sole purpose of entertainment. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. Well-known persons also have the right to respect for personal matters of the kind we are dealing with here. In this connection I place special emphasis on the fact that getting married is a very significant occasion in a person's life. ‘The article in Se og Hør cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality, and that the opposite parties are entitled to redress for pain and suffering from the appellants.’ ‘The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion.” ‘Using a zoom lens because of the personal and private nature of the event resembles the use of a hidden camera, which is a factor that also weighs against the appealing parties’

Two Norwegian nationals, Mr Lars Lillo-Stenberg and Mrs Andrine Sæther (“the applicants”) lodged an application against the Kingdom of Norway on 5 March 2009. The applicants alleged that their right under Article 8 of the Convention to respect for private life had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. The application was communicated to the Government, but it was decided to await the outcome of Von Hannover v. Germany (no. 2) [GC], nos. 40660/08 and 60641/08, ECHR 2012 and Axel Springer AG v Germany [GC] 7 February 2012. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine before Oslo District Court (Oslo tingrett) The magazine appealed to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), which by judgment of 13 February 2008 upheld the judgment. In recent years the Supreme Court has considered legal questions relating to violation of privacy in the judgments Rt-2007-687 (Big Brother) and Rt -2008-489 (Plata). My argument is based mainly on these judgments. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [Mr Justice U.S.], there is a need to appeal against the decision. The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships within the family are clearly of a personal nature. There would have been no question of violation of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the basis of an overall evaluation of the article, cf. paragraph 64 of the Big Brother judgment with further references. I would add that I see nothing in the article indicating that the couple had given the magazine permission to report on the wedding in return for payment. The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 is the most relevant principle to be weighed. I will now examine the circumstances in thepresent case in relation to the issue of legality. (40) The case is heard by a jury of three men and three women. The jury will deliver its verdict at a hearing to be held later this year. The verdict will be delivered by the jury of two men and one woman. The Court of Human Rights in the case of von Hannover and the subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court in the Big Brother case have premises that seem to go far in support of protection against the use of pictures and texts concerning an individual’s private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together, and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source, cf. paragraph 80 of theBig Brother judgment. That protection extends beyond the private family circle and also includes a social dimension. The Court reiterates the fundamental importance of protecting private life from the point of view of the development of every human being’ Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. (44) The right to protection of privacy is no weaker for well-known cultural personalities than it is for others. (45) A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families, friends and other persons close to them. (46) As mentioned above, a neutral description of two individuals’ wedding is not unlawful. (47) Neither the text nor the photos in the disputed magazine article contain anything unfavourable to the couple. The photos were taken from a headland about 200-250 metres from the islet where the ceremony was being held. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. A certain amount of weight must be given to the fact that the wedding was organised in a very unusual way, and took place in an area that is accessible to the public under the Outdoor Recreation Act. Many of the arrangements were such as to attract attention from third parties, for example the arrival of the bride in an open boat and the presence of a men’s choir singing a hymn. The case raises difficult and uncertain legal questions, clarification of which is in the public interest. The Court therefore allows the appeal. No award of costs should therefore be made.’ Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge’s general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article in Se og Hør can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. Weddings have always been a subject of general interest. Weddings should be respected in the sense that the wedding ceremony should be regarded as a personal matter within the meaning of section 390. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. The islet where the events reported by Se og Hør, and the marriage itself, took place is a relatively short walk away and directly linked with the hotel’s property. In my opinion the fact that there is a general right of public access to the islet under the Outdoor Recreation Act does not prevent this part of the wedding from also being of a clearly private nature. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. The names of guests with children were also given, and pictures were shown of the children and their parents. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding and that in my view underlines the private nature of the wedding. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. Well-known persons also have the right to respect for personal matters of the kind we are dealing with here. Se og Hør’s use of a zoom lens enabled the journalist and photographer to take close-up pictures of the bridal couple and their guests that make it look as if they were actually at the event themselves, when in fact they were hidden from those who were being observed. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. (70) For these reasons I am of the opinion that the article in Se og. Høre cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality, and that the opposite parties are entitled to redress.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 13 September 1991 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 13071/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 29 September 1986. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). The applicant was convicted at Sheffield Crown Court, inter alia, of one count of robbery and two counts of burglary. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The trial and appeal proceedings took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. The victim of the robbery (Miss Sizer) was awakened from her sleep to find a man standing over her. She remained tied up until she was freed the next morning. In a statement to the police she gave a description of the man and said she thought she would recognise him. It was this statement that led to the arrest of his co-accused. He was convicted of two counts of burglary and sentenced to life in prison. He appealed the sentence but it was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 21 May 1985. An independent investigation was ordered into the case. The Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against the officers. The applicant submitted to the Court of Appeal that the verdict should be set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case. At the trial one of the police witnesses had stated under cross-examination that no fingerprints were found at the scene of the crime. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. The applicant had not been informed of this by the prosecution before his trial. A further shortcoming complained of by the applicant related to the fact that the police had shown two volumes of photographs of possible burglars (including a photograph of the applicant) to the elderly victim of the robbery who said that she had caught a fleeting glimpse of the burglar. Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. Court concluded that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true. Although this is a matter which perhaps casts the police in a somewhat lazy or idle light, we do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions. Consequently, treating this matter as we have to according to section 17 of the Act, we think this appeal fails and must be dismissed.

He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. Various documents were filed by the applicant in the course of the hearing. The victim of the robbery in 1984 was an 82-year-old woman. She had her hands tied behind her back and was blindfolded. She made a statement to the police saying she thought she would recognise the man. The man was found guilty of two counts of burglary. He appealed but the case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 21 May 1985. The Director of Public Prosecutions decided there was insufficient evidence to bring charges against the police officers who had investigated the case. The case was eventually dismissed on the grounds of public interest immunity. The woman's case was never heard by the court again. It was not until 1988 that the case finally went to trial. The Court of Appeal rejected the application to set aside the verdict as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of shortcomings in the prosecution case. The application was made under section 17 (1)(a) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968. The reference was heard on 18 July 1986 and judgment delivered on the same date. The applicant had not been informed of this by the prosecution before his trial. A further shortcoming complained of by the applicant related to the fact that the police had shown two volumes of photographs of possible burglars (including a photograph of the applicant) to the elderly victim of the robbery. Her statement, read to the jury, said that she thought she would be able to recognise her assailant but she did not pick out the applicant from the photographs. Court of Appeal also rejected this argument: “The fact that Miss Sizer had a fleeting glimpse of her assailant, and the fact that such identification as she did make was largely directed to other matters of identification rather than his features, leads us to believe that the jury would not have been influenced to act other than they did if they had the full story of the photographs and of Police Constable Esdon’s activities with regard to that.” The court concluded as follows: ‘It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true’

name: Piotr Rachwalski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. A decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The case was decided on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants tried to argue with the policemen, to no avail. The first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheons. No information was provided about the grounds, purpose or legal basis for the search. During this time the police showered abuse on the students. They pushed and shoved them. This lasted for about half an hour. Afterwards, the police left the house and warned the students that some of them were in an illegal situation. The Wrocław District Prosecutor found that no criminal offence had been committed. The applicant had objected in a pretentious tone to having been woken up and to the check on the car taking place at night. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As the applicants were interfering with the arrest of D. S., they were hit with truncheons. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. Given that D. S. had been behaving aggressively, direct force had been used against him, including the use of truncheons and handcuffs. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. The police had entered private property and effected a search. The second applicant had woken all of them up in an attempt to find the owner. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently, he said. The outcome of the appeal was upheld on 20 May 1998 the Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the intervention of the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault.

The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The application was filed under former Article 25 of the. Convention for the Protection of Human. Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants lived in the house with the owner’s permission. They often received young visitors from all over the country. An unlocked car parked in front of the house had seemed very suspicious to the policemen A. C. and R. S., who thought it was a suspicious car. The applicants were ordered to stand against a fence. They were pushed and jostled and the policemen insulted them referring to them as “scum’, “slobs”, ‘queers’ (hołota, brudasy, pedały) The police left the house and warned the students that some of them were in an illegal situation as they were not registered as inhabitants. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. He found that no criminal offence had been committed. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The atmosphere was tense. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to a police car. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. The outcome of the appeal was decided on 20 May 1998 by the Regional Prosecutor, who ruled in favour of D. S.'s appeal against the arrest of him.

The applicants were called 'scum', 'slobs' and 'queers' by the police. They were beaten with truncheons and insulted by the officers. The applicants were examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police trunchetons. The police left, taking D. S. with them. They left the house and warned the students that they were in an illegal situation as they were not registered as inhabitants. The applicants behaved aggressively, loudly expressing opinions about the purpose and nature of the intervention. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. While he was being taken into custody by the police, he hit one of them in the face. Thereupon truncheons were used against him. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. He found that no criminal offence had been committed. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to a police car. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. As presented by the applicants the case may be summed up as follows: The applicants produced their identity cards and the registration card of the car, whose owner was asleep in the house. The police were not satisfied with their explanation and the dispute became more intense. In reaction to the opinions expressed about the intervention, in particular by D. S., the policemen used truncheons. The applicants were ordered to stand against a fence. They were pushed and jostled and the policemen insulted them referring to them as “scum’, “slobs”, ‘queers’ (hołota, brudasy, pedały). The police left the house and warned the students that some of them were in an illegal situation as they were not registered as inhabitants. The applicants behaved aggressively, loudly expressing opinions about the purpose and nature of the intervention. The police action was a result of the fact that the applicants did not comply with the police requests to provide necessary information. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. He found that no criminal offence had been committed. The case was settled out of court by a jury of six men and four women. The judge ruled in favour of the applicants in the case of the second applicant. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to the car. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the people present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal.

name: Alan Wainwright
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 13 December 2005, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant, but not the Government, filed further observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the applicants' claims. The case was decided by the Court on 14 December 2005. Governor ordered all Mr O’Neill’s visitors be strip-searched before visits. Two applicants were taken to HMP Armley, Leeds, to be searched. Neither had ever been to a prison before and were told they would be strip searched if they did not comply. They were then taken to separate rooms for the searches. The applicants were told that they would not be allowed to visit Mr O'Neill until they had been searched. The first applicant was told to take off her jumper and vest. One of the officers walked around her, examining her naked upper body. She was then instructed to remove her shoes, socks and trousers, which she did. The second applicant was then told that she would be searched for drugs. The first applicant was told to pull down her underwear and spread her legs. She was then told to bend forward and her sexual organs and anus were visually examined. She believed that anyone outside the prison looking at the windows in the room where she was being strip-searched could have seen her in a state of undress. Although none of the officers touched her, she felt threatened by their actions and considered that she had no alternative but to comply with their instructions. The first applicant told the officers that she might as well sign it as there was by that stage nothing else the officers could do to her and she then did so without reading it. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. On returning home, she removed her clothes and bathed because she felt upset, angry and dirty. She did not visit Mr O'Neill for a further four months. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. Dr Sims considered that the severe upset that she had experienced in the prison made her existing depression (for which she was receiving medication at the time of the visit) worse. The first applicant suffered intrusive recollections of her time at the prison and psychological distress at anything that resembled her experience. For about five weeks after the incident, he would not see his girlfriend, baby son, friends or anyone else and spent large amounts of his time in his bedroom. He was also examined by Dr Sims in October 1998. He concluded that, as a result of her aversive experience in the prison, the first applicant would be more vulnerable to future traumatic events and more prone to depressive reaction. As for the second applicant, on his return home from the visit, he went to his bedroom crying. He thought about being in prison almost continuously and broke out in a sweat and felt frightened when he recalled the incident. Striking search could not be justified by Rule 86 § 1 of the Prison Rules (see Relevant domestic law and practice below) The trial judge held that the strip-searches were an invasion of their privacy exceeding what was necessary and proportionate to deal with the drug smuggling problem. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act (save for the battery against the second applicant) had been committed. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. But this has been fully compensated. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages, irrespective of whether the defendant acted intentionally, negligently or accidentally. It is one thing to wander carelessly into the wrong hotel bedroom and another to hide in the wardrobe to take photographs. Lord Hoffmann says there should be a general tort of invasion of privacy under which the searches of the applicants were actionable and damages for emotional distress recoverable. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law. provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invasion of. privacy contrary to Article 8. The court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of invasion. of privacy. But in my opinion it shows no more than the need, in English law, for a system of control of the use of film from CCTV cameras which shows greater sensitivity to the feelings of people who happen to have been caught by the lens. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. If it is indeed the case that a person’s rights under Article 8 have been infringed by a public authority, he will have a statutory remedy. this is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle.” For these reasons I would reject the invitation to declare that since at the latest 1950 there has been a previously unknown tort of invade of privacy’. The creation of ageneral tort will pre-empt the controversial question of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State to provide remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.

Mary and Alan Wainwright were granted legal aid in 2004. They complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison. They had no effective remedy as required by Article 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. The applicant, but not the Government, filed further observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the applicants' complaint. The Court ruled that the application was admissible. Governor ordered that all Mr O’Neill’s visitors be strip-searched before visits. Neither of the applicants had ever been to a prison. They were taken across the courtyard from the south gatehouse by four or five prison officers. The first applicant was told to take off her jumper and vest. One of the officers searched them whilst the other officer walked around her, examining her naked upper body. She was then instructed to remove her shoes, socks and trousers, which she did. The second applicant was beginning to be distressed and the first applicant tried to calm him down. The applicants were then taken to separate rooms for the searches. Although there were roller blinds on the windows, they were not pulled down. First applicant was told to pull down her underwear and spread her legs. She was then told to bend forward and her sexual organs and anus were visually examined. The first applicant was shaking and visibly distressed. She believed that anyone outside the prison looking at the windows in the room where she was being strip-searched could have seen her in a state of undress. Although none of the officers touched her, she felt threatened by their actions and considered that she had no alternative but to comply with their instructions. The second applicant was taken to a separate room by two male officers. At first he refused to go into the room. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. After returning home, she removed her clothes and bathed because she felt upset, angry and dirty. Because of her experience, she did not visit Mr O'Neill for a further four months. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. At that time (approximately twenty-one months after the incident), she still thought about the strip-search about once a week. The first applicant was still feeling bad about the incident, had difficulty sleeping, and had nightmares about going into the room at the prison and of being strip-searched. The second applicant was suffering from PTSD (scoring 15 on the DSM-IV scale) and had a depressive illness. Dr Sims concluded that even after recovery the second applicant would remain vulnerable to further symptoms with lesser provocation than previously. On 23 April 2001 the County Court upheld the applicants’ civil claims against the Home Office, holding that the searches constituted a trespass to the person which the person had been searched for. The case is now before the European Court of Human Rights. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicants. The Home Office conceded battery following the trial judge’s factual findings. The judge rejected the applicants’ submission that Article 3 was relevant, holding that although strip-searches were unpleasant they did not amount to inhuman or degrading treatment. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act had been committed. The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. The House of Lords upheld the judgment of the Court of Appeal and dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. But this has been fully compensated. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages. Lord Hoffmann said there was no reason to adopt a high level principle of privacy to comply with Article 8 of the Convention. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invasion of privacy contrary to Article 8. The court expressed some impatience, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of privacy invasion. But in my opinion it shows no more than the need, in English law, for a system of control of the use of film from CCTV cameras which shows greater sensitivity to the feelings of people who happen to be caught by the lens. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. this is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle.” For these reasons I would reject the invitation to declare that since at the latest 1950 there has been a previously unknown tort of invading of privacy’. The creation of ageneral tort will pre-empt the controversial question of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State to provide remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.

The officer inspecting her body then asked the first applicant to pull her vest up again, asking for it to be raised higher and higher until it was above her breasts. The first applicant asked why that was necessary since they had already inspected her top half, but the officer ignored her and continued walking around her body. By this time she was crying. She believed that anyone outside the prison looking at the windows in the room where she was being strip-searched could have seen her in a state of undress. Although none of the officers touched her, she felt threatened by their actions. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The first applicant and the second applicant are suing for damages. First applicant awarded 2,600 pounds sterling (GBP) (comprising GBP 1,600 basic damages and GBP1,000 aggravated damages) Second applicant awarded GBP 4,500. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act (save for the battery against the second applicant) had been committed. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. But this has been fully compensated. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages. It is one thing to wander carelessly into the wrong hotel bedroom and another to hide in the wardrobe to take photographs. House of Lords said there should be a tort of invasion of privacy under which searches of applicants were actionable and damages for emotional distress recoverable. But Lord Hoffmann said there is nothing in the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights which suggests that the adoption of some high level principle of privacy is necessary to comply with Article 8 of the Convention. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invasion of. privacy contrary to Article 8 § 1 and not justifiable under Article 8 XV 2. The court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of privacy invasion. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. If it is indeed the case that a person’s rights under Article 8 have been infringed by a public authority, he will have a statutory remedy. this is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle.” The creation of a. general tort will, as Buxton LJ pointed out in the Court of Appeal, at [2002] QB 1334, 1360, para. 92, pre-empt the controversial question. of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State to provide. remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.

name: Orhan Akgül
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government did not designate a specific Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant denied the veracity of his signed statements taken in detention, alleging that they had been obtained under duress. He alleged that he had been forced to sign the impugment. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Orhan Akgül, and he was represented by Ms T. Aslan. The Grand National Assembly amended Article 143 of the Constitution and excluded military members from State Security Courts. The military judge hearing the applicant’s case was replaced by a civilian judge. On 13 October 1999 the State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 9 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. Two days later, the decision was pronounced in the absence of the applicant's representative. The decision was deposited with the registry of the Izmir State Security court for the applicant to review. The applicant was convicted and sentenced on 13 October 2000.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Izmir Security Directorate. He was charged with aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), contrary to Article 169 of the Criminal Code. He denied the veracity of his signed statements taken in detention, alleging that they had been obtained under duress. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate a specific Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 4 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant’s representative requested his release. The court dismissed his request and ordered his continued detention on remand. On 13 October 1999 the State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 9 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. Two days later, the decision was pronounced in the absence of the applicant's representative. The decision was deposited with the registry of the Izmir State Security court for the applicant to review. The applicant was convicted on October 13, 1999 and sentenced to 3 years' imprisonment. The judge who found the applicant guilty of making false statements under duress is still serving his sentence.

The request sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Articles 8, 9, 12 and 13. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 and 24 June 1986. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Gleeson and Mr. O’Reilly for the Government, by. Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Senator M. Robinson and Dr. Duncan for the applicants. The applicant’s representative was Mr. R. Macdonald (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). The Court decided under Rule 50 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was adjourned until June 25, 1986. The first applicant is Roy H.W. Johnston, who was born in 1930 and is a scientific research and development manager. The second applicant is Janice Williams-Johnston, who is a school-teacher by profession and used to work as director of a play-group in Dublin, but has been unemployed since 1985. The third applicant is their daughter, Nessa Doreen Williams- Johnston, whose father consented to his name being included in the Register of Births as the father. Under the Constitution of Ireland he is unable to obtain, in Ireland, a dissolution of his marriage to enable him to marry the second applicant. The matter has therefore not been pursued. The parties also mutually renounced their succession rights over each other’s estates. The third applicant has, under Irish law, the legal situation of an illegitimate child. Her parents are concerned at the lack of any means by which she can, even with their consent, be recognised as their child with full rights of support and succession in relation to them. They are also concerned about the possibility of a stigma attaching to her by virtue of her legal situation, especially when she is attending school. The first and second applicants state that although they have not practised any formal religion for some time, they have recently joined the Religious Society of Friends (the Quakers) in Dublin.

name: Sebastian Kliza
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8363/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Sebastian Kliza (“the applicant”), on 20 February 2004. The applicant was arrested on 26 January 2001 on suspicion of having committed a series of armed robberies as a member of an organised criminal group. On 28 January 2001 the Tychy District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that he be detained pending the outcome of the investigation. On 8 October 2001 the Katowice Regional Court prolonged the applicant's detention until 17 January 2002. The case involved armed robbery committed by an organised criminal group. The charges in the bill of indictment concerned 4 co-accused. The applicant's detention was extended on several occasions. The case was complex, given the number of accused and victims. The trial had not yet begun for reasons beyond the trial court's control. There were no special grounds, as specified in Article 259 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that would justify lifting the detention and imposing a less severe measure. The court relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question. The delays in the proceedings were to a large extent caused by the failure to escort the applicant to the trial. The applicant was accused of acting in an organised criminal group and sentenced to 8 years' imprisonment. He appealed. The applicant served prison sentences which had been imposed on him in other criminal proceedings. On 11 February 2005 the Katowice Regional Court amended the trial court's judgment, acquitted the applicant of the charge and reduced the applicant's sentence to 6 years' jail. The application form sent to the Court bears the following stamps: “Zabrze Detention Centre received on 16.02.2004” and “District Court in Tychy, censored” (Sąd Rejonowy w Tychach, cenzurowano), a hand-written sentence: ‘Z: without censorship’ (Z: bez cenzury) The stamps were issued on 8.04.2004. They contained the words “Zabrze Detention Centre” and “District Court in Tychy, censored” The stamps also featured an illegible signature and a censored version of the words. The stamps were released by the Polish Ministry of Culture and the Polish Government in Exile, a branch of the Polish National Committee for the Human Rights of the Disabled. The stamp was issued by the Czechoslovakian Ministry of Human Rights and the Czech Republic’s National Court of Justice, a part of the Republic of Poland, in 2004. They were issued by Poland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the National Court for the rights of the disabled.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on 14 May 2002 on suspicion of having intimidated witnesses. On the second day of the trial the witness who had identified the applicant did not attend and the trial had to be aborted. On 16 February 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Court ruled that the application was admissible under Article 29. Judge: “Without her evidence, plainly, we can't proceed. I offer no evidence. Verdicts must follow.” The applicant was duly acquitted. On his counsel's application for a defendant's costs order, the judge refused to make an order and stated: ‘That order will be refused. There is clear evidence on the court papers. The Crown have taken the view that they are not going to compel this witness although there is compelling evidence in respect of those matters.’ The applicant's attempted appeal was dismissed on 14 November 2003 as “to be appealable as a sentence, the order must be contingent upon conviction’.

name: Mustafa Yalgın
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the complaints and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The judge elected in respect of Turkey withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28): the Government appointed an ad hoc judge to sit in his place. The applicant was accused of being a member of the Dev-Yol, an illegal armed organisation. The applicant denied the allegations against him and said that the police officers took his statements under duress. name: Muammer Pakkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant was represented by Mr M. Filorinalı and Ms Y. Başara, lawyers practising in Istanbul. On 13 October 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the. same time as its admissibility. The Istanbul State Security Court remanded the applicant in custody in March 2000. On 1 August 2001 his objection was dismissed on account of the nature of the offence and the content of the case file. On 27 October 2004 the Istanbul Assize Court found the applicant guilty of the charges and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 13 July 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the decision on procedural grounds. The case is still pending and the applicant is still in detention on remand. The latest hearing was held on 2 December 2005. The applicant is currently serving a life sentence in prison for a crime he did not commit. The judge on the bench of the court had been changed on six occasions by 12 October 2001.

name: Kamil Prus
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5136/11) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 6 December 2010. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of Article 3 on account of the imposition on him of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government and upheld on 7 July 2014. The Lublin Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 4 April 2011. The court referred to the reasons given in the decision of 5 November 2010. On 28 April 2011 the Lublin Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission revoked its decision to classify the applicant as a ‘dangerous detainee’. It considered that the applicant’s behaviour had improved and that he no longer posed a threat to the security of the remand centre. The application was dismissed on 29 April 2011, with the prosecutor refusing to open an investigation in the case, holding that no offence had been committed. The case was eventually settled out of court by an agreement between the applicant and the prison authorities.

The judge ruled that the decision to apply the regime to the applicant had been lawful and justified. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal.

name: Mehmet Pehlivan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4233/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of affiliation to the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), an illegal organisation, and of having committed homicide. He was questioned by officers from the Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command on 22 April 1996. The applicant was charged under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code, and with killing B.C. in 1992. The applicant claimed that the murder was not linked to any terrorist activity. The court subsequently postponed the hearings until 24 December 1998 on account of the failure of the gendarmerie command to submit the relevant information. The First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand in view of the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the case file. In November 1999 the First Division ordered the judge to keep the applicant in custody. The applicant was convicted under Article 448 of the Criminal Code of homicide and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 26 March 2002 because the applicant had been unable to examine three witnesses against him during the trial. The case was subsequently remitted to the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The court found no convincing evidence that the offence committed by the applicant was linked to terrorist activities. The judge ordered the applicant’s release from prison in view of the length of his detention during judicial proceedings. The applicant was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment on 8 April 2004.

name: Helmut Kucera

name: Maria Gollner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49455/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings concerning her lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided for in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was heard by a court in St. Pölten on 1 November 2001. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The court requested the expert to supplement his opinion on 23 October 1995. The time-limit for filing observations on the expert’s opinion was fixed at 28 April 1995. On 8 August 1995 a further hearing was held. On 14 August 1996 the District Court gave judgment, partly dismissing the applicant's claim. Following her appeal, the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the decision for procedural errors on 13 December 1996 and referred the case back. On 25 February 1997, the applicant appealed against the decision. On 24 March 1998, the appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht). On 24 September 1998 it partly dismissed the applicant’S maintenance claim. On 29 October 1998 the motions for provisional maintenance were partly dismissed by the District Court. On 23 November 1998 the applicant appealed against this decision. On 3 March 1999 the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the judgment of 24 September 1998 for procedural errors and referred the case back. On 15 April 1999 the applicant therefore lodged a further appeal and requested that it be given suspensive effect to preserve the status quo before the Regional Court’s decision. A further hearing scheduled for 1 December 1999 was cancelled due to the judge's illness. Further hearings were held on 3 May 2000 and 15 June 2000. The judgment was served on 13 February 2001.

name: Jaroslaw Niedzwiecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58453/00) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of child benefits between July and December 1995 amounted to discrimination in the exercise of his right to respect for family life. By a decision of 17 June 2003 the Court declared the application partly admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant applied for child benefits according to Section 1 of the Federal Child Benefits Act (Bundeskindergeldgesetz, see relevant domestic law below) On 18 August 1995 the Labour Office dismissed the applicant’s request. The applicant lodged an action with the Würzburg Social Court (Sozialgericht) claiming that he had been residing in Germany since 1987 and that he should, therefore, have the right to child benefits. The court confirmed that only aliens with an unlimited residence permit or with a provisional residence permit were entitled to the payment of child benefits under Section 1 § 3 of the Child benefits Act, as in force until 31 December 1995. The applicant and his wife had paid taxes in 1995 but had not obtained child benefits. He claimed that the relevant provision of the Federal Child Benefits Act was discriminatory and racist. He alleged that the refusal of his request for child benefits infringed the principle of social justice (Sozialstaatsprinzip) The proceedings before the Tax Court are still pending. The proceedings concerning claims after 1 January 1996 have been transferred to the Nuremberg Tax Court (Finanzgericht). The case was decided by the Würzburg Social Court on 3 July 2001. It was decided that it was not competent to deal with the applicant’s claims regarding child benefits for the period after January 1996.

name: Anthony Boner
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 3 August 1993 by. the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It originated in an application (no. 18711/91) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 4 April 1991 by a British citizen, Mr Anthony Boner. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). Anthony Boner stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Lord Rodger and Ms Rae as well as replies to its questions. During the trial a prosecution witness, Mrs G., entered the courtroom prior to giving evidence. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter so that it could be determined whether Mrs G.'s attendance was due to any negligence or failure on the part of the Crown. The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. Mr Boner instructed new solicitors, who asked a different counsel to advise on the prospects of an appeal and to draft a note of appeal. In his opinion dated 10 June 1990 counsel stated his view that the only possible ground of appeal related to the ‘admissibility of the evidence of Mrs G’ The appeal court considered whether Mrs G.’s evidence was admissible. Mr Boner had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions. The applicant presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in Edinburgh and acting as an appellate court. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The Appeal Court considered the appeal court consider Mrs G’'s evidence. The appeal was decided in favour of Mrs Boner and the applicant was awarded legal aid by the Scottish Legal Aid Board. The Court of Appeal decided that the appeal had no merit and that the applicant should not receive legal aid. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The applicant did not address the court on the remaining grounds of appeal, these were not considered by the court. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. the first two grounds of. appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had. approached the matter properly. The appeal against. conviction was. unanimously dismissed and the judge said there had been ‘no miscarriage of. justice’ and ‘the trial judge’ had approached the. matter properly’

The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland also made an application. The object of the request and application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (art. 6-3-c). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Between 29 March and 10 April 1990 he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter so that it could be determined whether Mrs G.'s attendance was due to any negligence or failure on the part of the Crown. Subsequently, counsel for the applicant had the opportunity to cross-examine Mrs. G. on the matter of her attendance. In her evidence she stated that the. applicant had been at her home the evening before the robbery and had spoken of robbing the post office. The following morning he had left the. house and returned later with a bag, in a state of nervousness. The appeal court considered the appeal court's decision. Mr Boner decided to proceed with the appeal. He presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in Edinburgh and acting as an appellate court. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The applicant had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions. The Appeal Court’s decision was made by the Scottish Legal Aid Board (‘the Board’). The appeal was decided by the Court of Appeal of Scotland (“the Court”). The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The court found that the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case“. The case was settled in a jury trial at the Old Bailey in April last year. The jury found Mrs G guilty of perverting the course of justice and sentenced her to 10 years in jail. The verdict was quashed on appeal and Mrs G was sentenced to 15 years in prison. The appeal was later quashed again and the verdict was overturned on appeal.

name: Bahar Yeşilyurt
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15649/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant, Ms Bahar Yeşilyurt, was born in 1978 and lives in Batman. She was taken into custody by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation in October 1995. On 25 October 1995 she was brought before the investigating judge at the Istanbul State Security Court, who ordered her detention on remand. Diyarbakır Assize Court declared its lack of jurisdiction and transferred the applicant's case to the Diyarbakar Juvenile Court. On 17 October 2006 the Court of Cassation decided that the case should be heard by the Batman Assize court. On 4 December 2007 the Batman Assize Court acquitted the applicant of the charges against her. The applicant then applied for compensation for both non-pecuniary and pecuniary damage pursuant to Law no. 466 pertaining to the payment of compensation to persons unjustifiably arrested or detained. On 24 April 2008 the Midyat Assize Court awarded the applicant 11,881 Turkish liras (TRY) in respect of pec uniary damage.

The pre-trial detention (Untersuchungshaft) was confirmed by the presiding judge of the Regional Court on 2 November 1977. According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia querulans, which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. He was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could harm his health. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained under Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment, and was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM) Mr Herczegfalvy. made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. on his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making. An expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The director of the hospital advised the court not to terminate Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention as the treatment carried out, based on medication, had only a sedative effect. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 57345/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Four Turkish nationals, Mr Vahdettin Budak, Mr Mehmet Emin Yalçın, Ms Songül Karatağna and Mr Tayyip Ölmez (‘the applicants’), made the application on 21 April 2000. The applicants were represented by Ms T. Aslan, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. Vahdettin Budak, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçın were convicted of membership of an illegal organisation. Tayyip Ölmez was convicted of aiding and abetting an illegal group. All of the applicants were released from prison in 2005, except for Mr Budak. The applicants' representative informed the Court that all the applicants, except Mr Vahdettev Budak had been released from jail. The applicant’s representative said that Mr Budek was the only person to have been freed from prison. The application was filed under the Article 3 of the Criminal Code of Turkey, which stated that the applicant was a member of an illegal group.

Vahdettin Budak, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin. Yalçın were convicted of membership of an illegal organisation and Tayyip Ölmez of aiding and abetting an illegal group. On 29 March 2005 the applicants’ representative informed the Court that all the applicants, except for Mr Vah dettin budak, were released from prison. The applicants were released on 14 March 2005. The application was dismissed on 2 April 2005 by the Supreme Court of Justice.

name: Halit Tendik
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23188/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the period of their detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement, that the criminal proceedings brought against them were not concluded within areasonable time, and that they did not have an effective remedy at their disposal under domestic law in that respect. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. This case was assigned to newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) Following the promulgation of Law no. 4210, the case-file was transferred to the State Security Court. The Court of Cassation quashed the lower court’s decision, and the case was sent back to the original court. The case was then transferred back again to the first court, which continued to sentence the defendants to life in prison. The decision was quashed on the grounds that some of the defendants had not been provided with the necessary documents to prove their membership of the PKK. The court of cassation then upheld the original decision and the sentence was commuted to 16 years in prison, with the possibility of more time to serve.

The Court of Cassation quashed the lower court’s decision on the grounds that it did not respect the right of defence of the applicants.
