train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43748/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had been unreasonably long. By a decision of 21 October 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The case was decided in favour of the applicant. Gdańsk Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 21 January 1995. The court pointed out that the investigation had not yet been completed and that the group the applicant belonged to had brought improper pressure upon the witnesses to change their testimony. It found that in view of the seriousness of the offence he was charged with, the strong probability of his guilt and the danger that he (or another member of the group) would exert additional pressure on the witnesses, the applicant's detention was warranted. On 21 November 1994 an expert opinion on the state of the applicants mental health was issued. On 12 April 1995 the Gdażsk Court of Appeal ordered the applicant to undergo psychiatric observation. On 27 June 1995 the bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court against the applicant and eleven co-accused. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. The court remarked that the negative effect of the continuing detention upon his family situation was not such as to call for his release. In a separate set of criminal proceedings, the applicant was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. At the hearing held on 18 June 1996 the court dismissed the applicant’s request for release, considering the gravity of the charges against him. The applicant was detained until 31 December 1997. The case was adjourned several times due to the illness of the accused and the defending counsel. The Supreme Court granted the Regional Court’s request to prolong his detention. The Gdańsk Regional Court refused to release the applicant, observing that he had failed to indicate any new relevant circumstances in the case. However, the limit of the duration of the detention was set at 1 December 1997 and not at 31 December 1996. The hearing scheduled for 25 September 1997 was. adjourned as one of the hearings scheduled on 19 February 1997, 5 March 1997, 16 April 1997. and 11 June 1997. The hearing scheduled for 1 October 1997 was adjourned because of the illness of the judge rapporteur. The Supreme Court observed that a number of hearings had not been held due to the absence of either the co-accused or their defence counsel. The case was complex and multi-layered and the charges of a serious nature. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment on 22 October 2002 by which the court gave a judgment by which he was convicted and sentenced. The judge was released under police supervision on 30 April 1998 and the case was closed in October 2002. The application for bail was rejected.

On 5 April 1995 the applicant’s lawyer appealed against this decision. On 12 April 1995 he was ordered to undergo psychiatric observation. The applicant was released on bail on 30 June 1995. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. He was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine in a separate set of criminal proceedings in March 1996. Gdańsk Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention until 30 June 1997. On 11 January 2012 the Asylum Court quashed that decision. It stated that the Asylum Office had failed to update its country information regarding the risk of refoulement of asylum‑seekers from Hungary to Serbia. Hungary expelled asylum-seekers to Serbia, if their first asylum proceedings were terminated and there was no obstacle under the non-refoulement rule. A person lodging a subsequent asylum request was not allowed to remain in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities did not have a list of safe third countries and evaluated each case individually. However, in most cases Serbia was considered to be a safe third country. The Asylum Office concluded that it hence did not consider itself legally obliged to make use of the sovereignty clause and rejected the applicant’s asylum request. The applicant's appeal against that decision was awarded suspensive effect on 24 September 2012. The Asylum Court took note of a letter from the UNHCR Office in Vienna dated 3 February 2012, seemingly citing problems with the techniques of age assessment in Hungary. Thereupon, on 24 October 2011 the Hungarian authorities had discontinued his proceedings. The Asylum Court assumed that because of Hungary’s acceptance of jurisdiction under Article 16 § 1 (c) of the Dublin II Regulation the applicant would have access to asylum proceedings on the merits. The asylum proceedings would not be reopened upon his return to Hungary. If he was returned to Hungary, an asylum request would be considered a subsequent request which would not have automatic suspensive effect if there were no new circumstances supporting his application. The applicant was placed in a children’s home in Fót, where care and education was provided to them according to their age. The member State responsible for examining an asylum application of an unaccompanied minor shall be that where a member of his or her family is legally present, provided that this is in the best interests of the minor. An asylum application must be rejected as inadmissible if, under treaty provisions or pursuant to the Dublin Regulation, another State has jurisdiction to examine it. International documents describing the conditions of detention and reception of asylum-seekers in Hungary are extensively summarised in the judgment in Mohammed v Austria (no. 2283/12, §§ 32-50, 6 June 2013) In October 2012 the UNHCR published a note on Hungary and Serbia as countries of asylum and concluded that it maintained its previously expressed concerns regarding Hungary’s ongoing practice of treating most asylum claims as second applications. The UNHCR noted that the number of asylum‑seekers detained had significantly declined in 2012. Hungary no longer denied an examination of asylum claims on the merits where asylum-seekers had transited via Serbia or Ukraine prior to their arrival in Hungary. Asylum-seekers who applied for asylum immediately upon their arrival, or at the latest during their first interview with the immigration police, were no longer detained. Those who failed to apply immediately, or who otherwise failed to communicate such an intention, continued to be subject to detention for the duration of the entire asylum proceedings. The UNHCR appreciated the State’s reported intention to introduce additional legal guarantees concerning detention to ensure unhindered access to basic facilities. The proposed detention regime for asylum‑seekers would also foresee the detention of first-time asylum-seekers as well as those whose cases had started even before the adoption of the proposed regulations. Vulnerable people were not excluded from detention, with the exception of unaccompanied children. Alternatives to detention were available in the form of bail, a designated place to stay, and periodic reporting obligations. However, the scope of application of bail as alternative to asylum detention was not defined clearly enough, which it feared could result in the non-application of this measure in practice. UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention visited two detention facilities for irregular migrants and asylum-seekers in Nyírbátor and Békéscsaba. There were no psychologists working at the asylum detention facilities. Lawyers, family members and non-governmental organisations were able to access the detention centres, as long as they gave prior notice to the facility. Unaccompanied minors remained exempted from detention. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee noted that following the changes in legislation which took effect in January 2013, deportation could no longer be imposed during the asylum procedure. The issue of prolonging the detention of an asylum-seeker and the lack of proper judicial review were consistently raised during interviews. Detention should not be the common and first resort and should be for the shortest possible duration, especially when genuine asylum-seekers may be overlooked or detained unnecessarily without proper justification. It recommended that the measures introduced by the recent law, which were considered to be positive, should be implemented in a clear and defined manner.

In addition, access to asylum proceedings in Hungary had improved for those asylum‑seekers transferred to Hungary under the Dublin system whose claims had not been examined and decided in Hungary (in other words, those for whom no final decision on the substance of the asylum claim had been taken) The UNHCR noted that the number of Asylum‑seekers detained had significantly declined in 2012. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee noted that following the changes in legislation in January 2013 Dublin returnees were now considered as first-time applicants. They had the chance to substantiate the reasons for their application in a detailed ‘in-merit procedure’ and were not detained. Those asylum-seekers who had withdrawn their application, or had received a negative decision on the merits, may however be placed in immigration detention after being returned under the Dublin II Regulation. From 1 July 2013, pursuant to Act XCIII of 2013, the Asylum Act provides for a newly created detention regime called “asylum detention” These amendments widen the grounds for detention, applicable also to those who submitted their first asylum application immediately upon apprehension. Asylum seekers submitting subsequent applications remain subject to immigration detention. Between July and December 2013, 1762 asylum-seekers were detained under the asylum detention regime. Vulnerable people were not excluded from detention, with the exception of unaccompanied children. Alternatives to detention were available in the form of bail, a designated place to stay, and periodic reporting obligations. However, the scope of application of bail as alternative to asylum detention was not defined clearly enough, which it feared could result in the non-application of this measure in practice. The conditions of assessment were not properly defined by law, which casted doubt on its transparent and coherent application. Detainees complained about inadequate housing conditions. Lack of equipment and cleaning materials, inadequate water quality and difficulties in practising their religion. There were complaints of a lack of access to specialist medical care. But on a positive note, it was found that although the centres were usually at full capacity, there were no problems with overcrowding. Religious dietary requirements were always respected. Lawyers, family members and non-governmental organisations were able to access the detention centres, as long as they gave prior notice to the facility. Unaccompanied minors remained exempted from detention. UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention expressed its concern that there had been a significant focus on detaining asylum-seekers. The issue of prolonging the detention of an asylum-seeker and the lack of proper judicial review were consistently raised during interviews it conducted. Detention should not be the common and first resort and should be for the shortest possible duration, especially when genuine asylum-seekers may be overlooked or detained unnecessarily without proper justification. The Working Group called to the Hungarian Government’s attention the fact that the situation of Asylum-seekers and migrants in irregular situations needed robust improvements and attention to ensure against arbitrary deprivation of liberty. It recommended that the measures introduced by the recent law, which were considered to be positive, should be implemented in a clear and defined manner.

name: Philemon Löffelmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42967/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion. By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared that the application was not admissible and that the Government had not violated the applicant's rights. The Court also ruled that the Austrian Government did not have a duty to provide for the applicant’s protection. The applicant appealed against an order exempting him from military service. He claimed that he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. The Administrative Court found no concerns as regards the legality of the drafting order. It noted that the applicant had solely complained about section 24(3) of the Military Service Act in conjunction with the 1998 Act on the Legal Status of Registered Religious Communities. It referred to an earlier decision by which it had found that the obligation to perform military or civilian service raised no concerns for compliance with Article 9 of the Convention. The applicant was called to military service by the Lower Austrian Military Authority on 14 May 1998. He lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. The applicant filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted. Between 1 February 1999 and 31 January 2000 he performed his civilian service in a social institution. On 1 February 2000 the applicant joined the “Religious Order of the Jehovah’s Witnesses” (Orden der Sondervollzeitdiener der Zeugen Jehovas), where he lived and worked as a preacher.

By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant was ordered to undergo another examination as to his ability to perform military service pursuant to section 24(8) of the Military Service Act (Wehrgesetz), as in force at the relevant time. The applicant appealed against that order, claiming in particular that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. The Administrative Court (Verwaltungs-gerichtshof) dismissed the applicant's complaint on 26 March 1998. name: David Adetoro
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46834/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During the interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment’. The applicant also provided answers to all the questions which he had declined to answer during the police interviews in March and June 1997. The judge directed them as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to prove things. ... The next matter of law, is the standard. of proof, this is a very simple concept, that you must be sure. rely in court’ The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The applicant did not suggest that he was advised by his lawyer not to comment but said that he did not want to incriminate people in relation to stolen vehicles. He admitted that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that, was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery, as he had been, he didn't want to implicate them in the stealing of cars. On 18 June 1998 the jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged. He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing, inter alia, that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The court upheld the conviction and sentenced Mr Adetoro to prison for 26 years. The judge found that he was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The judge said he had six previous convictions dating from 1998, including a conviction for conspiracy to rob and described the applicant as a dangerous, cunning and intelligent man. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (‘CCRC’) referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of Appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant’s silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The court disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trialJudge, the conviction was safe. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation before they could have used it as supportive of the Crown's case. It concluded that: “The direction the judge gave could only have related to lies told byThe court referred to the accused's defence itself. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The Court of Appeal found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming, and concluded: “This was not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would have tipped the balance”. The applicant was found guilty of a charge of perverting the course of justice and sentenced to three years in prison. The conviction was later quashed on appeal and he was sentenced to a year in prison, but the sentence was overturned on appeal again. The case was heard at the High Court in London, and was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice, which upheld the conviction.

The judge directed the jury as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant’s. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30141/04) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged in particular that they were discriminated against as, being a same-sex couple, they were denied the possibility to marry or to have their relationship otherwise recognised by law. On 8 January 2007 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 February 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms B. Ohms, Federal Chancellery, Deputy Agent, Ms G. Paschinger, Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs, Mr M. Stormann and Mr K. Mayer, Counsel. The applicants argued that the legal impossibility for them to marry constituted a violation of their right to respect for private and family life. The Vienna Regional Court of Appeals ruled that the marriage could not go ahead. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, who ruled in favour of the applicants. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 3 January 2003. The application for a divorce was also rejected. The couple were allowed to leave the country, and their case was dismissed. The appeals court ruled in favor of the couple, and the appeal was thrown out of court on 7 January 2004. The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court of Europe, which ruled in their favour. The applicants alleged a breach of their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. They argued that in the event that one partner in a homosexual couple died, the other was discriminated against since he would be in a much less favourable position under tax law. The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) dismissed the applicants’ complaint. The European Court of Human Rights found in its Cossey [v. the United Kingdom] judgment of 27 September 1990 (no. 10843/84, [Series A no. 184], concerning the particular position of transsexual persons) that the restriction of marriage to this ‘traditional’ concept was objectively justified. The Civil Code provides: “The marriage contract shall form the basis for family relationships” The purpose of the Registered Partnership Act (Eingetragene Partnerschaft-Gesetz) was to provide same-sex couples with a formal mechanism for recognising and giving legal effect to their relationships. The rules on the establishment of a registered partnership, its effects and its dissolution resemble the rules governing marriage. “A registered partnership may be formed only by two persons of the same sex (registered partners) They thereby commit themselves to a lasting relationship with mutual rights and obligations” “It is unnecessary in the instant case to examine whether, and in which areas, the law unjustifiably discriminates against same- sex relationships by providing for special rules for married couples.”  registered partnership. involves cohabitation on a permanent basis and may be entered into between two persons of the same sex having legal capacity and having reached the age of majority. A registered partnership must not be established between close relatives or with a person who is already married or has established a still valid registered partnership with another person. As in the case of spouses, the partner who is in charge of the common household and has no income has legal authority to represent the other partner in everyday legal transactions. Registered partners have the same obligations regarding maintenance as spouses. Dissolution of a registered partnership occurs in the event of the death of one partner. The right to marry and to found a family is guaranteed in Article 9 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which came into force on 1 December 2009. A few countries, e.g. in the Netherlands and in Belgium, marriage between people of the same sex is legally recognised. Others, like the Nordic countries, have endorsed a registered partnership legislation, which implies, among other things, that most provisions concerning marriage, i.e. property distribution, rights of inheritance, etc., are also applicable to these unions. There is no explicit reference to ‘men and women’ as the case is in other human rights instruments, it may be argued that there is no obstacle to recognise same-sex relationships in the context of marriage. International courts and committees have so far hesitated to extend the application of the right to marry to same-sex couples. A number of directives are also of interest in the present case. Currently, six out of forty-seven member States grant same- sex couples equal access to marriage. In addition, the following thirteen member States do not grant same-'sex' couples access to married life. The state of relevant legislation in Council of Europe member States is as follows: Andorra, Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Iceland, Luxembourg, Sweden, Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. There are 19 member States in which same-sex couples either have the possibility to marry or to enter into a registered partnership. The legal consequences of registered partnerships vary from being almost equivalent to marriage to giving relatively limited rights. In most of the States concerned, registered partners obtain a status similar to marriage. The possibilities for registered partners to undergo medically assisted insemination or to foster or adopt children vary greatly from one country to another. Other consequences include the use of the partner’s surname, the impact on a foreign partner's ability to obtain a residence permit and citizenship, refusal to testify, next of kin status for medical purposes, and lawful organ donation.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their rights to respect for their private life and reputation had been breached. The court found that the journalists had failed to contact the applicants and that their allegations were, to a large extent, based on gossip and hearsay. It noted that journalists had a right and an obligation to inform society about important issues and that they enjoyed freedom of expression. The allegations had not been shown to have had a plausible factual basis. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicants sought an order requiring the defendants to take down the article from the newspaper’s website and publish a written apology. They sought compensation in the amount of PLN 11,000 for the non‑pecuniary damage. The court allowed the applicants’ claim in its entirety, by ordering the journalists and the editor‑in‑chief to pay, jointly, PLN 30,000 to a charity and to publish an apology in the newspaper. The obligations imposed by the courts were subsequently complied with by the defendant newspaper. As a result of this, the court ruled that the original article should be expunged. The Warsaw Regional Court, by a judgment of 28 September 2005, dismissed the applicants’ claim. The court was of the opinion that the discovery of a new source of publication, namely the newspaper’s website, of the defamatory article had given rise to a new claim on the applicants' part. It stressed that removing the article from the website would have been devoid of any practical purpose and would amount to censorship and to rewriting history. It was the journalists’ right and obligation to inform the general public of matters of public interest, the court said. It pointed out that the applicants have already received a public apology. Allowing the application to have a new apology published would not offer adequate protection. The applicants appealed. They argued that the case was important in that it raised new issues which had hitherto not been addressed by judicial practice. They submitted that each new reading of the article on the newspaper’s website, which was open to the general public, amounted to a new publication of that article. The court had unequivocally acknowledged that the impugned article had violated their rights. It had, however, limited itself to dismissing the claim. The Internet was not an instrument for archiving materials, but had to be regarded as a means of communication of information on current topics. The mere fact that a part of a website was called an “archive” did not affect this in any way. The Warsaw Court of Appeal rejected the appeal in so far as it related to the first applicant. It noted that the court fee paid in connection with the appeal had corresponded to the sum to be paid for an appeal lodged by one person only. No appeal was lodged against this decision. The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their rights to respect for their private life and reputation had been breached. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The court observed that the journalists had failed to contact the applicants and that their allegations were, to a large extent, based on gossip and hearsay. It noted that journalists had a right and an obligation to inform society about important issues and that they enjoyed freedom of expression, guaranteed by the Constitution. The applicants sued again the newspaper under the same provisions of the Civil Code. They alleged that they had recently found out that the article remained accessible on the newspaper’s Internet website. They sought compensation in the amount of PLN 11,000 for the non‑pecuniary damage. The court allowed the applicants’ claim in its entirety, by ordering the journalists and the editor‑in‑chief to pay, jointly, PLN 30,000 to a charity and to publish an apology in the newspaper. The obligations imposed by the courts were subsequently complied with by the defendant newspaper. As the applicants had already obtained a judgment in their favour, their request to have the article expunged was ill‑founded. The Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. The court was of the opinion that the discovery of a new source of publication, namely the newspaper’s website, of the defamatory article had given rise to a new claim on the applicants' part. It noted that removing the article from the website would have been devoid of any practical purpose and would amount to censorship and to rewriting history. It was the journalists’ right and obligation to inform the general public of matters of public interest. The applicants have already received a public apology. Allowing the claim to have a new apology published would not offer adequate protection to the applicants. The applicants appealed. They argued that the case was important in that it raised new issues which had hitherto not been addressed by judicial practice. They submitted that each new reading of the article on the newspaper’s website, which was open to the general public, amounted to a new publication of that article. Traditional principles governing the archiving of various printed materials and documents in traditional archives were not the same as those applicable to the operation of a website. The term “archive” was to be understood as a set of documents which had lost their currency. The Internet was not an instrument for archiving materials, but had to be regarded as a means of communication of information. The applicant, a lawyer and member of the administrative board of the Istanbul Human Rights Association, organised a demonstration in Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul, in the form of a march followed by a statement to the press, to protest against plans for “F-type” prisons. The police asked the group to disperse and to end the gathering, and informed them via a loudspeaker that the demonstration, for which advance notice had not been submitted, was unlawful. The demonstrators refused to obey and attempted to continue marching towards the police, who dispersed the group using a kind of tear gas known as “pepper spray” The police arrested thirty-nine demonstrators, including the applicant, and took them to a police station. On 29 June 2000 the public prosecutor’s office discontinued the proceedings on the ground that no offence had been committed. On 25 July 2000 the applicant applied to the Beyoğlu Assize Court seeking to have that decision set aside.On 25 September 2000 the AssizeCourt upheld the decision that there was no case to answer. The case has been referred to as the case of the two Turkish women who were unlawfully arrested and prevented from making the public statement scheduled for the end of the demonstration. The charges against the women were later dropped by the prosecutor's office and the case was thrown out of court on the grounds that it was not a case of unlawful arrest.

The first applicant is the mother of two children, P. and J.; the second applicant is J.’s father. The first applicant came into contact with the social authorities in 1984 while expecting her first child P. Following his birth, he and his mother stayed with her parents, then with her second applicant and, as from May 1985, with P’S. father. After the birth of her second son J. in 1986 the first applicant moved in with J. and his father. On 17 November 1997 the applicants sought to file a document. On 24 November the President, in consultation with the Chamber, decided not to accept the document for filing (Rule 39 § 1, third sub-paragraph) The first applicant moved to Västra Frölunda in order to be closer to her parents. In the summer of 1986 she moved to Högsbohöjd. On 8 February 1989, in the light of an investigation by the social authorities, the Chairperson of the Social District Council decided to take the children immediately into care on a provisional basis. The children were placed at the Bö Children’s Home in Gothenburg. The first applicant appealed against the decision to taking the children provisionally into care. However, the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) and the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten), of Gothenberg upheld the decision and the Supreme Administrative Court refused her leave to appeal. On 20 March 1990 the Chairperson of the Social Council (stadsdelsnämnden) of Högsbo decided, pursuant to section 16 of the 1980 Act, to restrict the first applicant’s access to her children to a 2½ hours’ visit in the foster homes every second week. The County Administrative Court quashed the decision in a judgment of 20 June 1990. That judgment was overturned on 6 July 1990 by the Administrative Court of Appeal. The first applicant appealed against the decision to the Supreme Administrative Court which, on 5 November 1990, refused leave to appeal. The case was referred back to the County administrative Court for determination of the merits of the access restrictions. The second applicant’s access to his son J. was granted on 23 July 1991. In June 1993 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ judgments as regards the restrictions on access. According to the Government, the delay in giving judgment appeared to have been due to the fact that it was awaiting the Strasbourg Court’S ruling in the case of Margareta and Roger Andersson v. Sweden (judgment of 25 February 1992, Series A no. 226‑A) which raised similar issues in relation to restrictions on telephone communications between mother and child. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 66689/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Revolutionary Communists’ Union of Turkey (“the TIKB”, Türkiye İhtilalci Komünistler Birliği) and placed in custody. She denied all the charges against her. She declared that her statement in police custody was taken under duress and that she had been given electric shocks. The judge ordered the applicant’s detention pending trial. The applicant was convicted under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of State Security Court on 20 September 1999. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Court ofCassation on 14 October 2000. The application was dismissed on 22 October 2000 and the case was returned to the court of cassation. The case is still pending at the   İzmir State Security  Court. It is unclear whether the applicant will ever be freed from jail. The organisation’s members are still imprisoned and participating in the demonstrations organised by the organisation. providing information to its members.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32435/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Hermann Kammerer (‘the applicant’) alleged that his right to be heard had been infringed. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The IAP dismissed the applicant's appeal and only amended a citation of the DAA's decision. It found that even though the car was used by somebody else the applicant, as the registered owner has to check that the car undergoes regular inspections, did not consider it necessary to question the witness. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court in which he complained, inter alia, that the IAP had convicted him in absentia. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the case since it did not involve a question of fundamental rights. The case was transferred to the Administrative Court on 29 July 2005. The Administrative Court refused to deal. with the complaint on 27 January 2006 since the amount of the penalty did not exceed EUR 750.

None of the applicants was legally represented at the hearings in front of the magistrates. Each applicant spent a period of time in prison. In all five cases the orders were quashed following the High Court’s approval of a consent order agreed between the applicants and magistrates who had sentenced them. The High Court has set out the relevant facts pertaining to each applicant in the table which appears at the end of the decision. Julie BEET (47676/99) spent a total of 2 days in prison. The applicant’s proceedings before the magistrates arose in respect of her arrears in payment of the community charge and took place after 1 June 1997. The orders of the magistrate were quashed by the High Court as a result of a consent order in which it was agreed that: “(i) The decision of the justices that the applicant had culpably neglected to pay her community charge without having conducted a proper inquiry into her circumstances as of the time that the liability became due was unlawful, see R. v. Leeds Justices ex parte Kennett [1996] RVR 53” It was agreed that costs be borne by the respondent justices see R. v. Newcastle upon Tyne Justices ex parte Devine [1998] RA 97. It was further agreed that: “... in view of the fact that the Hull Justices had acknowledged the same ground in quashing the committal in R.v. Hull justices exparte Shawcross (CO/265/98), the costs of this case should also be borne.” It was also agreed that the cost of the costs should be shared by the respondents, rather than paid by the court of appeal. The decision was made by the Supreme Court of Northumberland, which ruled in favour of the respondent.

name: Rolf Gustafson
train_texts: Case was referred to the Court on 18 December 1995 by the applicant, Mr Rolf Gustafson, a Swedish national. The applicant’s application bringing the case before the Court referred to Article 48 of the Convention (art. 48), as amended by Protocol No. 9 (P9), which has been ratified by Sweden. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The Court’'s Screening Panel decided not to decline consideration and to submit it to the court (Article 48 para. 2-2) The applicant claims that on two occasions, in April-June and June‑July 1991, he was the victim of kidnapping and extortion perpetrated by three persons. According to the applicant, one of the alleged perpetrators, a certain Mr L., had wanted to be paid for the part he played with him in the commission of certain economic crimes. The applicant requested the court, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 22 of the Code of Judicial Procedure (Rättegångsbalken) to order L. to pay him a total of 169,350 Swedish kronor (SEK) in compensation in respect of the following items: (a) material damages to his clothes; (b) SEK 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages. The applicant applied for compensation to the Criminal Damage Compensation Board (Brottsskadenämnden - hereinafter ‘the Board’) under the Criminal damage Act 1978. The applicant reserved his right to present further claims in respect of any such damage as he might suffer in the future. The Stockholm District Court convicted L. and sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay SEK 144,350 in damages to the applicant. The Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) reversed the District Court’s decision on the ground that the charges against L. had not been proven, acquitted L and rejected the applicant's claim for compensation. The Board rejected the applicant’s compensation claim on 26 August 1993. The applicant asked the Board to reconsider its decision. He argued that it was clear from the judgments of the District Court and the Court of Appeal that he had been the victim of a crime. He had identified two of the three persons who were allegedly involved in the offences; the fact that the only one to be charged, L., was guilty was not a reason to doubt that he was a victim of crime. The Board said it could not find it established that [the applicant] has suffered damage as a result of crime, Consequently, compensation for damage caused by crime cannot be awarded. Inspector S. had been the principal investigator into the economic offences of which the applicant had previously been convicted. He had interrogated both the applicant and L. on a number of occasions. His report and Crime Inspector S.’s testimony had in essence been reproduced in the District Court's judgment. The case was also heard orally before the Court of Appeal, where it was decided that L. had not committed any of the offences against which he was accused. L. was acquitted of all charges against him by the Appeal Court, and the case was dismissed on appeal. The appeal was decided on the grounds that the judge had made a mistake in his original decision. On 1 June 1994 the Board rejected the applicant’s request, for the following reasons: “The submissions in this case in support of the request for reconsideration are not such as to be a reason for the Board to change its previous decision. Nor is there any other reason for changing the decision.““He had more or less repeated the same evidence he gave to the District Court.”“The evidence was similar to what he had given in the previous hearing.’“. “There was no reason to change the previous decision,” said the Board. ”.

A colleague ... telephoned me to say that he had been informed that [the applicant] had been kidnapped ..., that the kidnapping had been staged by [L.] with the help of two ‘gorillas’, ... and that the kidnap had been combined with an extortion threat against [ the applicant] in the amount of SEK 5 million” On 1 June 1994 the Board rejected the applicant’s request, for the following reasons: “The submissions in this case in support of the request for reconsideration are not such as to be a reason for the Board to change its previous decision. Nor is there any other reason for changing the decision.” “He had more or less repeated the same evidence he gave to the District Court.’ “ “There was no evidence that the applicant had been involved in any way in any criminal activity.“ ‘He had no evidence to suggest that he was involved in a criminal offence’

name: Paul Matthew Coyne
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25942/94) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by Mr Paul Matthew Coyne, a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The applicant Paul Matthew Coyne made a claim for just satisfaction or costs. The Government offered to settle the case on the basis of the payment of the applicant’s reasonable legal costs and expenses. The Court decided that it would be necessary to hold an oral hearing. A hearing limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, and for the applicant Mr G. Blades, Solicitor. In August 1993 Mr Coyne was charged, pursuant to section 70 (1) of the Air Force Act 1955, with four civilian criminal offences. The charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. On 26 January 1994 the convening officer convened a district court martial, appointing all three members of the court martial by name. The court martial took place at the RAF Station, Brüggen on 26‑28 January 1994. After pleading not guilty to all the charges against him he was found not guilty on the first and second charges. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. The Court Martial Appeal Court rejected the appeal on 7 March 1994. The appeal was based on claims that the sentence was excessive. The Court Appeal Court ruled that the evidence was insufficient to prove that the charge was false. The Appeal Court made the decision on the basis that the conviction was not justified by the evidence. The decision was reversed by the Court of Appeal on 14 March 1994, and the appeal was rejected on 11 October 1994, on the grounds that there was insufficient evidence to support the conviction. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Australia, which ruled in favor of the appeal and ordered the conviction to be overturned. The court’s decision was overturned on 15 May 1994, with the appeal upheld.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25942/94) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The applicant, Mr Paul Matthew Coyne, was born in 1972 and lives in Bedford. He joined the Royal Air Force (“RAF”) in 1990. In June 1992, when he was serving as a non-commissioned officer in Br, Mr Coyne was involved in the death of a member of the British public. A hearing limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel. Mr Coyne was charged, pursuant to section 70 (1) of the Air Force Act 1955, with four civilian criminal offences. The charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. Mr Coyne presented a petition against conviction and sentence on 31 January 1994, claiming that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case, that he was not guilty on the first and second charges, and that no finding was made on the fourth charge. The petition was rejected and he was released from the RAF. The case is described in detail in the following pages. The appeal was made on 8 March 1994. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on the grounds that the charge was not supported by the evidence. The Appeal was then made to the Defence Council, which accepted the appeal. The case was dismissed on 11 October 1994 on the basis that the charges were not substantiated by the facts. The matter is now before the Supreme Court, which will make a decision on the appeal in May 2014. The result of the appeal will be known by the end of the year or in early 2015 when the case will be heard by the Court of Appeals.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 September 1996. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. On 24 April 1997 the President decided that legal aid should be granted to the applicant for the proceedings before the Court. The Government indicated that they had no submissions to make on the merits and offered to settle the case on the basis of the payment of the applicant’s reasonable legal costs and expenses. On 28 May 1997, the Court decided that it would be necessary to hold an oral hearing. A hearing limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Blades and Mr Eadie. Mr Coyne was charged with various offences of forgery and deception. Charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. Mr Coyne presented a petition against conviction and sentence on 31 January 1994. He claimed that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case, that he had been wrongly convicted and that the court martial had been unfair. The petition was rejected and he was discharged from the RAF in November 1994. The case was heard by a RAF court martial at the RAF Station, Brüggen, Germany on 26 January 1994. The Court Martial Appeal Court accepted the finding of guilt on one charge and the sentence on the other. The court made the decision on the basis of the advice of a single officer. The decision was made on the grounds that the officer had properly advised the court that the charge was not true. The Court Appeal Court made its decision on 8 March 1994. The appeal was rejected on 11 October 1994, and the conviction was upheld on the same grounds. The conviction was quashed on 14 March 1995, and a new appeal was made against the original conviction on 12 March 1995. The Appeal Court ruled that the conviction of the first charge was incorrect, and that the sentence was not excessive. The Appeals Court decided on 13 March 1994 that the second charge was true, and upheld the conviction.

name: Fedai Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21773/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Fedai Şahin (‘the applicant’), on 7 July 2000. The applicant was taken into custody within the context of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the TKP/ML – TIKKO (the Turkish Communist Party-Marxist Leninist - Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army). On 17 November 1992 the applicant was placed in detention on remand. The case was remitted to the Istanbul Assize Court for re-trial. The applicant appealed the decision. The proceedings are currently pending before the Court of Cassation. The case was re-tried between 12 May 2006 and 30 May 2007. The court found the applicant guilty of the alleged offence and sentenced him to life imprisonment, pursuant to Article 146§ 1 of the Criminal Code. The application is still pending and the judge has not made a ruling. The appeal is currently pending. The judge has yet to make a decision on the appeal. The applicants appeal against the decision, which was made by the judge, and the appeal is still awaiting a decision. It is hoped that the appeal will be heard in the autumn.

On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench of the Istanbul State Security Court was replaced by a civilian judge. The application is still pending at the Court Of Cassation, which will rule on the appeal in May. The judge also ruled that the case should be re-tried, and that the applicant should be sentenced to 15 years in prison.

name: Fatma Çamdereli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28433/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 4 May 2002. The applicant, a housewife, was born in 1953 and lives in Bursa. The alleged ill-treatment of the applicant took place on 18 February 1999. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It decided to give notice to the Government on 11 June 2007. The application was brought by Mrs Fatma Çamdereli, a Turkish national. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The Bursa Criminal Court of First Instance decided, in accordance with the relevant provisions of Law no. 4616, that the proceedings against the accused should be suspended and subsequently discontinued if no offence of the same or a more serious kind was committed by the offenders within a five-year period. The applicant’s objection against this decision, notably regarding the application of LawNo.4616, was dismissed on 9 January 2002. On 23 January 2006 the Burs a Forensic Medical Institute referred the applicant to the Court of Appeal for further proceedings. The court ruled that the charges against Mr T.Ü. and Mr M.A.G. should be dropped. The applicant bought an action in tort against Mr T.Ü. and Mr M.A.G. before the Bursa Civil Court of First Instance. She sought compensation in the amount of 1,500,000,000 Turkish liras [TRL] (approximately 2,700 euros [EUR] at that time) for non-pecuniary damage for the treatment she had received from Mr T., M. and A. The applicant’s lawyer informed the court that she had been paid the amount awarded in full. The criminal proceedings against the accused were dropped after the statutory time-limit for the offence had expired.

There was no evidence of entrapment or any other abusive action on the part of the police. The potential branches of the civil or criminal law and Article 8 do not affect the quality of the evidence.

The Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The case was settled in favour of the applicants and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) from 10 October 2000 to 11 October 2000. The decision was upheld by the ECJ and the appeal was dismissed. Two men travelled to Brazil and the first went to Los Angeles. The two applicants returned to London on 30 October. Armand was observed arriving at Heathrow carrying a black suitcase. On 2 November 1990 he met Thierry (who had been in France) and Mr Terrasson (coming from Brazil) at Heathrows. Mr Smolny was also on this flight, although there was no evidence of contact between him and the applicants. customs officers intercepted the luggage. They found that the two black suitcases were indeed very similar. One of the suitcases was to contain 18 kilograms of cocaine. The other black suitcase was not collected from the carousel. Armand Terrasson was arrested at Heathrow. Mr Smolny was arrested later in Zurich. All three men were interviewed and denied any knowledge of or participation in the offence. The prosecution case was that Armand had organised the importation, using Mr Smorny as the courier from Brazil to Copenhagen and London, and that he had instructed Mr Terrass on to collect MrSmolny’s suitcase as if in mistake for his own. There was no forensic evidence. Under cross-examination by the defence counsel, the customs case-officer claimed that the only relevant evidence held by the prosecution was two tapes of interviews with the applicants’ South London relatives. Armand Atlan, Thierry Terrasson and David Smolny were accused of trying to smuggle cocaine into the UK. The applicants claimed that rival jewel trader Rudi Steiner was an informer for Customs and Excise. But there was no evidence to connect Mr Steiner to Mr Molny’s suitcase full of drugs or to substantiate the suggestion that he was a Customs andexcise informer. All four defendants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence at the trial in London. The judge summarised the defence by saying, inter alia: “...Steiner had long since either directly or through the Brazilian authorities informed British Customs and. Excise that Armand Atlan and Thierries Terrassons were preparing to smuggling cocaine to England" Steiner sent a representative to Copenhagen to pick up diamonds from Armand Atlan. Atlan told British Customs of the itinerary of the various people to be delivered. Steiner then sent his representative off with a duplicate of Terrasson’s suitcase, believing it, of course, to be antiques and works of art. He lost the cost of sending his representative diagonally across the world and back [with the sample] with a bit of time in a hotel. The cost of 18 kilograms of 90 plus percent pure cocaine in Brazil is very, very much less than it would be in London, but ... you may think that 18 kilos of high quality cocaine like that would cost a substantial sum. Armand Thierry was sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment and a confiscation order of GBP 1,918,489.60 with a further ten years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. Rudi Steiner was one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine, which he was able freely to obtain from the Brazilian police. The applicants provided a copy of the report to the prosecution, which was given to the applicants’ solicitors. In a letter dated 4 December 1995, the Swiss Federal Police Office informed the applicants that the report was the property of the Tessin cantonal police. The applicants added a further ground of appeal coupled with an application for leave to call fresh evidence. The Court of Appeal indicated its view that the Mato Grosso Report would not be admissible in evidence because, inter alia, its author could not be found to vouch for its accuracy and be cross-examined on its contents. It decided not to rule on the application unless or until such time that, having considered the applicants’ application to introduce new evidence, it became necessary to do so. The applicants were granted legal aid to enable their solicitor to travel to Italy where, it was believed, Rudi Steiner was in custody awaiting trial for smuggling cocaine. Court of Appeal ruled that in principle it had jurisdiction to issue such a letter of request. Originally constituted court decided that the applicants’ proposed request to the Italian authorities was too wide-ranging and unlikely to elicit information which would be either admissible or of assistance in the appeal. Court of Appeal adjourned the case until after the conclusion of Mr Steiner’s trial in Italy in the Autumn of 1996. In the event, however, Mr. Steiner was released on bail and his whereabouts were unknown at the time of the appeal hearing in February 1997. The applicants added a further ground of appeal, alleging that the prosecution had failed to make full disclosure of the evidence in its possession. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. The court dismissed the application for leave to appeal. It observed that little, if any, of the material put before the Court of Appeal by the applicants’ counsel would have been admissible at the trial. However, in considering all the information put before us, we have not been able to avoid taking a view of its effect if, and to the extent that it were admissible and credible, on the outcome of this appeal, that is, whether ... it ‘[might] afford any ground for allowing the appeal’ Prosecuting counsel suggested Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end. Such a conspiracy between Steiner and the officers would have been hard for them to organise to an assured outcome. The jury, by its verdict, clearly rejected Thierry and Terrasson’s suggestion of it. There are also a number of other questions indicating the impossibility of the Atlans’ defence. Why, if they thought they were to collect diamonds from Steiner, not drugs, did they check their luggage onto the return flight without apparently enquiring by telephone why he had not turned up or whether he had been delayed? Why did Smolny and the two of them make no contact in Copenhagen and ignore each other on the plane to Heathrow? Prosecuting counsel’s submission, which echoes considerations voiced by the judge to the jury in the summing up, provides a logical and complete answer to the complaint based on Steiner's alleged role as an informer and drug smuggler. His only possible line of defence, though, for the reasons we have given, is a wholly unrealistic one. The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. All that activity pointed only to their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law. The Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear.

The case originated in an application (no. 36533/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied a fair trial in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. By a decision of 10 October 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicants and another man, Jean-Pierre Terrasson, were convicted of illegally importing 18 kilograms of cocaine (with a street value of GBP 2‑3 million) into Heathrow Airport, London, on 3 November 1990. Two men travelled to Brazil and Los Angeles in 1990. When they returned to London, they were intercepted by customs officers. The pair were arrested and the cocaine was found to be in their suitcases. They were sentenced to 10 years in prison and a three-year suspended sentence. The case has been described as one of the most notorious drug busts in the history of the UK. The trial took place in front of a jury in the High Court of Justice in London in November 1990. The defendants were convicted of conspiring to smuggle cocaine into the UK and sentenced to a total of 10 years behind bars. The verdicts were quashed on a technicality and the defendants were released. Armand Terrasson, a diamond dealer in England for a short time, was arrested at Heathrow. He said he had travelled alone to Copenhagen, taking with him a black suitcase, to meet a married woman friend. He was unable to meet her because her husband was home, so he returned immediately to London. Mr Smolny was arrested later in Zurich and claimed he had been instructed by a man called Mr Morgan to bring the black suitcase from Sao Paolo to Heathrow and to leave it on the luggage carousel. All three men were interviewed and denied any knowledge of or participation in the offence. There was no forensic evidence to support the prosecution's case. Defendants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. The applicants maintained that Armand worked principally as a jewel trader, but that he did not keep written records because he systematically avoided paying taxes and duties in Brazil. The illegality of his jewel trading had motivated their lies during their initial interviews with customs officers. The defence centred around a dispute between Armand and a rival jewel trader based in Brazil called Rudi Steiner. They claimed that, in order to avoid repaying his debt and for fear that the applicants would discredit him amongst other Brazilian traders, he had arranged falsely to implicate them in the importation of cocaine. But they had no evidence to connect Mr Steiner to Mr Molny’s suitcase full of drugs or to substantiate the suggestion that he was a Customs and Excise informer. Mr Steiner got Armand Atlan to believe that it was worthwhile going for the third time to Copenhagen for a delivery of the diamonds. He notified Customs of the itinerary of the various people which was to be foreseen from these arrangements, and that is how the incident you have heard about on the afternoon of that day came about. Steiner. off with the suitcase ... with the drugs in it, believing it, of course, to be antiques and works of art. It would be difficult for Steiner to ask the British Customs and Excise about Terrasson’s suitcase for that purpose, you may think, without revealing he himself was engaged in setting them up. On 5 July 1991 the jury, by a majority of ten to one, convicted the applicants and Mr Terrasson of importing the cocaine. Mr Smolny was acquitted. In spring 1994 the applicants learned from the French press (Libération) that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report. In early 1995 the applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine, which he was able freely to obtain from the Brazilian police. The applicants added a further ground of appeal coupled with an application for leave to call fresh evidence. They maintained that the Mato Grosso Report substantiated their suggestion at trial that Mr Steiner had access both to stolen jewels and cocaine. In their submission, the fact that the jury had not had before it evidence relating to these matters, and the judge, ignorant of the true facts, rendered their convictions unsafe. The applicants objected to the holding of an ex parte hearing, inter alia that the court was a tribunal of both fact and law and could be adversely influenced by material which was wrong or inaccurate. The Court of Appeal dismissed the objections and heard the prosecution’s ex partse application. Court of Appeal ruled that in principle it had jurisdiction to issue a letter of request. But the application was too wide-ranging and unlikely to elicit information which would be either admissible or of assistance in the appeal. The case was adjourned until after the conclusion of Mr Steiner’s trial in Italy in the Autumn of 1996. In the event, however, he was released on bail and his whereabouts were unknown at the time of the appeal hearing in February 1997. The applicants’ solicitor was able to obtain a number of documents relating to the Italian proceedings, including transcripts of interviews with Mr. Steiner, arrest warrants and a list of his previous convictions. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. Court of Appeal dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. Court observed: “Little, if any, of the material ... would have been admissible at the trial’. The applicants and their lawyers were not permitted to be present when the court delivered its judgment on disclosure. The court noted that the material was largely hearsay and unspecific as to events and dates. Much of it is wholly irrelevant to the central issue in this case, namely whether British Customs and Excise officers conspired with Steiner to ‘frame’ the Atlans. Prosecuting counsel suggested that Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end. Such a conspiracy between Steiner and the officers would have been hard for them to organise to an assured outcome. The jury, by its verdict, clearly rejected Thierry and Terrasson’s suggestion of it. Why did the Atlans tell so many lies on arrest and in interview about their activities together before the flight to Copenhagen and about the reason for it? Why did they later give wholly different accounts in evidence at their trial? Why. did Smolny make indirect telephone contact with someone on Armand's telephone number in Brazil on the day of the importation? Prosecuting counsel’s submission, which echoes considerations voiced by the judge to the jury in the summing up, provides a logical and complete answer to the complaint. The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. All that activity pointed only to their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law. ...” Whatever Steiner's possible role as an informer, the Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear,” the judge said. “His only possible line of defence, though, for the reasons we have given, is a wholly unrealistic one.”

In spring 1994 the applicants learned from the French press that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report, called ‘the Mato Grosso Report’. The applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. On 10 June 1996 a different constitution of the Court. of Appeal ruled that in principle it had jurisdiction to issue such a letter of request. It therefore decided that it was not in the public interest to issue a letter. of request, and adjourned the case until after the conclusion of Mr Steiner’s trial in Italy in the Autumn of 1996. It observed: “Little, if any, of the material [put before the Court of Appeal by the applicants’ counsel] would have been admissible at the trial.” The court dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. The case relates to whether British Customs and Excise officers conspired with Steiner to ‘frame’ the Atlans. The Atlans were charged with smuggling large quantities of cocaine from South America to Italy in 1995. Prosecuting counsel suggested that the only way Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end would have been to persuade the officers to ‘plant’ the drug on, or falsely attribute it to, Thierry or Terrasson. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39652/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The case was referred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 12 January 1999 the Chamber decided to adjourn the examination of the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings for rescission of the exclusion order. In a decision of 22 March 2000, the Grand Chamber declared the remainder of the application admissible, while reserving the issue of the applicability of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The French Government (“the Government”) each filed written observations on the merits of the case. The applicant, who was born in 1958 in Tunisia, entered France in 1980 at the age of 22. On 14 September 1992 he married a French national, an invalid whose disability had been assessed at 80%. On 1 December 1988 the Alpes-Maritimes Assize Court sentenced the applicant to six years’ imprisonment for armed robbery and armed assault with intent for offences committed in 1985. He was released on 14 April 1990. On 8 August 1991 the Minister of the Interior made a deportation order against him. An appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 1 June 1994 on the ground that the applicant had failed to challenge the legality of the deportation order in the courts below. In December 1992 the applicant sought judicial review of the deportation order. In a judgment of 14 February 1994 the Nice Administrative Court quashed the order of 8 August 1991. The applicant applied to the Principal Public Prosecutor’s Office at the Aix-en-Provence Court of Appeal on 12 August 1994 for rescission of the ten-year exclusion order made by the Nice Criminal Court on 19 November 1992. He contended that he was married to a French national and held a provisional residence permit. He initially obtained acknowledgment forms for applications for provisional residence permits (not work permits) for renewable three-month periods. On 4 September 1995, however, he was given a new 3-month residence permit incorporating the right to seek employment. The applicant received notice of a decision dated 2 April 1996 refusing him a residence permit. to live and work in France for a prolonged period, as he was married to a French citizen. He appealed to the Nice Administrative Court, but his appeal was dismissed on 27 September 1996. The applicant appealed on 24 December 1996 to the Lyons Administrative Court of Appeal. On 21 July 1998 the applicant obtained a temporary residence permit valid for one year (from 13 July 1998 to 12 July 1999) Recently he obtained a ten-year residence permit with the right to seek employment. The case is currently pending in the Marseilles Administrative court of Appeal – the court with jurisdiction.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was referred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 12 January 1999 the Chamber decided to adjourn the examination of the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings for rescission of the exclusion order. In a decision of 22 March 2000 the Grand Chamber declared the remainder of the application admissible, while reserving the issue of the applicability of Article 6 § 1 of the Hague Convention. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 5 July 2000. The applicant, who was born in 1958 in Tunisia, entered France in 1980 at the age of 22. On 14 September 1992 he married a French national, an invalid whose disability had been assessed at 80%, with whom he had been living since 1983. He refused to travel to Tunisia and was prosecuted for failing to comply with a deportation order. On 19 November 1992 the Nice Criminal Court sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment and made an order excluding him from French territory for ten years. An appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 1 June 1994 on the ground that the applicant had failed to challenge the legality of the deportation order in the courts below. The applicant sought judicial review of the deportation order. He contended that he was married to a French national and held a provisional residence permit. The applicant applied to the Principal Public Prosecutor’s Office at the Aix-en-Provence Court of Appeal on 12 August 1994 for rescission of the ten-year exclusion order made by the Nice Criminal Court on 19 November 1992. He initially obtained acknowledgment forms for applications for provisional residence permits (not work permits) for renewable three-month periods. On 4 September 1995, however, he was given a new 3-month residence permit incorporating the right to seek employment. He also sought to regularise his status with the immigration authorities. The case is still pending at the Marseilles Administrative Court of Appeal – the court with jurisdiction – where the case is currently pending. The applicant is married to a French citizen and was refused a residence permit in 1996. On 21 July 1998 the applicant obtained a temporary residence permit valid for one year (from 13 July 1998 to 12 July 1999) Recently he obtained a ten-year residence permit with the right to seek employment. The application is being heard by the Court of First Instance in Lausanne, Switzerland. The case is being argued by the Attorney General of Switzerland and is currently being dealt with by the Supreme Court of Justice of France.
