name: Memet Koçak
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the convention at the same time as its admissibility under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of thevention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant and five other persons were arrested by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate. The applicant alleges that, while there, he was blindfolded and forced to listen to the cries of other detainees being tortured. He was stripped naked, immersed in cold water and beaten with a truncheon on various parts of his body, including the soles of his feet. His hands were tied with a blanket and he was strung up by his arms and subjected to a form of torture known as “Palestinian hanging” He was subsequently coerced into signing a statement, of which he only signed the first two pages. On both occasions the applicant denied the accuracy of the statements that had been taken from him by the police. The applicant's injuries rendered him unfit for work for seven days. The applicant filed further petitions alleging that he had been subjected to ill‑treatment while in police custody. The Istanbul public prosecutor initiated an investigation into the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 20 December 1995 the Istanbul Assize Court acquitted the accused police officers, holding that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the accused had ill-treated the applicant. The judgment of 20 December1995 became final as the public prosecutor did not lodge an objection to the decision of 5 June 1995. The judge ruled that the applicant was not entitled to compensation for the injuries he had sustained. The applicant surrendered a 7.65 mm calibre pistol and seven bullets to the police officers. Several weapons and organisational documents were found and seized in the course of the police operation. On 26 November 1996 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The applicant was conditionally released from prison on 26 April 2003. The judge ruled that the applicant had supported the ideology of the PKK and believed that the PKK was the legitimate representative of Kurdistan. The court took into account the statements of three other accused, who had contended before the public prosecutor that the. applicant had collected money on behalf of the. PKK.

name: Arnaud Bédat
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 July 2014 a Chamber of that Section delivered its judgment (see A.B. v. Switzerland, no.56925-08, 1 July 2013), in which it declared the application admissible. The Court heard addresses by Mr Poncet, Mr Schürmann and Mr Hoffmann. The article in question concerned a set of criminal proceedings against M.B., a motorist who had been remanded in custody after an incident on 8 July 2003 in which he had rammed his car into pedestrians, before throwing himself off the Lausanne Bridge (Grand-Pont) The incident, in which three people had died and eight others had been injured, had caused much emotion and controversy in Switzerland. The applicant is a journalist by profession. On 15 October 2003 he published an article in the weekly magazine L’Illustré entitled “Drame du Grand-Pont à Lausenne – la version du chauffard – l’interrogatoire du conducteur fou’ (“Tragedy on the LaUSanne Bridge – the reckless driver’s version – Questioning of the mad driver”). The article was accompanied by several photographs of letters which M.B. had sent to the investigating judge. The article also included a brief summary entitled ‘He lost his marbles...’ (“Il a perdu la boule...”) The authorities responsible for the criminal investigation had themselves decided to inform the press of certain aspects of the investigation, which had led to the publication of an article in the Tribune de Genève on 14 August 2003. It appears from the file that the applicant’s article was not the only piece to have been published on the Lausanne Bridge tragedy. The application did not lodge a complaint against the applicant. M.B. was sentenced to one month's imprisonment, suspended for one year. The Lausanne Police Court replaced the prison sentence with a fine of 4,000 Swiss francs (CHF) (approximately 2,667 euros) The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. His appeal was dismissed on 30 January 2006 by the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Vaud. The Federal Court dismissed the appeals on 29 April 2008. Its decision was served on the applicant on 9 May 2008. The applicant’s representative stated that his client was intending to refund it after the proceedings before the Court. He also confirmed that the amount set by the criminal court had taken account of the applicant's previous record. Anyone who makes public documents, investigations or deliberations of an authority which are secret by law or by virtue of a decision taken by that authority, acting within its powers, will be punished by a fine. Complicity in such acts is also punishable. The court may decide not to impose any penalties if the secret thus made public is of minor importance (see paragraph 3). According to case-law, this provision proceeds from a formal conception of secrecy. In its Stoll v. Switzerland judgment of 10 December 2007, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that this formal conception. of secrecy was not contrary to Article 10 ECHR inasmuch as it did not prevent it. In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud (CPP/VD), all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The law also specifies that the following are bound by secrecy vis-à-vis anyone who does not have access to the case file: the judges and judicial staff, and also the parties, their friends and relatives, their lawyers, the latter’s associates, consultants and staff. However, disclosure to friends or relatives by the parties or their lawyer is not punishable (see Article 185a CPP/VD). The aim is to maintain the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights has already had occasion to deem such a purpose legitimate in itself. This is the inescapable conclusion as regards the records of interviews of the accused. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation and before the trial. We might point out here that it appears from the impugned publication that it is possible that the accused's letters to the investigating judge have been classified secret. It is also the only possible conclusion that the letters sent by the accused to the judge focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer. The content of the records of his interviews and his correspondence with the investigating judge was not of minor importance for the purposes of Article 293, paragraph 3, of the Criminal Code. The information in question may be described as being secret in substantive terms because it was only accessible to a restricted number of persons (the investigating judge and the parties to the proceedings). Furthermore, the investigating authority was desirous to keep them secret, with not only a legitimate interest in doing so but an obligation under the Cantonal Code of Criminal Procedure, the justification for which was mentioned above (see point 7.3 above). 7.5. The only remaining point at issue is the existence of justification. Lausanne Bridge was not a case of collective trauma on the part of the Lausanne population, which would have justified reassuring the citizens and keeping them informed of the investigation. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest in the disclosure of classified information. This type of information provides no relevant insights into the accident or the circumstances surrounding it. It relates to the private life, or indeed intimate sphere, of the person in custody. It is difficult to see any interest which its publication could satisfy other than a certain kind of voyeurism. Nor is it clear, as regards the records of his interviews, what political question or matter of public interest would have arisen or been worth debating in the public sphere. The cantonal court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not, as he claims, to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’, ‘the reckless driver's version’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a mad driver. The Court does not attach decisive importance to this fact when considering whether applicants have fulfilled their duties and responsibilities. The determining fact is that disclosure of the information was punishable by law. Journalist wondered whether the driver was in fact doing his best to ‘make himself impossible to defend’ The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case, without the least respect for the principle of presumption of innocence. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. That court cannot be criticised on that account. The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged (the least serious in the classification set out in the Swiss Criminal Code), how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 8790/79) lodged with the Commission on 19 September 1979 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mrs. Viera Sramek, a United States citizen. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (Art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the Republic of Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art.) 46. The Government’S application referred to Article 48 ( art.48) and the purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Court heard addresses by H. Türk, Legal Adviser in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr M. Matzka, Federal Chancellery, Mr. G. Liebl, Office of the Government of the Tyrol, Advisers. The Government filed a document during the course of the hearings. The Court decided on 27 March that the proceedings should continue without resumption of the hearing (Rule 26) The Government also replied to two supplementary questions which the Registrar had addressed to them on the instructions of the President (Rule 37 para. 1). The Chamber decided under Rule 50 of the Rules of Court to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The applicant, who is a United States citizen, lives in Munich in the Federal Republic of Germany. Wishing to build a holiday residence in Hopfgarten, a village in the Austrian Tyrol, she approached, with the assistance of municipal officials, the owners of a plot of land which had until then been used for agricultural purposes. Sale negotiations began in 1971 and apparently led, in 1973, to an initial contract. One year later, Mrs. Sramek paid to the vendors the greater part of the agreed price. However, the definitive contract was not drawn up until 13 January 1977. The contract could not take effect unless it were approved by the local Real Property Transactions Authority (Grundverkehrsbehörde) The Government Office of the Tyrol was organised in a number of “ groups’ and each group comprised several “divisions’ The contract in question was contrary to social and economic interests within the meaning of the above-mentioned Act. The applicant received a copy of the appeal but did not file any observations in reply. There were, in fact, already 110 foreign landowners in Hopfgarten and it could be seen from a series of decisions of the Regional Authority that this municipality was one of those where the danger of foreign domination was imminent. The judge of the Innsbruck Court of Appeal was a farmer experienced in real estate matters. The applicant stated that she had signed the initial contract (Erstvertrag), which could not then be found, on 13 March 1973. The Transactions Officer then requested the Authority to uphold his appeal on the ground that as there was already a risk of foreign domination in Hopfgarten, the acquisition of the land in question would be contrary to social and political interests. On the same day, that is 3 June 1977, the Regional Authority upheld the appeal: referring to the above-mentioned section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act, it refused to approve the transfer of title. Its decision (Bescheid) was dated 16 June. The application was brought by a woman who wanted to use the land for a holiday residence. The Regional Authority rejected the applicant's argument that she had already concluded a contract in 1973. The Authority emphasised firstly that it had to base itself on the factual and legal situation obtaining at the time when the decision had to be taken. On 22 August 1977, the applicant appealed to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) against the decision of the Regional Authority. She claimed that her right to inviolability of property had been infringed and relied on Article 5 of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundgesetz), Article 83 para. 2 of the Federal Constitution. Mrs. Sramek alleged that the Regional Authority had applied section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act in a misconceived (denkunmöglich) manner. She also claimed that the Authority was not an “independent tribunal’ within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 3 March 1979 (Erkenntnisse und Beschlüsse des Verfassungsgerichtshofes, 1979, vol. 44, no. 8501). It took the view that the. Regional Authority was indeed a “tribunal” within themeaning of Article. 6 (art. 6) of. the Convention and gave decisions which the executive. could neither annul nor vary.  Constitutional Court sat in camera and gave judgment without holding a hearing. Government stated that during the last ten years or so the Regional Authority had not approved any acquisition of real property in Hopfgarten by a foreigner. They supplied a list of thirteen refusals in the period between July 1973 and February 1983. According to the applicant, the list was insufficiently detailed to be conclusive. In the Tyrol (see paragraph 9 above), section 15(1) of the 1970/1973 Act obliges the purchaser to seek such approval within two months of the conclusion of the contract. No entry can be made in the land register until the transaction has been approved by the competent authority. The Transactions Officer, who is appointed for three years by the Government of the Tyrol, must be a person who is experienced in real property transaction matters. His secretariat is provided by a division of the Office of the said Government. If the case is referred to it, the Regional Real Property Transactions Authority takes a decision as the second and final instance. Its membership varies according to the subject-matter of the contract to be examined. In the case of agricultural or forestry land - whether the buyer be Austrian or foreign - its voting members are. “(a) a person experienced inReal Property transaction matters, who shall act as chairman; (b) a member of the judiciary (Richterstand); (c) a legally qualified civil servant from the Office. of the Regional Government, with training in realProperty transaction matters; (d) a lawyer (Rechtsanwalt or Notar).“ The Constitutional Court held, the Act did not fix the duration of the members’ term of office, conferred on the said Government the power of appointing the members. Only Austrian citizens who have reached the age of 25 years and are in full possession of their legal rights shall be eligible for appointment as members or substitute members. The details of the Real Property Transactions Authorities’ procedure (such as the convening of sittings, summoning of substitute members, conduct of voting, keeping of minutes and signing of decisions) shall be laid down by the Tyrolean legislature. Re-appointment is possible. Members and substitute members shall hold office for three years. The executive may neither annul nor vary their decisions. Members of Real Property Transactions Authorities receive for their work remuneration and a travel allowance. The parties have the right to be heard (rechtliches Gehör) and, inter alia, to adduce their arguments and evidence and comment on facts presented and submissions made by other persons appearing, witnesses or experts. In certain circumstances which may give reason to doubt his impartiality, the civil servant concerned must arrange to be replaced (section 7). The parties are entitled to consult the case-file (section 17) and must be given an opportunity of presenting their arguments (section 37). The competent authority may decide to hold a hearing (section 39(2), which will not take place in public. Under Article 3 para. 1, the Authorities shall deliberate and vote in the absence of the parties, if appropriate after oral hearings. The right to consult the case-file (Akteneinsicht), guaranteed by Article 17 of the General Administrative Procedure Act, does not extend. Decisions of a Regional Authority may be challenged before the Constitutional Court but not before the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Commission expressed the opinion, by eleven votes to one, that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. Austria's request to the Court was made in January 1984. The Government asked the Court to hold that the provisions of paragraph 1 of Article 6 (art. 6-1) of the Convention were not violated. The facts underlying the dispute do not indicate any breach by the Republic of Austria of its obligations under the Convention, according to the Government. The case was settled in October 1983 and the case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The appeal was dismissed in March 1984 and the ruling was quashed in March 1985. The Austrian government appealed the decision, saying that the decision was not in breach of the Geneva Convention or the Vienna Convention on Human Rights and that it had been made in good faith.

Regional Authority was indeed a “tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6 (art. 6) of. the Convention. As regards its members - who included a judge -, they had a degree of independence equal to that of judges. The Constitutional Court sat in camera and gave judgment without holding a hearing. The Government stated that during the last ten years or so the Regional Authority had not approved any acquisition of real property in Hopfgarten by a foreigner. The first-instance authority is the Höfekommission (“Farm Commission“) (section 13(1)(a)). The Farm Commission is established at the seat of the District Administration and has three members: the head of the. District Administration, or a legally qualified (rechtskundig) official of that Administration appointed by him, as chairman. name: Franz Ladner
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Franz Ladner (‘the applicant’) was convicted under Article 209 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to three months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. The applicant was released on 27 February 2001. The Vienna Court of Appeal quashed the Regional Court’s decision and referred the case back to it. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was dismissed on 3 December 2002. The applicant’s petition for a pardon was of no avail. The Federal Minister of Justice replied to questions put by members of Parliament concerning the granting of a pardon in cases of convictions under Article 209. The Minister stated that the conduct of the person concerned would also qualify as an offence under the newly introduced Article 207b, as in one case that person had taken advantage of the adolescent's predicament, i.e. the fact that the latter had, following a conflict with his parents, temporarily lived in that person's apartment. The decision was served on the applicant on 4 July 2003. It referred to the Constitutional Court's judgment of 21 June 2002 which found that Article 209 of the Criminal Code was unconstitutional.

name: C. Langum Becker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21272/12) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that she had been compelled to give evidence that would have enabled one or more journalistic sources to be identified. She is represented before the Court by Mr V. Strømme, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government’s Office (Civil Matters) as their Agent) were represented by Mr C. Reusch of the Attorney General's Office ( civil Matters) on behalf of the applicant. The price of DNO stock fell by 4.1% on Monday 27 August 2007, the first trading day after the content of the letter had become known in the press. On the same day, a new article on the topic was published in DN.no. During subsequent questioning by the Financial Supervisory Authority, Mr X confirmed that he had initiated the letter and been the source of the article. The applicant refused to answer questions about possible contacts between her and Mr X and other sources, if any, related to the publication by DN. no on 25 August 2007. She argued that she was under no obligation to give evidence on those points. The City Court held that the applicant had a duty to give evidence about her contacts with Mr X in relation to the letter of 24 August 2007 from Attorney Y to the bond trustee company. Mr X, through his counsel and co‑counsel, had submitted that he had described his contact with the applicant and that she could contribute nothing further of interest. Whether or not consent had been given by the source to the witness making her statement had no bearing on the obligation to give Evidence. The element of abuse should suggest that in a case like this the press would also have an interest in making a statement in order to avoid being abused in this way. Mr X was sentenced to one year and six months’ imprisonment, of which nine months were suspended for a probationary period of two years. An appeal by the applicant to the Supreme Court was rejected by three votes to two on 30 September 2011 (Norsk Retstidende – Rt. 2011 page 1266) The appeal had been directed at the High Court’s assessment of evidence as well as its application of the law. The Supreme Court disagreed on whether this provision was applicable if the source had stepped forward or the identity of the sources had otherwise been established. The majority observed that it did not appear from the wording of Article 125 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that it was relevant. An obligation on the press to give evidence in such cases was not thought likely to weaken the public’s general trust that the press would protect its sources. Once an informant had confirmed that he was the source, this fact would become known. Should the recipient of the information then refuse to giving evidence, this would normally appear futile. In such a situation, an exemption from the obligation to give Evidence would in reality not constitute a protection against having to disclose the source. It would rather be a right to avoid contributing to the debate. The majority further disagreed that there was no reason to treat a situation where the informant had identified himself or herself as the source differently from those cases where the source had consented to being identified. The majority held that this provision did not apply when the source had come forward and had confirmed his or her role. The principal justification for source protection, as elaborated by the Court in its case-law, was based on the consequences that the disclosure of a source’s identity might have for the free flow of information. The majority further noted that there was no decision where the Court had examined the situation where the source came forward and where in this sense there wasno source to protect. They observed that in the two British cases, a violation had been found under the necessity test even though strong countervailing arguments had been present. The charge in this case had been based. on the fact that the journalist had allowed herself to be used by the source. The European Court of Justice ruled that journalists have the right to refuse to reveal their sources. The purpose of protecting sources was to protect the public interest in free communication of news and opinions. If journalists were allowed to protect their sources, they would obtain information enabling them to uncover matters in society that were worthy of criticism more easily than they would otherwise. If the hearing of evidence on the identity of a source were to be allowed, the media’s working conditions would become considerably more constricted, the court ruled. If consent to source disclosure was required, the protection would be undermined. This would enable a source to be tracked down, even if a requirement for waiver of source protection was that the source be identified with a criminal standard of proof. Mr X had stated that he was the source. A person might incorrectly claim to be the source so that the actual source might be identified by a process of elimination. Even if it were true, it would erode the journalist’s right to source protection. Free speech did not protect only information and views that were positively received, but also those which offended, shocked or disturbed the State or parts of the population. Therefore, the fundamental right of journalists to protect their sources could not be dependent on the sources’ motives. The case was examined by the High Court, which summoned and heard the applicant as a witness on 13 January. The High Court ordered the applicant to pay a fine of 30,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK), approximately 3,700 euro (EUR) for an offence against the good order of court proceedings. The applicant did not appeal against that decision. By a judgment of the same date, the High Court convicted Mr X on the charges and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment. The court records contain the following passage: “When heard as a witness [the applicant] stated that she had received Attorney [Y]’s letter by fax on 24 August 2007 at 5.35 p.m.” There is extensive Supreme Court case-law concerning the main rule in Article 125 § 1 about the protection of journalists’ sources. If the author or source has revealed matters that it was socially important to disclose, the witness may be ordered to reveal the name only when this is found to be particularly necessary. When an answer is given, the court may decide that it shall only be given to the court and the parties at a sitting in camera and under an order to observe a duty of secrecy. The UN Human Rights Committee adopted General Comment no. 34 concerning Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (CCPR/C/GC/34) National laws should ensure that protections apply strictly, with extremely limited exceptions. Revealing or coercing the revelation of the identity of a source creates disincentives for disclosure, dries up further sources to report a story accurately. Any restrictions must be genuinely exceptional and subject to the highest standards, implemented by judicial authorities only. Such situations should be limited to investigations of the most serious crimes or the protection of the life of other individuals. The same conditions apply to investigative measures, such as searches, seizures and telephone tapping, with respect to journalistic sources.” “The right of journalists not to disclose information identifying a source must not be subject to other restrictions than those mentioned in Article 10, paragraph 2 of the Convention,” the European Court of Human Rights said. Disclosure of information identifying a source should not be deemed necessary unless it can be convincingly established that: i. reasonable alternative measures to the disclosure do not exist or have been exhausted by the persons or public authorities that seek the disclosure, and ii. the legitimate interest in the disclosure clearly outweighs the public interest. The above requirements should be applied at all stages of any proceedings where the right of non-disclosure might be invoked, the European Court of Human Rights said in its Recommendation. The Recommendation also said it was necessary to protect all kinds of information which are likely to lead to the identification of a source. The potential to identify a source determines the type of protected information and the range of such protection.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38629/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal in proceedings concerning social security benefits. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The Case was heard by the European Court of Human rights. The applicant. requested the Office to review its decision under chapter 20, section 10 a of the 1962 Act. He claimed that he had failed to fully state his need of assistance and his additional costs in the original application. On 12 July 1991 the Office found that there was no basis for a review of its earlier decision. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. It considered that the Office’s first decision had been based on insufficient information and that it should therefore have reviewed that decision. The applicant made submissions in response to the Board’s appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative Court of Appeal to hold an oral hearing. The applicant maintained that the Board had failed to adequately explain the reasons for its appeal. He requested that the court order the Board to clarify its position in the case. The court did not do so, however, and the applicant called into question the impartiality of the proceedings. By 3 votes to 2, the Court quashed the County Administrative Court’S judgment and confirmed the Office's decision. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) of 12 July 1991. The dissenting judges considered that the applicant was entitled to the disability allowance granted to him by the County Administrative Court. The applicant complained about the lack of an oral hearing in the Administrative Court of Appeal. On 24 February 1997 the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. The case was eventually settled in the High Court of Justice of Germany in November 1998. The High Court ruled that there had been no basis for a review of the Office’s first decision. Without giving any further reasons, it considered that there were exceptional reasons to change the Office's decision.

By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. He claimed that he had failed to fully state his need of assistance and his additional costs in the original application. On 27 April 1991 he asked the Office, alternatively, to consider his request as a new application and to grant him benefits as from November 1988. On 12 July 1991 the Office found that there was no basis for a review of its earlier decision. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. It considered that the Office’s first decision had been based on insufficient information. The applicant made submissions in response to the Board’s appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative Court of Appeal to hold an oral hearing in the case during which the person in charge of the case at the Office should give evidence relating to the meaning of its decision. The applicant also asked the court to obtain the opinion of a medical expert. The latter request was granted by a decision of 30 December 1992. By 3 votes to 2, the Court quashed the County Administrative Court's judgment and confirmed the Office's decision. By letters of 16 September 1994 and 10 January 1995 he reiterated his request for a hearing. As an allowance could be given retroactively only for the two years preceding the application, the Applicant was granted an allowance as from October 1994. By a decision of 12 December 1996 the Office found that he had special needs and costs due to his handicap which made him eligible for disability benefits under the 1962 Act. On 24 February 1997 the Supreme. Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal.

name: Teresa Jerzak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29360/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Sulejówek. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was brought by a Polish national, Ms Teresa Jerzak (‘the applicant’), on 3 July 2006. The President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The case is still pending before the District Court in Warsaw, Poland. The applicant lodged a complaint alleging a breach of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The court awarded the applicant 200 Polish zlotys (PLN – approximately 50 euros (EUR) by way of just satisfaction. The case remains before the Warsaw District Court, which is expected to rule on the matter in the next few months. The application is based on the 2004 Act, which entered into force on 17 September 2004. These delays had taken place before the date of entry into force the Act and had not been remedied afterwards. The High Court of Poland has ruled that the Act applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date and were not yet remedied.

name: Royce Darnell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15058/89) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 2 December 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The Court was constituted on 26 September 1992, with ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Dr Royce Darnell was a consultant microbiologist and Director of the Public Health Laboratory in Derby. He was fired by the Trent Regional Health Authority for non-compliance with laboratory staff appointment procedures. The Court heard addresses by Mr Baker for the Government, by Mr Loucaides for the Commission and by Ms Hampson for the applicant, as well as replies to its questions. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1993. The case concerns the length of time that proceedings relating to this dismissal have taken. The applicant's case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. Dr Darnell was dismissed on three months' notice with effect from 19 August 1984. A professional committee was appointed in accordance with paragraph 190 of the Terms and Conditions of Service of Hospital Medical and Dental Staff. The applicant challenged the fairness of the procedure leading to the Secretary of State’s decision. The High Court granted a declaration that this decision was invalid and indicated that the secretary of state should reconsider the matter. The Secretary ofState did not appeal. The paragraph 190 procedure has since been replaced by a new procedure which incorporates time-limits into the various stages of an appeal to the Director of Health and Social Security. Dr Darnell was fired by the DHSS in March 1988. He had appealed his dismissal to the Secretary of State. He also sought reinstatement, re-engagement and damages for dismissal by proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal ruled that the dismissal of the applicant was not unfair. The applicant was paid his salary in full until March 1988 when he was dismissed. He lodged his application (no. 15058/89) with the Commission on 2 December 1988. A pre-hearing assessment took place on 6 February 1989 in which the Tribunal determined that a hearing could take place with no cost consequences to the applicant. In June 1988 a separate action in the High Court claiming damages for the applicant’s suspension from work in June 1982 pending the outcome of the disciplinary procedure was struck out. The Commission declared the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings admissible and dismissed the remainder of his application. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) (unanimously) The full text of the Commission’S opinion and of the concurring opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The case was heard at the International Court of Human Rights in The Hague between 11 and 13 April 1991. The final termination of his employment. proceedings taken against him took an unreasonable length of time; he also alleged that the Secretary of State and the RHA had followed a procedure which was neither fair nor public and that the former was not independent or impartial.

name: Mehmet Ali Yılmaz
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning hisright to aFair Hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. In 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of being one of the founding members and a leader of the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court sentenced him to life imprisonment (in effect 18 years assuming good conduct) and permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service. The Court of Cassation (yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and the case file was transmitted to it. On 27 December 1995 the court upheld the applicant’s conviction.

name: İsmail Şencan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7436/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants signed contracts with third persons before the notary public to acquire de facto possession (zilyedlik) of a plot of land in Gökçeada. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The cases were remitted to the first-instance court. The Court of Cassation quashed the three judgments of the first-instance court in 1994. The cases were remitted to the Gökçeada Civil Court of General Jurisdiction. In its judgment, the court stated that the plot in question was not designated as “meadowland’ in the land registration records and that, therefore, it could be subject to private ownership. The court further held that the land should be officially designated as a second degree conservation area. The applicants' request for rectification was served on the applicants' representative on 30 April 2001. They were denied the right to register the land.

They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his kids should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the applicant and his wife agreed to a settlement. The settlement was never accepted by the applicant. The mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. The court ordered an expert opinion on the question of what attribution of custody rights and – should sole custody be awarded to the mother – what contact with their father would be in the children's best interest. The expert opinion was finalised on 31 August 2000. The mother had previously cancelled appointments for appraisals in connection with the drawing up of the expert opinion, thereby delaying its completion. The parties agreed that from 15 October 1999 the applicant would be entitled to visit his children every fortnight, accompanied by a representative of the Kleve child protection agency, and that he could have telephone contact with the children every two weeks at set time. The Court of appeal confirmed that, in view of the tensions and lack of cooperation between the. parents, the transfer of sole Custody was in the. children'sbest interest. Düsseldorf District Court set deadline of 20 July 2001 for parties to reach agreement on contact rights, failing which a court decision would have to be made. The court found that, in view of the lack of cooperation between the parents on matters concerning their children, joint custody was not an option. Since the children's main focal point for several years had been their mother, sole custody had to be awarded to her. The applicant appealed on 18 February 2002 and requested to be granted joint custody with the mother and to leave the right to determine children's place of residence with a guardian. The children attended the hearing but were not heard by the Court of Appeal. After the divorce the parties continued to argue about the applicant's contact rights. A court settlement stipulated that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence. The parties also agreed that with effect from 2003 they would plan at least one holiday per year. On 2 April 2004 the Düsseldorf Court of Court of Appeal ruled that the settlement constituted a binding agreement between the parties in this regard. A new expert was appointed who agreed to provide an opinion by the end of November 2005. The applicant objected to the new expert on the ground that she did not have the necessary professional qualifications and refused to be examined by her. An expert opinion could therefore not be established. The Federal Constitutional Court pointed out that it was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. The applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to lower courts. The court held that a decision could only be taken after the child had been given the opportunity to disclose its personal relations with the other family members. The applicant filed an application with the Emmerich District Court on behalf of and in the name of his children for the regulation of the children's contact rights with respect to their father. On 4 July 2001 (file no. 5 F 134/01) the District Court dismissed his request as inadmissible. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint concerning the separate custody proceedings (5 F 283/98) The applicant's parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. Since the applicant had failed to inform the Federal Constitutional Court of his new address the decision could only be served on him on 9 December 2006. The court pointed out that it was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. But there was no need to take a decision in this respect because in any event the applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage. The applicant requested the District Court to prohibit any contact by the grandparents with his children and alternatively to grant them contact only in the presence of a third person to be determined by the children's guardian. The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. The court found that the applicant could not represent the children in the proceedings since the power of representation was part of the right to custody which in proceedings no. 5 F 283/98 had been transferred solely to the mother. He completed the course in November 2012. He was transferred to HMP Northumberland on 5 November 2013. open conditions. name: Altan Karakullukçu
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr Ç. Hasdemir, a lawyer practising in İstanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 21 October 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the long proceedings to the Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court on 1 November 2004. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The court referred to the doctrine of “social risk’, which did not require the establishment of any causal link between the harmful action and the loss. The court reasoned that the damage caused by terrorism should be shared by the society as a whole in accordance with the principles of ‘justice’ and ‘social state’ The case-file was sent to an expert. The expert submitted its report to the Court. The Istanbul Administrative Court awarded the applicant an amount of compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage with legal interest running from 18 February 1992. The case became final on 30 April 1999.

name: Laleş Çeliker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75573/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. On 6 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. Diyarbakır State Security Court held nineteen hearings and heard a number of witnesses. During these hearings, the applicant renounced her statements taken during her detention in police custody. Witnesses heard by the court stated that the applicant was an active member of the PKK and that she had been involved in armed clashes with the security forces. Taking into account her confessions before the court, the death penalty was commuted to a life sentence of imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the first instance court on 19 December 2000. It reasoned that the decision was justified as the evidence in the case file was capable of proving the applicant's membership of an illegal organisation.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 54215/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr I.-J. Tegebauer, a lawyer practising in Trier. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The parties have four weeks to submit further submissions to the court. The court will rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The child's guardian ad litem case was heard for the first time on 27 September 2007. The District Court cancelled the hearing on account of the competent judge being ill. On 1 January 2008 the case was assigned to another judge and the judge scheduled the hearing for 18 March 2008. On 27 February 2008 the District Court refused to reschedule the hearing, inter alia, on the ground that the applicant still appeared to be represented by her former lawyer, who had not yet informed the court that his mandate had been terminated. On 17 March 2008 the judge ruled against the allegation of bias. On 30 July 2008 the Frankfurt/Main Court of Appeal quashed the decision and found that the judge was biased. The complaint was brought by the father of the child. The court refused to admit the case. The case was heard again on 15 April 2009. The child's father appealed the decision. The appeal was rejected on 18 June 2009. A new complaint was filed against the father on 19 December 2008. The decision was made to hear the matter again on April 15, 2009. It was decided that the case should be heard by an expert. The expert submitted a report on 24 February 2009. This report was accepted by the court and the case was dismissed. The father and the child are no longer in the custody of the court of first instance, but the case is still with the court.

name: Peter Maxwell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’s application referred to Article 48 (art. 48) The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). The applicant indicated in a letter postmarked 22 July 1993 that he did not wish to take part in the proceedings. On 17 November 1993 he submitted a claim for just satisfaction (Rule 50 para. 1) Peter Maxwell was sentenced to five years in prison for assault. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. Legal aid had been made available to the applicant for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Lord Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The applicant received the Government’s memorial on 10 January 1994. On 15 April 1994 the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations in reply. On 23 February 1994 the applicant, having obtained the President's leave, lodged written observations. in reply to the Government's memorial. On 29 May 1990 the jury found the applicant guilty of the charge. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him. There had been insufficient evidence to establish that the assault had resulted in the victim’s permanent disfigurement. The applicant was granted a further adjournment of the hearing of his appeal. On 17 December 1990 they lodged an application for legal aid to pay for representation at the hearing. They sought the advice of a new counsel on the prospects of success of the appeal. In an opinion dated 10 January 1991, counsel concluded that there was ‘no ground of appeal against conviction and no prospects of appealing successfully against sentence’ The applicant's solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. On 21 March 1991, the applicant addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal. The judgment gave full consideration to each of the grounds. of appeal, but was satisfied that they had no substance and that there had been no miscarriage of justice. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing.

name: Stanisław Marecki
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Stanisław Marecki alleged that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Brzozów. On 12 December 1998 the applicant was arrested on a charge of numerous counts of armed robbery and membership of a criminal gang. On an unspecified date in 2000 the Łódź Regional Prosecutor laid additional charges against the applicant (armed robbery committed as part of an organised criminal gang and homicide) The courts justified their decisions prolonging the applicant’s detention on remand and their refusals to release him by the need to hear evidence from the accused and witnesses, some of whom lived abroad. These considerations led the courts to assume that the applicant, if released, could obstruct the proper course of the proceedings. The courts found on several occasions that there were no special grounds, as specified in Article 259 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that would justify lifting the detention order and imposing a less severe measure. On 23 May 2002 the Łódź Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged a claim for compensation for wrongful detention. The proceedings are still pending. The applicant was acquitted and he was released from detention on 6 December 2004. The Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The matter is currently before the Court of Appeals of the Poland Regional Court. The application for compensation is still pending, and the case is still in the Regional Court of Appeal's preliminary judgment. The claimant has appealed to the Supreme Court of Poland. The case is currently being heard by the Supreme  Court of Justice of the Poland.

name: Rajko Medenica
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20491/92) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Assize Court of the Canton of Geneva had tried and convicted him in absentia. By a decision of 16 December 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. After consulting the parties, the Court decided to dispense with a hearing of the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. The Swiss Government was represented by their Agent, Mr P. Boillat, Head of the International Affairs Division, Federal Office of Justice. The applicant was accused of causing Yugoslavia’s welfare institutions to sustain substantial losses with the complicity of an official at the consulate of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva. On 27 October 1982 he was arrested and charged with fraud, intimidation and forging documents. On 1 February 1984 the applicant paid the stipulated sum and was released. He then travelled to the United States of America, where he acquired American nationality and practised as a doctor specialising in the treatment of certain serious forms of cancer. The trial of the applicant is set to commence on 17 April 1989 in the Canton of Geneva Assize Court. The applicant was never convicted of any crime. One of the applicant’s American patients applied to the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, Charleston Division, for orders requiring the applicant to continue to treat him until he could be replaced by another doctor. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the U.S. and requiring him to surrender his passport. The Swiss authorities, including the Principal Public Prosecutor of the Canton of Geneva, were given sixty days in which to respond. The applicant was requested to find replacement doctors for his patients. The hearing took place on 27 March 1989 before the President of the American District Court. After the hearing he returned to the US. The applicant lodged an application with the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina to have the restraining order of 28 March 1989 set aside. In a judgment of 26 May 1989 the Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. The applicant was also found guilty of forgery of documents for procuring the signing by his secretary of seventeen false receipts for expenses in a name she no longer used. The jury assessed the amount of alleged damage at approximately 1,000,000 Swiss francs. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted on 672 counts of fraud. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. It held that the applicant’s inability to appear before the Assize Court was his own fault in that he had made a decisive contribution to that outcome. The argument concerning the refusal to remit the case had been conclusively disposed of in its judgment of 27 June 1990. It further held that, in so far as they were not inadmissible as being out of time, the complaints of the applicant had been dismissed in the earlier proceedings. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court, seeking to have set aside the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation’s judgments of 27 June 1990 and 14 February 1991. He alleged, inter alia, a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant's absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure, in order to secure a judgment. On 26 July 1995 the applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States. He is currently serving a sentence of life in prison with a minimum of 15 years to be served, and a maximum of 25 years with a possible parole period of 20 years. The case has been referred to the U.S. Federal Court.

name: Magdalena Witek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13453/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Magdalena Witek alleged that her detention in a psychiatric hospital had been unlawful and in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr J. Gałkowski, a lawyer practising in Bielsko Biała. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was admitted to Lublin Hospital on 23 September 2006. days after her arrival there. The Psychiatric Commission on Preventive Measures submitted its opinion dated 17 August 2006 to the Kielce District Court. The court referred to the experts' opinion of 2000, which stressed that the applicant had behaved aggressively during her period under psychiatric observation in Morawica Hospital (in 2000) On 15 January 2007 the applicant filed an appeal against that decision. She stressed that over the previous five years her health had significantly improved and that her relations with her mother were very good. On 23 February 2007 theKielce Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision referring to the reasons given by the district court. Kielce District Court ordered the applicant's release from hospital. Court did not agree with expert psychiatrists opinions of 20 July 2007, 16 August 2007 and 25 September 2007 maintaining that the applicant should be kept in a psychiatric hospital. On the prosecutor's appeal, on 16 November 2007 the Kielce Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision. The applicant was released from hospital on the same day. The court concluded that the probability of the applicant committing another similar offence was very low. It referred to the applicant’s mother's testimonies confirming that since 2002 the applicant had never behaved aggressively towards her and their relations were very good.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49151/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a Rom of Spanish nationality, complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of her husband. She alleged that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the. Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 12 of. the Convention. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blasco Lozano, Ms Queipo de Llano López-Cózar and Mr S. Sánchez Lorente, Counsel. The application was for a survivor's pension for the wife of a man who died in 2000. The judge rejected the application because the woman had never been his wife prior to his death. The decision was confirmed by a decision of the National Institute of Social Security (Instituto Nacional de la Seguridad Social – “the INSS”) The couple had six children, who were registered in the family record book issued to the couple by the Spanish civil registration authorities (Registro civil) on 11 August 1983. They were granted first-category large-family status under the Large-Family Protection Act (Law no. 25/1971 of 19 June 1971) The applicant filed a claim with the Labour Court. In a judgment dated 30 May 2002 of Labour Court no. 12 of Madrid, she was granted an entitlement to receive a survivor’s pension with a base rate of 903.29 euros per month, her Roma marriage thus being recognised as having civil effects. The argument relied upon against the applicant in order to deny her a survivor's pension is solely the non-recognition of the civil effects of her marriage to the insured person. This is despite the fact that Spain has ratified the United Nations International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination of 7 March 1966. The refusal by the INSS to grant the applicant a survivor’s pension, the sole obstacle being that the marriage between the widow and the deceased is not recognised, reveals discriminatory treatment on grounds of ethnic affiliation. The Madrid Higher Court of Justice quashed the impugned judgment, giving the following reasons: “... It should be noted that the principle of equality and non-discrimination is based on the idea that equal situations should be treated equally” In a case of a Roma woman applying for a survivor's pension, her application was rejected on the grounds that her marriage was not recognised as a religious one. The INSS appealed, and in November 2002, the Madrid higher court of Justice ruled in favour of the applicant. In Spain there are statutory norms governing marriage. Roma marriage does not correspond, in the current framework of our law, to the nature of the marriages referred to above. Section 174 of the LGSS requires that a person be the spouse of the deceased in order to benefit from the survivor’s pension, and the notion of spouse has been interpreted strictly according to an established constitutional and ordinary case-law. A couple living together de facto as husband and wife and many others who, in reality, are not married under the applicable law, are excluded from the benefit of that pension.” The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, relying on the principle of non-discrimination in terms of race and social condition. Spanish court ruled there was 'no discrimination on social grounds' in the case of the surviving spouse. The court also ruled that the extension, by the legislature, of the survivor’s pension to other forms of partnership was not prohibited by Article 14 of the Spanish Constitution. 'There is no form of covert discrimination here against the Roma ethnic group,' the court ruled. The law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form, and that the legislature has not prohibited this, the court added. The applicant denies all the accusations against him and claims that the co-accused have been giving false information about him in order to benefit from the Reintegration of Offenders into Society Act (Law no. 4959)

name: Ulf Arne Hammern
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30287/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Norwegian courts in refusing his compensation claim. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr F. Elgesem, who acted as Agent until he left the Attorney-General's Office (Civil Matters) in June 2002. The application was allocated to the former Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: the Court changed the composition of its Sections in 2001. The applicant, who was an assistant at the kindergarten at the time, had sexually abused one or more of the children there. On 13 March 1992 the applicant was interrogated. He denied the accusations. On the same date he was suspended from his post. On 22 September 1993 he was formally indicted under Articles 195, 198 and 213 of the Penal Code for having allegedly committed various offences of sexual abuse against 10 kindergarten children. The applicant spent three periods in pre-trial detention – respectively 7, 7 and 32 days – a total of 46 days. The Court heard addresses by Mr Krokeide (counsel for Mr O, who pleaded the common issues relevant to both his case and that of Mr Hammern). The applicant's trial took place before the Frostating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with three judges and a jury, over a period of 43 days, between 15 November 1993 and 31 January 1994. They later claimed compensation under Articles 444 to 446 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (straffeprosessloven) The High Court, sitting with two of the judges who had taken part in the trial and a new judge (replacing the judge who had presided at the trial, disqualified from sitting in the compensation case), held an oral hearing between 13 and 15 February 1995. In its decision of 28 February 1995, the High Court ordered the State to award him the entirety of his claim of NOK 45,000 in compensation. The Appeals Selection Committee rejected the appeal. 's decision contained assumptions of criminal liability. He requested the Supreme Court to quash the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court concluded that the rules in Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not, as such, contrary to Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The compensation case must be determined on an independent basis and the rules on evidence applying in such compensation cases do not differ from those which apply to ordinary compensation claims. The legislator has as a starting point opted for a solution whereby the financial burden caused by the institution of criminal proceedings, which are discontinued or which end with an acquittal, must be borne by the accused. The Appeals Selection Committee said the High Court had to justify why it considered that the conditions for making an award for compensation under Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been fulfilled. The Committee affirmed that it would base itself on this view in its assessment of the present case. The High Court clearly specifies that Mr Hammern is not liable under the criminal law, the Committee said. It is further clear that the High court ... was aware of the rules in Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, the European Court's Sekanina judgment and the 1994 decision of the Supreme Court, it added. The Court of Appeal's decision is expected to be delivered by the end of the month. The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist, about abuse by Mr Hammern. The children markedly changed their behaviour, inter alia, in the form of bedwetting, refusing or expressing fear about going to the kindergarten. Several children had a sore crotch, sore abdomen and, on one or several occasions, blood on their underwear. The High Court finds it established that at the kindergarten it was possible to perpetrate such abuse without it being revealed either from a technical or practical point of view. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. Nor can a diagnosis which excludes paedophilia be deemed accurate. The Appeals Selection Committee found that the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined. In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected.” “The Committee once again emphasised that a refused compensation does not mean that the earlier acquittal has been undermined,” the Committee said. “It does not entail any infringement of the presumption of innocence laid down in the Convention,’ it added.

The High Court, sitting with two of the judges who had taken part in the trial and a new judge, held an oral hearing between 13 and 15 February 1995. The Appeals Selection Committee, considering that the applicant's appeal concerned the High Court's application of Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, rejected the appeal. Mr Hammern says the High Court's reasoning contains assumptions about criminal liability. The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist, about abuse by Mr Hammern. Several children had a sore crotch, sore abdomen and, on one or several occasions, blood on their underwear. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophilia. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. name: Fahriye Çetinkaya
train_texts: The case originated in three applications against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were arrested on suspicion of having participated in an illegal demonstration which took place in Ümraniye. The Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicants’ alleged ill-treatment in police custody, the right to an effective remedy in this regard, and the length of their detention in police. custody. It decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. The applicants were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examinations both in the evening of 3 August 2001 and in the morning of 4 August 2001. The medical reports drafted on these dates concluded that there were no signs of blows on the applicants’ bodies. On 7 August 2001 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicants with aiding and abetting the PKK under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The applicants denied all the allegations made against them. They contended that they had been forced to sign police statements without reading their contents. The court ordered their detention on remand. The first applicant contended that she had been tortured in police custody. The second applicant maintained that police officers had hit him, pulled his hair and insulted him. The applicants’ lawyer filed two separate petitions with the Fatih public prosecutor. He maintained that the first applicant had been beaten, cursed and threatened with rape in police custody. In the petition regarding the second applicant the lawyer argued that the police had intentionally remained passive when people had tried to lynch him. On 16 February 2004 the Ümraniye Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicants on account of lack of evidence. The investigation against the police officers against the applicants was dropped on 3 September 2002. The second applicant filed an objection against the decision of non-prosecution. On 17 December 2002 Beyoğlu Assize Court dismissed her objection.
