train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26118/10) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant waved a small placard reading “Casse toi pov’con” (“Get lost, you sad prick”) as the President’s party was about to pass by. He was prosecuted by the public prosecutor for insulting the President, an offence under section 26 of the Act of 29 July 1881 (see paragraph 16 below) In a judgment of 6 November 2008 the Laval tribunal de grande instance found the applicant guilty of insulting the president and fined him 30 euros. The Angers Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in its entirety. Mr Eon cannot reasonably maintain that he had no intention of causing offence. The purpose of the law is to protect the office of President, and he cannot claim the right to be treated on an equal footing. The small placard containing the phrase in question is indisputably a form of publicly conveying a message, which can take place by means of placards or posters on public display (section 23 of the 1881 Act). Accordingly, the actus reus of the offence has been made out. There is no need for lengthy discussion of the fact that describing the President as a ‘sad prick’ [pauvre con] amounts to insulting him. Hervé Eon is an activist and a former Socialist elected representative in the département of Mayenne. He had recently fought a campaign actively supporting a Turkish family residing unlawfully in national territory. The Court of Appeal further noted that the applicant had declined to apologise, which meant that he could not be given a discharge. It observed that the first-instance court had found that a simple warning was required and had given him a suspended fine of EUR 30 as a matter of principle. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation’s Legal Aid Board for legal aid. In a decision of 14 May 2009 the Legal aid Board refused his application, holding that no arguable ground of appeal could be made out. The applicant appealed to. the Court of Cassation, challenging the decision to refuse legal aid in the absence of an arguable ground of appeal. The Government stated that on 15 September 2009 the law firm instructed to represent him had sent the. Government a letter indicating that it did not intend to file further pleadings in support of. the appeal; nor had the applicant filed any pleadings himself. The applicant submitted that in view of his inability to pay the fees charged by the law. firm, the firm had informed him that it would not file any. pleadings. The appeal was declared inadmissible, finding that there were no grounds to warrant its examination.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37212/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the obligation imposed on him as a man in employment over age 60 to pay national insurance contributions, which did not apply to a woman in work of over that age, was in violation of Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a decision of 16 March 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant's earnings. was GBP 2,970 and he paid 10% of his earnings. in NICs (Class 1), amounting to GBP 215 per month. From April 2003, NICs increased to 11% of the amount up to the upper earnings limit, plus an additional 1% on all earnings above the limit. The applicant wrote to his Member of Parliament and the Paymaster General complaining about the difference in treatment for men and women. Both replied stating that since liability to pay national insurance contributions is linked to the state pension age, the treatment of men andWomen would equalise in 2020 when the state Pension age will equalise.

name: Ayşe Tezcan Uzunhasanoğlu
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35070/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Istanbul State Security Court which tried and convicted her. She further complained that the Court of Cassation had based its decision on witness statements taken at the police station, which the witnesses subsequently repudiated as having been made under duress. By a decision of 20 May 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The case was referred once again to the Istanbul State Security Court. The applicant was charged with aiding and abetting members of an illegal armed organisation. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's request for a hearing holding that the request had been introduced out of time. The case was then referred to the Supreme Court of Justice. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had refuted the confession statements she made in police custody and that the two witnesses had rejected their statements as they had allegedly been made under duress at the police station. The court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced her to three years and nine months' imprisonment.

name: Mesut Deniz
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently detained in Sincan prison. In the arrest and seizure report it was also noted that the applicant had false identity papers and, inter alia, a Kalashnikov rifle, bullets, night-vision binoculars and a walkie-talkie in his bag. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 April 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant claimed that he had been subjected to various forms of ill-treatment during his arrest and subsequent detention at the Samsun police headquarters and the Ankara police headquarters. He claimed to have been beaten, given electric shocks, hung by his arms, hosed with cold water, had his genitals and fingers squeezed, been made to lie on an icy surface and been raped by one police officer with a hose. The applicant was charged under the former Criminal Code with membership of an illegal organisation and attempting to undermine the constitutional order; he was remanded in custody. The application was dismissed by the Supreme Court in December 1999, and he was acquitted of all charges. The applicant filed a. complaint with the Samsun public prosecutor’s office, claiming that the applicant had been subjected to various forms of ill-treatment while being held at Samsun police. headquarters between 5 and 6 October 1999. In 2001 the applicant began to suffer from a mental disorder. According to a report dated 19 April 2002 issued by the Medical Board of the Ankara Numune Hospital, the applicant presented psychotic symptoms. The experts could not determine whether these symptoms were due to the hunger strike (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) or to schizophrenia. The medical expert concluded that it was not possible to determine the exact cause of the injuries noted in the medical reports. The Samsun Criminal Court convicted H.Ö. as charged and sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment and suspension from duty for a period of three months. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 16 April 2003, holding that the police officer should have been charged with torture under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The court then commuted the sentence to a fine and suspended its execution. On 26 September 2007 the Samsun Assize Court acquitted H. Ö. of the charges against him. In its decision the court held that while the forensic medical reports established that the applicant had been ill‑treated between 5 and 6 October 1999, the applicant could not formally identify the accused as responsible and, as such, there was insufficient evidence to convict him. The Samsun Assize Court held that the applicant could not lodge an appeal against the judgment of 26 September 2007 as he had not joined the proceedings as a civil party. January 2010 the applicant’s lawyer appealed against the first‑instance court's decision. On 4 May 2012 the higher court dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant and the accused should have been allowed to confront each other in order to give the former the opportunity to identify the latter, the applicant argued. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on 5 February 2010. The appeal was dismissed on 5 May 2012. The case is still pending at the High Court of Justice in Istanbul.

The case originated in an application (no. 36716/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Mesut Deniz (‘the applicant’), was born in 1975 and is currently detained in Sincan prison. The applicant was represented by Ms G. Altay, Ms F. Yolcu and Mr H. Karakuş, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 April 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant claimed he had been subjected to various forms of ill-treatment during his arrest and subsequent detention at the Samsun police headquarters and the Ankara police headquarters. He claimed to have been beaten, given electric shocks, hung by his arms, hosed with cold water, had his genitals and fingers squeezed, been made to lie on an icy surface and raped by one police officer with a hose. The applicant was charged under the former Criminal Code with membership of an illegal organisation and attempting to undermine the constitutional order; he was remanded in custody. He was released on bail in December 1998. He died on December 29, 1999. In 2001 the applicant began to suffer from a mental disorder. According to a report issued by the Medical Board of the Ankara Numune Hospital, the applicant presented psychotic symptoms. The experts could not determine whether these symptoms were due to the hunger strike (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) or to schizophrenia. The medical expert concluded that it was not possible to determine the exact cause of the injuries noted in the medical reports. A forensic medical expert also criticised the fact that the applicant had not been transferred to the Department of Urology and Neurology at Ankara Hospital, as requested in a medical report of 12 October 1999. In 2001 the Samsun public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment accusing a police officer, H.Ö., of ill-treatment under Article 245 of the former Criminal Code. The applicant claimed that he had been ill-treated at the Samsun police headquarters. The Samsun Criminal Court convicted H.Ö. as charged and sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment and suspension from duty for a period of three months. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 16 April 2003, holding that the police officer should have been charged with torture under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The court then commuted the sentence to a fine and suspended its execution. The applicant gave evidence before the Ankara Assize Court acting on letters rogatory. He reiterated that he was not certain whether the accused was one of those who had ill-treatment him and affirmed that he wanted those responsible to be prosecuted. On 11 January 2010 the applicant’s lawyer applied to the Samsun Assize Court to annul its previous decision (eski hale getirme) to serve its judgment on the applicant, on the ground that it should have been served on his legal representative. In her application, the applicant's lawyer also maintained that since the applicant suffered from Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, the rogatory court should have assigned him a lawyer, even if he had waived that right. According to information obtained by the Registry from the website of the Court of Cassation, on 4 May 2012 the higher court dismissed the applicants appeal.

name: Anthony M. Tyrer
train_texts: The Tyrer case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 21 September 1972. The purpose of the Commission’s request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the convention) and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court. President decided on 28 June 1977 that it was not necessary at that stage for memorials to be filed. He also instructed the Registrar to invite the Commission to produce certain documents. Oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 January 1978. There appeared before the Court: Mr. D.H. ANDERSON, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. L.J. BLOM-COoper, Q.C., Mr. J.W. Corrin, Attorney-General, Isle of Man, Counsel, Mrs S.A. EVANS, Legal Advisers’ Branch, Home Office. Anthony M. Tyrer was sentenced to three strokes of the birch in accordance with the relevant legislation. He appealed against sentence to the Staff of Government Division of the High Court of Justice of the Isle of Man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972; the court considered that an unprovoked assault occasioning actual bodily harm was always very serious and that there were no reasons for interfering with the sentence. The applicant was made to take down his trousers and underpants and bend over a table; he was held by two policemen whilst a third administered the punishment. The birching raised, but did not cut, the applicant’s skin and he was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927. “Any person who unlawfully assault or beat any other person, shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding thirty pounds or to be imprisoned for a term not exceeding six months.” “The instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod,” said the court in its sentence. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the whipping shall be inflicted privately as soon as practicable after sentence and in. any event shall not take place after the expiration of six months from the passing of the sentence; (b) the number of strokes to be inflicted, being in the cases of a. child not more than six strokes; and in theCase of a male person who is under the age of 14 years, a light cane not exceeding half an inch in diameter.“ The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts. The Island’s parliament, the Court of Tynwald, is one of the oldest in Europe. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. A report of the facts shall be forwarded immediately to His Excellency. The Court was advised at the hearing on 17 January 1978 that, in the light of the Commission's report, an amendment had recently been made by the Isle of. Man Government whereby the punishment is to be administered over ordinary cloth trousers in all cases. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948 and in Northern Ireland in 1968. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. In May 1977, by thirty-one votes for and only one against, Tynwald passed a resolution, inter alia, “that the retention of the use of judicial corporals punishment for crimes of violence to the person is a desirable safeguard in the control of law and order in this Island’”. In January 1978, the Attorney-General for the Isle. of Man informed the Court that recently a privately organised petition in favour of the retention. of judicial Corporal Punishment had obtained 31,000 signatures from amongst the approximate total of 45,000 persons entitled to vote on the Island. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. In 1975 there were 65 crimes of violence to the person, in 1976 58 and in 1977 approximately 46. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. The facts of the case raised issues of discrimination on grounds of sex and race. The Commission, having considered ex officio that the Facts of the Case raised Issues of Sex and Race, decided in favour of the applicant. The Commission expressed the opinion, by 14 votes to one, that the judicial corporal punishment inflicted on the applicant was degrading and was in breach of Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The applicant took no further part in the proceedings. The Commission decided not to proceed further with an examination of the original complaint under Article 14 ( art. 14) which the applicant had subsequently withdrawn. The report contains one separate opinion. There appeared before the Court: Mr. D.H. ANDERSON, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. L.J. BLOM-COOPER, Q.C., Mr. J.W. Corrin, Attorney-General, Isle of Man, Counsel, Mrs. S.A. EVANS, Legal Advisers’ Branch, Home Office. The Court heard Mr. Kellberg for the Commission and Mr. Blom-Cooper for the Government. Anthony Tyrer pleaded guilty to unlawful assault occasioning actual bodily harm to a senior pupil at his school. The applicant was sentenced on the same day to three strokes of the birch in accordance with the relevant legislation. His father lost his self-control and after the third stroke “went for’ one of the policemen and had to be restrained. The birching raised, but did not cut, the applicant’s skin and he was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. He appealed against sentence to the Staff of Government Division of the High Court of Justice of the Isle of Man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod.“ The expressions “child“ and “young person’ mean, respectively, an individual of or over the age of 10 and under 14 and an individual over the ages of 14 and under 17. The execution of the sentence was followed by a fine of not more than 30 pounds. The whipping shall be inflicted on the posterior over the child’s ordinary cloth trousers. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts and its own administrative, fiscal and legal systems. The Crown is ultimately responsible for the good government of the Island and acts in this respect through the Privy Council on the recommendation of Ministers of the U.K. Government in their capacity as Privy Counsellors. In that capacity, the Home Secretary is charged with prime responsibility for Isle of man affairs. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948 and in Northern Ireland in 1968. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. In May 1977, by thirty-one votes for and only one against, Tynwald passed a resolution. A privately organised petition in favour of the retention of judicial Corporal punishment had obtained 31,000 signatures from amongst the approximate total of 45,000 persons entitled to vote on the Island. Since 1969 its application has apparently been restricted in practice to offences of violence. At the hearing on 17 January 1978, the Attorney-General for the Isle. of Man informed the Court that recently a privately organised. petition in favor of the retaining of judicial corporal. punishment had won the support of more than 30,000 of the island’s electors. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. In 1975 there were 65 crimes of violence to the person, in 1976 58 and in 1977 approximately 46. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. The offence with which the applicant was charged had been omitted from the specified list of offences. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. In its decision of 19 July 1974, the Commission, having considered ex officio that the facts of the case raised issues of discrimination on grounds of sex and. The Commission decided not to proceed further with an examination of the original complaint under Article 14 (art. 14) which the applicant had subsequently withdrawn. The Commission decided that it could not accede to this request “since the case raised questions of a general character affecting the observance of the Convention which necessitated a further examination’. In its report of 14 December 1976, the Commission expressed the opinion that the judicial corporal punishment inflicted on the applicant was degrading and was in breach of Article 3 ( art. 3) of the convention. The report contains one separate opinion. The applicant took no further part in the proceedings.

name: Hasan Yağız
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31834/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 June 1996. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. The Court declared the application admissible on 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of. membership of the Dev and sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) on 26 December 1994. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the Dev. It sentenced the applicant to six years’ imprisonment. On 27 December 1995 the Court ofCassation upheld the above judgment.

name: Joe Anthony Ashendon
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal to award them their defence costs, after they had been acquitted in their respective criminal proceedings, was in violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention. On 23 April 2008 and 2 October 2009 respectively, the Vice-President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the applications and to communicate the complaints to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of each application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicants and the Government each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The first applicant’s jacket, shoes, trousers and underpants were found in the flat. Faecal material, which was found to contain components of B's DNA, was found on the first applicant's t-shirt. The first applicant denied having committed any offences and stated that he had no recollection of events. He was interviewed on a further four occasions and states that he co-operated with the police each time. The prosecution offered no evidence in respect of the burglary charge and a not guilty verdict was recorded. The trial judge's summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. ... We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken” Jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. First applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) His counsel stated that had a different criminal offence been charged he may have had no alternative but to plead guilty but costs have been expended on defending him on charges for which he has been found not guilty. In refusing the application, the trial judge said: “With regard to a defendant’s costs you [Counsel] are right, the costs should and almost invariably would follow the event.” He continued: ‘I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in the criminal courts in which it is more apparent that a defendant's conduct, albeit that it had led to him being acquitted, has led him to the court’ The second woman is accused of conspiring to steal from a bank. A tape was recorded of her giving advice to a friend on how to steal money. The second woman says she can't remember the date of the tape or the conversation. She claims that if she had, the bank would have dropped the charges against her. The bank denies this and says the tape was not taken out of context. The case is still before the Supreme Court, which will decide whether or not the tape can be used as evidence in the case against the second woman. The hearing is expected to take place in the next few weeks, and the case will be heard in full in September and October. The second applicant was acquitted unanimously of the two counts facing her. Three defendants, including A.R. and C.R., were convicted of the majority of the charges against them. The second applicant applied immediately for a defendant’s costs order, pursuant to section 16(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 (see relevant domestic law and practice below) The trial judge refused the application. He stated: ‘The relevant features, in my judgment, in this case are these: that [the second applicant], acting very much on the advice of her then solicitor [name omitted], exercised her right to silence when answering ‘no comment’ in her police interview’ The second applicant renewed her application in writing, relying inter alia on the fact the she had been unable to recall the conversation on the tape recording until the trial had started. The trial judge declined to hold an oral hearing on the renewed application and stated that he was unable to make the order for the reasons he had already given. ‘She has rightly been acquitted by this jury.’ ‘This decision is in no way meant to indicate that she is in any way guilty of this offence, she is not, she has rightly been acquitted' ‘I have come to the conclusion that to that extent she brought this prosecution upon herself and in my judgment that is a proper reason for refusing a defendant’s costs order'

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal to award them their defence costs, after they had been acquitted in their respective criminal proceedings, was in violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of each application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicants and the Government each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants are Mr Joe Anthony Ashendon and Ms Marilyn Jones. The Government is represented by their Agents, Mr D. Walton and Ms H. Moynihan. The first applicant was charged with burglary, rape (by penile penetration), and sexual assault. The prosecution offered no evidence in respect of the burglary charge and a not guilty verdict was recorded. The trial judge’s summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies. ... We are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken.” The jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. When the first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) his counsel stated: “This is a case in which [the first applicant] was inevitably going to be charged with a criminal offence, I do not doubt that for a moment” The trial judge refused the application, saying: ‘I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in the criminal courts in which it is more apparent that a defendant’s conduct has led to him being brought before the court’ Police made a recording of a conversation between a man and woman. The man was alleged to have told the woman how to steal. The woman denied the conversation took place. The tape was recorded in 2006 and played to the jury in 2007. The jury found that the conversation was not recorded in the way the woman claimed. The case was settled out of court, but the woman is still owed money. She is suing for damages, claiming she has been unfairly treated. The prosecution has denied this, saying the tape was a genuine conversation between the woman and the man, and not part of a conspiracy to steal money. The trial continues, with the jury expected to make a decision in the coming days. The second applicant was acquitted unanimously of the two counts facing her. Three defendants, including A.R. and C.R., were convicted of the majority of the charges against them. The trial judge refused the application for a defendant’s costs order, pursuant to section 16(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 (see relevant domestic law and practice below) The second applicant, acting very much on the advice of her then solicitor [name omitted], exercised her right to silence when answering ‘no comment’ in her police interview. Her failure to answer questions had the effect of bringing this prosecution on herself, allowing the police to believe that the case against her was stronger than it in fact has turned out to be. On 30 July 2007, the second applicant renewed her application in writing, relying inter alia on the fact the she had been unable to recall the conversation on the tape recording until the trial had started. The trial judge declined to hold an oral hearing on the renewed application and stated that he was unable to make the order for the reasons he had already given. In my judgment that is a proper reason for refusing a defendant’s costs order. In no way is that decision meant to indicate that she is in any way guilty of this offence, she is not, she has rightly been acquitted by this jury.” The judge concluded that she had not put the phone call into its true context and true timescale.

name: Mükremin Kılınç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48083/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal. The applicant was the Deputy Mayor of the Sincan District in Ankara at the time of the events. In his capacity as the deputy mayor, he was responsible for the activities of the Culture and Education Department. He was accused of having disseminated propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation, namely the Hezbollah. The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor on 13 February 1997. He denied being involved in any illegal organisation. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to three years and nine months' imprisonment. He was also debarred from public service for three years. He appealed to the Court of Cassation. The Chief Public Prosecutor submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. The opinion was not notified to the applicant, but was read out during the hearing. The appeal was dismissed on 21 September 1998 and the applicant was discharged from the military service and banned from the public service. The application was later rejected again on 7 December 1998, and the chief public prosecutor rejected his request for rectification.

name: Thomas John Crompton
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. In 1989 the applicant joined the Territorial Army (“TA”) as a pay and accounts clerk, a military post, carrying out duties such as filing, photocopying and maintaining a stationery store. In 1993 he was made redundant, following organisational changes in the TA pursuant to a process of civilianisation. The applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal in 1994. His claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board of the Defence Council. The Army Board, without holding an oral hearing or directing a Board of Inquiry to be convened, issued its decision on 7 May 1998, refusing the applicant's claim for redress. In 2001, an award of compensation was notified to the applicant but he disputed the calculation of the compensation. A further offer of settlement was made to him in November 2001, which he rejected. On 11 April 2003, the Board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67. The High Court of England and Wales ordered the defendant to pay compensation. The claim was that he should have been paid for six years of his salary. The claimant appealed the decision, but the appeal was rejected. The case was eventually settled out of court, but not before the judge ordered the company to pay back the money. The company made an offer of £2,000, which was rejected by the court. The court of appeals ruled that the company should pay the full amount. The judge ruled in favour of the company and ordered the payment of the full sum, plus an additional £1,000 in interest, to be paid to the victim. On 24 May 2005 the Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. The decision was made on the basis that the award had been incorrectly reached. The award of the award of 24 May 2004 to the applicant was rescinded on the grounds that it had been reached incorrectly. The awarding of the compensation of the applicant to the claimant was also incorrectly reached on the balance of probabilities. The compensation was increased to GBP 150,000.

The case originated in an application (no. 42509/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. His discharge from the Army, dated 18 February 1994, was formally made, incorrectly, on the basis that his services were no longer required. He later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical store-man post remained vacant. The applicant had claimed redress in respect of his redundancy from his Commanding Officer, under sections 180 and 181 of the Army Act 1955. His claim was rejected because the Industrial Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. The applicant applied for judicial review of the decision not to hold an oral hearing or convene a Board of Inquiry. The Army Board met to reach a determination on 11 April 2001. It issued its decision on 16 July 2001, ordering that the applicant be offered compensation. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary (minus the applicant's actual earnings during the relevant period) and a redundancy payment estimated on the basis of the application. The High Court ruled that the award had not been properly calculated. It also ruled that he should pay back the full amount that he had been owed. The case was not settled for more than a year. In April 2004, a further offer of £5,000 was made. The offer was rejected on the basis that the original amount was too low. In May 2005, the High Court again refused to settle the case. The matter was finally settled in February 2006. The award was rescinded on August 6, 2006. It was awarded again on August 18, 2007, for £4,000. The total amount of the award is now £6,936.05. On 24 May 2005 the Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. The applicants’ subsequent petitions and appeals, as far as the full Courts-Martial Appeal Court, were unsuccessful. March 1999 the Chamber decided to join the cases and not to hold a hearing on the merits. The Chamber also declared the applications admissible. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63207/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her right to remain silent and not to incriminate herself had been breached in criminal proceedings against her. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 18 March 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant was fined 1,500 Austrian schillings (ATS) with two days' imprisonment in default. She claimed that the obligation under section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act to disclose the driver of her car violated the presumption of innocence and her right not to incriminate herself. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. The case is still pending in the Federal Court of Justice of Austria, which is the seat of the District Administrative Authority in the town of Vorarlberg. The court's decision may be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court of Austria.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was settled by the Court of Appeal on 21 November 1999. The decision was unanimous. The judge ruled that the application was not admissible because of its lack of merit. On 17 December 1988, the applicant complained to the same doctor he had seen the day before of ill-treatment during the second and third interviews on the previous day. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.m. and his solicitor made notes on the applicant's allegations. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. On 18 December 1988 the applicant was interviewed for the last time about an unrelated matter. He was then interviewed about another matter between 10 a.m and 12.45 p.M. on the same day. The applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant applied under section 8 of the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (as amended) to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. A voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) began and the applicant gave evidence. The trial judge gave judgment on 21 December 1990. The judge noted that the applicant did not mention the names of or attempt to describe the two detectives in respect of whom he complained to the doctor on the morning of 17 December 1988. The trial judge found it impossible to accept that ill-treatment of the nature alleged by the applicant could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room where the applicant was questioned. The applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination. As to the ESDA evidence, the judge found that the witness was not credible. The applicant was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment in 1991. His appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland in 1993. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. On 17 December 1993 the applicant's appeal against his sentence was rejected. The trial judge found that it did not substantiate the applicant’s submission as to the lack of authenticity of the interview notes. Accordingly, the trial judge rejected the. applicant's allegations of ill-treatment and found that there was no reason to exclude the applicant.'s admissions or statement made during his detention in Castlereagh police station.

The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention and that he had been denied a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and declared partly admissible by a decision of 14 September 1999. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations on the merits. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicant complained to the same doctor he had seen the day before of ill-treatment during the second and third interviews on the previous day. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. At 1 p.m. the applicant was allowed to consult with his solicitor, who made notes on the applicant's allegations. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20pm. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. The applicant was charged with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. All the relevant witnesses, including the applicant, the police officers alleged to have been involved in the ill-treatment and the doctors who had seen the applicant gave evidence. The applicant did not subsequently give evidence at the trial. However, the trial judge cautioned the applicant. The judge rejected the application and admitted the applicant's admissions and statement into evidence. On 21 December 1990 the trial judge gave judgment. He noted that the only evidence against the applicant was the admissions and statement made while in custody at Castlereagh police station. The trial judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials of the allegations made by theApplicant. As to the ESDA evidence, the judge noted that not one single objective sign of the ill- treatment which the applicant alleged was found by any of the doctors who examined the applicant; and that on the morning of 18 December 1990, the applicant did not make any complaint about ill- Treatment. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 16 June 1993. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. On 17 December 1993 the applicant’s appeal against his sentence was rejected. The application was dismissed on the basis that the trial judge had had the great advantage of seeing the applicant give evidence, and that both an accused and the police officers involved can equally have an incentive to lie.

On 21 December 1990 the trial judge gave judgment. The judge outlined his detailed reasoning behind his decision further to the voir dire. He noted that the applicant did not mention the names of or attempt to describe the two detectives in respect of whom he complained to the doctor on the morning of 17 December 1988. The trial judge found it impossible to accept that ill-treatment of the nature alleged by the applicant could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room where the applicant was questioned. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the. applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were. not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials of the allegations. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment and found that there was no reason to exclude his admissions or statement made during his detention in Castlereagh police station. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 2 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22299/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 7 July 1993. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. The trial ended on the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the judge to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.“ Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue. However, defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Defence counsel based his recollection on the grounds of appeal and advice on appeal which he drafted shortly after the trial on 10 December 1991. Neither of these documents suggests that Defence counsel made an express request to the judge to discharged the jury, as defence counsel suggests. The jury retired at 12.50 p.m. after failing to reach a unanimous verdict. The judge told the jury that he could accept a verdict of at least a majority of ten. The jury returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings began on Monday at the Court of Appeal. The application was for an appeal against the conviction of the applicant for racially aggravated GBH. The case was heard in front of a jury of nine men and two women. The trial judge ruled that the applicant was not entitled to appeal against his conviction because he had not been discharged on the grounds of racial prejudice. Leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The court continued: “Matters of this kind raise delicate issues. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly, and cannot be faulted for a conclusion that the jury should continue the deliberations which they had given their oath to undertake. We, therefore, find no ground for complaint and we dismiss this application.“

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40909/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was lodged by Mr Krzysztof Kulik (“the applicant”), on 6 August 2008. The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Nowogród Bobrzański. The applicant relied on the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. As of August 2009 the proceedings were still pending. B. scheduled for 21 May 2008 was adjourned as another motion for the judge to step down was to be considered.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34236/06) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The German Government (“the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Government of Montenegro, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, have not indicated that they wished to exercise that right. The case was referred to a Committee after consultation of both parties, who did not object. On 2 March 2010 the Committee, having deliberated, decided to refer the application to a Chamber. Hamburg Regional Court dismissed the objection the applicant had made to expert M. on 15 June 1998. The applicant's appeal against this decision to the Hamburg Court of Appeal was to no avail. Hamburg Regional Court decided to obtain a decisive expert opinion (Obergutachten) on the question of whether the applicant's dental treatment had been carried out correctly. The case was settled out of court in December 2003 and the applicant left Germany in compliance with an expulsion order made by the Hamburg Aliens Office. The hearing was held on 27 June 2002 and the judge ruled in favour of the applicant in the case against K. He was expelled from Germany on 1 December 2003. The judge ruled that K. had carried out his dental treatment correctly and that the applicant should not be expelled. The applicant was ordered to pay medical fees amounting to EUR 10,587.93 plus interest at a rate of four per cent starting from 22 November 1996. The Hamburg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid as his appeal had no prospects of success. The applicant subsequently paid the court costs due in their entirety. He did not, however, pay the plaintiff the medical fees plus interest as ordered by the Regional Court's judgment. He also did not reimburse the plaintiff any of the latter's costs of the proceedings (EUR 2,846.95) for lack of any income or revenues. He took up residence in Hamburg on 3 August 2005.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' plots of land in İskenderun were expropriated by the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways. A committee of experts assessed the value of these lands and the determined amounts were paid to them when the expropriation took place. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996. The first-instance court ordered the administration to pay Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000 plus interest at the statutory rate on 7 October 1997. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The amount due was paid at the rate of 13,075,000,000.

The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Four Turkish nationals, Ms Gülizar Pembe, Mr Mıstık Ateş, Mr İsmail Karapınar and Ms Yüksel Bozkaya (‘the applicants’) filed separate actions for compensation with the İskenderun Civil Court of First Instance. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The administration of Turkey paid Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000 plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 23 October 1996 to 23 November 1996. The administration also paid İsmail Karapınar TRL 13,075,000,000.

On 27 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings to the Government. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The administration continued to pay the appealants the amounts due.

name: Dariusz Kwiatek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20204/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 4 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Dąbrowa Górnicza. On 22 February 2000 the applicant was arrested by the police. The investigation was terminated on 14 September 2000. On 15 September 2000 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court. The applicant was charged with 2 burglaries. The case file comprised at that time some 32 volumes. The prosecution had obtained voluminous evidence, including various expert reports. The first hearing was listed for 22 March 2001 but it was cancelled. On 14 May 2001 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be held in custody until 15 October 2001, relying on the same grounds as previously. It held that no other measures could prevent the applicant from attempting to interfere with the proceedings. In addition, it observed that so far the trial court had not commenced an examination of the merits. On 8 October 2001 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 17 January 2002. The Regional Court noted that the continued detention of the applicant and some of his co-defendants was necessary in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings in the case. That decision was upheld on appeal on 13 June 2001. Two hearings had to be cancelled due to the failure of the police to bring the detained co- defendants from prison for trial. The applicant and two other co- Defendants appealed against that decision. On 28 December 2001 the. Regional Court ordered that the applicant be held in custody until 22 February 2002. The applicant was detained pending trial until 15 June 2002. He was charged with armed robbery, a serious offence for the commission of which an offender was liable to a minimum sentence of 3 years’ imprisonment. In reality the charges of armed robbery were brought against other defendants and the applicant had been, and still was, charged with 2 burglaries. The Court of Appeal considered that the serious nature of the offences, the complexity of the case as well as the fact that the original grounds for keeping him in custody were still valid warranted a further prolongation of his detention. The applicant appealed against that decision, but to no avail. The trial court made yet another application to the Court of. Appeal to extend his detention until 1 October 2002. The trial court held hearings on the following dates: 31 January, 15 and 21 March, 11 and 25 April, 16 May 2002, 3 and 27 June, 31 July, 29 August and 12 September 2002. Four hearings were cancelled for the following reasons: the absence of some of the co-defendants and defence counsel. On 3 December 2002 the Regional Court closed the trial. On 10 December 2002 it gave judgment. The applicant was convicted of one burglary and sentenced to 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment, which was nearly (less 12 days) the period he had spent in detention on remand. In sentencing the applicant the trial court took into account his two earlier convictions for similar offences.

name: Niyazi Ekici
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28877/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were laid off by the Diyarbakır Sur municipality, with which they had been employed. The court ruled in their favour and ordered the municipality to pay the applicants certain amounts in Turkish liras (TRL), including costs, together with interest running from 15 June 1999. In the absence of an appeal, the judgments became final on 22 November 1999. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 3 July 2007. No settlement was reached in respect of the other applicants. However, the municipality deposited a partial amount in the relevant account at the local enforcement office, which was made available to the remaining applicants. On 21 February 2005 Salih Demircan was paid 822 New Turkish liras (TRY) in a settlement with the Municipality of Bursas. The settlement was agreed in advance of the payment being made on the 21st February 2005. The applicant, who is a journalist, distributed a leaflet concerning the conscientious objector Mr O.M.U. He also handed the leaflet to the public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court together with a petition stating that he should be prosecuted for having committed a crime. On 28 September 2004 the Court (Second Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court. The case, which was brought before the Ankara Military Court of the Office of the Chief of Staff, was concluded on 29 August. The army, unable to deal with us through judicial methods, think that they can draw the opponents of war away from the public view. I am not a soldier and I never will be. Until I am summoned, whenever that may be, there will be no changes to my lifestyle. They can find me here and take me by force. But I will resist to the end in the barracks, and I am underlining that I will refuse to do military service in any shape or fashion.” On 1 April 1998 the public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court took the applicant's statement in which he reiterated the content of his petition. The applicant claimed he was a defender of freedom of expression and challenged the independence and impartiality of the court. The court held that it had competence to deal with the case pursuant to the Constitution and domestic law. In its decision the court, referring to domestic law and the jurisprudence of the Court, held that the military courts had jurisdiction and competence to try the applicant and concluded that the judgment given by the General Staff Court was in accordance with the law. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who is a journalist, distributed a leaflet concerning the conscientious objector Mr O.M.U, outside the Ankara State Security Court. The latter had been previously convicted and sentenced on account of this press release. On 28 September 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint. The complaint concerns the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court, the alleged interference with the applicant's right to freedom of expression and the lack of an effective remedy to the Government. The case, which was brought before the Ankara Military Court of the Office of the Chief of Staff, was concluded on 29 August. The army, unable to deal with us through judicial methods, think that they can draw the opponents of war away from the public view. I am not a soldier and I never will be. Of course, I am aware that I will be summoned for military service, but until I am summoned, whenever that may be there will be no changes to my lifestyle. They can find me here and take me by force. But I will resist to the end in the barracks, and I will refuse to do military service in any shape or fashion.” The court held that it had competence to deal with the case pursuant to the Constitution and domestic law. The court, relying on Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, affirmed that freedom of expression and the free dissemination of ideas was not an absolute right. Citing relevant articles of the Criminal Code, it reasoned that the provisions under which the applicant was charged pursued the aim of eliminating threats to the unity of the country, national security and sovereignty. In its decision the court, referring to domestic law and the jurisprudence of the Court, held that the military courts had jurisdiction and competence to try the applicant and concluded that the judgment given by the General Staff Court was in accordance with law.

name: Leyla Şahin
train_texts: The case stems from an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Grosz, Mr Alpaslan and Mr Güran. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The Court held a hearing in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002. The woman was wearing a headscarf at the time of the incident. She was studying at the University of Bursa when the incident occurred. The student had been banned from attending lectures if her head was uncovered. She has since returned to the university to complete her studies. The woman was also banned from leaving the university without permission by the university's vice-chancellor. The ban was imposed on all students wearing the headcovering at all times. The headwear was removed after the incident, but the student was not allowed to leave the university until the matter had been resolved. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the student. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health for the same reason. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998 was dismissed on points of law. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for a semester in April 1999 for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. On 10 June 1999 the applicant lodged an application with the Istanbul Administrative Court for an order quashing the decision to suspend her. The applicant’s application to have the disciplinary penalty quashed was dismissed on 30 November 1999. In June 2000 the applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that the aforementioned legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant's appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1998. In the meantime the applicant had enrolled at Vienna University.

The case originated in an application (no. 44774/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms under Articles 8, 9, 10 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 2 July 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002 (Rule 59 § 3). The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits. The student was banned from wearing the headscarf for four years. The ban was imposed by the University of Bursa in 1998. She was also banned from attending lectures if she was not wearing a head scarf. The student was allowed to wear the head scarf for one further year. She wore it until she was forced to remove it. The university ruled that the ban was necessary for the safety of the students. The judge ruled in favor of the ban and the student was able to continue wearing the hair-covering. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which will consider whether the ban is a breach of international human rights law. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health for wearing a headscarf. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. That regulatory power had to be exercised in accordance with the relevant legislation and the judgments of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. She lodged an application with the Istanbul Administrative Court for an order quashing the decision to suspend her. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ He was arrested in April 1989, having returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. In July 1993 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review of his decisions to reject the board's recommendation for immediate release and to require him to spend a further two years in open conditions before the next review. On 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of the sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than two years are eligible for release. The Secretary of State acknowledged in the proceedings that there was not a significant risk that the applicant would commit further violent offences. He asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. 4 years were released after serving two-thirds of their sentence (section 33 of the 1991 Act) On 5 September 1997 Mr Justice Collins quashed the Secretary of. State's decision of February 1997, holding that it was beyond his power to detain a. life prisoner other than on the basis that there existed an unacceptable risk. of a future offence involving a risk to the life or limb of the public. On 16 December 1997 the applicant was moved to open conditions. In January 1998 the Secretary of State decided that the applicant should spend only six months in open conditions before his next review. In July 1998 the House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. The applicant was released on licence on 22 December 1998. He later died in a hospice in Chelmsford, Essex, in 2005. He was buried in a private funeral on 6 November 2011. His son, Michael, was awarded a posthumous knighthood in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee honours ceremony on 17 December 2011. He has also been awarded an MBE for his services to the community.

The applicant, sentenced to mandatory life imprisonment for murder, alleged that his detention after recall on life licence had ceased to be justified by the original sentence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert, Sir Nicolas Bratza and Mrs S. Dollé. The case was heard at the Court of Appeal on 20 February 2002. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967. He was released on licence in April 1979. His licence required him to cooperate with his probation officer and to remain in the United Kingdom. After release he left the UK in breach of his licence and went to live in South Africa. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ He was arrested in April 1989, having returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. In July 1993 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review of his decision to reject the board's recommendation for immediate release and to require him to spend a further two years in open conditions before the next review. He was released on 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of his sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than two years are eligible for release. The Secretary of State acknowledged in the proceedings that there was not a significant risk that the applicant would commit further violent offences. But asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. 4 years were released after serving two-thirds of their sentence (section 33 of the 1991 Act). The Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of. State's appeal. Lord Bingham CJ stated: “The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. This term has not been imposed on him by way of punishment, because he has already served the punitive terms which his previous, very serious, offences have been thought to merit” On 16 December 1997 the applicant was moved to open conditions. In January 1998 the Secretary of State decided that the applicant should spend only six months in open conditions before his next review. In July 1998 the House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. In his speech, with which the rest of the judges agreed, Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the Secretary Of State to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. He held that there was no fundamental common-law principle of retributive proportionality which restrained him from detaining a mandatory life prisoner by reference to a risk that he may in future commit a serious but non-violent offence.

name: Janusz Panek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38663/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 5 September 2002 the Court declared the application admissible and the case was dismissed. The case was reopened on 15 March 1994. On 13 January 1995 the Gdańsk Regional Court pronounced its judgment. It convicted the applicant as indicted, except for the count of murder, of which he was acquitted. The court sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. On 3 July 1995 the prosecutor lodged an appeal against that judgment, contesting its part relating to the acquittal. On 12 October 1995 the Court of Appeal quashed the contested part of the first-instance court's judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. A further hearing, listed for 14 October 1996, was cancelled because the judge rapporteur was ill. The subsequent hearing was held on 6 November 1996.
