name: Aydın Hanbayat
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant’s mother was represented by Mr and Mrs Kırdök, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The applicant was arrested by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate in the course of a police operation carried out against the illegal organisation the TKP/ML-TIKKO (the Turkish Communist Party/Marxist Leninist - Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army). The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal organisation. The Istanbul Assize Court acquired jurisdiction over the case in 2005. While the proceedings were pending before the Court of Cassation, the applicant died on 18 June 2005. The applicant was sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. The court dismissed the applicant’s requests that he. be released pending trial. It held that the applicant's detention pending trial should continue having regard to the nature of the offence with which he was charged, the state of the evidence and the date of the remand decision. The case was discontinued on 19 October 2005 after the applicant appealed against his conviction.

The applicant was arrested by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate in the course of a police operation carried out against the illegal organisation the TKP/ML-TIKKO (the Turkish Communist Party/Marxist Leninist - Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army) The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Istanbul State Security Court decided to disjoin the proceedings against the applicant from case no. 1994/183 and to join them to a case brought against him in 1997 (no. 1997/359) On 23 February 2005 the Istanbul Assize Court acquitted the applicant of the charge under Article 146 of the Criminal Code, but convicted him of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 2. It sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. While the proceedings were pending before the Court of Cassation, on 18 June 2005 the applicant died. Subsequently, on 19 October 2005 thestanbul Assize court decided to discontinue the proceedings.

name: Mehmet Zeki Doğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38114/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the use of the applicant's statements allegedly taken under duress by the Istanbul State Security Court. The applicant was convicted of being a member of an illegal organisation and sentenced to fifteen years, seven months and fifteen days' imprisonment, pursuant to Article 168§ 2 of the former Criminal Code. In convicting the applicant, the first court to do so, the judge found the applicant guilty of attempting to undermine the constitutional order. The applicant was convicted under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Istanbul State Security Court and rejected the applicant's appeal. The court relied, inter alia, on the police statement of the applicant. On 2 June 2003 the decision was deposited with the Registry of the  Istanbul State security Court. The case was adjourned until the end of May 2003. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against him on 4 May 2004. He was sentenced to a life sentence in prison in June 2005. The sentence was suspended until the applicant could serve his sentence under Article 144 of the Criminal Code.

name: Roland Schutte
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Government, in their observations, requested the Court to give a separate decision. However, the Court has found no reasons to discontinue the application of Article 29 § 3. As neither party appealed, the judgment became final. The judgment of the Court is as follows: The applicant was acquitted of the charge of resisting the exercise of official authority by driving towards police officers with his vehicle, thus threatening them with bodily harm. The applicant was charged with failure to comply with a request to stop for the purpose of a traffic control contrary to Section 97 § 5 of the Road Traffic Act (Straßenverkehrsordnung). The applicant submitted his defence on 4 February 1998, asserting in particular that the conduct of proceedings for the said traffic offence violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The Independent Administrative Panel dismissed the applicant's appeal on 15 December 1998. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) on 24 March 1999. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application as being unfounded on 19 June 2000. The case was referred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) by decision of 17 August 2000. The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 31 January 2003. The fine imposed did not exceed 726 euros and the case did not raise an important legal issue. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint pursuant to Section 33a of the. Administrative Court Act. The case was settled by a majority decision in favour of the applicant, with the decision of the Independent Administrative Panel. In its decision it said that the offences at issue differed in their constituent elements and that it did not consider the issue to be an important one.

The case originated in an application (no. 46245/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged in particular that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible on 14 January 2003. The case was transferred to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1) by the Court in November 2001. The decision was made by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 13 December 2003. It was the first case to be heard by the ECJ under the new rules of the ECHR. The case was brought by Unirol Ltd. to the Płock Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) On 18 November 1994 the Regional Court exempted Unirol from court fees. On 16 December 1994 the court held the first hearing. At that hearing the applicant submitted a counterclaim, seeking payment of profits to which he was entitled under the terms of the contract. On 5 March 1997 the court decided that it would not deliver the final decision and resumed the proceedings. On 9 June 1999 the court ordered the parties to specify their claims. On 15 October 1999 the hearing listed for 10 July 1998 was cancelled. On 27 August 1998 the regional court ordered that the lost case-file be reconstituted. Unirol Ltd. asked the court to appoint an expert in 2000. On 12 April 2000 the expert submitted the relevant opinion to the court. On 22 November 2000 the Płock Regional Court delivered a judgment. Both parties appealed. On 27 June 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed both cassation appeals. The plaintiff and the applicant lodged their cassation appeal with the Supreme Supreme Court. The appeal was dismissed on 27 June 2002. The case has been referred to as the Unirol vs. Poland case by the Polish High Court and the Polish Supreme Court of Appeal. The Supreme Court ruled in favour of the plaintiff and dismissed the appeal.

name: Anna Łakomiak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28140/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Anna Łakomiak (‘the applicant’) was born in 1948 and lives in Łódź. The applicant lodged an application for division of an inheritance and dissolution of co-ownership on 19 September 1996. The estate had fallen into debt on account of unpaid rent for the apartment. On 18 October 2006 the District Court ruled on the inheritance rights and awarded the applicant money and furniture. On 111 May 2007 the Regional Court issued a writ of execution in respect of the judgment. The applicant sought an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 20,684.79 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approximately 5,200 euros (EUR) The court referred to the overall length of the proceedings and to the complexity of the case. The applicant appealed. On 20 July 2005 the Regional Court rejected the appeal as inadmissible in law. The court awarded the applicant PLN 3,000 (approximately EUR 750) in just satisfaction. The application was dismissed on 20 August 2005 and the applicant appealed again. The appeal was rejected on 20 September 2005. The case has been referred to as the Poland 2004 Act (“the 2004 Act”)

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37252/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Numerous witnesses were heard on various occasions. Some of the defendants transferred part of their shares to others on different dates. The court held an on-site inspection on 23 June 1986.

He alleged a violation of Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13, 14 and 18 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No 1. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. By a decision of 2 September 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The applicant’s village was in celi province, in the then state-of-emergency region of Turkey. In 1994, terrorist activity was a major concern in this area. Since the 1980s a violent conflict had been going on in the region between the security forces and sections of the Kurdish population in favour of Kurdish autonomy. The inhabitants were suspected of “aiding and abetting terrorists” and accordingly they were strictly and frequently controlled by the gendarmes stationed near the village. The applicant moved temporarily into a prefabricated State disaster housing complex close to Ovacık. He then filed a petition with the Ovac Turkey Public Prosecutor’'s office complaining about the burning down and forced evacuation of his village. The applicant learned of the Ovacık Public Prosecutor’s decision of non-jurisdiction from his fellow villagers. He therefore stated that the authorities would not initiate an investigation into the alleged events. In his statements to the investigating authorities, the applicant failed to specify the identity of the perpetrators of the alleged crime. name: John Bryan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 29 October 1991. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The hearing was adjourned until 11 May 1995, when it was reconvened by the Court to consider the matter. It was decided that the Delegate would submit her observations at the hearing. The buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate. Numerous features of the buildings were more suited to houses than barns. The original openings in building No. 1 were said to be doorways for a veal calf unit. But this building did not incorporate internal drainage considered necessary for such stock. Other features in both buildings include the extensive use of Georgian-style windows and other windows made for domestic use. I understand that Mr Bryan’s contacts allowed him to buy these windows cheaply. But whatever their source, they contribute to an impression that the buildings look more like houses than Barns. The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal on grounds (b) and (g) also fail. The decision turns on the following main issues. Whether, if the development is inappropriate to the green belt, there are any special circumstances to justify the granting of planning permission. Whether the appeal buildings enhance or preserve the character or appearance of the conservation area. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. (17) ... (18) These objections amount to sound and clear-cut reasons why planning permission should be withheld. (19) You said that demolition of the buildings and the removal of the materials was an excessive requirement. I do not agree. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order”. The subsequent grounds of appeal dealt expressly with grounds (a) and (g) of the appeal to the Secretary of State (see paragraph 9 above). The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. I see no need to insist on a period which would make undue difficulty for him. I will increase the period to 6 months. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) because the applicant had those rights and wanted more time to erect a replacement or replacements. Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected, whether or not conditioned as suggested by the applicant, was a matter for judgment. The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. He was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The hearing was held in public. Inspector rejected appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. (13) The buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate. (14) Numerous features of the buildings were more suited to houses than barns. The appeal buildings lie in part of the green belt ... They also lie within the Higher Whitley Conservation Area. They did not look as if they had been designed for the purposes of agriculture. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. I do not agree that demolition of the buildings and the removal of the materials was an excessive requirement. The applicant appealed against this decision under section 289 TCPA (see paragraph 24 below). In his Notice of Motion, the applicant first alleged that the inspector had “erred in law in applying the wrong test in deciding whether the buildings were permitted development under the provisions of the ... General Development Order’ The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development’. The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. ‘I am unable to say that there was anything irrational in the inspector’s decision. It is to be remembered that, in order to stay within his General Development Order rights, the applicant must erect replacement buildings which, by their appearance and layout, could be considered as designed for the purposes of agriculture. If they are, their effect on the green belt, the countryside and the conservation area is irrelevant to the exercise of that right. That does not, however, in my judgment mean that the inspector acted irrationally in concluding that the buildings in fact erected without permission were objectionable and should be demolished. I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.’

It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. He was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The Commission produced to the Court the documents in the proceedings before it. Inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. They also lie within the Higher Whitley Conservation Area. They did not look as if they had been designed for the purposes of agriculture. The two appeal buildings look like part of a small estate of detached houses with access roads and suitable garden areas. The appeal on ground (a) fails. (b) ... (18) The appeal buildings have neither enhanced nor preserved the appearance of the conservation area, rather the reverse. name: Fouzia Dakir
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4619/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the ban on wearing in public places clothing designed to conceal the face deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil. The Government were given notice of the above-mentioned complaints and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was brought by a Belgian national, Ms Fouzia Dakir (“the applicant”), on 22 December 2011. Wearing of clothing concealing the face shall be forbidden at all times and in all public places. A helmet, balaclava or other headgear may be worn where authorised by the legislation on the safety of workers or other legislation. The applicant lodged an application with the Conseil d’État for annulment of Article 113bis. She argued that the provision in question expressly targeted the Islamic veil, which she wore, and that the resulting ban constituted an interference with her rights guaranteed by Articles 8, 9 and 10 of the Convention. She contended that the interference did not pursue a legitimate aim as the principle of secularism was not a constitutional principle and there could therefore be no blanket ban on wearing the veil. The judgment was served on the applicant on 23 June 2011. the opinion of the auditeur, dismissed the application for annulment of the provision. The judge also dismissed the applicant's application for an annulation of the law. The judgment was read out in full in the Court of Appeal on 25 June 2011, and was delivered to the applicant the next day. The application was dismissed by the judge, and the application was thrown out of court. The judgement was then appealed to the High Court, which ruled in favour of the applicant. The case was dismissed on 26 June 2011 and appealed again on 24 June 2012, with the judgment being read out again on 6 June 2013.

name: Heinz Luksch
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that disciplinary proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. As of 1 November 2001 the application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant appealed the decision to suspend his right to practise for one year. The Administrative Court granted the applicant’s complaint suspensive effect. On 28 February 1997 it dismissed the complaint. The decision was served on 22 March 1997. The Chamber of Accountants declared the suspension to be effective from 31 January 1995 to 30 January 1996. The Appeals Board dismissed the appeal on 7 May 1993 stating that the suspension should last for a year. This decision was serving on 30 January 1995. The case was transferred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) on 17 May 1995 and the complaint was dismissed on 28 Feb 1997.

Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The applicant was suspended for one year in 1992. The Appeals Board dismissed the appeal on 7 May 1993. On 15 March 1995 the Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint. The case was transferred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) on 17 May 1995. On 28 February 1997 it dismissed the complaint and the decision was served on 22 March 1997. The suspension was effective from 31 January 1995 to 30 January 1996. The appeal was dismissed on 2 March 1997 and the complaint was dismissed. The application was dismissed by the German Court of Appeal on 1 June 1997. It was not heard by the European Court of Human Rights.

name: Ünsal Öztürk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24874/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of the national courts to lift a confiscation order for a number of books published by his company violated his right to freedom of expression within the meaning of Article 10. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The application was heard on 10 March 2009. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The Second Chamber of the Ankara State Security Court lifted the confiscation orders in respect of a number of the books but held that there were no books to return. The applicant appealed against the decision of 22 November 2005. The prosecutor at the Court of Cassation also requested that the decision be quashed because he considered that rejecting the applicant's request on account of the assumption that the contents of the papers might be unlawful was not in accordance with the law and procedure. The appeal was dismissed on 8 April 2006. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for legal advice. The ECHR ruled that the material in question was not “in contravention of section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act”.

name: Dorothea Vogt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. The Government requested leave to submit an additional memorial and requested that the hearing initially set down for 23 November be postponed. Mr Ryssdal granted these requests. The Registrar received the Government's additional memorial on 5 January 1995 and the applicant's observations in reply on 3 February 1995. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge, together with the other members of the Chamber. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995, namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr R. Macdonald, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr J. De Meyer, Mr I. Foighel, Mr M.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. Mrs Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. She became a member of the German Communist Party in 1975. On 1 February 1979, before the end of her probationary period, she was appointed a permanent civil servant (Beamtin auf Lebenszeit) In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory. It was stated that she was held in high regard by her pupils and their parents and by her colleagues. The applicant had engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980. She had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Parliament (Landtag) of the Land of Lower Saxony. The proceedings were stayed in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had been a member of the “Executive Committee“ of the Bremen/North LowerSaxony regional branch. She was also accused of being a party official in a constituency and standing in federal elections of 6 March 1983. From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary (Dienstbezüge) The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations and her combat against neo-fascism were in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The DKP, whose aims had always been wrongly alleged (but never proven) to be anti- constitutional, was never proven to be pro-constitutional. The applicant argued that she had availed herself of the right of all citizens to engage in political activity. In its judgment of 15 October 1987 the Disciplinary Division dismissed applications by Mrs Vogt to have the proceedings stayed and witnesses examined. It considered that active membership of a political party that pursued anti-constitutional aims was incompatible with a civil servant's duty of political loyalty. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978 (see paragraph 22 below), were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. Through the active role which she played within the DKP the applicant had clearly supported aims that were contrary to the Constitution. Mrs Vogt was dismissed for having betrayed the relationship of trust between herself and her employer. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. The fact that she had done her work satisfactorily for many years and that she was held in high regard by her pupils and their parents alike was immaterial. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs Vogts had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income to be protected from immediate hardship. It pointed out that, by carrying out activities on behalf of the DKP, the applicant had breached the duty. of political loyalty. Civil servants must at all times bear witness to the free democratic constitutional system within the meaning of the Basic Law and uphold that system. As a result of her activities as a member of the DKP the applicant had failed to satisfy these requirements. The DKP's political aims were incompatible with that system, the court said. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of thebasic law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant as the provisions governing the civil service mentioned in Article 33 para. 5 of the Civil Service Act were general laws. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. Mrs Vogt's conduct had been unlawful. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. In its judgment banning the former Communist Party (KPD) (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held that the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. [It] also stated that intensive propaganda and persistent unrest aimed at establishing - even if this was not to be achieved in the near future - a socialist rule. The court considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves unequivocally from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. The attitude of civil servants who, even if they campaigned within the DK P for the renunciation of aims that were contrary to the Constitution, showed outside the party, through the political offices they held, that they unreservedly supported its programme and policy, was incompatible with such a duty. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher. The court added that a radical change in a civil servant's attitude could affect its assessment of the seriousness of professional misconduct. employ only those teachers who unreservedly supported the free democratic constitutional system. The State was under a duty to dismiss teachers who played an active role in an anti-constitutional organisation. It followed that a more lenient disciplinary measure, aimed at persuading her to abandon her political activities within the DKP, was bound to fail. Her otherwise blameless conduct in carrying out her teaching tasks did not change the situation in any way. The applicant's dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonic civil service (Ministerpräsidentenbeschluß - also known as the Radikalenerlaß - see paragraph 32 below) and had published regulations for dealing with “earlier cases“ (see paragraph 33 below)

Parents, who because of compulsory education had to send their children to State schools, were entitled to expect the State to rely on its servants' loyalty to the Constitution, the court said. name: Wolfgang Adam Wenner
train_texts: The applicant has been continuously addicted to heroin since 1973. He has also been suffering from hepatitis C since 1975 and has been HIV-positive since 1988. In 2008 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of drug trafficking and taken in detention on remand in Kaisheim Prison. His drug substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. On 3 June 2009 the Augsburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of drug Trafficking and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment. It further ordered the applicant’s placement in a drug detoxification facility, to be executed after a period of time. On 17 June 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant was transferred back to Kaisheim Prison on 30 April 2010. The prison doctors gave him various painkillers for chronic pain resulting from his polyneuropathy, on a daily basis. During his detention, the pain in his feet, neck and spine became such that, at least during certain periods, he spent most of his time in bed. The applicant was examined by an external doctor for internal medicine, H., on the prison authorities’ request in October 2010. H. did not consider any changes in the treatment of the applicant’s HIV and hepatitis C infections necessary. He suggested that the prison medical service reconsider the possibility of drug substitution treatment. He subsequently confirmed that the applicant should be examined by a doctor specialised in drug addiction therapy. The applicant claimed that drug substitution treatment was the only adequate treatment for his medical condition. He also claimed that he was in need of Interferon therapy in order to treat his hepatitis C infection. The decision of the prison authorities was to continue the drug substitution therapy that he had received prior to his detention. The applicant had been addicted to heroin for almost forty years, he stood hardly any chance of leading a totally drug‑free life on release from prison. His rehabilitation could therefore better be furthered by providing him drug substitutiontreatment. He claimed that, as confirmed by doctor H., the serious chronic neurological pain from which he was suffering could be considerably alleviated by drug substitution. The prison authorities argued that substitution treatment was neither necessary from a medical point of view nor a suitable measure for the applicant’s rehabilitation. After three years in detention, he no longer suffered from physical withdrawal symptoms. His condition with regard to his HIV and hepatitis C infections was stable and did not require any therapy for which substitution Treatment was a necessary precondition. As suggested by the prison doctor, the applicant should use the opportunity to wean himself off opioids, such as heroin and its substitutes, while in prison, as it was very difficult to obtain drugs there. The applicant had neither been given substitution treatment in the clinic, nor had the doctors recommended substitution Treatment in prison. The applicant appealed against the decision of the prison authorities to the Augsburg Regional Court. He argued that under the applicable administrative rules for substitution treatment in prison in the Land of Baden-Württemberg, he would be provided with drug substitution therapy. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill‑founded. On 10 September 2012 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The application was dismissed on grounds that the applicant had failed to prove that the prison doctors of Kaisheim Prison were not qualified to decide about the medical necessity of heroin substitution. The court ruled that it was not necessary to obtain the opinion of a drug addiction expert. The applicant complained that his right to respect for his physical integrity under the Basic Law had been breached. He was denied drug substitution therapy, the only suitable therapy to treat his chronic pain. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2263/12) On 3 December 2014 the applicant was released. When examined by a doctor on 5 December 2014 he tested positive for methadone and cocaine. The doctor confirmed that the applicant would receive drug substitution treatment from 8 December 2014 onwards. The applicant was advised to be taken to a drug rehabilitation clinic immediately on his release in order to prevent him from taking an overdose of heroine.

The case originated in an application (no. 62303/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment, including a refusal to have the necessity of such treatment examined by an external medical expert, breached Article 3 of the convention. On 17 June 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The case was heard by a panel of three judges, including two members of the European Court of Human rights. The decision was delivered by the Lord Advocate of the High Court of Justice. The judge heard that the case was brought by a German national, Wolfgang Adam Wenner (‘the applicant’), who had been granted legal aid. On 10 December 2009 he was transferred to a drug rehabilitation centre in Günzburg, Bavaria, where he underwent abstinence‑based treatment for his addiction, without additional substitution treatment. On 19 April 2010 the Memmingen Regional Court declared the applicant’s detention in the detoxification facility terminated and ordered his retransfer to prison. The applicant was transferred back to Kaisheim Prison on 30 April 2010. The prison doctors gave him various painkillers for chronic pain resulting from his polyneuropathy, on a daily basis. During his detention, the pain in his feet, neck and spine became such that, at least during certain periods, he spent most of his time in bed. He had secretly consumed methadone at the clinic and lacked motivation to lead a drug-free life. The applicant claimed that drug substitution treatment was the only adequate treatment for his medical condition. He claimed he was in need of Interferon therapy in order to treat his hepatitis C infection. In view of his poor physical and mental health, it was impossible to carry out such treatment without simultaneous drug substitution therapy. Substitution also helped to protect other prisoners from infection when using the same needles as he did for the consumption of drugs. He stood hardly any chance of leading a totally drug‑free life on release from prison. His rehabilitation could therefore better be furthered by providing him drug substitutiontreatment. The decision of the prison authorities to continue the drug substitution treatments had to be confirmed by a drug addiction specialist. The prison authorities argued that substitution treatment was neither necessary from a medical point of view nor a suitable measure for the applicant’s rehabilitation. The applicant, who was severely addicted to drugs, had not received drug substitution treatment prior to his current detention in Kaisheim Prison. He also considered that the prison doctors did not have specialist knowledge in drug addiction treatment and asked to be examined by an external specialist. After three years in detention, he no longer suffered from physical withdrawal symptoms. His condition with regard to his HIV and hepatitis C infections was stable and did not require any therapy for which substitutiontreatment was a necessary precondition. The applicant appealed against the decision of the prison authorities to the Augsburg Regional Court. He claimed that the authorities of Kaisheim Prison, where no substitution treatment had ever been provided, had omitted to examine the medical necessity of drug substitution therapy under the relevant criteria. He also argued that under the applicable administrative rules for substitution treatment in prison in the Land of Baden-Württemberg, he would be provided with drug substitution treatment. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill‑founded. On 10 September 2012 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court continue. The applicant complained that his right to respect for his physical integrity under the Basic Law had been breached. He was denied drug substitution therapy, the only suitable therapy to treat his chronic pain. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2263/12) On 3 December 2014 the applicant was released. When examined by a doctor on 5 December 2014 he tested positive for methadone and cocaine. The doctor confirmed that the applicant would receive drug substitution treatment from 8 December 2014 onwards. The applicant was advised to be taken to a drug rehabilitation clinic immediately on his release in order to prevent him from taking an overdose of heroine.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62303/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment, including a refusal to have the necessity of such treatment examined by an external medical expert, breached Article 3 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. The German Government were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.‑J. Behrens, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The Court decided in favour of the applicant, who was sentenced to three years and six months in prison. In December 2009 he was transferred to a drug rehabilitation centre in Günzburg, Bavaria, where he underwent abstinence‑based treatment for his addiction, without additional substitution treatment. On 19 April 2010 the Memmingen Regional Court declared the applicant’s detention in the detoxification facility terminated and ordered his retransfer to prison. The applicant was transferred back to Kaisheim Prison on 30 April 2010. The prison doctors gave him various painkillers for chronic pain resulting from his polyneuropathy, on a daily basis. During his detention, the pain in his feet, neck and spine became such that, at least during certain periods, he spent most of his time in bed. He had secretly consumed methadone at the clinic and lacked motivation to lead a drug-free life. The applicant claimed that drug substitution treatment was the only adequate treatment for his medical condition. Substitution also helped to protect other prisoners from infection when using the same needles as he did for the consumption of drugs. It had to be clarified whether, in the applicant’s case, further treatment for the hepatitis C from which he suffered was necessary. The decision of the prison authorities to refuse the applicant treatment with Diamorphin, Polamidon or another heroin substitute for his heroin addiction was taken as a rejection of the applicant's claim that he was in need of Interferon therapy in order to treat his hepatitis C infection. In view of his poor physical and mental health, it was impossible to carry out such treatment. The application was dismissed by the prison authorities in October 2011. On 16 January 2012, the authorities again dismissed the applicant’s request. The prison authorities argued that substitution treatment was neither necessary from a medical point of view nor a suitable measure for the applicant's rehabilitation. After three years in detention, he no longer suffered from physical withdrawal symptoms. His condition with regard to his HIV and hepatitis C infections was stable and did not require any therapy for which substitution therapy was a necessary precondition. As suggested by the hospital doctor, the applicant should use the opportunity to wean himself off opioids, such as heroin and its substitutes, while in prison. It was very difficult to obtain drugs there. The applicant appealed against the decision of the prison authorities to the Augsburg Regional Court. He argued that the authorities of Kaisheim Prison, where no substitution treatment had ever been provided, had omitted to examine the medical necessity of drug substitution therapy. He also argued that under the applicable administrative rules for substitution treatment in prison in the Land of Baden-Württemberg, he would be provided with drug substitution treatment. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill‑founded. On 10 September 2012 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The proceedings before that court are currently underway. The applicant’s objection against the Court of appeal's decision was rejected. The applicant was denied drug substitution therapy, the only suitable therapy to treat his chronic pain. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2263/12). On 3 December 2014 the applicant was released. He claimed, inter alia, that he had been unable to hear the original proceedings as the acoustics in the court had been inadequate. He also submitted a letter in which the prison officer who had guarded him in the dock during the trial confirmed that the applicant had on a number of occasions complained to him of his inability to see the witnesses. The applicant complained to the Solicitors’ Complaints Bureau about the solicitor’s failure to take action in respect of his difficulties in hearing the evidence. She gave her evidence with her head bowed answering questions often with one word answers in a soft voice. I was nearer to her than the defendant. I could hear what she was saying. It is clear that the jury, the judge and counsel could also hear. A similar complaint concerning acoustics in the courtroom in which the applicant had been tried, and which was in constant use from the time of its opening in 1988, was made in one other case over a year after the applicant’s conviction. As a result, the landlords of the court building commissioned a report from a company specialising in acoustic. The report concluded that a person speaking from the Bench was intelligible in the front seat of the dock with the glass screen in position. It was subsequently decided to instal a reflector panel above the dock to overcome the very small sound loss which was due to the glass screens.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37326/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was born in 1956 and lives in Warszawa. He was placed in police custody on suspicion of drug trafficking. On 20 November 2002 the Częstochowa District Court ordered that the applicant be detained on remand. On 9 September 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. Hearings were held on the following dates: 27 November 2003, 25 March 2004, 15 April 2004, 13 May 2004, 17 June 2004, 8 July 2004, 12 August 2004, 9 September 2004 and 27 September 2004. Over thirty-five witnesses were examined by the court. On 30 September 2004 the Częstochowa District Court gave a judgment. The applicant was found guilty of drug trafficking and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. The court ordered that the applicant remain in custody until the prison sentence could be enforced. He was referred to a prison hospital for observation and admitted to hospital on 1 July 2004. The Częstochowa Regional Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case on 22 June 2005. The proceedings are pending. He was released from detention on 24 October 2004 and on the same day he was released. On 6 December 2004 two appeals against the judgment of 30 September 2004 were lodged by the applicant's lawyers. The appeal has now been quashed and the case has been remitted by the CzUkrainian Supreme Court of Justice. The case is still pending in the Polish Supreme Court, and the appeal judge is still awaiting a decision on whether or not to reinstate the case. The original appeal was lodged in September 2004.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention in respect of the legal status of transsexuals in the United Kingdom. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 11 September 2001, a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert, Sir Nicolas Bratza and Mr. Traja, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. A hearing in this case and the case of I. v. the United Kingdom (no. 25680/94) took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 March 2002 (Rule 59 § 2) The applicant had a tendency to dress as a woman from early childhood and underwent aversion therapy in 1963-64. She was prescribed hormone therapy, began attending grooming classes and voice training. She underwent surgery to shorten her vocal chords in October 1986. In August 1987, she was accepted on the waiting list for gender re-assignment surgery. Her treatment and surgery was provided for by the NHS. The Court heard addresses by Ms Cox and Mr Rabinder Singh. The applicant divorced from her former wife on a date unspecified but continued to enjoy the love and support of her children. She claims that between 1990 and 1992 she was sexually harassed by colleagues at work. She attempted to pursue a case of sexual harassment in the Industrial Tribunal but claimed that she was unsuccessful because she was considered in law to be a man. She did not challenge this decision by appealing to the Employment Appeal Tribunal. The applicant was subsequently dismissed from her employment for reasons connected with her health, but alleges that the real reason was that she is a transsexual. Her record continues to state her sex as male and despite the “Despite the ‘ “ The applicant has had to choose between revealing her birth certificate and foregoing certain advantages. She has not followed through a loan conditional upon life insurance, a re-mortgage offer and an entitlement to winter fuel allowance from the DSS. Nor did she feel able to report a theft of 200 pounds sterling to the police, for fear that the investigation would require her to reveal her identity. name: J. Peter
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) A German national, Mr J. Peter, entered into a civil partnership with Mr Peter, né V., on 5 October 2001. In September 2002 the applicant applied for a survivor’s pension to the German Pension Fund (Bundesversicherungsanstalt für Angestellte), a public-law corporation. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat. The Federal Constitutional Court delivered its judgment in a case (no. 1 BvR 1164/07, hereinafter ‘the 2007 case’) which had been brought in 2007 concerning the pension rights of a surviving partner in a civil partnership. The court found that denying a partner the right to a survivor’s pension from the civil servants’ pension scheme violated the principle of non-discrimination as set down in Article 3 of the Basic Law. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) would be introduced. The applicant complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicant's constitutional complaint. The applicant said that it would have been obvious even from a cursory examination of the constitutional complaints that his complaint concerned the retroactive application of a legislative amendment. The application was denied on the grounds that it did not appear to be a particularly difficult one. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint under section 97a of the Federal constitutional Court Act. Citing Gast and Popp v. Germany (no. 29357/95, ECHR 2000‑II), the court noted that a chronic backlog of cases in the constitutional courts could not justify the excessive length of proceedings. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. decisions and judgments of the federal Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and had to be drafted with the utmost diligence. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged by 3 June 2012. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. The complaints panel shall decide by a majority. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The decision is not subject to appeal. Section 97e of the amended Federal Constitutional Court Act stipulated that, in the case of terminated proceedings whose length might still become or had already become the subject of a complaint before that court, it was not necessary to raise a complaint. prior to filing a complaint claiming compensation. That complaint had to be lodged with the Federal Constitutional court by June 2012 at the latest.

Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) was to be introduced. The applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long, even taking the position and function of the Federal Constitutional Court into account. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007. case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the. applicant's constitutional complaint. Germany (no. 29357/95, ECHR 2000‑II), the court noted that a chronic backlog of cases in the constitutional courts could not justify the excessive length of proceedings. The court further explained that it was in the nature of constitutional court proceedings that chronological case management was of subordinate importance. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. decisions and judgments of the German Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay only admissible if complainant has previously objected to the length of the proceedings. Complaint had to be lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court by 3 June 2012 at the latest. Transitional provision stipulated that, in the case of terminated proceedings whose length might still become or had already become the subject of a complaint before that court, it was not necessary to raise a complaint of undue Delay prior to filing a complaint claiming compensation. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The court maintained that the twelve-month wait in accordance with section 97b §1 had not been excessive considering that the court had opted to rule on a similar case concerning the pension rights. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. If the sum thus calculated is not equitable, the Federal Constitutional Court shall assess a higher or lower sum. Complaint of undue delay only admissible if complainant has previously objected to the length of the proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court. Complaint must be lodged in writing and set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of proceedings. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. The decision is not subject to appeal. The complaint had to be lodged by 3 June 2012 at the latest. It was a departure from the general transitional provision under section 23 of the Remedy Act (see for details Taron, § 27, and Garcia Cancio, § 36, both cited above)

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6813/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was the owner and the editor-in-chief of a publishing house, Aram Basım ve Yayıncılık, which published a periodical, Vesta. The Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of disseminating propaganda in favour of the PKK under section 7(2) of Law no. 3713. The application was communicated to the Government on 9 January 2012. The case continues. The court considered that the aforementioned passages and the article in its entirety constituted propaganda in favour of the PKK. It hence sentenced the applicant to ten months’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay a fine of 375 Turkish liras (TRY) Taking into account his good behaviour during the trial and his character, the court suspended the pronouncement of his conviction on condition that he did not commit another intentional offence for a period of five years, under Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hükmün açıklanmasının geri bırakılması). On 22 October 2008 the court dismissed an objection lodged by the applicant against the above-mentioned decision.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21906/09) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, violated Article 5. The application was initially represented by Ms M. Kronfeldner, his sister, and subsequently by Mr A. Ahmed, a lawyer practising in Munich. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin. Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention. The court considered that owing to his propensity to commit serious sexual offences, the applicant was dangerous to the public. It considered that the applicant suffered from a dissocial personality disorder since his youth and that it was very likely that he would reoffend if released. His disorder could only possibly be treated in a psychiatric hospital. The applicant was accordingly transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital on 15 December 2005. The execution of his preventive detention was interrupted in order to execute the applicant’s preventive detention on probation. Regensburg Regional Court quashed its decision of 26 October 2005 to execute the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison. Nuremberg Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the Regional Court on 22 July 2008. The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital to Straubed Prison on 19 June 2008. It is argued that the applicant did not suffer from a psychiatric illness or a mental disorder which diminished his criminal responsibility or called for a psychiatric therapy. The court found that the therapy in the psychiatric hospital, in which he might become even more dangerous, had not yielded any success. The Court of Appeal added that the reasons why the applicant’s therapy in Straubing Psychiatric Hospital had not been successful were irrelevant for the question whether there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit further sexual offences. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. It found, accordingly, that the continued preventive detention was lawful and proportionate. The decision was upheld by the Regional Court on 17 June 2008. The application was rejected on 3 November 2008. The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. It remitted the case-file to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal in order for it to review whether, applying a stricter standard of proportionality, the applicant’s preventive detention was to continue. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regensburg Regional Court of 26 July 2010. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. It had not been shown that the applicant, owing to specific circumstances, was highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The applicant was transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital thereupon. The Applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act (see paragraph 39 below). The court may order preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied or whether it should be declared terminated. For persons in preventive detention, this time‑limit is two years (paragraph 2 of Article 67e) If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The detention of a person with diminished criminal responsibility is allowed to be placed in a psychiatric hospital if a comprehensive assessment of the defendant and his acts reveals that, as a result of his condition, he can be expected to commit serious unlawful acts and that he is therefore a danger. The duration of the placement is determined by the provisions which apply to the measure ordered in the judgment (Article 67a § 4). The Detention of Mentally ill Persons is provided. for enforcement of a different measure of corrections and prevention. The court may quash that decision if it later emerges that no success can be achieved by placing the person in a. psychiatric hospital. A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken. Recent case-law of the Federal Constitutional Court on preventive detention has been cited in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above) The Act on Therapy and Detention of Mentally Disturbed Violent Offenders (Therapy Detention Act – Gesetz zur Therapierung und Unterbringung psychisch gestörter Gewalttäter) entered into force on 1 January 2011. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. It found that those provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot) These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The court ordered all provisions to remain applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. It added that the Constitution stood above the Convention in the domestic hierarchy of norms was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue between the courts. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above, § 129), it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff. It was also necessary to offer the detainees anindividualised therapy if the standard therapies available in the institution did not have prospects of success.

The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional (file no. 2 BvR 2029/01; see paragraph 36 below) The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. It remitted the case-file to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal in order for it to review whether, applying a stricter standard of proportionality, the applicant's preventive detention was to continue (Articles 67d and 67e of the Criminal Code) Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regensburg Regional Court of 26 July 2010. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. It had not been shown that the applicant, owing to specific circumstances, was highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act (see paragraph 39 below). The applicant was transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital thereupon. The case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) involves the order of preventive detention by the sentencing court. The sentencing court orders preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied or whether it should be declared terminated. For persons in preventive detention, this time‑limit is two years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The court may subsequently transfer a person against whom preventive detention. was ordered to a psychiatric hospital or to a detoxification facility if the person’s reintegration. into society can be better promoted thereby. The length of the placement is determined by the provisions which apply to the measure ordered in the judgment (Article 67a § 4). The decision at issue in the case of M. v. Germany was subsequently reversed (see paragraphs 41-45 below). A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken. A therapy detention may be ordered if a person concerned has been found guilty by final judgment of certain serious offences. The person must further suffer from a mental disorder owing to which it is highly likely that he will considerably impair the life, physical integrity, personal liberty or sexual self-determination of another person. The detention must be necessary for the protection of the public. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The Court stressed that the fact that the Constitution stood above the Convention was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue between the courts. The Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care to the persons concerned. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany, it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff. It was also necessary to offer the detainees an individualise therapy if the standard therapies available in the institution did not have prospects of success (see§ 113 and 113).

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been denied access to a lawyer while in police custody and that his police statements had been relied on by the trial court to convict him. The application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The Government has been invited to submit further observations, if they so wished, following the judgment in Ibrahim and Others v the United Kingdom ([GC], nos. 50541/08 and 3 others, 13 September 2016). The applicant’s lawyer appealed against the judgment, arguing that the applicant had been convicted on the basis of statements taken under duress. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicant was sentenced to two years and one month's imprisonment. He was released on bail after serving a year and a half of the sentence. The judge ruled that the judge should not have sentenced the applicant to prison because he had acted in self-defence. The court of cassation's decision was upheld on 3 March 2010. The appeal was rejected by the French Supreme Court in May 2011. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal in March and April 2009.
