name: Metin Gültekin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17081/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. On 2 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was filed by four Turkish nationals, Mr Metin, Mr Tanju, Ms Selma Karaduman and Mr Toğay. At 5.15 p.m. on 27 March 2004 he died at the GATA Hospital. No autopsy was performed. Toğay Gültekin had spoken to his commanding officer on 16 February 2004 and told him that a friend of his had hepatitis and that he suspected that he might also have contracted the same disease. His superior had then transferred him to the regiment’s infirmary where tests had been conducted, establishing that he did not have hepatitis. On 28 September 2004 the applicants initiated compensation proceedings against the Ministry of Defence before the Supreme Military Administrative Court (“the Military Administrative court”) Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. It argued that on 16 February 2004 Toğay. GüLtekin told his superior that his friend had contracted hepatitis and that. he suspected that he himself might have been infected as well. A blood test had been conducted, but the results had not revealed any abnormalities. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with ToğAY Gü ltekin’s medical problems. The applicants argued that it had been these inordinate delays that had caused Toğays Güeltekin's death. They pointed out that there was no evidence to show that a blood test was carried out. Military Administrative Court appointed three medical experts, namely two professors and an associate professor from the infectious diseases department of the Gazi University Medical School. Medical experts reached the following conclusion in their report of 20 September 2005: “... An examination of the documents and other information in the file shows that Toğay Gültekin started his military service on 22 August 2003. On 2 January 2004 he was treated for a retractile testicle at Çorlu Military Hospital. He was prescribed medication at the regiment’s infirmary for an upper respiratory tract infection. On 17 March 2004 the regimentalinfirmary doctor decided to refer him to an infectious diseases clinic, but that was not done. Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses. His liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) The Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim in October 2005. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18), and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for Toğay Güllekin’s death. No mention was made in the decision of the applicants' complaint regarding the failure to transfer to hospital on 17 March 2004. The Military Administrative Court refused to entertain the rectification request lodged by the applicants on 28 December 2005. Toğay Gültekin was accused of failing to refer to hospital between 17 and 23 March 2004. The appeal was dismissed on December 29, 2005. In March 2007, a court ruled in favor of the applicants, allowing them to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court of Justice. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights. In May 2009, the court found that toğay was not guilty of any crime. In April 2010, the appeals court ruled that the case was not a case of criminal negligence.

name: John Henry Hubley
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63480/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a letter of 11 June 2007 the applicant’s estate informed the Registry that the applicant had passed away and that the estate intended to continue these proceedings. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Leeds. His wife died on 19 March 1997. The couple had two children, born in 1981 and 1984 respectively. In May 2000 the applicant enquired about widow’s benefits. The benefits agency refused his claim because he was not a woman. The applicant appealed this decision. He received child benefit in the sum of GBP 70.20 per month. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) on 12 November 2013. The ECHR heard the case under Article 29 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The hearing was held under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention (‘the Convention’).

name: Leszek Kaszczyniec
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59526/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was charged with large-scale fraud to the detriment of the State Treasury. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's detention and of his trial to the Government. The application was dismissed on 1 April 2003, and the case was dismissed again on 3 April 2003. The case was settled by the Supreme Court of Poland, which upheld the decision of the Court of Appeal to reject the application. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 9 years' imprisonment and a fine. He lodged numerous unsuccessful applications for release and appealed – likewise unsuccessfully – against refusals to lift the detention. The applicant asked the courts to release him either on bail or under police supervision, or to accept a guarantee from a responsible person or persons who would undertake to ensure his presence at trial. On an appeal lodged by the applicant, the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. The Regional Court held the first retrial hearing on 20 June 2000. The retrial was to begin on 28 March 2000 but was adjourned since one of the defendants had to undergo psychiatric examination. The applicant appealed, invoking Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The Szczecin Regional Court dismissed an application for release on bail or subject to other guarantees or conditions. The Court of Appeal extended the applicant's detention until 30 April 2000, repeating the grounds mentioned in the previous decisions. The applicant appealed again, saying that his detention was so excessive that it amounted in reality to serving a prison sentence. On 11 January 2000 the Court of appeal rejected the appeal. It stressed that both the fact that the applicant had earlier evaded justice and the nature of his, in the court's words, “criminal relations” with certain witnesses involved in the case, indicated that detention was the only preventive measure which would effectively secure the proper course of the trial. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant had misconstrued Article 263. §§ 3 and 4 of the 1997 Code. The applicant had already been convicted at first instance, no time-limit for detention applied to his case, even though his original conviction had subsequently been quashed on appeal. The court found it necessary to extend his detention until 30 October 2000 because the summer holidays were approaching, which, for all practical purposes, meant that the examination of the case would be postponed. The application was dismissed on 15 September 2000 and the applicant requested that the three sets of criminal proceedings conducted against him be dismissed. He was found guilty on all charges and sentenced to 18 months in prison. The applicant's appeal, based on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 31 October 2000. The applicant's request to transfer the proceedings at issue, be transferred to other courts, was refused. He was convicted of large-scale fraud and breach of official secrecy and sentenced to 8 years' imprisonment and a fine. On 1 March 2004 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal and he was released on the same day. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, and is expected to last until the end of 2014. The application was brought by a group of Polish academics and lawyers. The suit was brought in the wake of the fall of communism in Poland.

The case originated in an application (no. 59526/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 1 April 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's detention and of his trial to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with large-scale fraud to the detriment of the State Treasury. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki and Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 9 years' imprisonment and a fine. On an appeal lodged by the applicant, the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. The Regional Court held the first retrial hearing on 20 June 2000. Subsequent hearings were held on 12, 18 and 19 July, 22 August, 20, 21 and 28 September, 17 and 18 October, 28 and 29 November and 20 December 2000. The retrial was to begin on 28 March 2000 but was adjourned since one of the defendants had to undergo a psychiatric examination. The next hearing scheduled for 9 May 2000 had to be adjourned due to the illness of a lay judge. The applicant appealed, invoking, inter alia, Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The Szczecin Regional Court dismissed an application for release on bail or subject to other guarantees or conditions. On 16 November 1999 the Regional Court extended the applicant's detention until 30 April 2000. On 11 January 2000 the Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It stressed that neither bail, nor police supervision nor any other guarantee would secure the proper course of the trial. It said detention was the only preventive measure which would effectively secure the appropriate course of proceedings. The decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant was sentenced to 9 years' imprisonment. The court noted that he faced an exceptionally heavy sentence to which he was liable. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant had misconstrued Article 263 §§ 3 and 4 of the 1997 Code. The applicant had evaded justice at the initial stage of the proceedings, the court also pointed out that his detention served the purpose of securing the proper conduct of the trial. The court found it necessary to extend his detention until 30 October 2000 because the summer holidays were approaching, which, for all practical purposes, meant that the examination of the case would be postponed. The application was dismissed on 15 September 2000 and the applicant requested that the three sets of criminal proceedings conducted against him before the courts in Szczecin, including the trial, be dropped. The applicant's appeal, based on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 31 October 2000. On 13 October 2000 his request was refused. On 18 October 2000 the Szczecin Regional Court prolonged the applicant's detention until 30 January 2001. The applicant appealed. On 28 March 2002 he was convicted of large-scale fraud and breach of official secrecy. He was sentenced to a cumulative sentence of 8 years' imprisonment and a fine. On 12 February 2003 the Poznań Court of appeal amended the Regional Court's judgment by reducing his sentence to 6 years. On 1 March 2004 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal.

The court found that there was a considerable likelihood that he had committed the offence with which he had been charged. The applicant appealed, invoking, inter alia, Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. He submitted that his right to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial was not respected. He maintained that his detention was so excessive that it amounted in reality to serving a prison sentence. The Szczecin Regional Court dismissed an application for release on bail or subject to other guarantees or conditions. On 16 November 1999 the Regional Court extended the applicant's detention until 30 April 2000, repeating the grounds mentioned in the previous decisions. On 11 January 2000 the Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It stressed that both the fact that the applicant had earlier evaded justice and the nature of his, in the court's words, “criminal relations” with certain witnesses involved in the case. The applicant's original conviction had been quashed on appeal. Since the applicant had already been convicted at first instance, no time-limit for detention applied to his case. The applicant requested that the three sets of criminal proceedings conducted against him before the courts in Szczecin, including the trial, be halted. The court found it necessary to extend his detention until 30 October 2000 because the summer holidays were approaching, which, for all practical purposes, meant that the examination of the case would be postponed. The High Court ruled that the Court of Appeal had misconstrued Article 263 §§ 3 and 4 of the 1997 Code, and that only the Supreme Court could prolong his detention. The applicant was detained by the Szczecin Regional Court in Poland until 30 January 2001. The applicant's appeal, based on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 31 October 2000. He was convicted of large-scale fraud and breach of official secrecy in 2002 and sentenced to 8 years' imprisonment and a fine. On 1 March 2004 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal and he was released on the same day. The appeal was eventually dismissed on 1 March 2005 by the Polish Supreme Court, and the applicant was released from prison on 1 February 2006. The case is still pending at the Polish High Court of Justice.

name: Yasin Böber
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62590/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The application was lodged by a Turkish national, Mr Yasin Böber (“the applicant’), on 6 November 2009. On 23 June 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. His right leg was broken as a result of the incident. The applicant was injured by Turkish police officers in June 2003. The police officers were sentenced to two months and fifteen days' imprisonment. The court suspended the sentence for a period of five years. The applicant lodged an objection to the judgment of the first-instance court in December 2008. The Istanbul public prosecutor filed an indictment with the 1st Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court against the police officers, charging them with ill-treatment of the applicant. The judge acquitted the applicant of the charges against him in respect of one of the officers. However, since the officer had overstepped his authority by his actions, the court decided not to convict the officer. The Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the application on 8 May 2009. As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, this decision was final. The decision was made without holding a hearing. The case was dismissed without a hearing, and without any further action being taken against the applicant. The appeal was rejected by the court on 14 June 2009. The trial was adjourned until September 2009, when the case was heard by the Istanbul Court of Appeal. The judge ruled that the case should be dismissed and the case returned to the original court of appeal. The hearing was held on 8 September 2008. The result was the rejection of the appeal, and no further action was taken.

The case originated in an application (no. 62590/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. He was arrested and taken to the Beşiktaş police station by the officers, as he was accused of having insulted them. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination of the applicant, his right leg was broken as a result of the incident. The applicant's leg was broken and he was unfit for 15 days. The court found that the police officers had beaten the applicant and had closed the car door on his leg and had thus caused the injuries found on the applicant’s body. The police officers were sentenced to two months and fifteen days’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an objection to the judgment of the first-instance court. The 1st Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court convicted the officers as charged on 23 December 2008. The judge suspended the sentence for a period of five years, pursuant to Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) The applicant said he would make more detailed submissions after he had been provided with a copy of the reasons for the reasons. The case was referred to the Istanbul Assize Court on 21 April 2009. The court made its decision on 8 May 2009. There was no need for an appeal, as the decision was made by the court. The case was dismissed without any further action being taken. The appeal was rejected on 15 May 2012. He was arrested and taken to the Beşiktaş police station by the officers, as he was accused of having insulted them. As regards the second officer, who had closed the car door on the applicant’s leg, the court found that the applicant had insulted him. The court sentenced the accused police officers to two months and fifteen days’ imprisonment. The first-instance court considered that the police officers would not commit any further offence. It therefore decided to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment (hükmün açıklanmasının geri bırakılması) for a period of five years. The Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the case without holding a hearing. As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, the decision to dismiss the case was final. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Turkey. The appeal was dismissed and a new case was brought before the High Court of Justice. The judge ruled that the case should be dismissed. The court did not hold a hearing to determine the case's legal status. The decision was made by the Appeals Court, which found the case not to be in the public interest. The ruling was made without a hearing, and the case returned to the Court of Appeal. The appeals court decided to uphold the original decision to drop the case.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 52479/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. He also complained that he had been unable to communicate with his defence counsel out of earshot of a person appointed by the prosecutor. On 9 October 2007 the Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints relating to the excessive length of his detention and the lack of unsupervised contacts with his lawyer at the investigation stage of the proceedings. The applicant's detention was prolonged twice, on 1 August, until 31 October 1996. An appeal lodged by the applicant against the decision of 1 August 1996 was unsuccessful. On 23 December 1996 the prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and his co-accused with the Wrocław Regional Court. The first hearing in the case was held on 21 March 1997. The court held subsequent hearings on 11 and 12 September and 18 November 1997, and 10 February and 3 March 1998. On 16 April 1998 the court heard evidence from two anonymous witnesses who answered questions which had previously been formulated in writing by the applicants lawyers. On 25 March 1998 they submitted a list of further questions to be put to one of those witnesses. The Wrocław Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention, which was about to exceed two years. The court found that apart from the reasonable suspicion that he and the two co-accused persons had committed the offence at issue, there existed an actual risk that they would obstruct the proceedings if released. The Supreme Court also recommended that the trial court should “schedule the hearings in a more rational way so as to avoid further intervals of several months in the instant case”. Subsequent hearings were held on 9 July, 16 September, 1 October and 3 November 1998. The application was dismissed on October 31, 1998. The applicant and his co-accused were found guilty of robbery committed by an organised criminal gang. The applicant was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and a fine. The Wrocław Regional Court closed the trial and rendered its judgment. On 28 June 1999 the applicant’s lawyers filed an appeal. They referred, inter alia, to procedural shortcomings and expressed the view that the proceedings had, as a whole, been unfair. On 16 November 2001 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal as manifestly unsubstantiated. The application is still pending at the Court of Appeal of Wroc Poland. The appeal is expected to be heard in November. The Wrocław Regional Court ruled that the applicant could see his lawyer whenever he requested. The restrictions imposed on his contacts with his lawyer did not impair his defence rights. The court further stated that the defence strategy could also be discussed in accordance with the law in the presence of a person appointed by the prosecutor. The only restriction imposed on the applicant concerned the possibility of having unsupervised contacts. with his lawyers. a defence strategy. The fact that a prosecutor was to be present during these visits did not affect the applicant’s defence rights at that stage, the more so as the restriction was to apply only during the investigations.

name: Yunis Bolukoç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35392/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1962, 1978 and 1980 respectively and were in Kandıra prison at the time of the lodging of the application. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance during detention in police custody, the length of the criminal proceedings against the first applicant, and the. lack of independence and impartiality of the State Security Court which tried him. The first applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on the same grounds as before, but in respect of acts which he had allegedly committed after he had been released pending trial. The court decided to join these proceedings to another case (no. 1997/543) pending before the 6th Chamber of the ISSC. In the course of these proceedings, the applicant was released pendingtrial. The second and the third applicant took part in a reconstruction of events where they admitted, inter alia, to throwing a Molotov cocktail at a building in Istiklal on 30 March 2000. The first applicant stated that he had refused to make a statement to the police because he did not accept the accusations against him. The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation. The second and the third applicants were also accused of throwing Molotov cocktails on various dates. The applicants were tried together with ten co-accused. In November 2002 the ISSC convicted the applicants as charged and sentenced them to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. In January 2004 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and upheld the judgment of the first-instance court in respect of the applicants. According to the documents in the case file, the case was still pending before the Court for Cassation on 10 November 2008. The court ordered the applicants' continued detention.

name: Martin Zumtobel
train_texts: Case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. Expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch. On 13 February 1986 the Office made an order for expropriation and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file, namely a report of the Court of Audit (Rechnungshof), an expert report on the environmental implications, and the decision taken by the local authorities. The first applicant also challenged the decision of 13 February 1986 (see paragraph 10 above) in the Administrative Court. Relying on substantially the same arguments as in the Constitutional Court, it now complained of breaches of procedural and substantive law. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports. Court rejected complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt for the purposes of Article 7 (1), sub-paragraph 4, of the 1950 Law. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right to a hearing. The fact that the Government Office had not made the commencement of construction work for the L 52 subject to a final decision on the length of the route was not incompatible with the Provincial Highways Law. In the absence of any formal requirement, there was nothing to prevent a written record being made of an orally delivered expert report. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50 (ATS). On 6 December 1987, the court ruled in favour of the first applicant. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988 the first applicant's appeal onpoints of law was dismissed. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) and who was given leave by the President to use the German language. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984.  expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch, which went through densely populated built-up areas. The Office considered the first request to be irrelevant to the case; as to the second, it stated that the official expert had not shown any bias in favour of the authorities and had submitted a convincing report. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the road network. The Administrative Court cannot hold to be unlawful the fact that the respondent authority had regard to road traffic requirements and based its decision principally on the consideration that no other more appropriate solution - than the construction of the proposed section of the L 52 - was possible. The court rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right to access the case file. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt for the purposes of Article 7 (1), sub-paragraph 4, of the1950 Law. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50. On 6 December 1987, the case was heard by the Court of Audit, who concluded that there was nothing to show that these documents could have been material to the applicant partnership’s case. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988 the first applicant's appeal onpoints of law was dismissed by the Supreme court. October 1988, the appeal was dismissed and the case was settled. October 1989, the first application was settled and the first appeal was rejected. October 1990, the second appeal was decided and the appeals were dismissed. October 1991, the third appeal was settled, and October 1992, the fourth appeal was agreed. October 1994, the fifth and sixth appeal were decided. October 1999, the sixth appeal was concluded.

name: Ecevit Piroğlu
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the executive board of the Izmir Branch of the Human Rights Association (“the Association”) at the time of lodging their applications. The Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning both applicants' right to a fair and public hearing, and the second applicant's right to freedom of expression and freedom of association. The application was rejected on the grounds that the first applicant's case concerned only the first set of proceedings, regarding the Association members with prior convictions. The applicants were banned from founding or becoming a member of an association. They were accused of non-compliance with section 4 of Law no. 2908. The applicants did not pay the fine within ten days. The Izmir Magistrates' Court found the applicants and the other co-accused guilty as charged and fined them TRL 213,548,4000 per person. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Izmir Criminal Court dated 6 February 2002 and the case file was remitted to the IzMir Magistrate's Court. The case was re-opened on 14 May 2003 and the applicants were allowed to remain on the Board. The Association, together with several local non-governmental organisations (NGOs), took part in a civil society movement called the “Platform of Conscientious Objectors to War” and made a collective press declaration in protest against the military operations of the United States of America (USA) in Afghanistan. On 31 December 2001 the Izmir Magistrates' Court, following the simplified procedure and thus without a hearing, convicted the second applicant as charged (case no. 2001/2160). By issuing a penal order, it sentenced her to an increased fine of TRL 213,548,400. However, the court suspended the sentence pursuant to section 6 of Law no. 647 on the execution of sentences. She argued that the. conviction infringed her right to freedom of expression. She further complained that the indictment had not been communicated to her and that the court had not obtained statements or heard counter-evidence from her. On 20 February 2002 the criminal court dismissed her objection, again without holding a hearing. She was convicted of a contribution to the establishment of an unlawful organisation and sentenced to five years in prison. The sentence was suspended for three years and suspended for five years on appeal. The conviction was later overturned on appeal and she was released from prison. She has since worked for a number of newspapers, including the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal.

name: Stephen Arthur Perry
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63737/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 September 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. No hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant is currently detained in HM Prison Brixton. An important part of the prosecution's case rested almost entirely on the ability of the witnesses to visually identify the perpetrator. Given the failure of the applicant to attend the arranged identification parades, the police decided to arrange a video identification parade. Permission to covertly video the applicant for identification purposes was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force under the Home Office Guidelines on the Use of Equipment in Police Surveillance Operations 1984. The video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant as the robber. The applicant was later acquitted on this count. He was acquitted on all five counts against him. The trial lasted 17 days, the applicant and 31 witnesses giving live evidence. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video and this had been shown to the court. Jury convicted the applicant of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant applied for leave to appeal against conviction, inter alia, alleging that the trial judge had erred in not excluding the evidence obtained as a result of the covert identification video. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. On 14 April 2000, the House of Lords rejected the application. The solicitors claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000 that the jury had been told of the complaints by the applicant. The jury were also made aware of the alleged breaches of the code of practice.

The case originated in an application (no. 63737/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 September 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), and the case was dismissed. The applicant was charged with two counts of armed robbery in 1997. He was acquitted of one count on 1 August 1997 and acquitted of the other on 1 September 1997. The applicant did not appear for identification on the specified date, stating later that he did not receive such notification as he had changed address. A compilation tape was prepared in which eleven volunteers imitated the actions of the applicant as captured on the covert video. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant. The police decided to arrange a video identification parade. Permission to covertly video the applicant was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force. The trial lasted 17 days, the applicant and 31 witnesses giving live evidence. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video. The judge ruled that the evidence was therefore admissible. In his summing-up to the jury, the trial judge warned the jury at considerable length about the “special need for caution” before convicting any defendant in a case turning partly on identification evidence. Jury convicted him of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. He applied for leave to appeal against conviction, inter alia, alleging that the trial judge had erred in not excluding the evidence obtained as a result of the covert identification video. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. On 14 April 2000, the House of Lords rejected his appeal. The solicitors claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000 that the jury had been made aware of his complaints about the honesty and fairness of his treatment by the police and alleged breaches of the code of practice.

name: Charles Bernard O’Neill
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 41516/10 and 75702/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first applicant was born in 1962 and is currently detained in HMP Glenochil in Scotland. He was represented by McClure Collins Solicitors, a firm of solicitors practising in Glasgow. The second applicant, born in 1976, is currently awaiting trial at HMP Edinburgh. The applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012 and 17 December 2012 respectively. The initial investigation into the disappearance of A.M. began on 16 February 1998 when R.M reported his ex-wife missing. The applicants were directly accused of the murder of A.M. in September 1998. Neither was arrested or charged with any offence owing to insufficient evidence. The applicants were released from custody on licence on 22 May 2003 and 18 January 2002 respectively. They both travelled to Spain without notification, thereby breaching the terms of their parole licence in contravention of the Sex Offenders Act 1997. The Scottish Executive subsequently revoked their licences. In April 2004 the applicants were arrested in Spain in connection with the apparent abduction of a fourteen year old boy. They were returned to the United Kingdom, where they were recalled to prison to serve the unexpired portion of their licence periods. On 4 April 2005 they were sentenced to a further three years’ imprisonment, which was reduced on appeal to eighteen months. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. They appeared on petition at Kilmarnock Sheriff Court were they were committed for further examination and remanded in custody. On 19 December 2005 the Crown decided to take “no proceedings meantime’ with regard to the 2005 petition. On 26 April 2006 the applicants were informed that there would be ‘no proceedings meanwhile’. By November 2006 both applicants had served the custodial element of their earlier criminal sentences and were released from prison. They both travelled to live in Scotland. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. in 2005. A number of additional charges relating to various sexual offences were added. On 9 September 2008 Crown Counsel concluded that there had been a material change in the prospects of securing a conviction against both applicants. The High Court found that the Crown had acted properly in investigating and reviewing the evidence between 1997 and 2008. Although the applicants were granted permission to appeal, their appeal was refused on 5 June 2009. At a preliminary hearing on 29 June 2009 the High Court allowed motions by the applicants to separate the murder charges from the sexual offences charges. The application was granted on 20 February 2009. The applicants were convicted of various sexual offences and murder. They were sentenced to periods of imprisonment ranging from eight to ten years to run concurrently. Both appealed against conviction and sentence. The applicants’ trials took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. The first applicant also argued that the murder charge against him should be dismissed for reason of delay. The second applicant did not appeal the decision. The application was dismissed on 26 November 2009 and the Supreme Court refused the first applicant leave to appeal on 22 February 2010. On 10 June 2010 a jury convicted the applicants of murder and attempting to pervert the course of justice and sentenced them to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. The main issue before the Supreme Court was whether the applicants could be said to have been ‘charged’ on 17 September 1998 or whether the appropriate ‘starting point’ for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 was 5 April 2005. The court assessed the evidence in light of the relevant case-law of the domestic courts and of this Court. The case was decided in favour of the applicants on 13 June 2013, and the appeal was heard at the Court of Appeal on 29 and 30 April 2013. The appeal was decided on the basis of the arguments presented in the Note of Appeal. Supreme Court observed that as the ‘fair trial’ guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the “reasonable-time” guarantee it had to be approached separately. The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant‘s appeal on 19 June 2014. The case was then remitted back to the Court of Appeal for further proceedings. The appeal was dismissed and the cases were sent back for further hearings.

name: Erwin Baischer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32381/96) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him relating to an administrative offence no oral hearing has been held. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 16 January 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard in the Third Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The applicant complained that the District Administrative Authority had incorrectly applied the law and failed to sufficiently assess the evidence before it. The applicant did not request a hearing, nor did he expressly waive this right. An oral hearing would have been necessary because his appeal was not limited to points of law. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The case was then transferred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) However, on 23 February 1996 this decision was served on the applicant's lawyer. On 10 May 1996 the Court of Appeal ruled that the case did not raise important legal issues.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by lawyers practising in Pamplona and Madrid. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) would be the Court's Fourth Section. The case was heard by Mr I. Blasco Lozano, new Agent of the Government and Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights, Ministry of Justice, until 31 January 2003. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The application was dismissed by the Audiencia Nacional on 15 February 2003. The case was settled on 16 March 2003. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan, which had not been drawn up when the project was approved. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In 1996, the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Aut autonomous Community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987, particularly with regard to the possibility of reclassifying the protection zone. The Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. In application of the Supreme Court's judgment, by a decision of 4 September 1997, the Audiencia Nacional declared final the interim enforcement measures ordered on 6 March 1996 concerning the prohibition on filling the reservoir and other related work. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. The Constitutional Court declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible. The court extended the question to include a new point raised by the applicant association. The Court gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government, and invited them to file their observations within fifteen days. The Speaker of the House of Representatives indicated that the Chamber would file its observations within three weeks. The Attorney General's observations were submitted on 29 September 1998. The Constitutional Court, sitting as a full court, held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the law. The Constitutional Court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three above-mentioned nature reserves. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. Court considered that a new law was not in itself incompatible with the right to execution of judicial decisions as enshrined in Article 24 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. It found that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the constitution. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. Outlined that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The application was dismissed and no further action was taken by the court. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court examined whether the impossibility of executing the Supreme Court's judgment as a consequence of the enactment of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was justified in view of the values and assets protected by the Constitution. It found that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. The Constitutional Court further noted that the system of peripheral protection zones introduced by this new law had not in itself been considered arbitrary in the Audiencia Nacional's decision. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance, and pointed out that the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 of the constitution. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. It was ruled that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The decision was published by the Government of South Africa in the official Gazette on April 14, 2000. Click here to read the judgment in full, or click here for a video of the entire verdict. The judgment is available to the general public via the official website of the South African Broadcasting Corporation and the official news agency, South African Press Association. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They also complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The application was dismissed on 1 April 2003, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan, which had not been drawn up when the project was approved. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In the context of the interim enforcement of its judgment of 29 September 1995, by a decision of 6 March 1996, prohibited the filling of the reservoir and displacement of the population concerned. On 17 June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Aut autonomous Community Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. In application of the Autonomous Community law of 1996, the Navarre government adopted Decree no. 307/1996 of 2 September 1996. This identified the peripheral protection zones for certain nature reserves and strict nature reserves in Navarre. According to the applicants, this Law enabled construction work on the dam to continue, with the consequent deterioration of the protected natural site. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz was saved from flooding. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could nonetheless be corrected. In the alternative, the applicant association requested that certain provisions in the Aut autonomous Community law be referred to the Constitutional court for a preliminary ruling on their constitutionality. The Constitutional Court ruled that the issues raised in the preliminary question were admissible in July 1998. The case was decided by a unanimous vote of the Spanish Court of Appeal. The decision was upheld by the Spanish Supreme Court. The Constitutional Court, sitting as a full court, held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court's judgment of 14 March 2000 was published in the journal of the Spanish Academy of Sciences and Humanities. It was published under the heading "Navarre Dam Case" and was published by the Spanish Association of Learned Societies. The Constitutional Court examined whether the impossibility of executing the Supreme Court's judgment as a consequence of the enactment of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was justified in view of the values and assets protected by the Constitution. It found that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. The Constitutional Court further noted that the system of peripheral protection zones introduced by this new law had not in itself been considered arbitrary in the Audiencia Nacional's decision. The court added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. out that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The application was dismissed and the judgment was published in the official Gazette on April 14, 2000. The case was settled in the High Court of South Africa, and the case was heard by the Supreme Court of Appeal on April 22, 2000, which ruled in favour of the government in the case. The appeal was upheld and the decision was made to dismiss the application. In the case of this appeal, the court ruled that the application was not necessary to be heard because the case had been dismissed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28520/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he was subjected to ill-treatment in police custody in breach of Article 3 of the Convention. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) by a decision of 29 June 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section on 1 November 2001, when the Court changed the composition of its Sections. The Government submit that the applicant was questioned by the police on 15 July 1994. He was strung up by his arms in the form of torture known as “Palestinian hanging’ His head was hit against the wall and he was held parallel to the ground on his hands and feet. The applicant further claims that he was coerced into signing a statement in which it was stated that he had worked for and had been involved in the terrorist activities of the PKK. After having signed the statement, he was allegedly kept in custody for one more week so that the signs of the ill-treatment to which he had been subjected would disappear. During that week, he claims that a police officer came to his cell at regular intervals and applied a medicine on his wounds in order to cover up the signs. The applicant claims that he told the State Security Court Judge that he had been tortured in police custody. However the case files show that the applicant did not claim to have being subjected to ill-treatment. He was not seen by a doctor before being questioned by the Prosecutor on 23 July 1994 and consequently he does not have any medical evidence concerning the torture he was subjected to on 22 July 1994. The Chamber of Medicine of Istanbul found that Dr T. Taner Apaydın had concealed signs of torture in the medical examinations conducted on several persons between 3 February and 7 October 1994 and he was, therefore, prohibited from practising as a doctor for six months. The applicant filed an objection with the Beyoglu Assize Court against the Public Prosecutor's decision. Forensic Medical Department, gave a decision of non-prosecution on account of lack of evidence. On 7 March 1995 the Beyoğlu Assize court dismissed the applicant's objections. üp Forensic Medical department, gave an decision ofnon-pro prosecution on account of lack of evidence. The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he was subjected to ill-treatment in police custody. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant was represented by Mr M.S. Okçuoğlu, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The Court ruled that the application was admissible on the merits. The applicant claims that he was subjected to torture known as “Palestinian hanging’ He was strung up by his arms and held parallel to the ground on his hands and feet. He was also electrocuted, threatened and insulted. He claims that a police officer came to his cell at regular intervals and applied a medicine on his wounds in order to cover up the signs of ill-treatment. The Government contested this argument and stated that the applicant was brought for the first time before the Public Prosecutor on 23 July 1994. The applicant admitted that he had been involved with PKK related activities in the past and had been convicted on that account by the Erzincan State Security Court in 1989. The applicant claims that he told the State Security Court Judge that he had been tortured in police custody. However the case files show that the applicant did not claim to have being subjected to ill-treatment neither before the Public Prosecutor nor the State security Court. He was not seen by a doctor before being questioned by the Prosecutor on 23 July 1994 and consequently he does not have any medical evidence concerning the torture he was subjected to on 22 July 1994. The Chamber of Medicine of Istanbul found that Dr T. Taner Apaydın had concealed signs of torture in the medical examinations conducted on several persons between 3 February and 7 October 1994 and he was, therefore, prohibited from practising as a doctor. The applicant filed an objection with the Beyoglu Assize Court against the Public Prosecutor's decision. üp Forensic Medical Department, gave a decision of non-prosecution on account of lack of evidence. On 7 March 1995 the Beyoğlu Assize court dismissed the applicant's objections. The case was settled at a later date in the same year. The applicant was sentenced to five years in prison. The sentence was reduced to three years and one month on appeal. The judge ruled that the applicant should be released from prison on bail. The trial was heard in the High Court in Istanbul, Turkey, on 7 February 1995. The hearing was adjourned until 8 March 1995.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43807/07) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1986 and 1980 respectively and live in Ağrı. On 21 March 2006 the applicants attended the Newroz celebrations in Patnos. During the gathering, the crowd shouted slogans. Subsequently, the Patnos Security Directorate initiated an investigation on account that some of the participants had shouted slogans praising the imprisoned leader of the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, an illegal organisation) The applicants indicated their wish to pursue their application. The applicants were charged with disseminating the propaganda of an illegal organisation, based on the slogans shouted during the Newroz celebrations. The court found the applicants guilty of praising both a crime and a criminal pursuant to Article 215 of the Criminal Code. It accordingly sentenced the applicants to twenty-five days’ imprisonment each. On 19 October 2007 the first applicant paid the fine. On 26 February 2008 the Erzurum Public Prosecutor reopened the proceedings against the second applicant for reconsideration of his case in view of Section 562 of Law no. 5728, which was published in the Official Gazette on 7 February 2008. As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, this decision was final. The court decided to suspend the enforcement of the judgment for a period of five years in respect of the second applicant. The second applicant had become entitled to benefit from Section 231 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Law no. 5271), which provided the possibility of suspending his sentence. The judge ruled that the second person was entitled to a reduction in his sentence to one year from his original sentence of 10 years. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal. The hearing was adjourned until February 14, 2012. The verdict was returned to the court of appeal on February 11, 2012, and the sentence was suspended for one year. The case was heard by the jury of three men.

The case originated in an application (no. 43807/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Turkish nationals, Mr Mehmet Fatih Kılıç and Mr Kemal Eren (“the applicants”), made the application on 1 October 2007. The applicants were represented by Mr C. Demir, a lawyer practising in Van. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) was represented by their Agent. On 11 December 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicants were charged with disseminating the propaganda of an illegal organisation, based on the slogans shouted during the Newroz celebrations. The investigating judge released the applicants when the interrogation was over. The Patnos Criminal Court declared that it lacked jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Erzurum Assize Court. The court found the applicants guilty of praising both a crime and a criminal pursuant to Article 215 of the Criminal Code. It accordingly sentenced the applicants to twenty-five days’ imprisonment each, before commuting the prison sentence to a fine of 500 Turkish liras (TRY) (the equivalent to 270 euros) As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, this decision was final. The court decided to suspend the enforcement of the judgment for a period of five years in respect of the second applicant. The second applicant had become entitled to benefit from Section 231 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Law no. 5271), which provided the possibility of suspending his sentence. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal after hearing the case for more than two hours. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court. The case was referred to the Supreme Court by the Appeal Court for further proceedings to be held. The Appeal Court rejected the appeal and ordered the judgment to be suspended for five years. The judgment was dismissed on a technicality. The court also ruled that the applicant had not been given a fair trial.

name: Mary Theresa Shanaghan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37715/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her son Patrick Shanaghan was killed by an unknown gunman in circumstances disclosing collusion by members of the security forces. She invoked Articles 2, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Hugh Jordan v. the United Kingdom, no. 24746/94, McKerr v the United UK, no., 28883/95 and Kelly and Others v the U.K. no. 30054/96 (see judgments of the same date). Patrick Shanaghan was a thirty-year-old Catholic and active member of Sinn Fein when he was killed. The Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC) suspected him of being an IRA member and that he was involved in terrorism. Patrick Shanaghan gave several written statements to his solicitors alleging physical assaults by RUC officers while in custody. The applicant alleged that on several occasions RUC detectives threatened to kill her son during interrogations, for example, by telling him that “Loyalists in Castlederg know you now and they'll get you’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff and declared the application admissible. Patrick Shanaghan instituted proceedings against the Chief Constable of the RUC for alleged assault, battery, trespass to the person, unlawful arrest and unlawful imprisonment in respect of his detention from 9 to 15 April 1986. The applicant also claimed that there was an attempt on Patrick Shanaghan's life, on 17 February 1989, but that he managed to escape. On 10 December 1990, a RUC detective informed him that security force documentation containing information about him, including a photographic montage, had accidentally fallen out of the back of an army vehicle. He was advised to take measures for his personal safety as there was a risk that the material had come into the hands of loyalist paramilitaries. The RUC responded to this letter by stating that the police investigation was concluded and that the document had been accidentally lost by the Army. Patrick Shanaghan was stopped and questioned by RUC and UDR officers on a daily basis. The Shanaghan family home, which the applicant shared with her son, was searched sixteen times between 1985 and 1991. According to the applicant, sometimes the RUC would not even enter certain rooms indicating that the search was not a concerted effort to locate and seize illegal material but was carried out solely to harass the family. The applicant alleged that the behaviour of the police at the scene was not consonant with any concern for her son's life or proper police procedures. The killing of Patrick Shanaghan on 12 August 1991 by a masked gunman was ruled a homicide. Patrick Shanaghan died from a bullet wound to the chest. The RUC discovered a car which they believed had been used by the people involved in the shooting. However, a forensic and fingerprint examination disclosed no evidence to connect it with any person suspected of the murder. Enquiries showed that the car had been recently bought for cash by unknown persons from a private vendor. Several suspects had been arrested and interviewed but no evidence of admission had been obtained from them. An inquest into the killing was opened on 26 March 1996, over four and a half years after the killing. The inquest was heard over six days, between 26 March and 20 June 1996. Patrick Shanaghan's family sought to introduce evidence in support of allegations that the RUC had prior knowledge that he was to be murdered. The High Court quashed the Coroner's decision, holding that the evidence is not relevant to the means by which Patrick Shanaghan was killed. The RUC Chief Constable applied for judicial review of those decisions. The case was heard by a jury and a Coroner who sat with a lawyer and was assisted by a lawyer. The Coroner and the jury were represented by counsel and a solicitor. The verdict was returned in favour of the jury and Mr Shanaghan died in a hospice in 1998. Patrick Shanaghan died on 12 August 1991 on Learmore Road in Castlederg from a bullet wound to the chest. The Coroner refused to admit in evidence statements made by Patrick Shanaghan to his solicitors. The applicant made a complaint about the conduct of the RUC at the scene of the shooting in denying Dr Stewart access to the body and in failing to call an ambulance. This complaint was investigated by an assistant chief constable, under the supervision of the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) As a result, the Inspector concerned was given advice which was recorded in the Divisional Discipline Book. The RUC officers who had interviewed D.C. on 14 and 15 May 1991 were themselves interviewed. Community inquiry was organised by family and friends after the inquest. It was chaired by a retired United States Judge, Andrew Somers. The witnesses included family, local residents and friends of the deceased. Evidence was given alleging that police officers had frequently stopped Patrick Shanaghan in the street and issued threats. The judge concluded that the applicant had been murdered by the British Government and, more specifically, with the collusion of the RUC. In January 1999, the DPP decided that there should be no prosecution in relation to the shooting. The applicant claimed damages for loss and damage sustained by her and the estate of her son by reason, inter alia, of negligence, breach of confidence.

name: Senanik Öner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 51962/12) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that there had been an interference with their right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 May 2013. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by Mr E. Talay, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The case was described as ‘the most important case of its kind in the history of the Court’. The applicants were sentenced to one year and eight months' imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court’s judgment. The applicants learned of this decision on 6 March 2012. The Diyarbakır Assize Court revised its judgment pursuant to Provisional Article 1 § 1 of the Law no. 6352 and suspended the execution of the applicants’ sentences. The application was dismissed on 12 October 2012, following an amendment to the law. The case is being investigated by the Turkish National Court of Justice and the Turkish Anti-Terrorism Court of Appeal. The court will make a decision on whether or not to proceed with the application.

The application was lodged on 27 June 2012 by two Turkish nationals, Mr Senanik Öner and Mr Ferhan Türk. On 21 March 2007 the applicants attended the Newroz celebrations in Kızıltepe, a district of Mardin, and made certain speeches concerning the problems of Kurdish people. Criminal proceedings were brought against the applicants. The applicants learned of this decision on 6 March 2012. Following an amendment to the law, the Diyarbakır Assize Court revised its judgment on 12 October 2012 and suspended the execution of the applicants’ sentences. The application was brought under the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and the applicants were found guilty as charged and sentenced to a year and 8 months' imprisonment. They were released on appeal on 6 June 2013. The appeal was dismissed on 13 June 2013, and the application was dismissed again on 15 June 2014.
