train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 10 August 1998. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Sosnowiec. On 12 June 1994 he was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. He was charged with homicide and remanded in custody until 12 August 1994 in connection with the investigation against him. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The court convicted the applicant as charged, and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed and the case was quashed and remitted for re-examination. The hearing scheduled for 17 February 1998 was adjourned. The case was reopened on 1 June 1998 and the court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 30 November 1998. It made reference to the reasonableness of the suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. The applicant’s lawyer appealed against the reasonableness of the charge against his client, maintaining that it was solely based on presumptive evidence. On 24 September 1998 the Katowice Regional Court gave judgment. It again convicted the applicant of homicide and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. The court deducted from the sentence the period spent by the applicant in detention. On 26 April 1999 the applicant”s lawyer lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court concerning the conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court dismissed that appeal on 6 March 2000. The case has since been settled in the High Court of Justice in Bratislava.

He appealed the conviction and the case was remitted for re-examination. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The hearing scheduled for 17 February 1998 was adjourned. The applicant’s counsel applied for his release, but to no avail. The court stressed the serious nature of the offence and the necessity to consider further evidence. the applicant might tamper with the evidence. The case was concluded on 1 June 1998. The applicant was convicted of homicide and sentenced to ten years in prison. His lawyer appealed against that decision, maintaining that the charge against his client was solely based on presumptive evidence. The applicant’s lawyer lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court concerning the conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court dismissed that appeal on 6 March 2000. The case is still pending in the courts of appeals in Poland and the Czech Republic. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 10 August 1998. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Sosnowiec. On 12 June 1994 he was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. He was charged with homicide and remanded in custody until 12 August 1994 in connection with the investigation against him. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The court convicted the applicant as charged, and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 30 May 1996 the applicant appealed. On 13 August 1996 the Katowice Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. The hearing scheduled for 17 February 1998 was adjourned. On 1 June 1998 the court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 30 November 1998. The applicant was found guilty of homicide in 1998 and sentenced to ten years in prison. His lawyer appealed his conviction and sentence. On 24 June 1998 the Katowice Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals. On 11 January 1999 the applicant challenged that decision before a court which did not have the necessary jurisdiction. On 6 March 2000 the Supreme Court dismissed that appeal. The applicant was sentenced to life in prison but was released on parole on 29 January 2001. The case continues at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, which is currently hearing an appeal on behalf of the father of two young children. The father’s appeal was dismissed in March 2000. The appeal is still pending at the High Court of Justice in Prague.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ consent, the case was decided in favour of the applicant. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). On 30 January 1981 the Erzincan Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. On 24 June 1997 the Ankara Assize Court decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time-barred. The application was declared admissible and the Court declared the Court's observations on the merits. The case was transferred to the Court ofCassation on 26 December 1994.

On 30 January 1981 the Erzincan Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. In a judgment of 24 August 1988 the Martial Law court convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the Dev Yol. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. The Court declared the application admissible.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged principally that he had not been arrested on a reasonable suspicion of committing an offence. He also alleged that he did not have an enforceable right to compensation in respect of these matters. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 March 2000, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 June 2001. The Court heard addresses by Mr MacDonald and Mr Freeland. The applicant was arrested in 1985 in relation to the murder of Kurt Konig. The Government submitted that Special Branch received intelligence that the applicant and three other persons were involved in the murder. The intelligence derived from four informants who had proved reliable in the past and had provided information leading to seizures of explosives or firearms. None of the informants had a criminal record. The information given by these four informants was consistent, in that all gave the same names as being involved, and independent. None was aware of the existence of the others and each gave the information at separate meetings with police officers. The applicant was taken to Castlereagh and arrested under section 12(1)(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984. The applicant was interviewed on thirty-four occasions. He was released without charge on 3 January 1986 at 9 p.m. after six days and 13 hours in custody. The applicant instituted a civil action for damages before the High Court in Northern Ireland in respect of, inter alia, assault, seizure of documents, false imprisonment and unlawful arrest. The judge found that the applicant’s counsel concentrated, as the trial judge found, on the issues of assault and confiscation of documents. It was common ground that the murder of Kurt Konig was a terrorist offence. The superior officer was not called as a witness in the proceedings. He did not state that Inspector B. had told him the grounds for his own suspicion. Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. The judge found on the evidence that the detective constable had a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in the murder of Kurt Konig and that this suspicion was reasonably based on information given to him by a superior officers at the briefing that morning. The High Court upheld the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer. The applicant gave notice of appeal to the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland concerning the claim of unlawful arrest and false imprisonment. The Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on 6 May 1994. The main issue between the parties is as to whether the [applicant] was assaulted and mistreated during the period of his detention ...” The appeal was dismissed by the Appeal Court on 6May 1994 on a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. The appeal court said that the decision by the learned trial judge was correct. The information given at the briefing to the arresting officer was admissible and although, in his words, ‘scanty’ it was sufficient to constitute the required state of mind. An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, with which the other judges agreed, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. The information acted upon by the arresting officer need not be based on his own observations, as he is entitled to form a suspicion based on what he has been told. The executive ‘discretion’ to arrest or not vests in the constable, who is engaged on the decision. to arrest and not in his superior officers. "A mere request to arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion," the court rules. "How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a requests to arrest someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s report," it adds. The court rules that the police should be able to use the powers of an arrest warrant to make an arrest.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Mr Gerard Patrick O’Hara (“the applicant”) alleged that he had not been arrested on a reasonable suspicion of committing an offence and that he did not have an enforceable right to compensation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. By a decision of 14 March 2000, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59: 1). German citizen Kurt Konig was murdered on 21 November 1985. The Provisional IRA claimed responsibility for his death. The Government submitted that Special Branch received intelligence that the applicant and three other persons were involved in the murder. The intelligence derived from four informants who had proved reliable in the past and had provided information leading to seizures of explosives or firearms and to prosecutions. The information given by these four informants was consistent, in that all gave the same names as being involved, and independent. None of the informants had a criminal record. The applicant was taken to Castlereagh and arrested under section 12(1)(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984 (‘the 1984 Act’) He was interviewed on thirty-four occasions. He did not respond to any questions. The applicant was released without charge on 3 January 1986 at 9 p.m. after six days and 13 hours in custody. He instituted a civil action for damages before the High Court in Northern Ireland in respect of, inter alia, assault, seizure of documents, false imprisonment and unlawful arrest. The High Court found that the applicant’s counsel concentrated, as the trial judge found, on the issues of assault and confiscation of documents. It was common ground that the murder of Kurt Konig was a terrorist offence. The superior officer was not called as a witness in the proceedings. He had been told by his superior officer, Inspector B., at that briefing that the. applicant was involved in the murder. 1990 Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. He accepted that both Mr Justice Carswell and the Lord Chief Justice had previously rejected the same submission in similar cases. He reserved his position on this issue and said he made no new submissions and produced no arguments to me which would cause me to depart from the reasoning in their decisions. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer. “Notwithstanding his concern that more detail of the briefing had not been given, the learned trial judge was able to conclude: ‘(1) that the arresting officer ... did have a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in a terrorist murder and it was implicit that that suspicion was genuinely held by him.’ These were factual findings and clearly contained all the essential proofs that the respondent was required to adduce to constitute lawful arrest under section 12(1)(b) of the Act” An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. He said the arresting officer must have equipped himself with sufficient information so that he had reasonable cause to suspect before exercising the power of arrest. The information acted upon by the officer need not be based on his own observations, as he is entitled to form a suspicion based on what he has been told. His reasonable suspicion may be based. on information which has been given to him anonymously, or it may bebased on. information which turns out later to be wrong. "A mere request to arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion," he said. "How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a requests to arrest someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s report," the judge added. He said: "It is accepted, and rightly accepted, that a mere request. to arrest ... is not sufficient"

Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The judge found that he had been wrongfully arrested by police officers who had purported to arrest the applicant for obstruction in failing to give his name when they were fully aware of his identity. The applicant’s counsel concentrated, as the trial judge found, on the issues of assault and confiscation of documents. It was common ground that the murder of Kurt Konig was a terrorist offence. The superior officer was not called as a witness in the proceedings. He did not state that Inspector B. had told him the grounds for his own suspicion. Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. He accepted that both Mr Justice Carswell and the Lord Chief Justice had previously rejected the same submission in similar cases. The judge found on the evidence that the detective constable had a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in the murder of Kurt Konig and that this suspicion was reasonably based on information given to him by a superior officers. The applicant gave notice of appeal to the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland in 1990. The appeal was dismissed on 6 May 1994, upholding the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer and that the arrest was lawful. “Notwithstanding his concern that more detail of the briefing had not been given, the learned trial judge was able to conclude: ‘(1) that the arresting officer ... did have a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in a terrorist murder and it was implicit that that suspicion was genuinely held by him.’ These were factual findings and clearly contained in our view all the essential proofs that the respondent was required to adduce to constitute lawful arrest’ An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, with which the other judges agreed, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. Lord Steyn stated, inter alia, concerning the general principles: “Certain general propositions about the powers of constables under a section such as section 12(1) can now be summarised. (1) In order to have a reasonable suspicion the constable need not have evidence amounting to a prima facie case. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrested. Such information may come from other officers ... (3) The information which causes the constably to be suspicious of the individual must be in existence to the knowledge of the police officer at the time he makes the arrest. (4) The executive ‘discretion’ to arrest or not ... vests in theconstable ... and not in his superior officers. "How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a request to arrest someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s’ said the court. The court said it is accepted, and rightly accepted, that a mere request to. arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion. the meaning of section 12 (1)’.
